papers.abstract: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.
authors: Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang, Yiheng He, XinJun Liu, Senhao Hou, Huichan Zhao, Xiaoqiang Tang
bullets: Addresses policy reuse challenges caused by differences in musculoskeletal morphology.
Combines individualized model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation.
Achieves 99.24% completion across 31 held-out models and reduces tracking error by 22.60% versus an unconditioned MLP.
Generalizes to single-image-based models and models with unilateral lower-limb shortening.
Simulations agree with measured ground-reaction forces and show channel-dependent agreement with electromyography.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the MyoAcross framework. a, The 64 source motions comprise 8 clips in each of 8 locomotion categories. CCW, counterclockwise; CW, clockwise. b, SKEL derives target skeletal measurements from SMPL body shape. Skeletal-guided regional scaling and mass calibration adapt the MyoFullBody template to construct 141 individual musculoskeletal models. Retargeting the source motions to each model produces 9,024 reference motions. c, Skeletal measurement fitting error across the 141 models. Template, Global fit and Regional fit denote the unchanged MyoFullBody template, fitting a single global scale factor and skeletal-guided regional scaling, respectively. Each point represents one model’s mean absolute error across 17 target skeletal measurements. Boxes span the interquartile range, central lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. The inset enlarges the distribution for regional scaling. d, Original models of 110 training individuals and their virtual variants support policy learning in parallel simulations; 31 individuals are held out for evaluation. A morphology encoder maps model-derived morphology features to a learned morphology representation, which conditions the actor and critic through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). The actor generates muscle excitations, and training uses proximal policy optimization (PPO).

Figure 5: Virtual model augmentation supports policy reuse across individual and asymmetric models. a, Training schemes and evaluation protocols. V0 uses 110 original training models without virtual model augmentation. Standard augmentation (V10) and asymmetry augmentation each add 10 virtual models per training individual, yielding 1,210 training models. Asymmetry augmentation increases the asymmetry perturbation scale while retaining the other covariance settings. All schemes use the MyoAcross policy architecture and the same interaction budget, with evaluation at 15,000 training iterations on models of 31 held-out individuals and 64 reference motions per individual. b, Completion, reference coverage and tracking error on the original held-out models for V0 and V10 (standard augmentation). Faint points represent individual-model means over the 64 reference motions; squares (V0) and circles (V10) indicate means across individuals. Out-of-range points appear as left- or right-pointing triangles at the corresponding axis limits, labelled with their measured values. c, The same metrics for standard augmentation and asymmetry augmentation under unilateral lower-limb shortening. Thigh and shank regional scale factors are reduced together by 1%, 2.5%, 5% or 10% on either the left or right side, giving nine conditions including the original model at 0%. Each test model retains its corresponding original model’s reference motions. Circles and dashed lines denote standard augmentation (labelled Standard); triangles and solid lines denote asymmetry augmentation. Symbols indicate means across individuals. Error bars in b and c show 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 subject-level resamples of the 31 individuals. Tracking error includes executed frames from incomplete trials.

Figure 3: Policy reuse across held-out individual musculoskeletal models. a, Training schemes and shared evaluation protocol for the template-trained MLP (labelled Template MLP), unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross. The unconditioned MLP is trained across individual models without morphology input. The three policies trained across models share the same training model bank, reference motions and interaction budget. Each policy is evaluated at 15,000 training iterations on 31 held-out individual models, with 64 corresponding reference motions per model and no individual fine-tuning. b, Completion, reference coverage and tracking error. Faint points represent individual-model means over the 64 reference motions; diamonds indicate means across individuals. Detail views enlarge completion and reference coverage for the three policies trained across models. c, Paired comparisons of individual-model tracking error. Each point compares MyoAcross with the unconditioned MLP or Concat for the same individual. Dashed lines indicate equal error; points below these lines indicate lower error for MyoAcross. d, Tracking error across eight motion categories for the unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross. Each category contains eight motions per model; symbols indicate means across individuals. Dotted, dashed and solid lines connect category means for the unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross, respectively, as guides to the eye. Error bars in b and d show 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals from 10,000 subject-level resamples of the 31 individuals. Tracking error is measured in world coordinates without alignment and includes executed frames from incomplete trials.

Figure 4: Biomechanical assessment of walking across individual musculoskeletal models. a, Workflow from labelled motion-capture markers and recorded body mass to individual musculoskeletal simulation. MoSh++ estimates SMPL-H body shape from the markers. SKEL-derived skeletal measurements guide regional scaling of the MyoFullBody template, and mass calibration matches recorded body mass. Model-derived morphology features condition the pretrained policy, which generates muscle excitations to track reference motions. Eight medium-speed KIT walking motions are retargeted to each of 120 Gait120 individual models. All policies are evaluated at 15,000 training iterations, with policy parameters and normalization statistics fixed and without individual fine-tuning. b, Subject-level tracking error for MyoAcross, Concat and the unconditioned MLP (n = 120 subjects per policy). c, Simulated vertical ground reaction force (GRF) profiles for MyoAcross and measured level-walking profiles from the corresponding Gait120 subjects, shown separately for the left and right feet. Forces are normalized by body weight (BW), and complete stance phases are interpolated to a common phase grid. Lines and shaded bands show population means and standard deviations, respectively (n = 101 subjects for the left foot and 107 for the right). d, Subject-level GRF agreement, quantified by Pearson correlation (left) and BW-normalized root-mean-square error (RMSE; right). Metrics are calculated separately for each foot and averaged within subjects with valid bilateral measurements (n = 101 per policy). e, Subject-level agreement between simulated muscle activations and measured electromyography (EMG), expressed as the mean Pearson correlation across 12 EMG channels (n = 120 per policy). In b, d and e, points represent individual subjects. Boxes span the interquartile range, central lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Waveform correlations are calculated within each subject before population aggregation. No correlation-maximizing temporal shifts are applied.

Figure 1: Muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models. a, Four example models illustrate variation in body dimensions, body mass and bilateral symmetry: A, 1.70m and 65 kg; B, 1.86m and 73 kg; C, 1.62m and 75 kg; and D, 1.67m and 65 kg, with 10% unilateral lower-limb shortening on the right side. Colours identify the same models throughout the figure. b, Motion sequences illustrate reuse of the pretrained MyoAcross policy across the four models for slow, medium-speed and fast walking, backward walking, left and right turns, and counterclockwise and clockwise circling. Each sequence shows four frames per model. Small coloured curves indicate the corresponding movement paths. CCW, counterclockwise; CW, clockwise.

Figure 7: Single-image model construction and policy reuse. a, Human Skeleton and Mesh Recovery (HSMR) estimates SKEL shape parameters from a single photograph. The resulting skeletal measurements are calibrated to measured height and combined with recorded body mass to construct an individual musculoskeletal model. Source motions are retargeted to the constructed model, which supplies its own morphology features. Control uses the pretrained MyoAcross policy trained with standard augmentation (V10) at 15,000 training iterations, without individual fine-tuning; the snowflake denotes frozen policy weights. The individual shown in a is an author of this study and provided informed consent for publication of the image; the face is anonymized. b, Sequential medium-speed walking poses of the image-derived model of MoVi Subject 65. Red muscles and warm-coloured bones depict the policy-controlled model; translucent purple bones depict the corresponding reference motion. Each model–reference pair is translated together for horizontal presentation. c, Completion and tracking error for 88 image-derived models, each evaluated on 64 reference motions. The cohort includes 63 individuals from the original training split (blue), 22 from the held-out split (orange) and three outside the registered training and evaluation collections (grey). Each point represents one model’s completion and mean tracking error over the 64 reference motions; the inset enlarges the high-completion region. Tracking error includes executed frames from incomplete trials.

Figure 6: Policy sensitivity to morphology feature and reference-motion input errors. a, Input perturbation design for the unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross, evaluated on 31 held-out individual models with 64 reference motions per model. Physical models, policy parameters and normalization statistics remain fixed. papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.
authors: Liang Li, Guoyao Zhang, Xingyu Chen, Sikai Wu, Qianyang Wu, Yuhang Lin, Renjing Xu, Mingliang Zhou, Diyun Xiang
bullets: Targets missing terrain adaptation in flat-ground-trained behavior foundation models, especially foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing.

Trains with task and foot-geometry rewards, suppresses unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distills privileged terrain information to onboard depth.
Evaluated on four frozen trackers across stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation.
Demonstrated real-world terrain traversal on a Unitree G1 using the adapted SONIC tracker, onboard depth, and unmodified references.

papers.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.
bullets: Targets low-cost SO-101 arms, addressing the lack of accessible benchmarks for spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks.
Provides four tasks across five evaluation families, 138 objects, seen/unseen splits, 916 episodes, and simulated demonstrations in an Isaac Lab digital twin.
Policy rankings in simulation exactly matched physical-robot rankings for five policies tested, though simulation overestimated success.
Best learned policies achieved about 61%, while an LLM code-writing agent paired with a learned grasping policy reached 83.2%.
Spatial placement, unseen object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain open challenges.

papers.abstract: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
authors: Fanqi Yu, Matteo Tiezzi, Cigdem Beyan, Tommaso Apicella, Vittorio Murino
bullets: Targets sequential learning from multimodal demonstrations without storing or revisiting past data.
Uses hierarchical dual attention to separate instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement.
Adds key-level geometric regularization to align representations within tasks and separate them across tasks.
Supports an expandable expert set for continual adaptation and reliable expert selection.
On LIBERO suites, including heterogeneous and paraphrased tasks, it improves AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting; gains are stronger under interference and language variation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HIDRA. A frozen pretrained multimodal policy produces an instruction query qinst and a context query qctxt . These drive a two-stage hierarchical dual-routing attention mechanism. Stage I performs instruction-level retrieval via qinst to select an anchor expert j∗ and an instruction candidate set Sj∗ over task-level keys {kinsj }. Stage II then uses qctxt to perform context-level refinement within Sj∗ using context keys {kctxj }, producing fused routing scores and selecting the active experts. Key-space regularization (Reg.) promotes intra-task compactness and inter-task separation, enabling stable and interference-resistant expert selection as new task-specific experts are introduced during replay-free lifelong adaptation.

Figure 1: Left: Existing methods (e.g., [26]) perform expert routing using a single projection over entangled representations, which is unstable without replay. papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP). While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified. We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL. We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation $\sigma$ has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques. We observe a significant effect of $\sigma$ on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments. Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
authors: Andrea Vasco Grieco, Evelyn D'Elia, Edoardo Caldarelli, Raffaello Camoriano
bullets: Analyzes loss of plasticity (LoP), where RL agents become less able to learn from new data.
Studies PPO with isotropic Gaussian policies and examines how policy standard deviation σ relates to LoP.
Provides theoretical and experimental evidence that σ substantially affects the extent of LoP.
Connects the findings to why commonly used LoP mitigation techniques may be effective.
Validates the analysis on LoP benchmarks and through deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.

papers.abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.
authors: Simone Manni, Annika Wollschl\"ager, Dario Bellicoso, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter, Simon Le Cleac'h, Jan Br\"udigam
bullets: Targets long-horizon tasks combining maneuvers such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion.
Uses a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated rewards, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to structure exploration.
Employs decoupled hierarchical control, separating low-level balance from high-level phase execution.
Demonstrates multi-stage skills on Unitree G1 and Boston Dynamics Spot with a manipulator arm.
Ablation studies validate the proposed design choices.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the phase-conditioned PPO framework. An environment state machine segments the task into phases (ψk) via local success conditions (e.g., distance d and phase-specific thresholds ϵ). To tackle exploration bottlenecks, a multiphase curriculum initially resets episodes into later stages before progressively shifting back to the initial phase as training advances. The actor outputs delta actions updating command targets ct, while an auxiliary head enforces phase internalization via cross-entropy loss (LCE) against the true environment phase. The critic conditions value estimation on state st and phase one-hot encoding ek, combining a base value Vbase with phase-specific residual heads. These are constrained by Lreg to keep the main learning burden on the base head. Finally, task rewards are dynamically gated based on the active phase ψk and combined with rewards for forward phase transitions and penalties for backward regression.

Fig. 5: Algorithmic Ablation Study on Spot and G1: Task success rate across training steps on (a) spot tire rolling and (b) g1 push two boxes, comparing our method (Ours) against baseline architectures (MLP, Multihead), an unguided variant (No phase prediction), and execution without multi-phase episode initialization (Initial phase reset). Solid curves and shaded regions denote the mean and variance across 3 random seeds, respectively. (c) Spot Phase Analysis: Evaluation of phase-prediction accuracy across 1,000 successful episodes of spot tire rolling task. Because individual phase durations vary across rollouts, evaluation episodes are temporally anchored at phase transitions with intermediate timesteps linearly warped to uniform phase durations. The top plot shows that the auxiliary head’s online phase predictions tightly track the ground-truth phase steps with minimal variance, while the bottom plot highlights the object-to-goal distance as a proxy for task progression.

Fig. 2: Overview of the low-level whole-body policy. The policy commands leg and waist joints to execute stable locomotion, low crouching, and crouch-walking. Training stability is achieved via inverse kinematics (IK) keyframe initializations that spawn the robot in valid postures, coupled with a feasibility-constrained command space. For standing environments, this region is bounded by the convex hull of admissible IK keyframes, whereas for dynamic environments, the feasible command envelope dynamically contracts as target tracking velocity increases.

Fig. 4: Hardware deployment of the g1 lift box task using onboard state estimation and ArUco marker detection. The right panel shows the Unitree G1 humanoid executing the lift, while the insets display the state estimation visualization (top-left) and the onboard first-person camera view tracking the ArUco marker (bottom-left).

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.
authors: Era AI Lab Team, Jianhao Lai, Zhihao Zhan, Zhiquan Liao, Qichang Li, Shubin Chen, Zhiyuan Liu, Hongsen Lei, Jianman Lin, Xiaoxin Lin, Ke Gong, Baiyue Gu, Shiming Chen, Junlin He, Longqi Yang, Junrong Xiao, Haolin Luo, Xiaojuan Su, Jianfeng Li, Yu Luo, Xu Sun, Likui Zhang, Jusheng Zhang, Qinhan Lyu, Tianshui Chen, Liang Lin, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Targets the limitation of video- or vision-language-centric world-action models, where 3D geometry is auxiliary rather than foundational.
Uses a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone for both world modeling and action prediction.
Predicts future 3D states alongside actions to model geometric world dynamics.
On RoboTwin 2.0, achieves 89.90% success in clean settings and 50.09% in randomized settings without embodied-data pretraining.
Pretraining on over 160k robot trajectories improves real-world manipulation success by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a geometry-native world-action model predicting future 3D states and actions, spanning Embodied AI, World Models, and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling
papers.tldr: E0.5 makes 3D geometry the native foundation for world-action modeling and jointly predicts robot actions with future 3D states, improving simulated and real-world manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles is a critical yet formidable challenge in aerospace engineering, primarily due to highly nonlinear dynamics, stringent precision require- ments, and inherent environmental uncertainties. While reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional model-based control, existing approaches frequently rely on flat training paradigms and highly simplified initial conditions, drastically limiting their real-world applicability. This paper proposes a comprehensive curriculum-driven deep reinforcement learning framework designed to master both far-range navigation and precision landing. By employing a three-stage curriculum augmented with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting, alongside a high-dimensional observation vector utilizing a full 3 X 3 rotation-matrix, the agent is trained to navigate from an initial horizontal distance of 1,000 to 1,500 units vastly farther than prior benchmarks before executing a soft touchdown. Crucially, we intro- duce a redesigned reward function that reduces unnecessary computational overhead and addresses limitations of earlier formulations, including poorly calibrated reward components and potentially conflicting optimization objectives. The redesigned function bounds the per-step reward magnitude by (O(1)), while its progress term accumulates the total distance closed over the trajectory. The available 100,000-episode results report a 99.98% success rate for the proposed policy and 68.31% for the baseline under the evaluation conditions. In the evaluation, the proposed policy retained 69.1% of its initial fuel capacity and achieved a mean final distance from the pad centre of 7.07 units, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline. Landing visualizations are available in Video 1 and Video 2.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining long-range navigation with precision vertical landing under nonlinear dynamics and uncertainty.
Uses a three-stage curriculum, critic warm-up, rehearsal to limit catastrophic forgetting, and observations containing a full 3×3 rotation matrix.
Introduces a bounded, computationally simpler reward function whose progress term tracks cumulative distance closed.
Under the reported evaluation, the policy achieved 99.98% success versus 68.31% for the baseline.
The proposed policy retained 69.1% initial fuel and had 7.07 units mean final pad-distance, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Curriculum-driven deep RL for autonomous far-range navigation and precision landing; directly relevant to learned embodied navigation and control.
papers.title: Curriculum-Driven Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Far-Range Rocket Landing
papers.tldr: A curriculum-driven deep RL framework enables autonomous rocket landing from far greater initial distances while achieving high success and precise touchdowns in simulation.

papers.abstract: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without observing real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Furthermore, ZAP also generalizes to an unseen embodiment as well as new objects, goals and strategies never seen during training. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining task understanding with robot motion control without real-world robot training data.
Uses a pretrained 27B vision-language model, then supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks via a tool harness.
Achieves 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra while running 3× faster and costing 17× less.
Generalizes to unseen embodiments, objects, goals, and strategies; reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 points above the cited VLA/WAM baseline.
Scope: results are reported for the described harness and selected real-world benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: ZAP sim-to-real robot policy using a VLM pre-trained on a 27B model, fine-tuned on simulation, achieving high real-world success and generalization.
papers.title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
papers.tldr: ZAP combines pretrained world understanding with simulation-based control training to achieve strong zero-real robot manipulation and compositional generalization.

papers.abstract: Learning generalizable humanoid loco-manipulation remains bottlenecked by costly real-world demonstrations. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, but requires visually faithful, physics-ready scenes and executable whole-body motions. We present Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that transforms smartphone captures and simulated source demonstrations into scalable training data for humanoid loco-manipulation. Gaussian-guided agentic real-to-sim reconstruction aligns visual and physical scenes; motion-environment co-adaptation uses rollout feedback to correct whole-body references and interaction geometry. We generate 4,800 physically validated demonstrations for zero-shot transfer across three Unitree G1 tasks. Simulation-trained GR00T N1.7 achieves 66.7% mean full-task success, versus 46.7% with real-data training. On generalized configurations, expanded simulation training raises pooled success from 23% for base-trained real-data policies to 69%, without additional real demonstrations. Project page: https://young-bit.github.io/zero-hlm/
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited scalability of collecting real-world humanoid demonstrations.
Uses Gaussian-guided agentic real-to-sim reconstruction to align visual and physical environments.
Applies motion-environment co-adaptation with rollout feedback to refine whole-body motions and interaction geometry.
Generates 4,800 physically validated demonstrations for three Unitree G1 tasks.
Simulation-trained GR00T N1.7 reaches 66.7% mean full-task success and 69% pooled success on generalized configurations.

papers.abstract: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.
bullets: The study investigates how animals generate autonomous exploratory actions without external rewards or sensory cues.
Whole-brain recordings show that future spontaneous decisions are represented more than 10 seconds before action.
A neuromechanical Drosophila digital twin uses hierarchical policies that select discrete low-level motor primitives.
Among 20 curiosity-, entropy-, and competency-based methods, DIAYN best jointly matched fly behavior and prospective neural coding.
The model also reproduced individual exploration variability and a biological interhemispheric kinematic encoding rule.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Agent Architecture Overview. (a) The FlyGym simulator provides visual, proprioceptive, and olfactory observations from a biomechanically realistic fly body. Modality-specific CNN and MLP encoders embed these observations into a shared representation ϕt, which is provided to the actor–critic and intrinsic drive module. When applicable, the policy is additionally conditioned on a sampled skill z. The intrinsic drive module computes an intrinsic reward from the encoded state transition and selected action. The actor outputs a categorical distribution over discrete motor primitives, while the critic estimates the state value. The policy selects a new motor primitive every 100 ms. (b) Locomotor primitives are translated into joint-level commands by a low-level central pattern generator (CPG) controller, while grooming is executed using a kinematic replay. These motor commands are applied within the FlyGym physics simulation, which is integrated with a timestep of 100µs. Thus, each policy action is executed for 1,000 physics steps before the next action is selected.

Figure 1: Environment Overview. (a) The fly policy is trained in an environment with obstacles and multiple odor sources. (b) The policy is then evaluated in a tethered-ball environment where the fly is head-fixed. The angular and forward velocities are read from the ball, analogous to the biological experiment of Brezovec et al. (2023). (c) The policy receives olfaction as a weighted sum of intensities sampled at the antennae and maxillary palps. (d) The policy’s proprioceptive input comes directly from NeuroMechFly and includes joint angles, joint velocities, and body-frame gravity, height, and linear and angular velocities. (e) Vision is also provided to the policy by simulating the ommatidia mapping of pale and yellow type cells to pixels.

Figure 4: Turning Bias. (a) Distribution of turning bias across evaluation rollouts for each method. Points indicate individual rollouts, with the mean and range shown for each method. DIAYN produces a broad distribution of turning biases spanning more of the fly-to-fly variability than the other evaluated methods. Methods with a rollout containing no turns or turns in only one direction are excluded because log(NR/NL) is undefined for those rollouts. (b) Virtual x-y trajectories integrated from the ball state of the nine flies and the nine DIAYN evaluation skills drawn from a common origin.

Figure 3: Turn-direction decoding from neural and behavioral data. Prospective coding is quantified as balanced accuracy in predicting future left/right turns. (a,c) Neural (a) and behavioral (c) prospective coding in the fly and models using elastic-net logistic regression in the −15 to −8 s window. (b) Neural and behavioral decoding before (−15 to −8 s) and during (−0.4 to +0.4 s) turns. (d) Behavioral versus neural prospective coding. The dashed line defines the fly’s behavioralto-neural accuracy ratio, which DIAYN closely matches. (e) Models with no turns or only one turn direction, precluding stratified cross-validation.

Figure 5: Low-dimensional internal structures relate to ω and v. (a) Reconstructed from Brezovec et al. (2023), the IPS of the fly brain has an interhemispheric relationship of z-scored activity that is correlated with angular (interhemispheric difference) and forward velocity (interhemispheric sum). (b) As a functional analogue of the bilateral supercluster pairs in Brezovec et al. (2023), we use PCA to find principal components in the network activation of the LSTM layer of the Actor in the policy whose difference correlates with angular velocity and whose sum correlates with forward velocity. This structural relationship appears in DIAYN’s Actor LSTM layer (b) but, does not appear in (c) the randomly initialized DIAYN model. (d) We rank each IDM by the mean of the squared Pearson correlations of its angular and forward heatmaps with the fly’s. Higher is a closer match.

papers.abstract: Large-scale vision, language, and video pretraining has substantially improved the perception and generalization capabilities of robotic manipulation models, but action generation for complex dexterous manipulation remains constrained by the scarcity of robot demonstrations. Limited robot demonstrations must be used to learn both action representations and task-conditioned action distributions, making it difficult to adequately learn action representations and, in turn, limiting the ability of downstream generative models to generate complex dexterous actions. To address this limitation, we propose ARPG (Action Representation Pretraining and Generation), which explicitly separates action representation learning from action generation: we first pretrain an action representation encoder on large-scale human manipulation data. We then freeze the encoder and train a compact generative backbone (130M parameters) to learn task-conditioned action distributions in the encoder's representation space. Experimental results show that ARPG achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DexJoCo benchmark and improves the average success rate on bimanual dexterous manipulation from 10.1% for $π_{0.5}$ to 44.7%. Scaling experiments further show that broader coverage of human manipulation behaviors effectively improves downstream performance. These results indicate that action representation pretraining provides an independent scaling dimension for improving complex dexterous manipulation capabilities.
bullets: Problem: Scarce robot demonstrations must support both action-representation learning and task-conditioned action generation.
Method: Pretrain an action encoder on human manipulation data, freeze it, and train a compact generative backbone in the learned representation space.
Result: ARPG achieves state-of-the-art performance on DexJoCo and raises average bimanual dexterous-manipulation success from 10.1% to 44.7% versus π₀.₅.
Scaling human behavior coverage further improves downstream manipulation performance.
Scope: The approach targets complex dexterous and bimanual manipulation, with results indicating action pretraining as an independent scaling dimension.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have recently achieved remarkable success in motion tracking. However, during real-world deployment, robots inevitably encounter dynamics gaps arising from either extra physical disturbances or inaccurate simulation modeling, resulting in a significant training-deployment gap. Therefore, effectively leveraging real-world data to fine-tune policies represents the crucial last mile for robust deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose HumanoidNDM, an online fine-tuning framework for humanoid motion tracking driven by a real-world-trained neural dynamics model. First, in the data collection stage, we introduce a low-frequency reference perturbation method with an adaptive intensity mechanism, balancing deployment feasibility and exploration efficiency. Second, for the model training stage, we train a robust history-based, proprioceptive neural dynamics model in Euclidean space by incorporating differentiable forward kinematics, eliminating the reliance on costly motion capture systems. Finally, in the policy fine-tuning stage, we directly fine-tune the policy via backpropagated model gradients, achieving high data efficiency. Through physical validation on the Unitree G1 robot, we demonstrate that HumanoidNDM enables rapid real-world adaptation to various perturbations, representing the first online, MoCap-free fine-tuning framework for humanoid tracking policies.
bullets: Addresses the training–deployment gap caused by unmodeled disturbances and inaccurate simulation dynamics.
Collects feasible exploration data using low-frequency reference perturbations with adaptive intensity.
Learns a robust history-based proprioceptive neural dynamics model with differentiable forward kinematics, avoiding motion capture.
Fine-tunes the tracking policy directly through backpropagated model gradients for high data efficiency.
Physical validation on a Unitree G1 shows rapid adaptation to various real-world perturbations.

papers.abstract: Successful tool-use trajectories are not necessarily useful supervision. Even successful interactions may underrepresent multi-step dependencies or contain actions that are unjustified by the information visible to the agent at decision time. We identify two coupled requirements for effective trajectory supervision: compositional coverage, so that important observation-action dependencies are represented, and decision grounding, so that each supervised action is supported by the learner-visible interaction history. We introduce Trajectory2Gym, which constructs executable interactions around under-supported compositional structures and derives supervision only from grounded decisions in their realized executions. Structural-support selection allocates the resulting experience, while parent-normalized supervised fine-tuning preserves the semantic interaction as the unit of training weight. This reframes trajectory generation as the deliberate construction of learnable interaction experience, rather than the collection of successful trajectories. Across five Qwen3 scales, Trajectory2Gym improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL at every tested scale, increasing the equal-weight three-benchmark mean by 16.9-29.8 percentage points. The gains are strongest in stateful and multi-turn interaction, where later decisions depend on earlier observations and feedback. Our results suggest that scaling tool-use agents depends not only on collecting more successful trajectories, but on constructing interactions whose dependencies are represented and whose decisions are learnable from the agent's visible history.
bullets: Successful trajectories can still provide weak supervision when multi-step dependencies are missing or actions are unsupported by visible information.
The method builds executable interactions around under-supported observation–action structures and supervises only decisions grounded in their realized histories.
Structural-support selection allocates experience, while parent-normalized fine-tuning keeps each semantic interaction as the training unit.
Across five Qwen3 scales, it improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL, with the largest gains in stateful and multi-turn tasks.
The study argues that learnable interaction construction matters more than simply collecting additional successful trajectories.

papers.abstract: We present MOTIO, an agentic skill-engineering system that turns ordinary human-action videos, reality-grounded 3D assets, motion references, and reusable robot skills into executable humanoid loco-manipulation programs. Through in-context task and contact reasoning, an agent constructs staged robot-native interactions and improves them using physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation---without task-specific teleoperation or robot demonstration collection. Agentic 3D supplies metric product and environment assets, while existing whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces realize the programs. Across 33 timestamped first approvals, the median recorded agent-turn time is 97.0 minutes and request-to-approval duration is 2.80 hours. Simulation-side layout and object variation prepare a long-horizon bottle-disposal skill for a continuous 101.75-second physical G1 execution in a scanned office; physical refinement reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%. Agent-generated skills additionally supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one shared reference policy, completing 18 simulated tasks under the same checkpoint without inference-time expert intervention. Project page: https://iiiiqiiii.github.io/motio/
bullets: Uses in-context task and contact reasoning to build staged, robot-native interactions.
Improves programs through physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation.
Combines metric 3D assets with whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces.
Demonstrates a 101.75-second physical bottle-disposal task and reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%.
Generated skills can supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one policy that completes 18 simulated tasks without inference-time expert intervention.

papers.abstract: Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by visual observations. We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion-force control, it contains a unified interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned motion-wrench chunks as control references. A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion-wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow-fast control system that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input. It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads. Our framework with an admittance controller reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, respectively, with smaller force fluctuations during successful execution. Project website: https://cw-wam-project.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit contact and load information in visual observations.

Compared with WAM without wrench input, insertion success rises from 25% to 70% for square pegs and from 40% to 95% for power adapters.
Reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, while improving lifting-height accuracy across loads.

papers.abstract: Among on-policy deep reinforcement learning methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has become the de facto standard, due to its consistently strong empirical performance across diverse application domains. However, on-policy methods are inherently sample inefficient: fresh data collected under the current policy is used for just a few updates before being discarded. Off-policy methods avoid this inefficiency via experience replay, achieving notable sample efficiency gains, but at the cost of training instabilities or extensive tuning. This motivated the rise of hybrid strategies that augment PPO with off-policy data reuse. Existing sample-reuse variants of PPO demonstrated improved sample efficiency over vanilla PPO, yet a systematic study of when reuse helps, in which scenarios, and to what extent remains missing. In this work, we study the effectiveness of sample reuse in PPO by instantiating two variants within a multiple importance weighting framework. Both retain the core PPO mechanics, reusing only samples from a window of recent iterations, thereby isolating the effect of data reuse from other factors. The variants, termed wPPO-U and wPPO-BH, employ vanilla importance weights or balance-heuristic-corrected ones, respectively. For both, we derive policy improvement lower bounds providing theoretical grounding for their respective losses. We use them to empirically study when and how data reuse improves sample efficiency or final performance of PPO across continuous control tasks.
bullets: Introduces two PPO reuse variants within a multiple-importance-weighting framework: wPPO-U and wPPO-BH.
Reuses samples only from a window of recent policy iterations to isolate the effect of data reuse.
Uses vanilla importance weights in wPPO-U and balance-heuristic-corrected weights in wPPO-BH.
Derives policy-improvement lower bounds to theoretically support both objectives.
Evaluates when and how reuse affects sample efficiency and final performance across continuous-control tasks.

papers.abstract: Large-scale manipulation demonstrations are essential for learning robust visuomotor policies, yet real-world data collection is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulation offers a promising alternative, but physical and visual discrepancies can limit the transferability of synthetic data, particularly for manipulation with soft grippers. We present PhyVisGen, a physically and visually high-fidelity framework for scalable robotic manipulation data generation. On the physical side, PhyVisGen introduces an arm-gripper coupling method based on the Incremental Potential Contact (IPC), enabling high-fidelity soft contact throughout complete manipulation trajectories. On the visual side, it combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to generate visually realistic observations while preserving captured scene appearance. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate the physical and visual fidelity of PhyVisGen. Policies trained exclusively on synthetic manipulation demonstrations achieve 65-95% success across five real-robot tasks, without real-robot demonstration data or policy fine-tuning.
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability challenges of collecting real-world robotic manipulation data, especially with soft grippers.
Uses Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) for high-fidelity arm–gripper coupling and soft-contact simulation across complete trajectories.
Combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to produce realistic observations while preserving scene appearance.
Quantitative evaluations show high physical and visual fidelity.
Policies trained only on synthetic data achieve 65–95% success across five real-robot tasks without policy fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation of surgical robots requires tissue that deforms, can be grasped and lifted, and reproduces the anatomy in which the robot will operate. We present a simulator in which this tissue is reconstructed from a fixed-view RGB-D recording of the surgical field, composited to remove the instruments, closed into watertight volumes and tetrahedralised; the pipeline was applied unchanged to three specimens of two species (thirteen organs, 146,061 tetrahedra, no inverted elements). For one specimen, the organs are placed in a bimanual cell in which two Franka FR3 arms operate motorised instruments through 6 mm trocars. The core contribution is the numerical and contact design that keeps this cell stable: implicit integration, simulation meshes separate from collision meshes, numerical guards, and a grasp constraint captured at the live tissue pose. In 45 repeated grasp-lifts, a friction grasp held the tissue in 0 of 15 trials and each constraint grasp in 13 of 15; on displaced tissue, a rest-pose constraint produced one-step snaps of up to 17.8 mm, which live-pose capture eliminates. Against the recording, front-surface depth error is 1.33 to 1.41 mm, organ silhouette IoU is 0.80, and in five grasp-lifts reproduced from video the landmark displacement RMSE is 11.8 mm against 14.2 mm for a static prediction. Biofidelity is not claimed; the environment is intended for closed-loop feasibility, safety, contact and policy screening.
bullets: Reconstructs watertight, tetrahedralised organs from fixed-view RGB-D recordings with instruments removed, applied to 13 organs across three specimens and two species.
Uses implicit integration, separate simulation and collision meshes, numerical safeguards, and grasp constraints captured at the live tissue pose for contact stability.
Constraint grasps succeeded in 13/15 trials, while friction grasps succeeded in 0/15; live-pose capture removes displacement-induced snaps up to 17.8 mm.
Simulation matched recordings with 1.33–1.41 mm front-surface depth error and improved landmark displacement RMSE from 14.2 mm to 11.8 mm versus a static prediction.
Designed for feasibility, safety, contact, and policy screening; the authors do not claim full biofidelity.

papers.abstract: Prioritized experience replay (PER) improves sample efficiency by replaying high-priority transitions, usually according to absolute temporal-difference error. In stochastic environments, PER can distort the distribution of realized outcomes replayed from transitions with the same state-action pair. We call this within-group self-selection. We quantify the resulting changes in within-group outcome frequencies and mean Bellman targets. We decompose PER into between-group allocation and conditional sibling selection, and derive fixed-buffer corrections that preserve current group-level priority mass: SAMPLE selects a group through PER and trains on a uniformly sampled sibling; AVG averages sibling Bellman targets; and MODEL samples from an empirical full-outcome model. In exact state-action environments with rare high-magnitude outcomes, sibling-aware replay improves learning efficiency over PER, although matched parameter sweeps show that tuning can narrow some gaps. In MinAtar, approximate VQ-VAE groups with SAMPLE mitigate degradation under mean-preserving reward tails in four of five games. Sibling-aware replay thus retains the focus on high-priority state-action regions while recovering their empirical outcome frequencies.
bullets: PER can overselect particular stochastic outcomes among transitions sharing a state-action pair, distorting outcome frequencies and Bellman targets.
The paper separates PER into group-level allocation and conditional sibling selection.
It proposes SAMPLE, AVG, and MODEL corrections that preserve group-level priority mass while restoring or modeling sibling outcomes.
In exact state-action settings, sibling-aware replay improves efficiency for rare high-magnitude outcomes; in MinAtar, approximate SAMPLE mitigates degradation in four of five games.
Benefits depend on tuning and the quality of approximate state-action grouping.

papers.abstract: The paper proposes a novel data-driven framework for designing and training a feedback linearizing controller by explicitly incorporating relative degree based conditions into the learning process. This enables the conventional feedback controller components to be replaced by neural Lie derivatives, thereby facilitating a fully data-driven feedback linearization framework. Furthermore, practical closed-loop stability is established by deriving sufficient conditions under which bounded identification errors lead to bounded tracking errors. The derived theoretical results are validated through their application to an armature controlled DC motor.
bullets: Targets fully data-driven feedback linearization without requiring conventional analytical controller components.
Incorporates relative-degree conditions directly into neural controller training.
Uses neural Lie derivatives to construct the feedback-linearizing controller.
Derives conditions showing bounded identification errors yield bounded tracking errors, supporting practical closed-loop stability.
Validates the theoretical results on an armature-controlled DC motor.

papers.abstract: Low-cost planar air-bearing testbeds have matured into a standard proxy for free-flying spacecraft GNC, but they remain largely thruster-only and are rarely equipped for contact-rich, inertia-coupled manipulation. Building on the open-source ATMOS testbed, we contribute a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, integrated as first-class control actuators through a unified ROS 2 abstraction layer. On top of the software stack we build a reinforcement-learning training environment and digital twin, and a controller that exploits these added degrees of freedom, letting classical optimal controllers and learned policies be swapped on the same hardware without modification. We validate the integrated system, PINGU, across four benchmark tasks: point-to-pose navigation (classical LQR vs. sim-to-real PPO), dynamic disturbance rejection under arm-induced center-of-mass shifts, reaction-wheel momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking. The results show that these additions extend an ATMOS-class emulator into the contact-rich regime and bridge classical optimal control and reinforcement learning on one reproducible platform.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of thruster-only planar spacecraft testbeds for inertia-coupled manipulation and contact-rich operations.
Integrates a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms with interchangeable end-effectors through a unified ROS 2 interface.
Provides a reinforcement-learning environment and digital twin supporting interchangeable classical optimal controllers and learned policies.
Validates the system on navigation, disturbance rejection, momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking tasks.
Demonstrates an ATMOS-class emulator extended into the contact-rich regime on a single reproducible platform.

papers.abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
bullets: Addresses tasks where coordinated hand forces and whole-body motion cannot be defined by kinematic trajectories alone.
Learns from robot-free demonstrations using force-sensing handheld grippers and wearable body-motion trackers.
A diffusion policy combines vision, proprioception, and measured contact wrenches to predict actions and per-hand force commands.
A hybrid compliance controller tracks commanded forces while maintaining balance and preserving motion accuracy in simulation.
Across three robot tasks, FLORE succeeds in 80% of rollouts versus 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de Saxc\'e-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: https://diffcontact.github.io
authors: Gijeong Kim, Seungbin Oh, Dongyun Kang, Hae-Won Park
bullets: Addresses the lack of first-order information when frictional contacts transition between modes.
Uses a central-path relaxation of frictional complementarity only during backpropagation, while retaining the exact hard-contact forward solve.
The resulting sensitivity is continuous across contact-mode transitions and approaches the exact sensitivity as relaxation vanishes.
With 100,000 samples and under 2 minutes of desktop training, the learned policy transfers to hardware without fine-tuning.
Hardware and trajectory-optimization demonstrations show robustness to pushes, debris, slippery ground, and contact-rich solutions missed by baseline gradients.

papers.abstract: Robot corrections allow people to adjust a robot's behavior, but a single correction changes many features. Also, preferences about object attributes and relationships between objects cannot be expressed by moving the robot. We propose environment edits as a complementary form of feedback. The robot's motion is held constant as the human edits the scene, so the only explanation for the edit is the moved object. We introduce Feature Learning from Environmental and Robot-Relational Edit Traces (FERRET), which learns preferences from both robot and environment corrections. We show that environment edits are able to disambiguate features and learn preferences that robot corrections alone cannot.

bullets: Robot corrections can change multiple features at once, making preferences ambiguous.
They cannot directly express preferences about object attributes or inter-object relationships.
FERRET learns preferences from both robot corrections and environment-edit traces.
Keeping robot motion fixed makes the edited object the likely cause of the feedback.
Experiments show environment edits disambiguate features and reveal preferences that robot corrections alone miss.

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic data collection remains a major bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) policy learning, especially for tasks requiring accurate end-effector positioning and camera-action alignment. This challenge is particularly severe in electronic-waste disassembly, where robots operate in cluttered assemblies of densely packed, visually similar components. Full digital-twin simulation is difficult because many parts are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level meshes and contact models difficult to obtain. In this work, we focus on pre-contact reaching and propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based data generation pipeline for wrist-camera VLA adaptation. Our method reconstructs the real workspace with 3DGS and renders diverse wrist-camera observations from robot-aligned poses. These observations are paired with smooth, structured reaching trajectories to provide robot-aligned visual-action supervision for VLA fine-tuning. We further augment the VLA policy with an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that estimates target proximity and provides reliable termination before physical interaction. Experiments in motherboard disassembly demonstrate precise VLA-based reaching using wrist-camera observations alone, without an external side-view camera. With $\pi$0.5, 1,500 generated trajectories achieve 80.0\% precise-reaching success across three targets, compared with 58.7\% using 150 teleoperated demonstrations, while requiring less than 10 minutes of active human capture. Project website: https://001-wang.github.io/PrecisionReach-GS/

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. On a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, RoboDoctor achieves a five-dimension mean score of 57.10, with a native success rate of 49.44%. Recorded interactions illustrate strategy changes, selective correction, and grasp revision. These findings characterize execution-time adaptation in the evaluated system; controlled trials remain necessary to isolate the contribution of cross-episode experience.

papers.abstract: Training robotic manipulation policies in simulation is widely adopted due to safety and cost efficiency; however, tasks involving obstacles remain under-performing and often converge slowly under Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). To address this challenge, we propose a task decomposition framework for DRL that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) with Reward Redesign (RR) to improve learning efficiency and robustness in obstacle environments. The TL strategy selectively transfers only the first-layer critic parameters across structurally related tasks, since that layer captures general state--action representations while deeper layers encode reward- and obstacle-specific value geometry; RR decomposes tasks into staged sub-objectives to provide denser optimization signals. Experiments on the PyBullet Panda platform show consistent gains in obstacle settings. On Push with obstacle, our method achieves $0.83 \pm 0.05$, outperforming the strongest baseline (Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC), $0.77 \pm 0.06$) by approximately $7.8\%$. On Slide with obstacle, performance reaches $0.95 \pm 0.02$, exceeding Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) ($0.84 \pm 0.06$) by about $11\%$ success rates. In addition to higher final performance, forward transfer reduces convergence time by up to $70\%$ in obstacle tasks, and RR shortens sparse-reward Pick-and-Place training from roughly $0.75$M to $0.20$M steps ($\approx73\%$ reduction). The best policy is deployed on a real Franka Emika FR3 robot as a qualitative feasibility demonstration.

papers.abstract: Existing manipulation data collection methods typically offer either accurate robot-state acquisition through kinematic-chain-based teleoperation or convenient, portable operation through vision-based approaches. We present DEX-PHD, a portable handheld device that combines these advantages for dexterous manipulation by integrating a dexterous robot hand, continuous per-finger control, and multimodal logging. The system records proprioceptive information, fingertip contact data, and wrist-camera video, while the operator directly controls the robot hand through joint-level mapping. Its untethered design enables data collection across diverse environments. We demonstrate DEX-PHD on contact-rich tasks requiring coordinated multi-finger manipulation and deploy the collected demonstrations through open-loop replay on a physical humanoid robot. The results show that open-loop replay preserves the main temporal patterns of finger motion and task-relevant contact. Therefore, DEX-PHD provides a practical platform for portable, multimodal dexterous manipulation data collection.

papers.abstract: Data-enabled predictive control has recently emerged as a promising control paradigm, enabling a transparent optimal-control formulation without the need to learn an explicit dynamics model. This paper presents a number of extensions paving the path towards its use in real-time robotics tasks. Following recent work, we utilize a nonlinear predictor based on Gaussian kernels to represent the relationship between input and output data. We propose a damped Gauss-Newton method that enables real-time control by efficiently exploiting the least-squares structure of the control problem. In addition, we introduce a hybrid buffer management strategy that incorporates informative online data while retaining relevant offline data, allowing the predictor to account for changes in the dynamics. We demonstrate the tracking performance and computational suitability of the proposed method in MuJoCo using a Franka Research 3 arm pushing a block across surface, without prior knowledge of its changing friction values.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive's collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird's-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop. We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label. A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand. Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly. Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive's scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.
authors: Khaled M. Seyam (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Julian Wiederer (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Samar Fathalah (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Markus Braun (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Bin Yang (University of Stuttgart, Germany)
bullets: NeuroNCAP analysis attributes 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s collisions to planning failures rather than perception.
The method attacks each planner through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its planning head, avoiding video rendering during search.
Automated quality-diversity search generates 50 attack scenes per planner, each paired with a safe escape trajectory for fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning roughly halves collision rates for SparseDrive and DiffusionDrive on NeuroNCAP, from 28.0% to 12.2% and 37.5% to 19.2%, respectively.
Cross-planner transfer is limited, indicating that targeting the specific planner is important; scope is demonstrated on two planners and NeuroNCAP.

papers.abstract: Estimating forces acting on Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is challenging due to their underactuated nature. However, reliable contact estimation is crucial to precisely control them and enable safe manipulation tasks. Differently from the various approaches presented in the literature, this work adopts a probabilistic formulation where the DLO state and sensor data are related through conditional distributions. In particular, factor graphs are used to determine the magnitude, direction, and location of a 3D force acting on a DLO, while simultaneously reconstructing its shape. Since DLOs are not actuated and are typically thin, like cables and wires, strain gauges and actuation readings are usually impractical. Therefore, to overcome this issue, this work is tested using one type of sensing information only, thus developing a generic technique suited for a wider variety of tasks. Realistic tests are performed by introducing noise into the measurements while the DLO follows a prescribed path in the presence of external forces that are accurately estimated.
authors: Annika Delucchi, Vincenzo Di Paola, Bruno Marco Quadrelli, Matteo Zoppi
bullets: Addresses reliable contact-force estimation for underactuated DLOs such as cables and wires.
Models the DLO state and sensor observations through conditional probability distributions.
Infers force magnitude, direction, and location alongside DLO shape.
Designed to avoid impractical strain-gauge or actuation measurements by using one sensing type.
Realistic noisy-measurement tests show accurate force estimation as the DLO follows a prescribed path under external forces.
