papers.abstract: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.
authors: Zhang Zhang, Shengjun Zhang, Simin Huang, Min Chen, Chong Xia, Xin Fei, Yueqi Duan
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static, post-hoc rollout reflection, which updates harnesses without autonomously validating them through interaction.
Maintains a harness graph to track version lineage, reuse effective mechanisms, and avoid repeated failed explorations.
Generates rollouts, probes failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively updates the harness based on execution evidence.
Evaluated on LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin, where it progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can select among discrete candidates for pick-and-place manipulation or generate continuous action chunks for motion control. Improving both forms of decision making through a common mechanism while retaining the capabilities of a pretrained policy is an important adaptation problem. Inspired by Jev's structured, probabilistic decision interface, we propose JevVLA, a lightweight energy-based adaptation framework for VLA policies. JevVLA instantiates this inspiration by modeling the relative quality of action proposals: with the base policy frozen, it learns a differentiable scalar energy conditioned on observations, task context, and actions, using execution feedback, expert corrections, or demonstration-derived preferences. JevVLA uses this single learned action preference function in two ways: its values compare discrete candidates, while its action gradients correct continuous actions or guide their generation. Candidate selection and continuous control thus share one trainable decision core. Each benchmark uses independently trained weights and fixed input/output encodings, while retaining the same core network with approximately 80,000 trainable parameters. On the held-out test sets, JevVLA improves task success over the respective matched base-policy controls by 1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points on MetaWorld MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and CLIPort, respectively. These results support the feasibility of a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy model for adapting both discrete action selection and continuous action guidance. The JevVLA implementation will be open-sourced at https://github.com/ZJU4EmbodiedAI/JevVLA.
authors: Wei Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Zheqi Lv, Zheng Dong, Yingjie Niu, Jiaqi Zhu, Jun Xiao, Chao Li, Yueting Zhuang

papers.abstract: Grasping is a foundational capability in robotic manipulation. Scene-level 6-DoF grasp synthesis relies on point clouds for metric geometry, yet real-world point observations are often noisy, incomplete, and over-smoothed. RGB images provide object-region, boundary, and appearance cues, yet two bottlenecks limit their effective use in scene representation and local grasp reasoning. We present MMGNet, a Multi-Modal Grasp Synthesis Network that addresses these bottlenecks through hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection and rotational graspness modeling. Hierarchical injection integrates multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation, while the rotational graspness jointly predicts the grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation before organizing local image-informed features through grasp-shaded grouping. Ablation studies show that these two modules provide complementary gains. MMGNet achieves a mean AP of 60.34 on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense, surpassing all compared methods. In real-world experiments with adversarial grasp objects, MMGNet improves the grasp success rate over AnyGrasp by 8.46 percentage points. \emph{Code, models, and data will be released upon publication.}
authors: Rui Cao, Jia-Hui Pan, Yichuan Li, Yunfan Yu, Chi-Wing Fu, Jiangliu Wang, Yun-Hui Liu
bullets: Addresses incomplete, noisy, and over-smoothed point clouds by incorporating complementary RGB cues.
Injects multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation.
Jointly predicts grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation, then organizes local features via grasp-shaded grouping.
Achieves 60.34 mean AP on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense and improves real-world grasp success by 8.46 percentage points over AnyGrasp.
Ablations indicate the two proposed modules provide complementary gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of MMGNet. Given a single-view RGB-D observation, the image backbone extracts dense image features, which are aligned with the scene points through pixel–point correspondence and injected into successive stages of the 3D backbone to form image-informed 3D features. Rotational graspness prediction then scores joint view–in-plane rotations at candidate grasp centers. Based on the selected rotations, grasp-shaded grouping aggregates local image-informed features within the corresponding gripper frames. Finally, the operation head predicts the remaining depth-wise grasp scores and gripper widths to produce the final 6-DoF grasps.

papers.abstract: Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution.
authors: Haoyang Jiang, Dana Kulic, Michael Burke, Pamela Carreno-Medrano
bullets: The paper identifies an objective mismatch between generative behaviour quality and downstream RL training utility.

Training on a distribution different from the true testing behaviour distribution can sometimes produce better policies than training directly on the true distribution.

papers.abstract: Visual captures provide detailed scene appearance, but converting them into interactive simulation environments requires object reconstruction, physical modeling, and correction of intermediate errors. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that coordinates these steps through simulator-based visual inspection and repair. The pipeline processes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), photogrammetry, LiDAR captures, AI-generated 3DGS scenes, and 4D videos of dynamic scenes, and combines object segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation. To support policy learning, SceneAgent generates diverse object variants ("digital sisters") and scripted demonstrations. On a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D, SceneAgent raises F1 at 1 cm for every coding agent with scorable outputs both with and without its skills, and its reconstructions are better than SimFoundry: all agent configurations exceed SimFoundry's F1 score, with a best of 60.75% versus 6.9%. On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09%. We further demonstrate diverse simulated interactions and preliminary policy transfer to a real robot.

papers.abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.
authors: Jonathan DeCastro, Thomas Balch, Emily Sumner, Deepak Gopinath, Laporsha Dees, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Elliot Weiss, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Todd Rowell, John Leonard, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
bullets: Targets the challenge of proactive yet understandable assistance in tightly coupled human–vehicle control.
Extends a recurrent state-space world model with human-intent inference and trains the assistive policy through fictitious co-play.
Includes a deployment pipeline with policy down-selection, reward restructuring, and iterative human–machine interface design to address the sim-to-real-human gap.
Validated in three human-subject studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment covering high-speed racing and urban driving.
Intent conditioning improved torque alignment and collision rate; the work also reports deployment insights for safety-critical human–robot teaming.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs. Furthermore, RAB enables systematic comparisons of standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures under a unified planning-execution-verification framework. Extensive experiments reveal substantial gaps between manipulation and autonomy, demonstrate the advantages of agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and highlight the remaining challenges toward open-world robot autonomy.
authors: Lingjun Mao, Jinglin Cao, Lukun He, Wenpeng Xu, Yuchen Yan, Hengyu Jin, Zijun Zhang, Jinzhou Tang, Songyao Jin, Ziche Liu, Yifei Shao, Junbo Huang, Fang Nan, Ruobing Han, Ziqiao Xi, Ziming Xu, Shuang Liang, Sibo Zhu, Wenyi Wu, Xinyue Wang, Yiming Huang, Xinkai Zou, Gao Zhu, Kun Zhou, Biwei Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between benchmarks for isolated robot capabilities and the integrated demands of open-world autonomy.
Introduces 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks across atomic, short-horizon, long-horizon, and open-ended scenarios.
Evaluates five task-level abilities: task discovery, contextual reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness.
Measures scenario-level autonomy, including how agents combine these capabilities to satisfy high-level user needs.
Experiments show a substantial manipulation–autonomy gap, benefits from agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and persistent challenges for open-world deployment.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts. We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively. Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision. We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for $\pi_{0.5}$, where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%. These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.
authors: Hanwen Cui, Yuanyuan Li, Qing Guo, Zhida Zhang, Chao Chen, Xi Chen, Jie Cao
bullets: Controlled ablations in FastWAM and OpenWAM isolate future-video prediction while holding architecture, initialization, data, and training steps fixed within each family.
Predictive supervision substantially improves success on clean, seen tasks: +24.38 and +72.91 percentage points in FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively.
Trajectory analysis suggests gains reflect better execution within existing trajectory patterns, not only shifts in which patterns occur.
Under unseen tasks and environmental randomizations, improvements are inconsistent or absent, with both models performing poorly in the evaluated shifts.
Adding a lightweight training-only Transformer predictor to π₀.₅ raises success from 82.94% to 89.19%, showing that large pretrained video diffusion models are not required in this setting.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor trajectory tracking under unmodeled disturbances often relies on online residual adaptation, but short out-domain residuals can corrupt the learned disturbance model when constant-step updates treat every residual gradient uniformly. We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size. DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with $L_1$-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.
bullets: Targets corruption of online disturbance learning caused by treating all residual gradients equally.
Retains DAPL’s random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares residual adaptation.
Compares current gradients with short- and long-term memories to classify adaptation regimes.
Uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates and recover after persistent domain shifts.
In numerical tests with four mixed disturbances, DGC achieved the lowest mean position RMSE among the evaluated baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of Dual Gradient Consensus for online adaptive learning under mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances. Left: the residual pipeline forms a packed gradient gt from the RFF predictor, a low-pass residual, and the least-squares loss. Center: Long-Term Gradient (LTG) and Short-Term Gradient (STG) memories classify gt into four regimes; only (0, 1) hands LTG over to STG. Right: a confidence map sets the step length of the (α̂, σ̂) update on mixed in-domain/out-domain residuals. Bottom: the applied learning step size remains high in-domain, drops on transients, and recovers after a completed domain shift.

papers.abstract: We introduce PhysLadder, a hierarchical Sim-Real benchmark for evaluating physical interaction capabilities in contact-rich manipulation. Its 16 household tasks span three cumulative levels: contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), force regulation within sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3). Each task is instantiated in physically and visually matched simulated and real-world environments, with shared task definitions and success criteria. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. Real-world success rates decline from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical success counts across environments; the remaining six differ by one success out of three trials. Across both environments, recurring difficulties in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination often prevent local physical progress from accumulating into task completion. These findings characterize Astra's observed capability boundary across increasing interaction demands and, for this model, support matched simulation as a repeatable, scalable testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that limit reliable manipulation.
authors: Haibao Yu, Jiaqi Meng, Zijian Zhang, Bowen Jing, Lei Yang, Yue Hu, Chenchen Ge, Yiming Hou, Chenbo Xin, Dawen Ye, Haifang Qin, Jin Li, Weitao Zhou, Jianing Qiu, Jiankai Sun, Dandan Zhang, Zaiqing Nie, Ping Luo, Ding Zhao
bullets: PhysLadder is a hierarchical Sim-Real benchmark with 16 household contact-rich manipulation tasks across three cumulative difficulty levels.
Tasks progress from contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), to sustained force regulation (L2), to coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3).
Astra’s real-world success rates were 80.0% (L1), 47.6% (L2), and 0.0% (L3); simulation rates were 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%.
Simulation and real-world outcomes closely matched: 10 of 16 tasks had identical success counts, while the other six differed by one success in three trials.
Recurring limitations involved spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordinating local progress toward task completion.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map a language instruction and the current observation directly to actions, without checking whether the instruction has been completed. For long-horizon tasks, a single failed step therefore goes unnoticed and leaves the whole task unfinished. Such failed episodes, however, often end with the task partially complete. Moreover, the unfinished steps are reusable atomic skills that recur across demonstrations. A failed attempt can thus be recovered by composing with atomic skills. We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual-system framework that uses code as the interface between a coding agent and two VLAs. The agent writes a program that lets a full-task VLA attempt the whole task and checks whether it is complete; on failure, an atomic VLA finishes the remaining steps. Since the agent emits no actions and only decides which VLA for execution, RoboDuo wraps an existing full-task VLA without updating its weights. To train the atomic VLA and the coding agent with the completion-checking ability, we build LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from a single set of LIBERO demonstrations. RoboDuo consistently improves X-VLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks, and recovers failed rollouts of a frozen full-task VLA on a real robot.
authors: Jie Wang, Bo Zhang, Renzhi Lu, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses unnoticed failures in VLAs that can leave long-horizon tasks incomplete.

The coding agent selects which VLA executes actions and does not require updating the full-task VLA’s weights.
Introduces LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge, built from existing LIBERO demonstrations.
Improves X-VLA and π₀.₅ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, especially for long-horizon tasks, and recovers failures on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. Project website: https://arielchen07.github.io/behavior-spatial/.
authors: Sirui Chen, Huang Huang, Qineng Wang, Wenlong Huang, Manling Li, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu

papers.abstract: Robots that learn from people often see several valid ways to do the same task: pass an obstacle on the left or on the right, open the microwave or move the kettle first. A policy that re-decides at every step can waver between these ways mid-task. We ask when the action head (the part of a policy that turns the state into actions) matters, and how it should make this choice. On a controlled task, heads that sample one way succeed far more often than a head that averages the ways when the demonstrations contain several ways and the state gives no hint which to take (+0.72 success with two ways); this trend was not reproduced on the other tasks we ran. We then present ElevateHead, a head that decides once at a learned decision point, commits to that choice for the episode, and exposes the choice as an input a user can set. We designed it by diagnosis: each version was frozen and tested on tasks it had not seen, and the next version changed only what a measured failure pointed to; predictions were registered before each run. The first four versions each fell below BeT on at least one held-out task. The fifth completed all four subtasks of the held-out Franka Kitchen task in 45.2% of episodes against 29.3% for BeT, the strongest baseline across our tasks (+0.160, 95% CI [+0.129, +0.188]); when a mode was forced, the first completed subtask matched it in 95% of successful episodes. Diagnosis also located where commitment breaks: varied start positions (repaired on the controlled task: commitment 0.22 to 0.81, success 0.74 to 0.91) and varied object placement (partly repaired: in an exploratory variant, commitment 0.03 to 0.59 on aligning with no detectable change in success). On held-out block stacking, version 4 was comparable to BeT and did not exceed it. A real-robot test with predictions fixed in advance is planned for a follow-up version of this paper.
bullets: Per-step averaging can fail when demonstrations contain multiple valid strategies and observations do not reveal which strategy to choose; sampling performed better on one controlled task, but this trend did not generalize to all tasks.
ElevateHead selects a mode once, commits to it, and lets users set the selected mode explicitly.
Through iterative diagnosis on unseen tasks, the fifth version achieved 45.2% success on all four Franka Kitchen subtasks versus 29.3% for BeT.
Forced modes matched the first completed subtask in 95% of successful episodes, supporting controllable behavior.
Commitment was sensitive to varied starts and object placements; performance was comparable to BeT on held-out block stacking, and real-robot evaluation remains future work.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances.
bullets: Addresses long-horizon manipulation where object properties cannot be determined reliably from appearance.
Integrates task-directed information-gathering actions with interleaved planning and execution.
Plans optimistically, verifies interactive outcomes, and replans only the remaining necessary connections.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot across tasks involving movable objects, ink-filled pens, openable drawers, and empty containers.
Supports continued execution despite uncertain interaction outcomes and external disturbances.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Example execution trace with online monitoring and recovery. Blue blocks show the initial plan and successive updated plans, containing retained actions and newly introduced bridging actions. The initial plan consists of actions a1, . . . , a12, while aki,j denotes the kth action of a bridge plan reconnecting execution after ai to retained action aj . After each interactive information-gathering action, AFTERCHECK updates the symbolic state from the observed outcome (green blocks), recording that the object has been checked and whether the tested property holds. VALIDATOR removes actions that are no longer valid: orange crosses denote collision-infeasible actions, while red crosses denote actions whose symbolic preconditions are infeasible. Before each retained action, PRECHECK verifies executability (red blocks). Detected precondition mismatches trigger RECOVERYREPLAN (yellow blocks), which searches for a bridge to the next retained action or, if unsuccessful, to a later retained action. Each successful repair produces an updated plan combining the recovered bridge with the retained suffix. The system executes the bridge and resumes the retained plan, repeating state updates, validation, and on-demand repair until the goal is reached. Robot snapshots show the corresponding physical execution from the initial scene to the goal state.

Fig. 4. Representative simulation experiments in two domains. Top: Container-Emptiness, where a negative interaction result (non-empty mug) leads from picking to pouring. Bottom: Drawer-Openability, where a positive interaction result (openable drawer) leads from pulling to placing the mug inside.

Fig. 3. Recovery replanning through bridge construction. After executing a1 and a2 (gray), the current planning state s′2 differs from the predicted state s2, and a3 fails its PRECHECK (red). RECOVERYREPLAN searches from s′2 for a bridge that establishes Pre(a3); if unsuccessful, it tries later retained actions in order. The first bridge found is prepended to the retained suffix beginning at its target action. If no bridge is found to any retained action, global replanning searches from s′2 toward the active goal set G (green), producing a new action sequence [a′3, a ′ 4, . . .]. If this search also fails, the algorithm returns failure.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robotic control requires simultaneous management of distinct functional demands under motor noise, energetic costs, and communication delays. We investigate how learning responsibility should be organised across modular controllers and the two arms in a simulated musculoskeletal system with two communicating recurrent controllers. Using a 2 x 2 design, we compare differential versus shared controller objectives and fixed versus balanced hand-task assignments. Task-aligned functional specialisation was strongest when differential objectives were combined with a fixed assignment aligned with contralateral control routing. This condition achieved the highest canonical-task performance and control efficiency, reaching 81.33% bimanual success. Its advantage over shared objectives increased with motor noise but narrowed under stronger energy penalties. Stronger specialisation also reduced hand-role flexibility: reversing the hand roles decreased bimanual success by 80.46 percentage points under Differential-Fixed training, compared with 1.51 percentage points under Shared-Balanced training. These results show that controller objectives and hand-task experience jointly determine functional organisation. Stronger role-specific specialisation favours performance and efficiency when roles remain stable, whereas more distributed training favours interchangeability when roles change.

papers.abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.
authors: Guile Wu, Shuangzhi Li, Xingxin Chen, Chengjie Huang, Sam Hosseini, Tongtong Cao, Yingxue Zhang, Dongfeng Bai
bullets: Addresses high inference latency that limits real-world deployment of world action models.
Adaptively aggregates representations from different world-model layers based on the evolving action-denoising state.
Uses structured action supervision to modulate layer-wise gradients and improve representation learning.
Reduces inference cost by executing fewer world-model layers and caching relevant representations across denoising steps.
Experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks show low latency with competitive task success rates.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the TurboWAM framework. The structured world representation aggregation module adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to the current action denoising state. The structured action supervision mechanism modulates action-supervision gradients across world model layers during the backward pass. Together, these complementary designs reduce inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates.

(c) Influence of individual world model layers at different denoising steps in Faster-WAM, measured by the relative change in predicted action velocity when the key/value pairs from a given layer are excluded from fusion. papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires actions whose validity depends on earlier interactions, yet visual progress can conceal missing task prerequisites. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. Stage-shuffle supervision encourages execution-order sensitivity, recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, and two-round training refines trajectory segments using predicted progress. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. Sparse terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by triggering correction for repeated high-scoring failures. Pretrained on demonstrations from 88 RLBench tasks and Open-X data, RoboLongR achieves 31.8% average success on 18 long-horizon tasks excluded from reward pretraining, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. Across four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5% success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. Reward-level controls probe sensitivity to synthetic order perturbations, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components to policy improvement.

papers.abstract: Language is a natural way to command robots, but converting a single instruction into a long-horizon, contact-rich hand-object interaction remains challenging: synthesized references are noisy, human-to-robot retargeting introduces embodiment bias, and fixed-reference tracking lets small errors snowball. We address this with AdaDexTrack, a modulator-in-the-loop framework for language-conditioned manipulation tracking. A distilled generalist tracker serves as the skill carrier, while a tightly aligned modulator performs three feedback corrections: reference modulation (continual adjustment of what to track), object-latent modulation (online adaptation of the object representation to recruit suitable skills), and positional-target modulation (small state-dependent refinements for execution). The tracker is learned via large-scale specialist to generalist distillation on a corpus of language-conditioned hand-object trajectories; the modulator is trained with RL under the same task objective, ensuring tight coupling. Across large-scale evaluations, AdaDexTrack consistently outperforms prior SOTA on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object sets in both average tracking error and success rate, demonstrating robustness and generalization. We further show zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real hardware, where adding the modulator yields substantial gains over a tracker-only variant. AdaDexTrack reframes language-conditioned dexterous manipulation as modulated tracking, replacing the open-loop, fixed-reference tracking with in-loop modulation that adjusts the reference, object latent, and positional target, yielding drift-resistant execution from noisy text references.
authors: Jianibieke Adalibieke, Qianwei Han, Xueyi Liu, Yuzhe Qin, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses noisy language-generated references, embodiment bias, and error accumulation in long-horizon contact-rich manipulation.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of $1.91\times$ over P-RoPE and $5.34\times$ over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.
authors: Xiaodi Huang, Zilin Wang, Jinpeng Liu, Pengchuan Xiao, Zhenlei Shao, Zhang Zhang, Shuxiang Lu
bullets: Represents each token’s observation footprint as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times.

Evaluated across four robot-policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, plus reconstruction, depth estimation, and novel-view synthesis.

papers.abstract: A robot in a home it has never seen must open doors, drawers, lids and taps whose physics a picture does not show. Instructions such as "open the drawer halfway, gently" depend on that physics: how far a part travels, how it resists, and what locks it. We present Open-World Law-to-Action (L2A). A vision-language model (VLM) proposes, for each movable part, its motions, the terms of its law of motion, and what may lock it. Each proposal becomes a prior with a floor, so that touch can always overturn it. The robot identifies each part's law online by Bayesian linear regression with closed-form evidence, for parts that move in one way or in two, and keeps a hypothesis that an unseen part or motion locks the target. We prove that touch alone cannot rule this hypothesis out, derive when another look is worth its cost, and show that a constant load and friction cannot be told apart while a part moves one way. All experiments are in simulation, developed on some scenes and run once on held-out ones. In new kitchens the robot completes 80% of tasks from the VLM's proposals, against 98% when every part is known. Proposed physics raises success on objects that need new terms from 353 to 378-383 of 400 episodes, and a second look raises success in mixed scenes from 284 to 329 of 366 tasks. A mobile robot that takes nothing from the simulator completes 70 of 100 requests in new scenes, against 62 when the simulator says which part each box is (after one change made between two held-out tests).
bullets: Targets open-world tasks such as opening doors, drawers, lids, and taps according to force- and motion-sensitive instructions.
A VLM proposes part motions, motion-law terms, and possible locks; touch can revise these priors online.
Bayesian linear regression identifies one- or two-way motion laws while maintaining an unseen-lock hypothesis.
The analysis characterizes limits of touch-only identification and when an additional visual observation is worthwhile.
In simulation, proposed physics and second looks improve held-out task success; a mobile robot completes 70/100 requests in new scenes.],

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
authors: Qingyuan Cai, Bo Zhang, Yongzhen Huang, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of robot data and the human–robot embodiment gap.
Learns factorized latent actions that disentangle shared manipulation primitives from embodiment-specific signals.
Transfers manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations to robots with different kinematic structures.
Supports both parallel grippers and dexterous hands.
Reports consistent gains over no-pretraining baselines on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.
authors: Xuebin Li, Jinpeng Xiao, Zong Chen, Pierluigi Arpenti, Bruno Siciliano, Jiebao Sun, Yiqun Li
bullets: Targets coordination across robots with different motion capabilities and a shared, unfixed payload.
Uses hierarchical CTDE: a centralized critic trains high-level coordination policies, while embodiment-specific low-level controllers execute commands.
Diffusion policies represent flexible, potentially multimodal coordination responses beyond single-Gaussian policies.
Robots act from local robot and payload observations without partner-state inputs or inter-robot communication.

Simulations report higher mean returns and velocity-tracking success, with lower velocity errors than evaluated baselines; real-world tests include quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot transport.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion trackers reproduce diverse behaviors, but sharing a policy across bodies requires accounting for differences in structure, morphology and dynamics. We present MimicAll, a reinforcement-learning framework for shared whole-body motion tracking across heterogeneous humanoids. A structured embodiment descriptor is encoded into global and joint-aligned conditions, which are combined with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets. Physics-consistent embodiment randomization, body-calibrated retargeting and heterogeneous simulation support training across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families. We introduce a benchmark of 464 bodies across five distribution strata to evaluate motion generalization, within-family embodiment shifts and unseen-family transfer. Controlled ablations show that embodiment information improves motion completion with simple concatenation, while self-attention yields the lowest global position errors. With equal training transitions, shared training achieves 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies in 100STYLE, versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist. With Flat-MLP encoding and concatenation, continued training on a motion subset excluding obstacle categories achieves 98.3% and 93.5% 30-second success on 100STYLE for sampled training bodies and out-of-distribution variants within seen families, respectively. On an eight-motion LAFAN1 subset excluding ground and get-up sequences across 464 bodies, mismatched body conditions reduce self-attention's 30-second success from 61.7% to 47.0%, demonstrating a closed-loop benefit from embodiment information.
authors: Jia Li, Lingyun Xu, Yitang Li, Hao Zhao
bullets: Addresses morphology, structure, and dynamics differences that hinder cross-humanoid policy sharing.
Encodes embodiment globally and per joint, combining it with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets.
Uses physics-consistent embodiment randomization, calibrated retargeting, and heterogeneous simulation across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families.
Evaluates generalization on 464 bodies across five distribution strata, including within-family shifts and unseen-family transfer.

Embodiment conditioning substantially improves closed-loop tracking; shared training reaches 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist, while self-attention gives the lowest global position errors.

papers.abstract: We present RAIWAY, an in-house wheeled bipedal robot with 20-inch wheels, together with a contact-informed control approach for rolling locomotion across irregular and discontinuous terrain. Such locomotion is fundamentally contact-dominated, governed by local wheel--terrain interaction that is impractical to instrument directly and depends on more than terrain geometry alone. The proposed framework exploits the contact information available in simulation, distilling multi-contact events into a latent representation. At deployment, the controller infers this representation online from proprioception, requiring no contact sensing. In real-world experiments, the proposed system traverses diverse environments including steep slopes, gravel beds, studded surfaces, and rocky terrain, and demonstrates continuous ascent on the tested outdoor staircases with riser heights up to 15~cm. On our platform, the proposed controller further outperforms baselines without the contact-informed mechanism across challenging indoor and outdoor settings. The video can be found at https://youtu.be/Ch0divLg64w.
authors: Kyungmin Nam, Jiseong Lee, Donghyuk Choi, Jeongsoo Park, Woojin Kim, Jemin Hwangbo
bullets: Addresses contact-dominated rolling locomotion where wheel–terrain interactions are difficult to measure directly.
Distills simulated multi-contact events into a latent representation and estimates it online during deployment.
Demonstrates locomotion across slopes, gravel, studded and rocky surfaces, plus stair ascent with risers up to 15 cm.
Outperforms controllers without contact-informed representations in tested indoor and outdoor environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the proposed contact-informed policy learning framework: The large wheels of our platform produce informative multi-contact patterns, yielding a diverse set of spatially distributed contact events during training. These noisy multi-contact events from the simulator are assembled into a structured vector ct. A recurrent encoder maps this vector sequence into a latent representation, which a student module learns to infer from onboard proprioceptive history for deployment. The GRU encoder has a hidden size of 128, the estimator and policy are [256, 128] MLPs, the teacher encoder is an LSTM with a hidden size of 8 producing the 32-dimensional latent lt, and the student is a [256, 128] MLP, all with LeakyReLU activations.

Fig. 1. Real-world experiments across diverse challenging environments: Representative deployments include (A) rapid stair descent, (B,C) steep-slope descent and ascent, traversal of (D) gravel bed, (E) studded slope, and (F,G) rocky terrain, and continuous stair ascent at (H) 9 cm, (I) 14 cm, and (J) 15 cm riser heights.

Fig. 7. Responses to abrupt contact events during outdoor deployment: Two representative episodes involving challenging contact conditions. The plots show base angle, leg-joint positions, the event-relevant estimator output, and two latent components (l3, l4). (a) The left wheel spins against a wheel-radiusscale rock in (i)–(ii), after which the left leg rolls over the rock on its wheel in (iii), producing a pronounced body oscillation after landing in (iv). (b) The studded slope shifts the wheel–terrain contact locations laterally.

Fig. 4. Temporal filtering during a representative simulated rollout: The robot traverses a flat–stairs–drop–flat terrain sequence, where the flat sections feature low-amplitude fractal height variations. The graphs compare the xs-coordinate of the first angularly sorted contact position for the two wheels before and after temporal filtering. On the flat terrain, the raw signal flickers despite continuous rolling contact, whereas the filtered signal preserves variation. During stair ascent, the filtered signal captures the stepedge locations with a distinct piecewise evolution. During the drop segment, a true aerial phase is induced, and the debounce filter introduces a short delay in the contact-state transition.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors. Yet, existing reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines are limited in system-level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback. We present ViT-H, a video-to-humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm. ViT-H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion-tracking outcomes to post-train the generator with direct preference optimization. We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability. We further show that ViT-H scales favorably with model size and with both pre-training and post-training data scale, while motion-tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers.
bullets: Addresses scalability limits of separately optimized reconstruction–retargeting–tracking pipelines.
Uses a diffusion model to generate humanoid reference motions directly from video, avoiding explicit reconstruction and retargeting.
Applies direct preference optimization based on motion-tracking outcomes to improve executability.
An autoregressive variant supports real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency.
Experiments on the Unitree G1 show improved motion quality and executability, with favorable scaling across model and data size.

For post-training (middle), candidates sampled for the same video are executed by a deployable tracker, which scores local pose accuracy and success, and by a privileged tracker, which scores global motion accuracy and success. At deployment (right), the offline generator drives video-to-humanoid control and the autoregressive generator drives real-time teleoperation.

papers.abstract: The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. As a result, the same motion can appear at widely different speeds across demonstrations, and policies trained on such data may inherit operator-specific timing along with task behavior. We propose to learn a speed prior directly from large-scale demonstration data. Given a task instruction, a motion path and the images along it, it predicts a distribution over execution speed along the path, from which a chosen quantile defines a consistent clock for retiming each demonstration. Existing methods derive the acceleration signal from the very data they accelerate, so each new task costs another fit, annotation, or pair of predefined rates. A single trained speed prior instead covers every task in a corpus. We fit a speed prior on both robot teleoperation data and handheld demonstrations in which a human arm, rather than a robot arm, moves the gripper, and use it to retime robot demonstrations to the handheld pace before fine-tuning a vision-language-action policy. For execution, we pair the policy with a real-time optimal-control layer that tracks predicted action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace. On 120 RoboLab tasks, policies fine-tuned on our learned clocks succeed more often and move with up to half the jerk compared with policies fine-tuned on the original demonstration timing and uniformly accelerated to the same speed. On a real robot, our policy stacks cups in 3.50s, 1.72$\times$ faster than the default policy's 6.02s while succeeding as often, in 29 of 30 trials. Videos and further material are available at https://mllab.snu.ac.kr/projects/learned_speed_prior.
authors: Seungyong Moon, Deokjae Lee, Hansang Lee, Munkhtselmeg Battsengel, Youngin Kim, Seonghyeon Yun, Sungjin Jeon, SongEun Kim, Jeongmin Park, Hyun Oh Song
bullets: Teleoperator timing can vary across demonstrations and cause policies to learn operator-specific speeds rather than task-relevant motion.
The method predicts a distribution of execution speeds from the task instruction, motion path, and path images; a selected quantile defines each demonstration’s new clock.
One speed prior trained on robot and handheld demonstrations can retime demonstrations across tasks without fitting a separate acceleration model per task.
A real-time optimal-control layer tracks policy action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace.
Across 120 RoboLab tasks, learned retiming improved success and reduced jerk by up to half; a real robot stacked cups in 3.50s with 29/30 successes.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Success rate (left) and TPR (right) against speed-up on RoboLab. Gray labels give the commanded speed-up. TPR (Appendix G) is in successes per minute, with the time limit of each task. Bars are 95% intervals of the gain over the uniform curve, bootstrapped over tasks.

Figure 5: Mean task progress over time on the real-robot placing bananas task, over 30 trials per condition. Each banana placed in the tray within the 30 s limit adds half of a trial, and curves average over trials, so curves further up and to the left progress faster.

Figure 1: Learning the pace from demonstrations. (1) Paths are resampled every 2 cm of arc length and read in windows of 17 nodes. (2) The prior predicts a distribution over the log speed of every interval. (3) Reading a source path with the target label gives a quantile of the speed along the path. (4) Integrating this speed gives the clock.

papers.abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) has demonstrated strong performance in various offline reinforcement learning (RL) tasks by conditioning action generation on expected future returns and historical trajectories. However, treating expected future returns as the condition provides an incomplete description of the future, as trajectories with different state transitions and behaviors may share similar returns. Moreover, expected future returns inherently depend on task-specific reward functions, which makes policy learning reliant on reward-labeled datasets and restricts its scalability to tasks with similar but unseen rewards. Recently, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have emerged as a promising paradigm of self-supervised learning-based world models, which learn predictive representations of future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing future states in the original space. Inspired by JEPA, we propose DT-JEPA, an offline pretraining and online fine-tuning framework that learns general knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories and achieves excellent adaptation to unseen tasks. Instead of predicting a single deterministic future embedding, we design a novel probabilistic predictor to model the conditional distribution of future representations in the latent space, thereby capturing both predictive information and uncertainty about future dynamics. Theoretically, we show that 1) the JEPA objective seeks to maximize a variational lower bound on the mutual information between historical representations and future trajectories; and 2) predictive future-conditioned policy learning admits a finite-sample performance bound with an O(N-1/4) estimation term. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that DT-JEPA achieves efficient adaptation across varying offline RL tasks, outperforming traditional DT-based and other offline RL methods.
authors: Changxu Ni, Yiyang Ni, Jun Li, Feiran You, Hongyang Du, Haitao Zhao, Shi Jin
bullets: Decision Transformer return-conditioning can miss distinct future dynamics and depends on task-specific reward labels.
DT-JEPA learns general predictive knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories before online task adaptation.
A probabilistic latent-space predictor models both future dynamics and their uncertainty instead of reconstructing future states.
Theoretical analysis connects the JEPA objective to mutual information and establishes a finite-sample performance bound.
On D4RL benchmarks, DT-JEPA adapts efficiently across tasks and outperforms DT-based and other offline RL methods.

papers.abstract: The growing population of orbital debris has intensified interest in active debris removal and on-orbit servicing, for which dual-arm space manipulators offer improved grasping stability and load distribution relative to single-arm systems. However, coordinating two manipulators under inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, and sensing uncertainty remains challenging. This paper develops a coordinated reinforcement learning framework for cooperative motion planning of a dual-arm space manipulator in a target-reaching task with inter-arm collision-avoidance constraints. A centralized state representation combines joint-space, end-effector, and target-relative information, while a multi-objective reward function promotes target-reaching accuracy, orientation alignment, motion smoothness, synchronized task completion, and collision avoidance. Within this framework, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) are compared as representative on-policy and off-policy algorithms, and the learned policies are further evaluated for generalization to previously unseen target configurations. Across five random seeds, SAC substantially outperforms PPO within the considered fixed-base simulation scenarios: it reaches an 80% success threshold in every seed (median 1.6M environment steps) whereas PPO does not reach it within a 4M-step budget, and it attains a higher mean success rate (78.6% versus 7.4%) with lower position and orientation errors and tighter bimanual synchronization. Both algorithms degrade on unseen boundary targets, but SAC retains most of its performance while PPO's collapses. The results also expose a failure mode of PPO: under the two-phase shaped reward, it tends to converge to a reward-loitering local optimum rather than committing to the precision task. This behavior highlights the sensitivity of on-policy learning to reward shaping.
bullets: Addresses dual-arm space-robot coordination with target reaching, inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, synchronization, and sensing uncertainty.
Uses centralized joint-, end-effector-, and target-relative state information with a multi-objective reward for accuracy, smoothness, alignment, synchronization, and safety.
Compares PPO and SAC across five random seeds and evaluates generalization to unseen target configurations.
SAC reached the 80% success threshold in every seed and achieved a 78.6% mean success rate; PPO achieved 7.4% within the stated training budget.
Both methods degraded on unseen boundary targets, while PPO often converged to a reward-loitering local optimum.

papers.abstract: The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation. On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization. We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon. In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 degrees. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.
bullets: Earth-trained policies retain 0.64–0.75 survival on flat rigid ground at lunar gravity, but lunar-trained policies fail to stand at Earth gravity.

Gravity-randomized rough-terrain training achieves seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 on the Moon across key tests up to 20°.

papers.abstract: Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time. It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing among multiple valid recovery motions based on scene and task requirements.
Learns a recovery vocabulary linking intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback.
Uses a visual diffusion planner to predict future body-state intent and steer it with task costs.
Generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent to shape recovery execution.
Simulation shows diverse, terrain-adaptive, and steerable recoveries; real-world demonstrations are provided on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and kinematically feasible for the target robot. Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generators supply diverse, language-specified demonstrations, but they synthesize motion in human (MANO) space. The embodiment gap is therefore deferred to post-hoc retargeting, where trajectories deployed on the robot can fail to maintain contact with objects and also degrade policy learning. Our key idea is that robot reachability should constrain the interaction trajectories while they are being generated. We present EmbodyHOI, which runs a differentiable inverse-kinematics (IK) solver for a specific humanoid embodiment inside the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI trajectory generator. We feed back gradients from the embodiment-aware IK solver into the HOI sampler and jointly optimize the position of the humanoid with respect to the object. Because guidance acts only at inference, one HOI trajectory generator trained on human hand poses transfers across humanoid embodiments without retraining. On ARCTIC trajectories with two contrasting humanoids (Unitree G1 and H1-2), our proposed guidance-based method cuts the retargeted wrist error from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm while leaving text-to-HOI generation quality intact, and raises task success from 68% to 79% on 50 random G1 tasks and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite. Critically, cheaper alternatives for bridging the embodiment gap fail to beat EmbodyHOI. Post-hoc wrist refinement and compute-matched best-of-N selection both reach lower IK energy than our guidance yet train worse policies. For simulation results, see our website: https://embodyhoi.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human-space HOI generation and humanoid robot execution, which can cause contact failures and poor policy learning.
Integrates a differentiable inverse-kinematics solver into the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI generator.

papers.abstract: Generalization in multi-arm collaboration can be studied as composing familiar atomic skills in new ways across arms. However, existing evaluations offer limited insight into which training and architectural choices support this ability under different coordination requirements. We introduce \textbf{ACG-Bench}, a benchmark for \emph{Arm-wise Compositional Generalization} that provides a common testbed for studying skill recomposition in dual-arm policies. It contains 23 task--condition pairs across 8 task families, with 6 in-domain conditions and 17 unseen compositions covering reordering, synchronization, their combination, and cross-task composition. All methods receive the same per-arm atomic prompts, and success requires achieving the task goal while satisfying physical milestones and specified order or timing constraints. Using $π_{0.5}$ as a common vision-language-action backbone, we compare representative data-augmentation and architectural strategies with shared source data and a common evaluation protocol. Our architectural study examines arm-token grouping, skill-specific LoRA adapters (SkillLoRA), and arm-wise attention (AWA), highlighting the complementarity of skill-conditioned parameters and attention structure. Combining these choices yields \textbf{AE-VLA}, which achieves 21.53\% generalization success in simulation, compared with 2.94\% for Single $π_{0.5}$, 3.06\% for MA-VLA, and 5.53\% for two independently controlled $π_{0.5}$ policies. On physical SO101 robots, AE-VLA reaches 39.00\% mean success across five unseen conditions, compared with 10.00\% for the strongest baseline. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing dual-arm policies that generalize beyond fixed training routines.
bullets: Introduces ACG-Bench: 23 task–condition pairs across 8 task families, including 17 unseen compositions.
Evaluates policies using shared per-arm atomic prompts and requires both task success and physical order/timing constraints.
Studies arm-token grouping, SkillLoRA adapters, and arm-wise attention, finding their design choices complementary.
Combining these components in AE-VLA achieves 21.53% simulation success versus 2.94% for Single π₀.₅ and 39.00% mean success on physical SO101 robots versus 10.00% for the strongest baseline.
Scope: the study focuses on dual-arm compositional generalization under the benchmark’s specified conditions and protocols.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for embodied control remains constrained by the difficulty of reward specification. Although recent large language model (LLM)-based methods can synthesize reward functions from natural-language descriptions, they often fail to capture subtle behavioral properties that humans care about, such as natural gait, posture, and movement style. This limitation arises because many desired behaviors are easier to recognize visually than to encode in a reward function. We introduce Reward Optimization via Observable Trees (ROOT), a framework for discovering reward functions that align learned policies with user-specified embodied behaviors. Rather than relying solely on scalar training statistics, ROOT casts reward design as an observation-guided search over a persistent experiment tree that stores reward programs, trained policies, and rollout observations, together with behavioral insights distilled by a video-language model, to diagnose behavioral failures and guide subsequent reward refinements. We evaluate ROOT on seven tasks across four embodiments: simulated Hopper, HalfCheetah, Ant, Unitree Go2, and as well as the real-world Unitree Go2. ROOT produces behaviors that better align with user intent than those generated by existing LLM-based reward-generation methods, achieving up to 86.8% locomotion-completeness accuracy and improving Vid-LLM behavioral alignment from 3.56/5 to 4.14/5, a 16.5% improvement over baselines. Human evaluations further support these results, with ROOT preferred in 51-63% of pairwise comparisons.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of encoding visually recognizable behaviors—such as natural gait, posture, and movement style—into scalar rewards.
Searches over a persistent experiment tree containing reward programs, trained policies, rollout observations, and video-language-model behavioral diagnoses.
Evaluated across seven tasks and four embodiments, including simulated and real-world Unitree Go2 robots.
Achieves up to 86.8% locomotion-completeness accuracy and raises Vid-LLM alignment from 3.56/5 to 4.14/5 over baselines.
Human evaluators preferred ROOT in 51–63% of pairwise comparisons.
