papers.abstract: Adapting a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to a new robot, environment, or task requires demonstrations that are collected locally and often discarded. Federated learning is a promising approach to exploiting such distributed demonstrations by learning a shared policy. However, whether it can adapt large pretrained VLAs remains an open question, and a lack of reproducible benchmarks for pretrained VLAs and reusable training frameworks makes existing results difficult to compare. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study of federated fine-tuning of three modern pretrained VLA policies on the 40 simulated tasks of the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, and on six real-world tasks in two real-robot experiments, with demonstrations collected across two and three sites, respectively. Our study analyzes the key choices in this setting, spanning multiple federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and evaluation under distribution shift. Based on the study, we derive a series of lessons, including the dominance of the federated scope over the choice of aggregation algorithm and the difficulty of matching centralized fine-tuning on physical robots, where cross-site heterogeneity is stronger than simulation captures. We also highlight opportunities for federated VLA learning, such as the ability to match centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data, to remain at least as robust as centralized fine-tuning under distribution shift, and to personalize, with each client federating part of the policy and keeping the rest local, which helps where the policy's pretraining is weak but leaves no usable global model. We open-source \decentvla{}, the model- and runtime-agnostic testbed behind the study, to facilitate future research and fair comparisons in federated VLA learning.
bullets: Evaluates three pretrained VLA policies on 40 simulated LIBERO tasks and six real-world tasks across multiple sites.
Studies federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and robustness under distribution shift.
Finds that the federated parameter scope matters more than the aggregation algorithm.
Federated learning can match centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data and remain comparably robust to distribution shift, but matching centralized performance on physical robots is difficult.
Personalized federation can help when pretraining is weak, though it does not produce a usable global model.

papers.title: An Empirical Study and Open Testbed for Federated Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.abstract: Fine-grained object (FO) manipulation requires robots to distinguish a specified FO from visually similar objects and execute actions reliably despite scene distractors. However, scene-level visual conditioning lacks explicit object selection, while category-level guidance cannot reliably distinguish FOs within the same category. We present a SAM3-guided visuomotor policy framework that addresses these challenges through persistent object memory and focused visual conditioning. First, we introduce FO Memory-driven SAM3 (FOM-SAM3), which learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view registration images, while keeping SAM3 fully frozen. Through one-vs-rest learning, these tokens encode persistent memories for localizing target FOs and rejecting similar alternatives, which can be stored in a memory bank for reuse. Second, we propose Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE), which combines in-FO appearance features with explicit bounding boxes to condition action policies, including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT). The effectiveness of the proposed FOM-SAM3 is validated on the FO-30 dataset comprising 30 physical objects across four coarse categories. Across three real-robot FO manipulation tasks, our FOM-SAM3-guided policies demonstrated robustness against distractors, discriminative ability of similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.
bullets: Targets fine-grained manipulation where scene-level or category-level guidance cannot reliably select a particular object.
FOM-SAM3 learns reusable target-object memory tokens from limited multi-view images while keeping SAM3 frozen.
FSAE combines target appearance features with bounding-box information to condition Diffusion Policy and ACT controllers.
Validated on 30 physical objects across four categories and three real-robot manipulation tasks.
The framework showed distractor robustness, discrimination among similar objects, and extension to new objects.

papers.abstract: Fast-WAM shows that video-action co-training improves control without generating future video at inference, making the representation from a single video diffusion Transformer forward central to action generation. However, future-observation prediction does not explicitly prioritize the future dynamics and visual structure needed for control. We present MT-WAM, which retains the original training objectives and adds complementary supervision for future two-dimensional point trajectories and visual features. A lightweight dual-stream branch copied from the video backbone's final blocks provides target-specific processing, while a structured attention mask prevents cross-stream attention. Motion-stream tokens supply additional dynamics conditions to the action expert. Future visual-feature prediction provides supervision in a feature space that captures object and spatial structure. This supervision trains the video backbone to provide more informative visual context for action generation under changing visual conditions, without adding visual-feature-stream tokens to action conditioning. At inference, MT-WAM uses video and motion caches computed once per replan and skips future-video prediction. Without additional embodied policy pretraining, MT-WAM achieves 98.2% success on LIBERO and 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding Fast-WAM by 23.8 percentage points on the latter. On RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Rand, Random success increases from 6.30% to 19.40%; across four real-world tasks, average success increases from 67.0% to 77.8%.
bullets: Targets a limitation of future-observation prediction: it does not explicitly emphasize control-relevant dynamics and visual structure.
Adds supervision for future 2D point trajectories and visual features while retaining Fast-WAM’s original objectives.
Uses a lightweight dual-stream branch with masked cross-stream attention; motion tokens condition the action expert, while visual-feature tokens are excluded from action conditioning.
Inference remains efficient: video and motion caches are computed once per replan, and future-video prediction is skipped.
Reports gains across benchmarks, including 98.2% success on LIBERO, 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, and improved real-world average success from 67.0% to 77.8%.

papers.abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms.
authors: Xi Chen, Fengqi Hu, Zeyu Shen, Jiaying Xu, Shangding Gu, Pan Xu, Anqi Liu, Laixi Shi
bullets: Addresses limited reusability and unclear empirical boundaries in robust RL.
Integrates 17 representative online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under one interface.
Provides evaluations across real-world shifts, humanoid tasks, and vision-language-action tasks.

Offers an open-source, reproducible, and extensible platform for research and application.

papers.abstract: Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in-hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real-world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with in-hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in-the-wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in-the-wild data.
authors: Amber Xie, Jiawei Fu, Xiaofeng Guo, Carmelo Sferrazza, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi

For bimanual scanning and drawer stowing, the operator is occasionally visible, but we do not post-process the data to remove the operator.

Reusing the same module preserves hand embodiment and camera-to-hand extrinsics. (b) Ergonomic Redesign: The final hardware interface places the operator’s grasp near the assembly’s center of mass and adds a support strap, shortening the moment arm and reducing wrist torque. (c) Skill Control Mapping: Quest 2 inputs start and stop demonstration episodes, select hand or screw mode, and modulate thumb, grasp, and screwing skills. papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.

papers.abstract: In medical robotics, data-driven soft-tissue shape control requires deforming tissue toward desired morphologies through sequential physical interactions. This challenge is particularly important in microscale manipulation, where localized deformation is difficult to observe, represent, and control, while physics-based models can be computationally expensive and difficult to adapt to realistic environments. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides high-resolution volumetric perception of tissue deformation, but target-conditioned control requires effective representations of both observed and desired tissue states. In this work, we introduce an OCT-guided data-driven framework for tissue shape control, learned from user-guided demonstrations and executed with closed-loop OCT feedback. We study full-volume, tissue-masked sparse-volume, and voxelized point-cloud representations, with or without residual conditioning, using deterministic (Explicit) and generative diffusion (Diffusion) policies. Across 12 configurations and 576 phantom rollouts on 3-DoF depth and 6-DoF directional tasks, OCT-derived 3D representations support both Explicit and Diffusion policies, with performance depending on representation and residual conditioning. Residual conditioning reduces directional Shape RMSE from 0.748 to 0.555 mm for full-volume Diffusion, while voxelized point-cloud Explicit with residuals achieves 0.534 mm for depth and 0.443 mm for directional control, with comparable accuracy at intermediate unseen targets and consistent performance across deployments. We further evaluate the framework in 60 ex vivo porcine rollouts, extending to biological tissue with final geometric errors comparable to human demonstrations. These results establish volumetric OCT as current and goal representations for learned closed-loop tissue shape control across deterministic and generative action models.
authors: Chaoyu Zhang, Guangshen Ma, Mark Draelos

An additional 60 ex vivo porcine rollouts achieved final geometric errors comparable to human demonstrations, supporting transfer beyond phantoms.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $\pi$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $\pi$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.

On LIBERO-Long, reduces failure rates by 19–48% and improves success by up to 7.4 percentage points; gains are smaller on easier suites, while all tested MetaWorld configurations improve.

Otherwise, the policy’s actions are executed normally. The resulting state is observed by the unchanged VLA and the control loop continues. Achieved motion is added to the buffer during normal policy execution; motion executed during backtracking is not. The diagram abstracts over differences in action generation between the evaluated VLAs.

papers.abstract: HoloBoxing presents a simple recipe for learning humanoid boxing by building on a pretrained whole-body controller. The recipe separates reusable motor skills from task decisions: a compact planner requests future body-point targets, while the frozen controller handles joint-level execution. A learned decoder maps 32-dimensional actions to structured target windows, and measured-state imitation initializes the planner before reinforcement learning. Task learning then refines interaction behavior while reusing the decoder and controller, avoiding the need to relearn whole-body control. This combination keeps task optimization focused on a compact upper policy and supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration. Starting from that available controller, the recipe accounts for about seven minutes of additional training, including reused representation fitting and a single-GPU task run. This excludes controller pretraining, data preparation, evaluation, and search. Simulated boxing experiments and component controls evaluate the resulting behavior and the roles of imitation initialization and the target representation.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.
authors: Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Obaidullah Zaland, Monowar Bhuyan
bullets: Human corrections vary in modality, urgency, behavioral scope, and privacy sensitivity across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments.
Naively shared updates may improve mean performance while suppressing rare safety interventions or causing unsafe behavior on other robots.
Corrections should retain their context and uncertainty when determining what to share.
Each candidate update should be evaluated in the receiving robot’s closed loop before deployment.
The paper proposes counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda; it reports no experimental results.

papers.abstract: Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) has provable robustness guarantees that should ease the transfer of policies from simulation to robots, known as sim-to-real. Yet, weakly regularised algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) remain the de facto choice in sim-to-real pipelines, while the practical benefits of regularisation for transfer remain poorly characterised. In this work, we study the sim-to-real performance of commonly used RL algorithms, with the aim of characterising the effects of regularisation on robotic performance. To that end, we derive Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a novel regularised RL algorithm based on the soft mellowmax value function, which carries strong robustness guarantees. On MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks, SMM-AC is competitive with baselines like Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). On real robots, SMM-AC achieves higher return, while exhibiting greater robustness to perturbations in observations, the environment, and dynamics than baselines. Together, these results demonstrate that regularised RL improves real-world policy deployment through better robustness to the sim-to-real gap, and changing real-world conditions.
authors: Danilo Vucetic, Mohamad H. Danesh, Florence Clerc, Hsiu-Chin Lin, Jonathan Tremblay
bullets: Sim-to-real transfer is difficult because simulation and deployment conditions differ.
The study characterises how regularisation affects robotic policy transfer.
It introduces Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a regularised RL algorithm with robustness guarantees.
SMM-AC is competitive with SAC on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks.
On real robots, it achieves higher return and greater robustness to observation, environment, and dynamics perturbations.

papers.abstract: Quantitative and dense task progress feedback is essential for robotic manipulation across data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Existing progress annotations often rely on sparse keyframe markings derived from subjective manual judgments, limiting their scalability and cross-task consistency, particularly in long-horizon manipulation. To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification, a unified progress specification that decomposes long-horizon trajectories into object-level subtasks via a vision-language model (VLM) and assigns weighted action credits to capture fine-grained execution dynamics. Using VLM auto-labeling and human calibration, we construct an 800+ hour training video dataset and LOOM, a long-horizon progress benchmark containing 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames. To model these dense progress dynamics, we introduce NimCritic, a predictive progress critic trained via Joint Video-Progress Learning. We further incorporate Historical Progress Perturbation to mitigate sequential drift, and design a contrastive Video-Progress Alignment objective that bridges asymmetric expert streams by mutually grounding intermediate visual dynamics and denoised progress trajectories. NimCritic matches or outperforms state-of-the-art process reward models (PRMs) on the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB) and LOOM, surpassing GVL (GPT-6-Sol) on VPB by about 65% in terminal success accuracy (TSA). On the large-scale RoboArena policy evaluation benchmark, it also retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with about 97% overall recall. These results establish action-aware quantification as a scalable foundation for dense progress feedback in robotic manipulation.
authors: Tianchi Xu, Yalin Zheng, Yangxin Zhu, Ruonan Ren, Zheng Fu, Yunlong Wang, Yuanxin Zhong

NimCritic uses Joint Video-Progress Learning, Historical Progress Perturbation, and contrastive Video-Progress Alignment to predict dense progress.
Matches or exceeds leading process reward models, achieves about 65% higher terminal success accuracy than GVL on VPB, and about 97% recall on RoboArena rollout retrieval.

papers.abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.
authors: Yves Delley, John Coller, Zachary Cutts, Alexander Daryin, Mathias Bellaiche, Jun W. Kim, Oscar Donosa, Srinidhi B. Seshadri, Tanner Clary, Sandy Klemm, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias, Pooja Rao, Petar Sirkovic, Annalisa Pawlosky
bullets: Addresses the gap between high-level AI-generated protocols and variable, error-prone physical laboratory execution.
Provides queryable lab introspection, time-compressed protocol simulation, persistent experiment traces, and safe-execution support.
Uses aqueous dye and deionized-water case studies to validate its optical and fluidic foundations.
Enables early protocol-error detection, mid-run recovery, and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures.
Records structured multimodal data for analysis, knowledge mining, and future agent training; demonstrated scope is foundational rather than broad biological validation.

papers.title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
papers.tldr: VERID is a semantic digital twin that helps AI agents safely design, simulate, monitor, recover, and learn from automated wet-lab experiments.

papers.abstract: Inspired by infants' ability to learn novel tasks by imitating others, in this work we evaluate to what extent Conditional Neural Processes can autonomously learn representations of actions that are informative about their underlying goal. We show that the addition of an attention mechanism in the hidden space fosters the emergence of robust goal representations early on in the observation of an action sequence, making it a promising model for a robotic self-supervised general learner.

Suggests potential for self-supervised, general-purpose learning in robots.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. These skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in hand-designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers an alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that combines anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes the initial probe pose as the reference frame for scanning. A flow-based policy then generates scanning motions from anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact forces, while a termination head predicts task completion. This avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 unseen participants, task success reaches 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned pi_0 model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with lower time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablations support the complementary roles of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large-scale human motion data, motion retargeting, and motion imitation have enabled increasingly capable whole-body control for individual humanoids. Cooperative carrying is more challenging because successful coordination requires not only plausible individual motions, but also consistent cross-agent and agent-object relations, including shared grasp, relative configuration, and whole-body support. We introduce CoCarry, a cooperative-carrying dataset containing 220 synchronized two-person sequences across 21 task schemes, five shared-object geometries, four terrain types, and approximately 61 minutes of motion. We further propose Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting, which starts from nominal individual motions and jointly refines both humanoids around the same prescribed object trajectory. Cooperation-aware object-local hand anchors preserve compatible four-hand grasp relations, while complementary upper object-interaction and lower support structures retain object-relative geometry and coordinated support. Across all 220 CoCarry sequences retargeted to two A3 humanoids, our method achieves 0.9995 contact preservation, reduces penetration duration by 67.0% and 71.0% relative to GMR and OmniRetarget, respectively, and maintains a 100% retargeting success rate. On CORE4D with Unitree G1 humanoids, it achieves 0.9906 contact preservation with zero measured sliding. We further validate the generated references through physics simulation and multiple real-world cooperative carrying experiments on two physical A3 humanoids, demonstrating their usability for downstream dual-humanoid control.
authors: Ziyu Lin, Shihang Du, Tianhang Wang, Xiaodong Liu, Runze Zhang, Zongyou Yu, Haodong Zhang, Alois Knoll, Guang Chen
bullets: Introduces the CoCarry dataset: 220 synchronized two-person sequences spanning 21 task schemes, five object geometries, and four terrain types.
Proposes Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting, which jointly refines both humanoids around a prescribed shared-object trajectory.
Uses object-local hand anchors plus coordinated upper-body interaction and lower-body support structures to maintain cooperation.
Achieves high contact preservation, reduced penetration, and 100% retargeting success on CoCarry; also shows zero measured sliding on CORE4D.

papers.abstract: Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error. While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability. To address these challenges, we propose $R^2E$, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization. $R^2E$ employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures. A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation. To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, $R^2E$ incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
authors: Shouhao Chang, Xuan Liu, Hongye Zhu, Xinning Chen, Shigeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the costly manual trial-and-error required to design effective RL reward functions.
Uses an Explorer for novelty, a Guardian for stable refinement, and an Evolver for crossover and mutation.
Dynamically shifts from broad exploration to focused exploitation during optimization.
Maintains a Global Elite Pool to preserve strong rewards and support collaboration across roles.
Experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of R2E. The framework operates in three main stages: (Stage 1 Initial Iteration): Reward candidates are generated through a broad exploration phase based on the environment code and task descriptions, and then trained on IsaacGym or Bi-DexHands tasks to initialize the Global Elite Pool with the Top 5 functions. (Stage 2 Dynamic Role-driven Iterations): In each iteration, a total of N = 16 candidates are generated through dynamic scheduling by the Explorer, Guardian, and Evolver roles. After RL training and evaluation, the pool is dynamically updated by replacing the worst-performing reward. (Stage 3 End of Iterations): After the search concludes, the Top 1 reward is selected and re-evaluated across five random seeds to produce the final output. (Global Elite Pool): A fixed-capacity memory (K = 5) that stores and ranks the best-performing reward functions across iterations.

If iteration T + 1 regresses, the LLM references only T + 1 for T + 2, discarding high-performing rewards from T . (Our Method) populates a Global Elite Pool via initial exploration. Specialized roles query historical elites from the pool to iteratively evolve diverse reward candidates.

papers.abstract: A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.
authors: Zongyao Zhao, Cheng-Jie Zhao, Ruihang Jiang, Bing Zheng, Zhaolin Wang, Yuanwei Liu
bullets: GRPO assigns one trajectory-level advantage to every action, so recovery attempts in failed rollouts may be penalized with preceding errors.
The method uses success-probability and policy-score martingales to characterize stopping points where removing later gradients has zero conditional expected effect.
A LoRA-fine-tuned VLM identifies the last visible error without observed recovery in complete rollout videos and retains feedback only through that interval.
For retrospective boundaries, the work analyzes changes in gradient expectation and variance relative to ideal stopping conditions.
Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 report higher success rates than full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of execution-grounded memory. The memory has two parts. The system keeps the record: one log line per executed action with the measured gripper state, and every note the model has written. The model chooses what to see: after an action only the recorded frames that changed near the watched points are returned, and a demonstration is skimmed before the model inspects the ranges it asks for. papers.abstract: Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged. Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics-aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action. This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task-irrelevant scene content. We introduce DynaSlots, an action-free, label-free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per-slot level rather than the scene level. A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model, paired with a self-supervised interaction head, predicts each slot's future state while learning pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. Experiments on Meta-World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65-B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene-level baselines. It achieves superior success rates in simulation and exhibits strong robustness to scene clutter and unseen objects in real-world manipulation. Code is available at \href{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}.
authors: Meng Li, Lijiang Chen, Qi Zhao, Jun Jiang, Longhao Zou, Shuchang Lyu, Guangliang Cheng
bullets: Addresses scene-level dynamics modeling, which conflates multiple moving parts and incorporates task-irrelevant content.
Decomposes point-cloud frames into a small set of temporally consistent slots without actions or labels.
Learns per-slot latent actions through inverse dynamics and predicts future slot states with diffusion-based forward dynamics.
Uses a self-supervised interaction head to capture pairwise proximity-and-motion relationships.
Outperforms scene-level baselines in Meta-World and Adroit, with robust performance amid clutter and unseen objects on a RealMan RM65-B robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. DynaSlots framework. (a) Three point-cloud frames are encoded by a shared Point Transformer and propagated by a temporal slot binder into K=6 aligned soft slots. The IDM extracts per-slot latent actions from feature differences, and the cross-slot encoder conditions a diffusion FDM on current slot features, centroids, and actions. An EMA target branch supplies noised future slot features, while an auxiliary interaction head predicts pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. The displayed losses are noise prediction, slot VICReg, relation BCE, and assignment entropy. (b) Previous slots query current point tokens through competitive assignment, weighted aggregation, and residual refinement, repeated three times per frame. (c) Two observed point clouds and the robot state produce slot condition tokens for the diffusion policy, which predicts the action sequence using cross-attention and FiLM.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation requires a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy to execute diverse skills across scenes and instructions. However, current multi-skill VLA policies often leave two aspects of an instruction insufficiently modeled: which primitive skill to execute and where/how to contact and move objects. We propose MAST-VLA (Multi-skill Adaptation with Skill-conditioned experts and Trajectory-affordance priors), a dual-conditioning framework for robot manipulation. MAST-VLA introduces skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts (LoRA-MoE) adapters in the LLM backbone, where skill-query tokens and routing biases guide low-rank expert specialization, and converts a predicted affordance heatmap into a patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial prior for the action head. On the CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D long-horizon multi-skill cross-scene generalization setting, MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an Avg. Len of 4.65 over five-subtask evaluation sequences. Real-robot multi-skill sequence experiments further validate its deployability under real perception and control noise.
authors: Jiachi Yang, Zhiyi Xu, Hongquan Zhang, Xin Tan, Zhizhong Zhang, Jingyu Gong, Yuan Xie
bullets: Addresses insufficient modeling of primitive skill choice and object contact/movement in vision-language-action policies.
Uses skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts adapters with skill-query tokens and routing biases in the language-model backbone.
Converts affordance heatmaps into patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial priors for the action head.
Achieves an Avg. Len of 4.65 on CALVIN ABC→D long-horizon cross-scene evaluation and is validated in real-robot sequence experiments.
Scope includes robustness to real perception and control noise; broader limitations are not specified in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Learned humanoid controllers are usually trained in one simulator and then checked in a second one before they go near hardware. We ask what that check says about command delay. We train motion-tracking policies for a 24-joint humanoid on five motions taken from monocular video and test them in an independent CPU MuJoCo harness, which we first verify against the training model. Every policy completes its motion in at least 26 of 30 episodes under the training randomization. With 40 ms of constant command delay, however, survival drops to 15% on average (0% - 45%), and the delay margin is only 20 - 30 ms. Randomizing the delay during training (0 - 50 ms) lifts survival at 40 ms to 95% on average (75% - 100%) and moves the margin to 50 - 70 ms. A control arm trained for the same number of extra iterations without delay does not improve, so the gain comes from the randomization itself. This holds for all five motions with three training seeds each, and a policy trained in PhysX behaves the same way. The price is slightly looser tracking (0.02 - 0.06 rad on four motions) and, for the most dynamic motion, less robustness to other perturbations. We also show that the first sim-to-sim gap we saw came from the harness, a missing floor and a wrong timestep, and not from the physics engines. The 0 - 20 ms delay ranges common in locomotion training lie inside the margin an unrandomized tracker already has. The benefit comes from randomizing beyond it, so the range should be set from the robot's measured latency, and delay margin belongs next to other sim-to-sim metrics.
bullets: Without delay randomization, 40 ms of constant command delay reduced average survival to 15%, with a 20–30 ms delay margin.
Randomizing delays from 0–50 ms raised 40 ms-delay survival to 95% on average and extended the margin to 50–70 ms.
The improvement was consistent across five video-derived motions, three seeds, and a policy trained in a different simulator.
Extra training alone did not produce the gain, indicating that delay randomization was responsible.
The approach slightly worsened tracking and reduced robustness to some other perturbations in the most dynamic motion; simulator discrepancies were traced to harness errors.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are typically pretrained on broad, diverse datasets and subsequently fine-tuned on a comparatively small dataset tailored to a specific target robot. Such adaptation recipe is now widely established, achieving its most mature results on fixed-base arms due to their static base dynamics and consistent reference frame. Mounting the same arm on a quadruped extends the workspace to the entire floor, but fundamentally changes the embodiment: rather than controlling the arm in isolation, the policy must jointly coordinate base navigation, body posture, and end-effector motion. In this work, we study the practical demands of this embodiment change across data collection, model adaptation, and inference design to achieve closed-loop loco-manipulation on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm. We report the choices that made this real-robot deployment feasible, namely model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions, together with a study tailored to a pick-and-place task, separating data coverage from model capacity. We show that expanding demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%, and incorporating secondary skills (such as pushing rather than grasping) introduces new behavioral modes without degrading baseline performance. Finally, closed-loop real-world experiments show how dataset composition shapes success and failure, validating the pipeline for more complex loco-manipulation.

bullets: Studies the embodiment shift from fixed-base manipulation to coordinated navigation, posture, and end-effector control on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm.
Examines practical deployment choices across data collection, model adaptation, and inference, including model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions.
Finds that broader demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%.
Shows that adding secondary behaviors such as pushing introduces new modes without degrading baseline grasping performance.
Validates the pipeline in closed-loop real-world pick-and-place experiments and analyzes how dataset composition affects success and failure.

papers.abstract: Recent robot manipulation policies commonly predict continuous action chunks directly from observations, without explicitly modeling reusable structure in the action space. However, manipulation demonstrations often contain recurring short-horizon motion patterns that are shared across tasks. We introduce \textsc{RoboCode}, which learns these patterns through a shared soft-gated primitive action interface. Rather than assigning each action chunk to a single discrete code, \textsc{RoboCode} represents it as a soft composition of multiple learned primitives, providing a flexible intermediate representation of short-horizon actions. The primitive interface is learned from action chunks pooled across multiple tasks and then frozen while task-specific state encoders are trained to map current state inputs into the shared latent space. Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks address three questions. First, the learned primitive interface reconstructs action chunks with an average reconstruction MSE of 0.0187. Second, analysis of code activations reveals structured code reuse across tasks. Third, \textsc{RoboCode} achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success rate on all evaluated tasks, with an average success rate of 75.6%, compared with 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for the larger Diffusion Policy baseline. These results suggest that soft-gated primitive codebooks provide an effective and interpretable intermediate action representation for robot manipulation.
authors: Xianyue Peng, Devi Amarsaikhan, Iman Soltani
bullets: Addresses the lack of reusable action structure in policies that directly predict continuous action chunks.
Learns a shared soft-gated primitive interface, representing each action chunk as a composition of multiple primitives rather than one discrete code.
The primitive interface is learned from action chunks across tasks and frozen while task-specific encoders map states into the shared latent space.
On five ManiSkill tasks, it reconstructs action chunks with 0.0187 average MSE and reveals structured cross-task code reuse.
Achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success on every task, averaging 75.6% success versus 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for Diffusion Policy.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. In this work, we show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations of OpenVLA activations contain outcome-predictive information and can be used to predict task failure before the robot reaches an unrecoverable state. Moreover, to provide insights into what common behaviors may contribute to these outcomes, we identify individual SAE features whose strong activations are associated with specific stages of success or failure, and uncover recurring behavioral patterns by localizing temporal intervals where these features exhibit significant activation changes. We further develop a VLM-based interpretation pipeline to generate behavioral descriptions of these patterns and validate their correspondence to feature activations on held-out intervals.
authors: Christian A. Rogers, Qian Lin, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of diagnosing why vision-language-action robot policies succeed or fail.
Uses sparse autoencoder representations of OpenVLA activations to identify outcome-predictive information.
Links individual SAE features to specific stages and recurring behavioral patterns in task outcomes.
Localizes temporal intervals with significant feature-activation changes to identify relevant behaviors.
Uses a VLM-based pipeline to describe these patterns and validates the descriptions on held-out intervals.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains a popular on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm owing to its stability and ease of implementation. Its clipping threshold, however, is fixed, so every training sample receives the same trust-region width regardless of how reliable the corresponding policy update is. This work examines adaptive-clipping variants of PPO in which the constant clipping parameter is replaced by sample-dependent thresholds computed from policy and return statistics. The central method, Dual-Adaptive Z-Score PPO (PPO-DAZ3), sets the clipping interval for each sample from two signals: action confidence, given by the probability of the selected action under the current policy, and update confidence, given by the normalized advantage magnitude. The rest of the standard PPO training pipeline is left unchanged. Evaluation on three classic control benchmarks (LunarLander-v3, CartPole-v1, and Acrobot-v1) indicates that adaptive clipping improves learning in some settings but not all. PPO-DAZ3 performs best on LunarLander-v3, the smooth advantage-based variant PPO-AZ3S leads on Acrobot-v1, and standard PPO stays competitive on CartPole-v1, suggesting that adaptive clipping is most beneficial on harder control tasks.
bullets: Standard PPO uses the same trust-region width for every sample, regardless of update reliability.
PPO-DAZ3 adapts each clipping interval using selected-action probability and normalized advantage magnitude.
The standard PPO training pipeline remains otherwise unchanged.
Across LunarLander-v3, CartPole-v1, and Acrobot-v1, adaptive clipping helps in some environments but not all.
PPO-DAZ3 performs best on LunarLander-v3, PPO-AZ3S on Acrobot-v1, while standard PPO remains competitive on CartPole-v1.

papers.abstract: Robot-assisted dressing is particularly challenging due to narrow openings and articulated body parts. Even small errors in the relative pose between the body part and garment opening can cause snagging, missed insertion, or incomplete dressing. To address these challenges, we formulate dressing as a geometry-aware insertion problem that represents task-relevant spatial relationships between the body part and object opening, rather than relying on the full deformable-object state. Based on this formulation, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework combining a staged curriculum, which progressively guides the policy from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement, with a finger-wise insertion soft gate that provides continuous feedback on individual finger insertion progress and helps suppress premature insertion. We evaluate the framework on rigid and deformable bracelet dressing tasks through component ablations, systematic variations in the initial hand pose, and closed-loop execution of the learned policies on a real robotic system. On the post-training deformable evaluation, the full method reaches 84.7 +- 1.2% success. The insertion gate accounts for the largest gain, and adding the curriculum on top of that gate reaches the top score. On a mannequin hand the same full policy succeeds on 15/20 real-robot trials.
authors: Takuma Tsukakoshi, Elle Miller, Tamon Miyake, Namiko Saito, Yushi Wang, Shigeki Sugano, Tetsuya Ogata, Sethu Vijayakumar
bullets: Models dressing through spatial relationships between the body part and garment opening instead of the full deformable-object state.
Uses a staged curriculum from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement.
Introduces a finger-wise soft insertion gate that gives continuous progress feedback and reduces premature insertion.
Evaluated on rigid and deformable bracelet tasks with ablations, varied initial poses, and real-robot closed-loop trials.
Achieves 84.7 ± 1.2% success on post-training deformable evaluation and 15/20 successes on a mannequin hand.

papers.abstract: Traversability analysis in off-road settings remains a fundamental challenge for mobile robots. Key difficulties include constructing an accurate and expressive local map from multimodal sensor data, and using the map to design traversability rules that yield desirable navigation behavior. Importantly, this system must be resilient to the limited sensing regime brought about by complex environments and high speeds. In this paper, we present TravSUITE, a traversability system suitable for high-speed navigation in off-road environments. TravSUITE consists of two major components: 1) an efficient voxel mapper that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) to build a rich geometric-semantic local map from streams of on-board sensor data, and 2) a unified neural network that jointly predicts traversability-relevant quantities in bird's eye view (BEV), including geometry, semantics, speed and cost. Our training strategy is entirely annotation-free and self-supervised, leveraging tasks such as map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn both map representations and traversability. We perform a thorough ablation study and comparison to state-of-the-art approaches, and the results indicate that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting each contribute significantly to planning quality, and their combination is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in off-road path planning. We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method's uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.
authors: Samuel Triest, Amirreza Shaban, David D. Fan, Wenshan Wang, Sebastian Scherer
bullets: Addresses robust traversability estimation under limited sensing, complex terrain, and high-speed motion.
Builds a geometric-semantic voxel map from onboard multimodal sensors using visual foundation models.
Jointly predicts BEV geometry, semantics, speed, and cost with annotation-free self-supervised learning, including map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning.
Ablations show that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting improve planning quality, with their combination needed for state-of-the-art off-road planning.
Real-world experiments report 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal when combining inpainting with uncertainty-based risk estimation.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. An overview of our network architecture. papers.abstract: Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function \(Q^*\) from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although \(Q^*\) is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating \(Q^*\) requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning. We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate \(Q^*\). We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that $Q^*$ inherits H\"older regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any H\"older index $\beta$, the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\big(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\big),$ where $d$ is the total dimension of the state and action spaces. In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
authors: Hao Cheng, Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Chen Zhong
bullets: Addresses offline soft Q-learning when reward distributions and dynamics are unknown.
Uses conditional diffusion models based on probability-flow ODEs to estimate reward and transition distributions.
Learns Q* with deep neural networks through a data-driven soft Bellman operator.
Provides nonasymptotic total-variation and excess Bellman-residual guarantees, without requiring Bellman completeness.
Experiments support the theory and show the method is effective; the stated rate depends on Hölder regularity and state-action dimension.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang, Ziheng He, Xiangnan Wu, Yingda Li, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: Problem: Solver depth and open-loop execution horizon are usually tuned independently, creating a responsiveness–stability trade-off.
Method: Jointly adjust numerical sampling depth and execution horizon, using coarse integration as an implicit regularizer during extended open-loop execution.
Key insight: Numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, reducing compounding drift.
Results: The approach consistently improves task success and substantially lowers inference latency across simulated and real-world manipulation settings and multiple VLA backbones.
Scope: Coarse integration can hurt precision during rapid replanning, so its benefit depends on the execution horizon.

papers.abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Behavior cloning is limited by costly, narrow demonstration data and insufficient coverage of successful states.
A privileged, latent-conditioned RL generator uses a parallel reverse curriculum and success-gated diversity objective to discover multiple solution modes.
Generated behaviors are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for imitation learning.
Across four manipulation tasks, downstream success rises from 40% to 62% in simulation and from 39% to 78% on a real robot.
The approach is evaluated with a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection.

papers.abstract: Distilling interactive LLM agents requires choosing between teacher-generated demonstrations and student-generated experience, corresponding broadly to off-policy and on-policy distillation. While both have proven effective, we argue that this distinction is inherently hierarchical: the policy that induces an interaction history need not be the same as the policy that generates the token prefix of the current action. We introduce a hierarchical agent distillation framework that formalizes these two levels of on-policiness and enables explicit control over their pairing, mixture proportions, and training schedule. We study this problem through self-distillation, where a frozen teacher has access to task guidance unavailable to the student, and conduct a three-stage controlled study across three models and four interactive environments. We find that student-induced histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone training signal, whereas following the student at both levels generally performs worst. Nevertheless, fully on-policy data becomes beneficial when incorporated into a mixture with other configurations. Moreover, mixtures with identical teacher/student proportions at each level can yield substantially different performance, showing that how the two levels are paired matters beyond the overall amount of on-policy data. Finally, front-loading fully teacher-generated contexts and delaying fully on-policy contexts improves over a static mixture. These findings provide practical principles for deciding where, how much, and when agent distillation should follow the student.
authors: Ya Gao, Zhengtao Zou, Pekka Marttinen
bullets: The study reframes on-policy versus off-policy distillation as two hierarchical choices: history generation and action-prefix generation.
Student-generated histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone signal.
Following the student at both levels usually performs worst, but fully on-policy data helps when mixed with other configurations.
Mixtures with the same teacher/student proportions can perform differently depending on how the two levels are paired.
A schedule that starts with fully teacher-generated contexts and gradually introduces fully on-policy contexts outperforms a static mixture in the studied settings.

papers.abstract: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site selection and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.
authors: Ray Verma, Eliseo Ferrante, Anthony Tzes
bullets: Addresses swarm assembly without requiring a predefined list of attachment sites during deployment.
Combines neural cellular automata with site selection and collision-aware control.
Introduces decentralized discovery by sharing local NCA states among robots already in the formation.
Uses sparse-retention fine-tuning and false-positive loss to adapt NCA growth to gradual physical assembly.
Simulations scale to several hundred robots, while Crazyflie experiments validate the integrated pipeline using externally tracked, robot-relative observations.

papers.abstract: Data-driven robots must learn to avoid collisions with as few demonstrations as possible to avoid collecting large datasets of destructive collision examples. We explore whole-body proximity sensors as inductive biases for learning reflexive collision-dodging behavior and find that lossy sensors with low resolution were stronger biases than high-resolution coverage. We also found that, perhaps unintuitively, anticipating when and where contact happens on the body of a robot reduced its learning sample efficiency. We investigated eight candidate representations in a reinforcement learning environment, which included latent compression, future contact anticipation, lossy corruption, and privileged state estimation. The candidate representations were tested by training over 200 humanoid robots to play a simplified version of dodgeball end-to-end under an intentionally constrained sample and compute budget.
authors: Carson Kohlbrenner, Niraj Pudasaini, William Xie, Naren Sivagnanadasan, Nikolaus Correll, Alessandro Roncone
bullets: Whole-body proximity sensors provide useful inductive biases for reflexive collision avoidance.
Lossy, low-resolution sensing outperformed high-resolution coverage as a learning bias.
Anticipating future contact location and timing unexpectedly reduced sample efficiency.
Eight sensor representations were evaluated in reinforcement-learning simulations with over 200 humanoid robots.
The study focuses on end-to-end dodgeball behavior under intentionally constrained resources.

papers.abstract: Swarms of small robots are an attractive way to survey lunar caves and lava tubes. Missions such as NASA's CADRE will fly cooperating rovers for distributed mapping, but only in daylight. The 354 h lunar night drops the surface towards 95 K, and the radioisotope heaters that let single rovers survive it cannot be supplied at swarm scale. In this study we investigate whether a swarm can instead use its own members as thermal shielding. We train one policy, shared by all twenty robots, by reinforcement learning with an evolution-strategies estimator. The policy receives a single reward, once, at the end of the night: the mean temperature of the five coldest robots. Nothing in that reward refers to position, spacing, exposure or motion. Two behaviors nonetheless emerge. The swarm aggregates, and robots circulate between the sheltered core and the exposed rim, the same pair of behaviors with which emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter. We measure the survival threshold, the smallest stored energy per robot at which every robot is still alive at sunrise. Across ten runs it is 155.6 +/- 1.3 pcm-h, where one pcm-h is 7.2 kJ of stored heat. That is 37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound, and at a budget where the motionless huddle loses six robots, every robot survives. The behavior needs no shared spatial reference and no robot-robot contact, and transfers from twenty robots to forty without retraining.
authors: Anais Jeger, Harry Holt, Lennart Puck
bullets: Motivation: Swarm-scale radioisotope heating is impractical for surviving the lunar night, which can cool the surface to 95 K.
Method: Train one policy for 20 robots using evolution-strategy reinforcement learning and a single end-of-night reward based on the five coldest robots’ mean temperature.
Emergent behavior: Robots aggregate into a sheltered core and circulate between the core and exposed rim, despite no explicit spacing, position, exposure, or motion objectives.
Result: The swarm’s survival threshold is 155.6 ± 1.3 pcm-h—37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound.
Scope: The behavior requires neither shared spatial references nor robot-to-robot contact and transfers from 20 to 40 robots without retraining.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Twenty simulated robots during the 354h lunar night, from one rollout of the learned policy. Ring color is each robot’s sky exposure χ on the scale of Fig. 3. Top: the scattered start at hour 0. Every robot is red: with no neighbor close enough to block it, each one radiates to the full sky. Bottom: hour 73, after the swarm has gathered. The interior is blue, shielded by the bodies around it, and only the rim stays warm-colored; all twenty are alive.

Fig. 4. Transfer to larger swarms. Change in survival requirement relative to N = 20, the size at which all five policies were trained; they were evaluated at N = 30 and N = 40 without retraining. Squares are the mean across policies with bars spanning best and worst; faint points are the individual policies. The grey region is the change available from the equalization bound.

Fig. 2 shows the full system. The optimization term consists of the terminal temperature of the coldest quintile of robots. For N = 20, this corresponds to K = 5. We use the coldest quintile rather than the swarm average so that the objective is dominated by the robots closest to failure, while remaining less sensitive to a single outlier. We use a sparse reward which is returned only once, at the end of the lunar night, and no reward shaping takes place during the episode. We leave out any terms which could influence our emergence claim, such as position, spacing, sky exposure, circulation, huddling, or motion. The only motivating factor is therefore to improve survival.

papers.abstract: Dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs) remains challenging due to underactuated, high-dimensional dynamics, delayed deformation responses, and the presence of multiple feasible motions under obstacle constraints. This paper presents BM2PC, a Bayesian Multimodal MPC framework for agile manipulation of DLOs. Building on the control-as-inference posterior, BM2PC formulates multimodal planning as a set optimization problem that balances control quality and behavioral diversity. An efficient incremental update maintains multiple promising control modes with low additional computational overhead. For real-world deployment, BM2PC incorporates an execution dynamics model that predicts actual end-effector motion and compensates for execution mismatch during fast manipulation. We evaluate BM2PC on rope tracking and obstacle avoidance in simulation and hardware, and on simulated disturbance rejection. In trajectory tracking, BM2PC generalizes better to unseen trajectories than a learning-based baseline without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate long-horizon tracking, reducing RMSE by 44.0% on the longest task. In obstacle avoidance, BM2PC achieves comparable performance to existing multimodal MPC methods while reducing planning time by 29% to 66%. These results demonstrate accurate dynamic control and efficient multimodal planning within a unified MPC framework. The core implementation of BM2PC and supplementary videos are available at https://github.com/Longyouyuan/BM2PC.
authors: Youyuan Long, Gokhan Solak, Arash Ajoudani
bullets: Addresses underactuated, delayed, high-dimensional DLO dynamics and multiple feasible motions under obstacles.
Formulates multimodal planning as Bayesian set optimization balancing control quality with behavioral diversity.
Uses incremental updates to maintain promising control modes efficiently, plus an execution dynamics model for fast-motion mismatch compensation.
Evaluated on rope tracking, obstacle avoidance, and disturbance rejection in simulation and hardware.
Generalizes to unseen trajectories without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning; reduces longest-task tracking RMSE by 44.0% and planning time by 29–66% versus relevant baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed BM2PC framework. Candidate control sequences are sampled around the multimodal warm-start set and evaluated through parallel rollouts using the execution dynamics model, DLO dynamics model, and collision detection. Based on rollout costs and trajectory features, BM2PC performs an incremental multimodal update to maintain a diverse set of high-quality control modes. One mode is selected for execution, while the updated multimodal set is propagated to the next MPC iteration.

Fig. 4: Trajectory tracking results (Sim). The proposed method achieves accurate tracking across most trajectories, while SPiD fails to reproduce fine geometric details, particularly on complex trajectories with sharp turns and rapid local variations. Thus, SPiD is not shown in the longer cases (T>12s) to avoid clutter.
Fig. 9: A test-time example of the execution dynamics model.

Fig. 3: Execution dynamics model. A GRU-based history encoder processes recent measured and desired end-effector states to initialize a latent representation of the current execution dynamics. Conditioned on this latent state and the desired future trajectory, the rollout cell recursively predicts future EE motion. At each rollout step, an MLP predicts the executed acceleration, which is integrated by a physicsinformed (PI) head to obtain the next velocity and position.
