papers.abstract: Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) stands as a fundamental challenge in robotics, essential for enabling autonomous agents to execute complex, long-horizon tasks in diverse environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new paradigm for TAMP by leveraging extensive common sense, their inherent reasoning limitations hinder direct application, and fine-tuning strategies to enhance these capabilities are currently bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality datasets. Existing automated generation methods often suffer from homogeneity, limiting model generalization, and unsolvability, where hallucinated scene graphs create physical mismatches with task goals. To address these issues, we propose Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction (SCOPE), an automated framework designed to generate diverse and executable TAMP datasets. SCOPE incorporates multi-level diversity metrics to maximize the information entropy of scenarios. Crucially, it introduces a Plan Feedback Error-correction pipeline that utilizes planner execution failures as feedback signals to retroactively rectify logical inconsistencies in scene graphs, ensuring physical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that SCOPE exhibits greater robustness to erroneous scene graphs and generates higher-quality data. When utilized for LLM fine-tuning, SCOPE-generated data yield a downstream TAMP model that achieves an absolute 12.33% gain in success rate over its counterpart fine-tuned with data generated by DELTA, a state-of-the-art PDDL-based planner.
authors: Chaoyue Li, Zeyu Gao, Yanfeng Lu, Fan Luo
bullets: Addresses scarce, homogeneous, and often unsolvable datasets for long-horizon robot planning with LLMs.
Uses multi-level diversity metrics to increase scenario information entropy.
Applies plan-execution failures to retroactively correct logical inconsistencies in scene graphs.
Produces more robust, higher-quality data and improves downstream TAMP fine-tuning success by 12.33 percentage points over DELTA-generated data.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the SCOPE framework. The pipeline consists of three main stages: (1) diverse scene generation based on statistical feedback and dynamic sampling; (2) Chain-of-Thought driven task instruction generation; and (3) scene graph construction optimized by planning feedback and autoregressive error-correction.

Fig. 1. An end-to-end task planning framework demonstrates the complete pipeline from environmental perception to plan generation. First, hierarchical scene graphs are extracted from the AI2-THOR environment. Subsequently, these graphs and natural language instructions are fed into the Qwen2.5-7BInstruct model. This model is fine-tuned on the SCOPE dataset via LoRA for efficient task planning. Finally, the model outputs an ordered plan sequence Π = {π0, π1, . . . , πn}, which is executed by the AI2-THOR simulator.

Fig. 4. Failure analysis of the SCOPE-fine-tuned model. The errors are classified into high-level cognitive deficits and low-level grounding issues to illustrate the bottlenecks in the planning pipeline.
Fig. 3. Simulation snapshots of the execution process of a long-horizon task.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone. Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force. We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing. VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns. The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4x4 array. We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments. In controlled single-taxel tests over 1-5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces. A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use. Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.
authors: Jian Hou, Xin Zhou, Adam J. Spiers
bullets: Addresses the lack of shear-force sensing in many low-cost flexible tactile arrays.
Uses a piezoresistive layer and passive silicone nubs to encode normal and shear forces as pressure patterns.
A 4×4 array costs under $35, is 6 mm thick, and can be fabricated without specialized equipment.
Controlled tests report 0.39 N normal-force RMSE and 0.16 N shear-force RMSE; flat calibration remains effective when curved.
Demonstrations include preventing balloon puncture with a scalpel and improving power-plug insertion.

Compression reduces the resistance of the silver-fiber resistive layer, increasing current between paired electrodes within a quadrant. (B) The assembled sensor stacks the cast silicone and resistive layer over the FPC. Normal force raises the four quadrant readings uniformly, whereas shear creates across-quadrant difference.

(5) Cyanoacrylate glue dots are applied only at the marked locations on the FPC. (6) The resistive layer is placed over the FPC. (7) The FPC and resistive layer are slid into the molded silicone layer produced in step (4). (8) A small batch of Dragon Skin 30, prepared as in step (2), is injected through the openings; the bottom plate from step (1) is reused as a press under a 200 g load during the approximately 8 h cure.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an important paradigm for robotic manipulation by unifying visual perception, language understanding, and action generation. Since reliable manipulation requires sufficient observation of objects, end-effectors, and their spatial relationships, multi-view inputs are widely used to provide complementary spatial information. However, our experiments show that existing VLA models do not fully exploit such multi-view complementarity. The policy tends to persistently rely on the wrist view, lacking the ability to dynamically adjust global-local view dependency across manipulation stages, which limits stage adaptability and robustness. To address this issue, we propose FocusVLA, a stage-aware multi-view routing framework. FocusVLA predicts future interaction intent from historical actions and uses it to guide dynamic view routing during action generation. By adaptively coordinating global and local observations across different task stages, FocusVLA improves multi-view utilization. On RoboTwin 2.0, FocusVLA improves the average success rate over the strongest baseline $\pi_{0.5}$ by 10.10 pp. In real-world evaluation, FocusVLA improves the success rate from 71.7\% to 85.0\%, achieving a 13.3\% gain over $\pi_{0.5}$. Moreover, the intent prediction and dynamic routing modules of FocusVLA can be integrated into existing VLA frameworks without modifying their core architectures.
authors: Huixin Xu, Ziya Yu, Peng Li
bullets: Existing VLA policies often over-rely on wrist views and fail to adapt view selection during manipulation.
The method predicts future interaction intent from historical actions to guide stage-aware multi-view routing.

On RoboTwin 2.0, it improves average success by 10.10 percentage points over π₀.₅.
In real-world tests, success rises from 71.7% to 85.0%; the modules can be integrated into existing VLA architectures.

papers.abstract: Vision and touch provide complementary cues for object pose and local contact geometry, but external cameras are often occluded at the contact site. We present GelSlim 5.0, a fingertip sensor that acquires visual and tactile observations with one fixed camera and a continuous UV-responsive contact layer. By switching illumination, the camera sequentially acquires through-membrane visual images and contact-sensitive tactile images from a shared viewpoint, avoiding inter-camera extrinsic calibration. To combine these observations, we introduce VisTacFusion, a multimodal transformer with separate prediction paths for planar object pose and contact geometry. Asymmetric bottleneck fusion incorporates visual context while preserving tactile spatial features for depth and surface-normal estimation. Modality dropout enables inference with paired inputs or either modality alone. On real validation data from 12 known objects, paired inputs reduce depth MSE, angular error, and translation $L_1$ by 61.2%, 72.3%, and 61.3%, respectively, relative to tactile-only inference with the same model. Relative to visual-only inference, the corresponding reductions are 93.7%, 6.1%, and 8.6%.
authors: Xiangdong Wang, I-Hsuan Huang, Xiaohao Xu, Xili Yi, Nima Fazeli, Xiaonan Huang
bullets: Addresses occlusion and calibration challenges caused by external cameras at contact sites.
Uses a fixed camera with a UV-responsive contact layer and switched illumination to capture visual and tactile images from one viewpoint.
VisTacFusion uses separate pose and contact-geometry prediction paths with asymmetric bottleneck fusion.
Modality dropout supports inference from paired inputs or either modality alone.

On 12 known objects, paired inputs substantially reduced depth, angular, and translation errors versus tactile-only and visual-only inference, with the largest gains over tactile-only depth and angular errors.

The geometry path retains tactile maps from blocks 3, 6, 9, and 12, applies gated conditioning from visual-context state B4, and decodes contact depth and surface normals with DPT. papers.abstract: Exoskeletons have shown great potential for augmenting human physical capabilities, yet generating reliable assistance remains challenging because human motion patterns and interaction requirements vary substantially in practice. To address this problem, a dual-loop assistance strategy is proposed to couple multimodal exoskeleton trajectory generation with variable admittance control, where trajectory variance links the outer-loop generator and the inner-loop controller. The generator synthesizes future exoskeleton trajectories through denoising, primarily using whole-body human motion and exoskeleton proprioception, with task descriptions as auxiliary semantic cues. To reduce cross-modal representation mismatch, a three-stage training pipeline is introduced to progressively optimize the human motion encoder, the exoskeleton proprioception encoder, and the trajectory generator. In the inner loop, multiple future trajectories are sampled from the generator to estimate the trajectory mean and variance. The mean is used as the control reference, while the variance provides an uncertainty measure for prediction reliability. This measure is further incorporated into a stiffness regulation law, enabling compliant assistance with input-to-state stability under bounded lumped interaction input. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces muscle activation levels compared with standard baselines, while also decreasing users' metabolic energy expenditure relative to the unassisted condition.
authors: Muyuan Ma, Long Cheng, Lijun Han, Haotian Zhai, Xinpan Meng, Xiuze Xia, Houcheng Li, Zeyu Liu

papers.abstract: Synthesizing physically grounded dexterous hand-object interactions is important for VR/AR, gaming, and robotics, yet remains challenging because subtle contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, and target trajectories must be jointly respected while maintaining natural grasps. Existing methods either track mocap trajectories with limited transfer to novel objects, or rely on hand-only generative priors that fail to capture coupled hand-object motion, sacrificing contact fidelity and sample efficiency. To tackle these challenges, we introduce PiHand, a Physically grounded Interaction-aware Hand motion synthesis framework. PiHand first trains expert policies that track mocap demonstrations in simulation, distills them into a unified hand-object interaction prior using a goal-conditioned VAE, and finally solve diverse dexterous manipulation tasks through bounded residual exploration in its latent space. With only a single reward and no complex curriculum training, this yields general tabletop manipulation policies that generalize to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB. The same prior transfers to object catching and bimanual handover, two tasks that are rarely seen in its training data. Across all tasks, PiHand consistently outperforms baselines in all metrics. We will release the processed data and model checkpoints.
authors: Niklas Berndt, Xianghui Xie, Enes Duran, Yixiao Wang, Gerard Pons-Moll
bullets: Addresses the challenge of jointly modeling contact dynamics, diverse object geometries, target trajectories, and natural grasps.

Uses a single reward without complex curriculum training.
Generalizes to unseen objects and trajectories on GRAB and DexYCB, and transfers to object catching and bimanual handover.
Reports consistent improvement over baselines across all evaluated metrics; data and checkpoints are planned for release.

papers.abstract: Real robot data, rich across tasks and morphologies, is often treated as the bottleneck for training robot learning models, including embodied foundation models that aim for zero-shot physical transfer. In this paper, we investigate the degree to which such models can acquire necessary structure using data from systems without embodiment. To this end, we test if inexpensive, procedurally generated synthetic data can yield useful priors before a model observes any real-world behavior. We study this through robot action prediction, a natural pretraining objective and a direct test of whether structure learned from arbitrary synthetic tasks transfers to embodied settings. We introduce three data generation pipelines that model mathematical abstractions of robotic control, and use them as pretraining priors for a Transformer. We demonstrate that a model trained purely on this non-robotic data attains non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen physical robot tasks via an in-context learning mechanism, and that our specialized control priors notably improve upon generic causal priors. We also compare against a compute-matched baseline trained on real robot data, and find that it outperforms our model but only on the datasets it was trained on. These findings suggest that procedurally generated, mathematical abstractions can yield useful robotic priors, offering a potential complement to expensive embodied data collection.
authors: Mateusz Odrowaz-Sypniewski, Michael Amir, Jasmine Bayrooti, Ajay Shankar, Amanda Prorok
bullets: Real robot data is expensive and limited for training broadly capable robot-learning models.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).
authors: Chenyuan Chen, Ran Ding, Lechen Zhang, Zewen He, Yoshihiko Nakamura
bullets: Addresses non-Markovian manipulation scenes where important visual cues disappear or leave view.
Uses SAM3 to track objects and select key event frames within an adaptive memory budget.
An action expert reads selected frames via cross-attention alongside object tokens encoding appearance, geometry, and time.
Introduces HuMeGo, a benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
Raises success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot; also improves SIMPLE tasks from 70.2% to 86.9%.

papers.abstract: Capturing a loose object inside a spacecraft requires a robot to approach a target that can translate and rotate, and whose motion changes when contact is made. These conditions motivate evaluation beyond manipulation of supported objects. We introduce AstroBench, an open benchmark for free-floating capture and space robotic manipulation with a fixed-base arm. The task suite combines four initial-motion tracks with sample-storage operations based on MELFI hardware and cap and captive-screw servicing based on the Robotic Refueling Mission. The two workcells provide nine task definitions and 29 task-target combinations. A metadata-filtered Objaverse inventory supplies 8,414 object instances for asset expansion, alongside five cabin visual contexts and versioned task instructions. We report two acquisition-focused experiments using existing checkpoints. A frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ DROID joint-position policy captures 2 of 200 static targets and 4 of 200 moving targets across twenty object identities. A cube-specific ACT policy captures 8 of 10 static targets and 6 of 10 moving targets in a separate experiment. Each experiment retains its recorded observation, action and capture configuration. The results document difficult direct transfer for the tested generalist checkpoint and successful task-specific capture behavior, while identifying concrete settings for studying motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control. Code, task definitions and editable workcell assets are available at https://github.com/AstroUpLab/AstroBench.

papers.abstract: Tilt-rotor quadcopters redirect thrust for translation without banking, but complicate modeling, state estimation, and disturbance rejection. This paper presents a simulation-based flight stack for a \SI{2.00}{\kilo\gram} tilt-rotor quadcopter. The system uses a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear model with first-order motor dynamics and two-axis rotor tilt, parameterized using a 3D CAD model. A cascaded PD controller commands forward and lateral tilt angles. A 14-state EKF fuses sensor data across hover, early-transition, and transition modes using a hysteretic (Schmitt-trigger) classifier to prevent covariance discontinuities. Because the proportional position loop leaves a steady-state offset under constant wind, a small bounded neural residual is added on top of the unmodified PD controller. It is trained by behavioral cloning from a teacher with privileged access to the true wind, while the deployed network never observes wind. In simulation, the EKF achieves a post-settling position root mean square error (RMSE) of \SI{0.226}{\metre} (horizontal) and \SI{0.03}{\metre} (vertical) and an attitude RMSE below \SI{0.8}{\degree}, and it estimates a wind velocity of $(\num{2.0}, \num{-1.2})\,\unit{\metre\per\second}$ to within \SI{0.15}{\metre\per\second} per axis. The residual reduces steady-state station-keeping error under wind by approximately \SI{49}{\percent}, from \SI{0.117}{\metre} to \SI{0.060}{\metre} at \SI{1.5}{\metre\per\second} and from \SI{0.319}{\metre} to \SI{0.162}{\metre} at an out-of-distribution \SI{3.9}{\metre\per\second}. The framework provides a basis for hardware-in-the-loop and flight-test studies.

In simulation, the EKF achieves 0.226 m horizontal and 0.03 m vertical position RMSE, with attitude RMSE below 0.8°.
The residual reduces steady-state position error by about 49% under both 1.5 m/s and out-of-distribution 3.9 m/s wind.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a demonstration-based robotic feeding framework that integrates human demonstration, Dynamic Movement Primitive-based motion planning, vision-based scene perception, and robot control. A human operator first demonstrates the scooping and feeding motions while the position and Euler-angle orientation of the spoon are recorded using a motion-capture system. The recorded trajectory is segmented into scooping and feeding motions, which are encoded using separate Dynamic Movement Primitives. Before task execution, an RGB-D camera estimates the participant's mouth position, while two AprilTags are used for robot-frame registration and tray localization. The detected tray pose is used to position the scooping motion, whereas the detected mouth position defines the positional goal of the feeding motion. The approach, scooping, and feeding trajectories are then executed sequentially by a Kinova Gen3 manipulator through a ROS~2-based framework. A real-world experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the integrated pipeline and shows that the learned spoon motions can be reproduced within the detected experimental scene.

papers.abstract: End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations. However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments. Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations. Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery. In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation. Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods. We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment. Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.

The study is evaluated in simulation and focuses on laparoscopic robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies. Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head. We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision. UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent. The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks. On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%. It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation of soft objects, such as garments, is a critical skill for service and household robots to adopt, but remains challenging due to its high-dimensional state space, and material-dependent deformations. Humans address this challenge by using mental world models that "imagine" the shape and material properties from partial observations, which enables them to predict how actions affect future states. As such, embedding such world models in robots allows for better generalization in manipulating a wide variety of garments in the real world. However, learned world models typically require large amounts of real world data that is strenuous to collect, and a mechanism to infer latent properties that govern dynamics. We present a Soft-Object World Model that performs generative full-state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction using a transformer backbone trained on large-scale simulated soft object interactions, with measures to mitigate the sim-to-real gap. By learning to infer latent shape and material cues through in-context learning over a variable-length partial point-cloud history, the model generalizes across robot embodiments, material parameters, garment types and shapes, and manipulation coordination modes without weight updates. The world model is then integrated with a Goal-Conditioned action planner for motion synthesis. We validate the approach in simulation and real world for bimanual garment folding, reporting improvements in reconstruction fidelity, prediction accuracy, and task success.

papers.abstract: Stable grasping under task-specific disturbances is important for robotic manipulation. However, most dexterous grasp synthesis methods are developed for highly actuated hands in free space, and low-DoF hands may not be able to realize the contact topologies required by these grasps. Meanwhile, support surfaces can provide useful contact forces, but are often treated only as geometric constraints. We present a support-aware grasp synthesis framework for object immobilization with low-DoF coupled hands. Given irregular object geometry, our method represents both hand and object local surface regions as graphs and searches for kinematically feasible matchings between them. We then refine the wrist pose and motor state for geometric contact feasibility and validates the refined grasps through physical rollouts. Starting from the validated grasp pose, an optional task-guided local search explores nearby grasp configurations by varying the wrist pose and motor state, and selects one according to the specified task condition. Experiments on diverse objects show that our method generates various grasp configurations that achieve high grasp success and strong disturbance resistance. Real-world experiments further demonstrate physically executable grasps which enable object immobilization in cooking scenario.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation in everyday environments, yet progress is difficult to assess across differing policies, controllers, and task settings. LocoManiLab provides an integrated testbed spanning data collection and generation, policy training, evaluation, and physical deployment. Its task suite covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation. The evaluation covers twelve policies with a shared controller across task and scene splits and perturbation levels, two policies across five controllers, and studies of demonstration scale and data-source mixtures. Success rates fall on unseen tasks and scenes and generally decline as visual perturbations increase, with differences in generalization and robustness across policies. For data generation, a humanoid motion generation model is fine-tuned for loco-manipulation to study the alignment of its outputs with task execution requirements and its integration into the data generation pipeline. Three simulated loco-manipulation tasks closely match real-world setups, enabling evaluation of three policies in both domains. Similar policy rankings support the reliability of simulation-based evaluation.
authors: Dewei Wang, Jinrui Han, Jiyuan Shi, Chenyun Zhang, Xianbo Lu, Jiabao Wu, Jiqin Feng, Jipeng Kong, Ping Luo, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li

Evaluates policy and controller choices under task/scene splits, visual perturbations, demonstration scales, and mixed data sources.
Finds reduced success on unseen tasks and scenes, with further degradation under stronger visual perturbations and varying robustness across policies.
Includes loco-manipulation motion generation fine-tuning and examines how generated motions support task execution and data generation.
Three simulated tasks mirror real-world setups; consistent policy rankings across domains support simulation-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion-tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition. A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot process. STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening. Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion-tracking policy. We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree~G1 and~ROBOTIS K1. Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long-horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP-project
authors: Taehyun Byun, Taemoon Jeong, Yoonbyung Chai, Woojin Wie, Insu Park, Kyungjae Lee, Sungjoon Choi
bullets: Addresses failed transitions caused by incompatible relative position, heading, and timing between motions.
Retargets robot motions to a human rig, where an alignment model ranks candidate boundary conditions and durations.
Uses a human motion prior to generate the transition, then retargets the result back to the robot for policy training.
Evaluated on Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1, with physical demonstrations of long-horizon motion sequences.
Scope: transition quality depends on suitable alignment and the capabilities of the human motion prior.

papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Lei Wei, Guangyuan Dong, Sihan Liu, Yingjie He, Siheng Wang, Shuaibo Li, Rongchao Zhang, Zhen Tian, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao Hu
bullets: Pixel prediction quality can misalign with policy utility: lower next-frame MSE may yield worse policy gradients.

DRILL-VWI is a rollout-free surrogate that weights errors by policy visitation, GRPO advantage, and model confidence.
DRILL-IMG differentiates through the inner update with truncated Hessian-vector products; DRILL-VWI approximates its local one-step gradient under stated assumptions.
Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG improves mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World.

papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.
authors: Jingyu Ru, Xiangyuan Xie, Lixuan Jin, Jian An, Xingming Zhang, Binghao Li, Siyu Wang, Xiang Zhou, Lei Yuan, Hongli Xu, Yang Yu

ALMA uses a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions.

An evolutionary process guided by an LLM analyzes control difficulties and proposes new arm-motion structures for training.
In simulation, position RMSE falls by up to 24.7%; on a real aerial manipulator, zero-shot transfer reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion.

papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history. Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.
authors: Adam Lee, Mutian Xu, Yukang Cao, Shulin Tian, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the entanglement of dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis in existing video-based world models.
Uses a lightweight 3D dynamics network to predict object-centric motion and deformation from an initial scene and future hand trajectory.
Transports appearance through predicted 3D motion, letting video generation focus on uncertain or newly visible content.
Reports 27–40% lower moved-point error than PointWorld across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, plus 47% higher object-fidelity IoU+ on HOT3D under a shared renderer.
Two-step causal generation provides a reported 57× speedup relative to the authors’ 14B bidirectional configuration.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.
authors: Shivakanth Sujit, Luca Nunziante, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Kai Arulkumaran
bullets: Flow-matching VLA policies typically require iterative ODE integration, which limits deployment control frequency.
Across six flow-matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale.

The finding depends on models having sufficient training and capacity.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi-task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA-MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token-level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre-trained capabilities and task-specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA-MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA-7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla-moe.
authors: Shiyang Zhang, Miao Yang, Zhengda Li, Yang Shao, Ruifang Zhai, Hui Peng, Peng Song
bullets: Addresses the limited multi-task capacity of lightweight VLAs that rely on one dense action expert.
Replaces action-expert FFNs with parallel experts and a token-level router, activating only one expert per token at inference.
Adds a tunable shared expert to balance pretrained capability retention with task-specific specialization.
On four LIBERO task suites, achieves an 84.25% average success rate versus 82.75% for SmolVLA and 76.5% for OpenVLA-7B.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robotic surgery has drawn increased attention in recent years due to its potential to relieve surgeons of time-consuming, mentally straining, and tedious tasks, particularly during prolonged operations. One suitable task for automation is suturing, which involves tracking the thread as it deforms during needle retrieval, de-tangling, knot tightening, and other tasks. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, deformable thread manipulation has no fixed pose to track and effectively infinite degrees of freedom, making its configuration difficult to predict and requiring the thread's state to be re-estimated rather than assumed. At the same time, thread manipulations involve sequential motions that depend on past and current thread contact points, which must be accurately and continuously tracked. This paper presents an image-to-manipulation pipeline that concurrently generates live thread reconstruction while conducting safe and optimized sequential manipulations to achieve long-horizon tasks.
authors: Emma Huang, Omar Hernandez, Zih-Yun Chiu, Michael Yip
bullets: Targets autonomous suturing tasks such as needle retrieval, de-tangling, and knot tightening.
Addresses the thread’s deformability, infinite degrees of freedom, and changing configuration.
Continuously tracks current and past thread contact points during sequential manipulation.
Combines live visual thread reconstruction with safe, optimized manipulation planning.
The abstract does not report specific experimental results or limitations.

papers.abstract: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.
authors: Yi Loo, Siddhant Shrivastava, Minh Long Pham, Malika Meghjani
bullets: Addresses the limited study of VLA-based collaboration among robots and humans.
Uses decentralized collaborative planning to generate executable multi-robot task plans.
Converts these plans into collaborative demonstrations for decentralized VLA fine-tuning.
The resulting models match the task performance of models trained on human-teleoperated collaborative data.

papers.abstract: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.
authors: Xiongbo Shi, Shihang Du, Zongyou Yu, Ao Zhou, Xudong Zhang, Ziyu Lin, Haodong Zhang, Junqiao Zhao, Guang Chen
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of uniform per-frame optimization, especially when accurate body–object relations matter only at critical stages.
Uses a vision-language model to select relevant motion signals and body parts, then detects keyframes from signal changes.
Assigns extra solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to selected body parts.
Adds Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring to refine object-surface contacts, and STRL uses adaptive key-stage sampling with contact-aware rewards.
Simulation and real-world experiments show improved contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, with better downstream task completion across diverse interactions.

papers.abstract: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.
authors: Maximilian St\"olzle, David M\"uller, Agon Serifi, Ruben Grandia, Espen Knoop, Moritz B\"acher
bullets: Addresses physically implausible motion trajectories that limit diffusion models’ use in simulation and control.
Combines surrogate kinematic constraints with dynamic feasibility checks from an inverse-dynamics cone program.
Uses gradient-free Sep-CMA-ES to optimize diffusion noise and an autoregressive scheme to generate long sequences.
On an SMPL humanoid across 100 motion styles, it reduces ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%.
On 11 custom-biped sequences, it reduces acceleration-reconstruction error by 89.5% and inverse-dynamics residual by 79.5% in the median.

papers.abstract: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.
bullets: A pre-registered study compares memory-augmented retrieval, weight-distilled policies, and fixed student policies with the teacher’s retrieval buffer attached.

Distilling memory-augmented behavior into weights improved performance by only 1 percentage point over an action-only control; the test was underpowered, so the claim was withdrawn rather than refuted.
Attaching the frozen retrieval buffer to student weights produced a large gain (+34 percentage points), matching the memory-augmented teacher’s 49.3% reference performance.
Follow-up controls found the buffer substantially improved the base model and other adapters, while adapters added no detectable benefit once retrieval was attached.
On a harder second task, the retrieval advantage was smaller and not significant, with exploratory evidence linking the reduction to limited memory coverage.

papers.abstract: Learning useful representations from continually changing value targets remains a challenge in deep reinforcement learning. We study the temporal horizon of this supervision: smaller discounts make these targets less sensitive to distant bootstrap changes, but using them for behavior changes the control objective. We introduce Short-to-Long (S2L), which supplies a long-horizon behavior learner with features trained by smaller-discount source networks. Detached connections prevent the behavior value loss from updating the sources, allowing each source to follow its own value objective while the behavior discount remains unchanged. Across Atari, online continuous control, and offline continuous control, the approach yields aggregate performance gains, improving the paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games. Matched Atari ablations support the roles of feature transfer, smaller source discounts, and gradient isolation. Fixed-trajectory measurements further show reduced drift in source value targets with mixed discounts.
authors: Tong Che, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
bullets: Addresses representation instability from continually changing long-horizon value targets in deep reinforcement learning.
Uses smaller-discount source networks to learn more stable features, while the behavior learner retains its original long-horizon discount.
Detached connections isolate source networks from the behavior value loss, letting each network optimize its own value objective.
Across Atari, online continuous control, and offline continuous control, S2L improves aggregate performance; it improves paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games.
Ablations support feature transfer, smaller source discounts, and gradient isolation; fixed-trajectory measurements show reduced source-target drift with mixed discounts.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.
authors: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Tactile sensing exposes physical contact information important for robust and dexterous manipulation.
Mechanics-driven methods interpret tactile signals using contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning to form state representations and guide actions.
Data-driven methods learn tactile representations and manipulation policies from data, including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models.
The paper surveys tactile sensing fundamentals and developments across both perspectives.
It identifies open challenges and future opportunities for broader, more robust tactile-enabled robotics.
papers.selection_reason: Review of tactile-based manipulation covering mechanics-driven and data-driven approaches, including imitation learning, RL, VLA models, and predictive models.
papers.title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
papers.tldr: This review traces tactile robotic manipulation from mechanics-based reasoning to data-driven learning and outlines challenges for scalable, generalizable, and robust systems.

papers.abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.
authors: Van Chung Nguyen, Hung Manh La
bullets: Addresses conflicting, robot-specific, and unstable reward shaping in humanoid RL.
Applies Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping (Multi-PBRS) to unify reward configuration.
Uses the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot metadata.
Reports more consistent scaling and reduced tuning sensitivity than standard shaping.
Preserves the optimal policy while guiding exploration through potential differences.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
authors: Huiwon Jang, Suhyeok Jang, Hyeonmo Kang, Seungku Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sihyun Yu
bullets: WAMs use future video representations to guide action prediction without costly iterative video denoising.
FRED self-distills representations predicted from noise using representations from ground-truth future observations as targets.
Historical observations provide temporal context for more accurate future representation prediction.
Across real-world manipulation tasks, FRED outperforms competing WAMs, especially on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks.
For skills shown only in human videos, FRED reaches 50.0% task success versus 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4). Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.
bullets: Evaluates robustness under sensor lag, grip slip, unreachable targets, planner-output corruption, and concurrent faults.
Matches an LLM agent with a deterministic Scripted Oracle across 150 simulated episodes using identical conditions.
The Oracle succeeds in 64.0% of episodes versus 44.0% for the LLM.
Excluding planner-output corruption, both planners achieve 55.0% success with no discordant outcomes.
The performance gap is isolated to the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface, not physical robustness or reasoning deficits.

papers.abstract: Real-time whole-body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization-based retargeting pipelines and future-frame conditioning. Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body-part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules. In this work, we present HuMiT, a whole-body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body-part transformations, and even future frames. Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication-to-inference latency of $\sim$20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types. We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split-second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco-manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu-art.github.io/Track/.
bullets: Addresses latency and upstream-module dependence in optimization-based whole-body teleoperation.
Uses a unified tracking policy conditioned on root height, root velocity, and SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints.
Avoids requiring full joint states, dense body transformations, or future frames.

papers.abstract: Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment. Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently. This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base, body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS~2 pipeline records synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified 11D action shared by teleoperation and policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection, force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 \cite{MOLMO} on pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics. Code available at: https://github.com/iit-DLSLab/LocoPilot
bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting demonstrations that coordinate legged-base and manipulator motion while preserving robot-specific observations and commands.

Estimates interaction forces without a dedicated force/torque sensor and provides passivity-constrained haptic feedback.
Records synchronized multimodal data with a unified 11D action interface shared between teleoperation and deployment.
Demonstrates the full pipeline on multiple tasks, including physical pick-and-place deployment after fine-tuning MolmoAct2 without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/
bullets: The study examines how robot-hand rendering affects novice demonstrations and downstream imitation learning.
PointHand renders a multi-fingered hand as fingertip and joint keypoints, matching the policy’s hand observations.

Diffusion policies using keypoint observations benefited most from demonstrations collected with the matching thumb-and-index rendering, improving from 46.3% to 57.3% success within 400 steps.
The findings are limited to a simulated task, a specific teleoperation interface, and the tested renderings and keypoint-based policy observations.

papers.abstract: Embodied VLMs can execute increasingly complex manipulation tasks, yet execution errors can leave the environment in states that require replanning for recovery. Existing recovery methods either rely on inference-time mechanisms with fixed policies or learn from failure examples and reference corrections rather than verified action outcomes. To enable recovery learning through verifiable interaction, we introduce the Embodied Replanning for Recovery Environment (ERR-Env), which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors. We further construct ERR-Bench, a benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states for evaluating recovery capability and execution reliability. We then propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation, and use it to train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM. Evaluation on ERR-Bench reveals a mismatch between task progress and execution reliability across diverse VLMs. AGT-GSPO improves ERR-VLM by 10.25 percentage points in Strict Success Rate for error-free completion and 22.95 percentage points in Recovery Rate, while ablations and zero-shot transfer further validate the effectiveness of our method.
bullets: Introduces ERR-Env, which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors for recovery learning.
Introduces ERR-Bench with held-out nominal, intermediate, and error-state tasks to evaluate recovery and execution reliability.
Proposes Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO, combining turn-level progress/error rewards with action-grouped advantage estimation.
Trains a compact 2B ERR-VLM; on ERR-Bench, it improves Strict Success Rate by 10.25 points and Recovery Rate by 22.95 points.
Finds that task progress and execution reliability can diverge across VLMs; ablations and zero-shot transfer support the method’s effectiveness.

papers.abstract: Shared autonomy is a control paradigm that combines human cognitive abilities with robot precision to enable effective remote manipulation in complex environments. A key challenge is how to adapt the level of autonomy using information extracted from the human, task, and/or environment. In this paper, we propose a novel arbitration strategy that dynamically adjusts the level of autonomy in the system using the entropy of a belief distribution derived from a multimodal intent inference. Human intent is modeled with a Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN), which updates beliefs over goals given real-time operator gaze data and robot arm motion during teleoperation. We then formulate the blending of human input and autonomous control as a Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem, where the system's autonomous behavior is guided by the belief distribution. This approach enables continuous, gradual transitions across the full spectrum of autonomy levels, from direct teleoperation to full autonomy. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments to compare the performance of our proposed algorithm against two MPC-based shared autonomy methods. Compared to the baselines, our approach achieved reductions of at least 61% in object retrieval time, 44% in trajectory length, and 60% in human control input. Participants reported high perceived control, predictability, intent recognition, and responsiveness, along with low workload.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing the appropriate autonomy level in shared remote manipulation.
Infers operator goals with a Dynamic Bayesian Network from real-time gaze and robot-arm motion.
Uses belief entropy to arbitrate between human commands and autonomous MPC control.
Supports continuous transitions from direct teleoperation to full autonomy.

Compared with two MPC-based baselines, experiments found at least 61% lower retrieval time, 44% shorter trajectories, and 60% less human control input; users also reported strong usability and low workload.

papers.abstract: Placing a grasped book into a tight shelf is a compact but difficult contact-rich control problem: millimetre-scale pose error can turn a geometrically valid approach into jamming, failed release, or incomplete seating. We study this final phase after grasp acquisition and global approach, and ask how control authority should be divided between known geometry and learned behaviour. Our method retains a nominal task-space controller for structured insertion and seating, while residual PPO supplies bounded local corrections and decides when to release. Only the brief open-retreat-reclose transition is scripted. For the final policy used on hardware, a deployment-matched simulation evaluation over 512 fixed conditions yields 98.50 percent mean success (0.23 percentage-point sample SD) across three independent training runs, compared with 37.89 percent for nominal control. On the physical xArm7, 60 trials over 30 matched conditions show the same qualitative advantage: residual control raises success from 26.7 percent to 63.3 percent, reduces failures from 22 to 11, and wins 13 of the 15 matched conditions in which the two controllers differ. Robustness tests show that performance remains above 87 percent under initialization perturbations up to 1.5x, while very tight clearances expose the geometric limit of local correction. These results support a hybrid design in which geometry preserves reliable task structure and learning is concentrated on the contact-sensitive behaviour that fixed rules handle poorly.

papers.abstract: A geometrically valid placement can still be difficult to execute because the selected grasp changes the required end-effector pose, collision geometry, and transport motion. Placement is formulated as a pre-execution ranking problem in which supplied grasp-placement candidates are scored before planning. The model combines a typed target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads for planning success and execution success conditioned on planning. On a 30-object, 1,235-scene dataset with scene-group-held-out splits, three-seed top-1 success on covered test groups reaches 85.63 +/- 1.08% for joint selection and 79.84 +/- 0.16% for fixed-target ranking. For the designated frozen seed-42 checkpoint, top-1 success improves from 72.84% to 85.78% over full-pool cuMotion for joint ranking and from 59.65% to 79.67% for fixed-target ranking. Frozen transfer to xArm7/MoveIt requires no xArm-specific retraining. Across 27 locked cases, 13 complete end to end (48.15%). Of the 16 cases that pass Top-5 preflight and begin execution, 13 succeed (81.25%). Candidate-level deployment-feasibility prediction reaches 81.25% recall, 85.20% specificity, and 83.23% balanced accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometric placement validity and practical execution difficulty caused by grasp-dependent poses, collisions, and transport motions.
Uses a target-conditioned point cloud with three pose descriptors and hierarchical heads predicting planning success and execution success conditioned on planning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot learning, with performance improving as models and datasets scale. Scaling robot data collection, however, remains challenging because data are naturally distributed across robots, tasks, and locations, making centralization costly or impractical. Federated learning offers a way to train on decentralized robot data, but applying it to VLAs requires accounting for heterogeneous robot client data distributions. We present Co-VLA, which applies consensus optimization using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers~(ADMM) to federated VLA training. We show that the same algorithm supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with both fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters. The name Co-VLA reflects both consensus and collaboration: clients with different local robot datasets collaboratively train a shared model without sharing their data. Our experiments demonstrate that Co-VLA achieves performance comparable to centralized training in both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings. The project website and videos of our real-world experiments are available at https://embodiedvision.github.io/co-vla/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling robot data collection when data are distributed across robots, tasks, and locations.
Applies consensus optimization with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to federated VLA training.
Supports both full-model training and parameter-efficient fine-tuning with fixed-rank and rank-adaptive adapters.
Experiments show performance comparable to centralized training in both training settings.
Scope: designed for heterogeneous client data while keeping local robot data private to each client.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
