papers.abstract: Flow-matching policies adjust inference cost through the number of solver steps, but reinforcement learning at a single fixed solver budget can hide degradation at cheaper deployment budgets and even erase useful one-step behavior present in a pretrained policy. We introduce Action-Ratio-Clip Flow (ArcFlow), a deployment-aware algorithm for training one flow policy across a specified range of solver budgets. ArcFlow combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection. For reconstruction objectives, its bridge aggregates temporal probes into one surrogate ratio and one PPO-style clip per action, with a boundary residual exactly equal to deployed one-step reconstruction error. Cycling exposes the shared field to the deployment range, and selection optimizes its performance floor. For native velocity objectives, multi-budget endpoint supervision applies the same principle without replacing the native update. Both realizations preserve the architecture and deployment-time cost. Across DM Control, manipulation, and locomotion, ArcFlow attains the highest mean one-step return among five flow-policy baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under each method's reported training settings. Component studies identify complementary improvements from boundary supervision, the fixed-grid bridge, budget exposure, and deployment selection. These results establish deployment-budget-aware training as an effective route to strong low-step control with one policy serving multiple inference costs.
bullets: Targets degradation at low solver budgets caused by training at only one fixed budget.
Combines action-aligned supervision, budget exposure, and worst-budget checkpoint selection.
Provides reconstruction and native-velocity variants while preserving the policy architecture and deployment cost.
Reports the highest mean one-step return among five baselines on 25 of 30 tasks under the reported settings.
Component studies find complementary gains from boundary supervision, fixed-grid bridging, budget exposure, and deployment selection.

papers.abstract: World models let agents compare imagined outcomes before acting, but an agent must still decide which alternatives to explore and when a proposed plan should replace its learned policy. We introduce SDI (Sibling Disagreement in Imagination), which connects these decisions through a shared actor-based reference. SDI compares action sequences imagined from the same model state, using repeated rollouts of the actor's own sequence to measure variation under fixed behavior. This reference scales both the spread across candidate returns, which provides an exploration signal, and a proposed plan's predicted advantage, which governs action acceptance. The agent executes a planned action when its advantage exceeds the reference variability by a fixed factor; otherwise, it follows the actor. SDI reuses the base agent's world model, actor, and critic without requiring an additional disagreement ensemble. Exploration and planning guide training data collection, while evaluation uses the learned actor alone. Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI achieves a higher observed task-average score than every compared baseline in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline's performance on 15 of 18 tasks. Component ablations and robustness analyses further examine the roles of exploration, planning exposure, and action acceptance. Paired evaluations from identical simulator states show that the gate improves both recovery from actor failures and preservation of successful behavior relative to ungated planning, while substantially reducing return degradation. Together, these results support comparing imagined alternatives against a shared actor reference as a unified approach to exploring and planning with world models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of selecting alternatives to explore and safely accepting plans in world-model agents.
Compares imagined action sequences from the same model state and measures variability in repeated rollouts of the actor’s sequence.
Uses this reference to scale exploration signals and accept a plan only when its predicted advantage exceeds reference variability by a fixed factor.
Reuses the base world model, actor, and critic without an additional disagreement ensemble; evaluation runs the learned actor alone.
Across Meta-World, Adroit, and DM-Control, SDI has the highest task-average score among compared baselines in each suite and matches or exceeds the strongest baseline on 15 of 18 tasks.

The lower branch normalizes, clips, and weights the exploration bonus b to augment the first imagined reward r̃. The bonus anneals after the first training success. papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose and force controller for physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI). In pHRI tasks, robots are expected to perform task-space motions robustly while remaining compliance with human disturbance, which proposes distinct control objectives. Most existing approaches focus mainly on either robustness or compliance and rely on force sensors for real-time tracking. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. Firstly, a neural network (NN) is trained to improve the observer performance by compensating for system friction and unmodeled dynamics. Secondly, a task-null-space decomposition is applied to separate the joint velocity and reduce the effect of the human disturbance on the observer. Finally, a hybrid pose and force controller is introduced to achieve the end-effector pose and force tracking. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust and accurate wrench estimation while maintaining reliable pose and force tracking performance. The proposed approach offers an effective solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements which can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which do not have force/torque sensors.
authors: Nuo Chen, Ya-Jun Pan, Onur Toker
bullets: Targets pHRI tasks requiring both robust task-space motion and compliance to human disturbances.
Uses a neural network to compensate for friction and unmodeled dynamics in the wrench observer.

Employs hybrid pose and force control for simultaneous end-effector pose and force tracking.
Experiments report accurate wrench estimation and reliable tracking without force/torque sensors.

The task-space velocity q̇t is sent to the NN to reduce the effect of human disturbance on force estimation, while q̇n is used for null-space compliant control. The proposed hybrid pose and force controller provides reliable position, orientation, and force tracking while maintaining compliance in the null-space.

papers.abstract: In human-robot interaction (HRI) tasks, humans may interact with the robot in either an active guiding or passive following state, resulting in distinct control objectives for each interaction mode. Most existing approaches rely on predefined switching thresholds to distinguish interaction modes, but their performance can be sensitive to measurement noise. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. First, a neural network (NN) trained via meta-learning is developed to recognize human intention without manually defined thresholds. By successfully incorporating force-dependent parameters from the controller, the recognition rates are improved from 90.1\% to 99.1\% for the passive mode and from 79.8\% to 97.1\% for the active mode. Second, an adaptive meta-learning controller is introduced to compensate for human disturbances and enable online adaptation to varying interaction forces. Third, a multiple-trajectory meta-learning algorithm is designed to jointly learn an environment-basis representation and force-dependent parameters, allowing the controller to deal with unmodeled dynamics efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust and accurate control performance, while providing reliable mode recognition for safe and adaptive physical HRI.

papers.abstract: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly deployed with asynchronous inference in real-world settings, where the next action chunk is generated while the robot is still executing the previous one. By the time the new chunk is committed, the robot and scene have changed, so the chunk is conditioned on a stale observation and task success drops sharply as this inference delay grows. Generating multiple candidate chunks could let newer observations inform the final choice, but existing multi-candidate methods either rank candidates with the stale inference-start observation or repeatedly switch between candidates during execution, which can make the executed action sequence discontinuous. Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework that generates candidates from the inference-start observation and selects one using this pre-commit observation. Its scoring function, FlowRes, measures the residual between each candidate's implied flow direction and the velocity predicted by the frozen policy under the pre-commit observation, requiring no separate verifier. A pipelined implementation overlaps observation processing with candidate generation and batches scoring, so selection adds no control-step delay on the evaluated hardware. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and it further improves existing delay-robust methods. On three real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 60% to 82% over naive asynchronous execution with the same frozen $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when action chunks are generated from stale observations during asynchronous inference.

papers.abstract: Recent studies have explored the potential of multimodal large language models for robot control, yet the models' embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized across models, tasks, and execution settings. We conduct a multidimensional comparative evaluation on RoboColiseum across four tracks: Instruction Following, Spatial Reasoning, General Manipulation, and Robustness. We implement Agent2Act, a control harness that integrates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon into the evaluation environment through shared observation, action execution, and feedback interfaces. Under common task settings and scoring criteria, all four models exhibit a consistent capability profile: high instruction-following scores, with three approaching perfect performance; strong spatial reasoning; and general manipulation scores below those of the other three tracks. Within the evaluated configurations, Astra leads instruction following and robustness, while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and overall performance. These results reveal complementary strengths across models and a persistent gap between task understanding and reliable physical execution. Component comparisons on selected tasks further show that harness design affects task success, planning cost, and execution time. Additionally, case studies with Astra examine whole-body coordination, manipulation across robot embodiments, precision manipulation, dexterous-hand manipulation, and real-robot tasks, providing further insight into the model's capabilities and limitations across embodied tasks.

papers.abstract: Reliable contact establishment remains a critical challenge for autonomous on-orbit servicing (OOS), particularly when interacting with non-cooperative targets. Gecko-inspired dry adhesives provide a lightweight, passive, and residue-free solution for robotic capture in space, yet current systems operate in open loop, without the ability to estimate their own contact or adhesion state during interaction. This paper presents a real-time interaction-awareness framework that enables sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces to estimate their contact state throughout the adhesion lifecycle using embedded capacitive sensing. Five discrete interaction states (idle, proximity, contact, engaged, and disengaged) are classified using experimentally collected and augmented sensor data, enabling a comparative evaluation of six lightweight machine learning models suitable for embedded deployment. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest achieved the highest offline classification accuracy of 95.65%. For online deployment, combining Random Forest with a rule-based state machine improved accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14%, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.9343 while maintaining a 53 ms inference cycle. These results demonstrate that incorporating physics-consistent state constraints significantly improves robustness during realtime inference, representing a step toward interaction-aware capture in future autonomous orbital servicing missions.

papers.abstract: Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground, a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100, a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons. https://winniechen2002.github.io/Agent-bench-website/

papers.abstract: Differences in hand geometry, joint parameterization, and kinematic topology pose challenges for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation. However, spatial relations among links alone are insufficient to fully capture the hand's kinematic topology. We propose DexGraspFlow, a conditional link-level $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ flow-matching framework integrating geometric relations and kinematic topology. The framework encodes local object geometry, link geometry, and current poses. A dual-stream DiT models link--link coordination and link--object interaction, while attention biases derived from kinematic-tree distances provide explicit structural information for modeling evolving geometric interactions. The model jointly learns translational and rotational velocity fields, integrates them to generate link poses, and recovers joint configurations through inverse kinematics. Additionally, inference-time palm-orientation guidance enables controllable grasp generation without retraining. Across three robotic hands and 30 object--hand pairs, DexGraspFlow achieves a 95.33\% average simulation success rate, with an average generation latency, including inverse kinematics, approximately 49\% lower than that of a state-of-the-art baseline. Further experiments demonstrate zero-shot adaptability to seven finger-removal variants and palm-orientation control. A model trained on demonstrations for the deployed hand achieves a 91\% success rate over 100 real-robot grasping trials, supporting the framework's applicability to physical grasp execution.
bullets: Addresses cross-embodiment grasp generation despite differences in hand geometry, joint parameters, and kinematic topology.
Uses a conditional link-level SE(3) flow model with geometric features and kinematic-tree distance biases.
A dual-stream DiT models link–link coordination and link–object interaction, then inverse kinematics recovers joint configurations.
Achieves 95.33% average simulation success across three hands and 30 object–hand pairs, with about 49% lower generation latency than a stated baseline.
Demonstrates zero-shot adaptation to seven finger-removal variants, palm-orientation control, and 91% success in 100 real-robot trials.

(c) Flow to executable grasp: Continuous velocity fields are numerically integrated from prior distributions to generate target link poses, which are mapped into executable joint configurations via batched inverse kinematics.

papers.abstract: Dexterous grasping in cluttered scenes remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation, as it requires high-dimensional hand coordination under complex object-environment constraints. To address this problem, we introduce one of the largest simulation benchmarks to date, comprising around 0.5B grasp annotations across eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects. Furthermore, we propose T(R,O) Grasp++, a scalable diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis in cluttered environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88% across eight dexterous embodiments. Meanwhile, our pipeline achieves only 0.3s inference latency while improving inference sample efficiency by over 10 times.
bullets: Introduces a simulation benchmark with around 0.5B grasp annotations spanning eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects.
Presents a diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment grasp generation under complex object-environment constraints.
Reports an average success rate of 88% across eight embodiments.
Achieves 0.3-second inference latency and over 10× improved inference sample efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions. This task requires a transition from representations that describe the scene and instruction to representations that support action generation. Many continuous-action VLAs leave this transition implicit and supervise it mainly through the final action-prediction loss. We introduce PAIR, a framework that learns a shared perception-action representation between these two spaces. During training, a Masked Action Autoencoder encodes expert action chunks into horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens. A Bridge Module extracts task-relevant features from the current visual-language representations. PAIR aligns these features with the Action Latent Tokens to form Bridge Tokens that preserve task information and capture the structure of expert actions. The Bridge Tokens are then projected into the action-token space and injected into the initial Action Tokens, providing an action-ready starting point for Action Expert refinement. At inference, the autoencoder is removed, and the Bridge Tokens are generated only from the current observation and instruction. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC-D show gains for the evaluated OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter models. On LIBERO-Plus, PAIR raises VLA-Adapter's success rate from 59.1% to 64.2%. On CALVIN, it increases VLA-Adapter's average completed sequence length from 4.42 to 4.53. Across seven real-world tasks, PAIR raises OpenVLA-OFT's success rate from 51.4% to 65.0%. Representation analyses show that Bridge Tokens retain task information while making continuous-action information accessible before Action Expert refinement. These results support a shared intermediate representation as a useful interface between perception and action in continuous-action VLAs.
bullets: Addresses the implicit transition from scene and instruction representations to continuous actions in VLAs.
Uses a Masked Action Autoencoder to create horizon-aligned Action Latent Tokens from expert action chunks.
A Bridge Module aligns task-relevant visual-language features with action latents, producing Bridge Tokens that initialize action generation.
At inference, Bridge Tokens are generated from observations and instructions without the autoencoder.
Improves evaluated models across LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and seven real-world tasks, including OpenVLA-OFT success rising from 51.4% to 65.0% and VLA-Adapter on LIBERO-Plus from 59.1% to 64.2%.

papers.abstract: Trajectory optimization (TO) under nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits and collision avoidance constraints is a fundamental problem in robotics, albeit especially challenging due to its highly non-convex nature. For this setting, Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) is an efficient second-order shooting method, yet its local structure renders it vulnerable to suboptimal basins. Sampling-augmented variants mitigate this susceptibility through stochastic exploration, but often sample only around the few trajectories they retain for reoptimization, based solely on their cost which restricts exploration breadth. We introduce Pareto-Optimal Entropy-Regularized DDP (PER-DDP), an entropy-regularized population framework derived from the free-energy/relative-entropy inequality. Our method combines prior-guided sampling that shapes exploration around each retained trajectory, with expanded rollout evaluations that probe these sampling policies beyond the few retained candidates, and Pareto filtering for preserving task-constraint alternatives across iterations. This decouples sampling effort from the optimization population size and broadens exploration without sacrificing the second-order structure that makes DDP effective. Across multiple systems and hundreds of environments, PER-DDP achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art sampling-augmented TO methods and finds reliable solutions in environments beyond the reach of all baselines.
bullets: Targets non-convex trajectory optimization with nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits, and collision-avoidance constraints.
Uses prior-guided sampling around retained trajectories, expanded rollouts, and Pareto filtering to preserve diverse task-constraint alternatives.
Decouples sampling effort from optimization population size, enabling broader exploration without abandoning DDP’s local second-order structure.
Across multiple systems and hundreds of environments, it achieves higher success rates than existing sampling-augmented methods and solves some environments all baselines miss.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code is available at https://github.com/du-owen/VLA-ACL.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of processing redundant visual tokens during robotic control.
Trains a lightweight pruning policy with action-level consistency supervision, using full-context predictions as a teacher and ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision.
Keeps the base VLA model completely frozen, avoiding costly end-to-end fine-tuning.
On LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks, prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5× inference speedup.
Demonstrates a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods.

On the right, vision embeddings enter our differentiable soft pruning gate and produce the soft-pruned action. b) During inference, the hard pruning gate only lets through K patches per view with the highest patch scores, obtained by the trained patch scorer. papers.abstract: Continuous asynchronous replanning is essential for real-time generative robot policies, but independent stochastic initialization can cause mode switching and inconsistent continuation across action chunks. We propose Execution-Aligned Progressive Noise (EAPN), which introduces structured stochasticity at both inter-chunk and intra-chunk levels. Across replanning steps, EAPN propagates a shared noise trajectory and aligns it with the actual execution displacement, establishing execution-aligned inter-chunk correlation. Within each action chunk, it models temporal correlation along action time. The aligned stochastic history is further combined with committed action context to condition subsequent generation, allowing new chunks to continue from execution-consistent generative states rather than restart from independent noise. We evaluate EAPN on D3IL, Kinetix, LIBERO, and real-world manipulation tasks. EAPN improves multimodal behavior consistency on D3IL and achieves an average success rate of 88.59% on Kinetix. On LIBERO, it remains robust and maintains strong task performance even under long inference delays. Real-robot experiments further achieve 90.0% success on Object Storage and 96.7% on bimanual Cloth Folding, demonstrating reliable continuous execution under asynchronous replanning.
bullets: Addresses mode switching and discontinuous behavior caused by independently initialized action chunks.
Propagates an execution-aligned shared noise trajectory across chunks and models temporal correlations within each chunk.
Conditions new generation on aligned stochastic history and committed actions to continue from execution-consistent states.
Improves multimodal consistency on D3IL and achieves strong performance across Kinetix, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation tasks.
Reports 88.59% average success on Kinetix, 90.0% on Object Storage, and 96.7% on bimanual Cloth Folding; remains robust under long inference delays on LIBERO.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated promising capabilities as in-context policy optimizers for Reinforcement Learning (RL), enabling policy search driven by both numerical reward signals and natural language reasoning. However, deploying such methods in practice requires transmitting raw policy parameters and rewards history to cloud-based LLM APIs, exposing proprietary control strategies to third-party service providers. To address this issue, this paper introduces Privacy-Preserving Prompted Policy Search (PP-ProPS), a framework that enables LLM-guided policy optimization while keeping policy and environmental parameters confidential. PP-ProPS encodes policy parameters and reward values using secret client-side transformations before they are included in each API request, ensuring that the LLM provider observes only encoded policy parameters and scaled reward information. Furthermore, unlike Vanilla ProPS, the proposed framework does not require the true optimal episodic return to be known or disclosed to the LLM. Beyond protecting the optimization data, PP-ProPS improves the search process in two ways. First, it provides the LLM with individual reward components instead of only a single total return, offering more informative feedback about each candidate policy. Second, it uses a bounded history that prevents the prompt from growing indefinitely, improving search with high-dimensional policies and supporting the use of open-weight LLMs. The proposed PP-ProPS is evaluated on both continuous and discrete control problems spanning Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) locomotion, classic control, highway driving, and robotic arm manipulation. Compared to Vanilla ProPS, the proposed PP-ProPS outperforms ProPS in seven of the ten evaluated tasks, and surpasses conventional RL methods including PPO, SAC, and TRPO, in five of the six tasks.
bullets: Addresses the exposure of proprietary policy parameters, environmental parameters, and reward histories when using cloud LLM APIs for RL policy optimization.
Applies client-side secret transformations to policy parameters and rewards, and avoids requiring the true optimal episodic return.
Provides individual reward components to give the LLM more informative policy feedback.
Uses a bounded prompt history to prevent indefinite growth, supporting high-dimensional policies and open-weight LLMs.
Evaluated across continuous and discrete control tasks; it outperformed Vanilla ProPS on 7 of 10 tasks and conventional RL methods on 5 of 6 tasks.

papers.abstract: Active perception is essential for robotic manipulation when fixed viewpoints leave task-relevant information occluded or unobserved. However, enabling vision-language-action (VLA) models to reason across changing viewpoints and actively acquire informative observations remains challenging. We present ActiveScale, a framework that advances active perception through coordinated model, data, and hardware designs. Our model augments a VLA with historical video observations and explicit camera-pose supervision, using per-frame pose tokens and a lightweight prediction head to associate observations across viewpoints and support a coherent understanding of the scene. To learn from the camera motion naturally present in human activity, we introduce a scalable human--robot mid-training recipe using 1000 hours of egocentric and robotic data, adapting the model to temporal inputs and pose supervision. We further introduce Active-perception Mobile-manipulation Platform (AMP), a robotic platform that supports active perception and mobile manipulation through single-operator teleoperation, enabling scalable collection of demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes and manipulation. Experiments demonstrate improved success rates on active-perception tasks, while ablation studies validate the contributions of camera-pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training. Together, these components provide an integrated foundation for studying and developing active perception in robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses occlusion and missing task information caused by fixed viewpoints in robotic manipulation.
Augments a vision-language-action model with historical video, per-frame camera-pose tokens, and pose supervision.

Introduces AMP, a teleoperable platform for collecting demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes with manipulation.
Experiments report improved active-perception success rates; ablations support pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training.

papers.abstract: Robotic data generation is a promising paradigm for scaling robot learning without collecting large-scale real-world data. However, generating geometrically diverse yet physically valid data for contact-rich tasks remains challenging, especially when success depends on precise geometric interfaces. Standard shape augmentation methods often distort task-critical interfaces, resulting in invalid contact relationships, e.g., fit mismatches or interpenetration, rendering downstream interactions infeasible. To address these limitations, we propose a function-preserving Real-to-Sim-to-Real framework that generates synthetic demonstrations from reconstructed assets without teleoperated source trajectories. Our method augments task-relevant object geometries through constraint-guided mesh deformation, together with physically consistent transfer of task poses and collision proxies. Visual domain randomization is further applied during simulation rollouts, enabling robust zero-shot policy deployment without real-world fine-tuning. Extensive experiments in both real-world and simulation settings demonstrate that our method enables robust generalization across unseen object geometries and diverse visual conditions in contact-rich and long-horizon tasks. Our method provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning for contact-rich tasks via shape deformation.
bullets: Addresses invalid contacts caused by standard shape augmentation in contact-rich manipulation.
Uses constraint-guided mesh deformation to preserve task-critical geometric interfaces.
Transfers task poses and collision proxies consistently while applying visual domain randomization in simulation.
Generates demonstrations without teleoperated source trajectories and supports zero-shot real-world deployment.
Experiments show robust generalization in simulated and real settings across unseen geometries and diverse visual conditions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our function-preserving Real2Sim2Real pipeline. Geometry-aware Real2Sim reconstructs and aligns the background mesh Msce and object meshes Mobj . Starting from Mobj , we generate diverse, functionally valid geometries Md by applying slippage-preserving reshaping for stretching and as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) deformation for bending, while preserving annotated task-critical interfaces, mesh topology, and vertex correspondences. These correspondences enable the consistent transfer of task poses Gd and collision proxies Cd, yielding augmented asset bundles (Md, Gd, Cd) that maintain task-critical contact relations. The augmented assets are then used across parallel, domain-randomized simulation environments to generate a synthetic dataset D for policy training. Finally, the policy πθ enables zero-shot deployment across unseen object shapes and visual perturbations.

Fig. 1. Overview of our function-preserving data generation framework for zero-shot Real-to-Sim-to-Real manipulation. Starting from geometryaware reconstructions of the workspace and objects, our shape augmentation increases geometric diversity while preserving task-critical interfaces. In contrast, axis-aligned scaling and shape-library curation may produce invalid geometries (e.g., interface distortion and fit mismatches). The augmented assets are combined with visual and calibration domain randomization to generate synthetic demonstrations for policy training, enabling robust zeroshot deployment to unseen object geometries and visual perturbations.

Fig. 6. Qualitative comparison of shape-augmentation methods in simulation. Axis-aligned scaling [12] can distort task-critical interfaces, causing assembly mismatch or interpenetration. Shape-library curation [11] may yield missing or incompatible functional structures. In contrast, our method preserves mesh correspondence, functional constraints, contact surfaces, and transferred task poses, producing diverse yet physically executable variants.

Fig. 7. Simulation success rates for FPSA and two shape-augmentation baselines. All methods use identical randomization settings, with 3,000 training episodes and 50 held-out test environments per task. While all methods perform similarly on the pick-up task, our method consistently outperforms both baselines on the contact-rich and long-horizon tasks, underscoring the importance of preserving task-critical interfaces and contact relations.

Fig. 8. Policy performance versus the number of augmented training shapes under a fixed budget of synthetic episodes. Greater shape diversity consistently improves success rates, with pronounced gains on contact-rich and long-horizon tasks. the importance of function preservation depends on the degree of geometric interaction. All methods achieve nearly saturated performance on pick-up because its coarse grasp affordances tolerate moderate geometric mismatch. The performance gaps widen substantially for contact-rich tasks: FPSA achieves success rates above 80% on screw fastening, assembly, and single-gear extraction, whereas both baselines remain at or below 65%. This advantage persists in longhorizon gear extraction, where bore mismatches can cause multiple stacked gears to simultaneously interpenetrate the central shaft, leading to severe numerical instability. These results demonstrate that geometric diversity alone is insufficient for contact-rich data generation. Reliable policy learning requires augmented instances to preserve task-critical interfaces and contact relations.

papers.abstract: Robotic piano playing has emerged as a standard benchmark for dexterous bimanual manipulation, yet progress on it has been measured almost entirely by note accuracy -- which keys are pressed (pitch) and when (onset) -- leaving the musical dynamics essential for expressive performance neither rewarded nor evaluated. We propose CANTABILE, a dynamics-aware framework for robotic piano performance that (i) closes the score-to-contact loop by conditioning the policy on upcoming velocity goals and mapping each key's angular velocity at onset back to MIDI velocity, (ii) couples a velocity-fidelity reward with an onset-coverage reward, so that dynamics cannot be improved by omitting difficult notes, and (iii) refines a frozen dynamics-aware base policy with an alpha-scaled, finger-only residual that localizes strike-intensity adaptation away from nominal note execution. On EXPRESSIVE-51, a dynamics-rich 51-song subset of RoboPianist, CANTABILE raises Velocity F1 -- jointly measuring pitch, onset, and intensity within a +/-8 MIDI-velocity tolerance -- from 0.06 to 0.34 over the RoboPianist baseline, improves all 51 songs, more than halves matched-note velocity error, and reduces log-mel distance to reference audio by 8%. Intensity-randomized training further enables runtime control of performance intensity without retraining.
bullets: Addresses the gap between conventional pitch/onset metrics and musically expressive performance.
Conditions control on upcoming velocity goals and maps key angular velocity to MIDI velocity.
Combines velocity-fidelity and onset-coverage rewards to discourage skipping difficult notes.
Uses a frozen base policy with an alpha-scaled, finger-only residual for strike-intensity adaptation.

On EXPRESSIVE-51, improves Velocity F1 from 0.06 to 0.34, more than halves matched-note velocity error, and reduces log-mel distance by 8%; intensity can also be adjusted at runtime without retraining.

papers.abstract: Dexterous in-hand manipulation requires policies that coordinate high-DoF hand joints through intermittent, contact-rich interaction. Beyond target-orientation tracking, such policies must discover finger gaits that preserve object stability while adapting to geometry, anisotropy, pose, contact, and sensing changes. We propose \method, a tactile-conditioned behavior prior model for dexterous reorientation. \method distills multi-scale sphere specialists into a latent controller and lets downstream policies reuse the fixed tactile prior through residual latent actions, reducing renewed exploration from raw joint commands. The prior conditions on tactile-proprioceptive history so latent behavior reflects the current hand-object interaction. We evaluate arbitrary-pose transfer across anisotropic objects, commanded-axis rotation, and an arm-hand Grasp-to-AnyPose task in which the robot must grasp, lift, transport, and reach goal poses for novel tool geometries and generalized placements. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method accelerates training and enables stable policies where matched raw-action PPO remains near failure, with successful sim-to-real transfer in in-hand and arm-hand tasks.
bullets: Targets contact-rich, high-DoF manipulation requiring finger gaits that maintain object stability under changing geometry, pose, and sensing.
Distills multi-scale sphere specialists into a latent controller conditioned on tactile-proprioceptive history.
Downstream policies reuse the fixed prior through residual latent actions instead of exploring directly from raw joint commands.
Evaluated on arbitrary-pose transfer, commanded-axis rotation, and arm-hand Grasp-to-AnyPose tasks involving novel tool geometries and placements.
Experiments report faster training, stable policies where matched raw-action PPO nearly fails, and successful sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.
authors: Yuxuan Kuang, Jiashun Wang, Yixuan Sun, Yufei Ye, Sungjae Park, Umar Iqbal, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Shubham Tulsiani
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between natural human-like behavior and robustness to varied object poses and goals.

Supports demonstrations from mocap or hand–object reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video.
Learns skills including functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and throw-and-catch.
Reports improved generalization and functionality over baselines, with transfer across simulators and to the real world.

papers.abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual-tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.602 to 0.885. Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases $\pi_{0.5}$'s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1% SFT baseline to 70.8%. These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. authors: Zebin Xing, Yuhang Zheng, Yupeng Zheng, Yichen Zhang, Zichen Li, Shangqing Zhou, Yujie Zang, Yuchen Liu, Zhongpu Xia, Haoran Li, Qichao Zhang

papers.abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
authors: Xinxin Liu, Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Ming Li, Wentao Bao, Chen Chen, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses reliance on powerful closed-source planners by improving the planner model itself.
Combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning.
Uses harness-specific adapters to unify training across VLA skill invocation and control-code generation while keeping execution components fixed.
On LIBERO-PRO, raises a 9B planner’s success rate from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory.

papers.abstract: Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability. Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.
authors: Rundong Luo, Yunong Liu, Di Cao, Matthew Tancik, Shyamal Buch, Colton Stearns, Wenqi Xian
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible reconstruction and physically correct object placement.
Combines geometric, visual, and physical tools with agent-driven edit-and-validate loops in a physics simulator.
Improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement across diverse inputs.
Produces physically stable scenes that better predict real-robot policy outcomes than the baseline.
Supports more reliable replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.

Geometry, material, and lighting agents construct the surrounding scene. papers.abstract: Humanoid-human interaction requires robots to operate under severe partial observability: during close physical contact, the human partner is occluded, truncated, or outside the robot's field of view, causing pose estimation to fail and often necessitating external tracking or privileged human state. At the same time, heavy mutual occlusions introduce errors into the human-human motion-capture data used for learning. We present REACT, a framework for learning deployable humanoid-human interaction policies from human-human demonstrations. REACT treats semantic contact structure as the key supervisory signal connecting demonstration processing, interaction learning, and onboard control. First, a VLM-guided contact modeling and retargeting pipeline identifies semantically meaningful contacts and transfers them onto humanoid-human geometry while preserving interaction structure. Using these annotations, privileged interaction policies learn physically grounded behaviors through interaction-aware contact rewards and are then distilled into deployable egocentric depth policies trained entirely from onboard sensing using photorealistic human depth rendering. To address severe partial observability, we introduce generative partner-state modeling objectives that predict partner motion from occluded egocentric views. We evaluate REACT in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid across five contact-rich interactions. Semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interactions, while generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most under heavy occlusion. On real hardware, REACT performs all five interactions using onboard sensing alone.
authors: Yuto Shibata, Kotaro Amaya, Kashu Yamazaki, Lalit Jayanti, Yoshimitsu Aoki, Mariko Isogawa, Katerina Fragkiadaki
bullets: Addresses partial observability and occlusion that make human pose estimation unreliable during close contact.
Uses semantic contact annotations to retarget human-human demonstrations onto humanoid-human geometry while preserving interaction structure.
Learns privileged interaction policies with contact-aware rewards, then distills them into egocentric depth policies using onboard sensing.
Generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall in four of five evaluated interactions, especially under heavy occlusion.
Demonstrated all five contact-rich interactions in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 using onboard sensing alone.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of REACT. REACT first annotates semantic contacts in human–human demonstrations with a VLM and retargets them onto the humanoid while preserving them. A privileged teacher then learns the interaction with contact rewards and is finally distilled into an egocentric depth student that predicts the partner’s motion and runs on the real robot.
Figure 4: Student rollouts on held-out motions in simulation (inset: egocentric depth input)

Figure 6: Long-horizon behavior: three consecutive hugs in a single episode. A continuous ∼30 s rollout in which the policy completes the hug interaction three times in a row, with no reset or re-initialisation between repetitions. The ten snapshots are read in boustrophedon order, following the arrows. After each embrace the robot releases the partner, re-approaches, and re-establishes contact, so the three hug cycles appear as three separate close-contact phases across the panels. The policy sustains repeated contact-rich interaction over a long horizon rather than a single one-shot contact.

Figure 7: VLM skill-selection state machine. Solid boxes are states and dashed boxes are the policies they invoke: the HOMIE locomotion controller for Search, Approach, and Retreat, and one of the five per-interaction students for Interact.

Figure 3: Within each interaction, frames are split into moments when the partner is hard to see (blue), either too close to fit in the view or largely out of view, and the remaining frames (gray). (Appendix C.4).

Figure 13: Qualitative retargeting comparison. Rows: the five contact-rich actions (hug, handshake, pat-on-back, high-five, link-arms). Columns: the original human–human demonstration and four retargets (GMR, OmniRetarget, Ours w/o VLM filtering, Ours), each at the action’s peak-contact frame. The red arrow marks the demonstrated contact the retarget must reproduce on the G1. Ours establishes the touch on the robot surface where the baselines reach short or push apart.

Figure 10: Why the external pose estimation-based method fails at contact range. Temporally ordered snapshots of an external-pose rollout, read left to right, with the ground-truth partner (green, Human (Sim)) and the HMR2.0 reconstruction (red, HMR2.0 Prediction) overlaid against the robot (black). Left three: high-five; as the partner’s hand leaves the robot’s egocentric field of view, the reconstructed hand position deviates sharply from the ground truth at the moment of contact. Right three: hug; at the instant of embrace the partner’s torso occludes the camera, and the reconstruction collapses into a large error behind the true mesh. The estimator degrades precisely in the close-contact, self-occluded regime that REACT’s end-to-end student handles directly from depth.

Figure 12: Body correspondence projects the SMPL-X mesh onto either the G1 or the partnercapsule surface. The offline registration introduced in Sec. D.2 establishes a dense body correspondence that maps every SMPL-X body vertex to a (link, plocal) pair, so the same mesh can be projected onto either target surface, the Unitree G1 robot or the partner’s SMPL-X collision capsules. The three columns show one identical set of colour-coded SMPL-X vertices in three configurations, from left to right: projected onto the G1 robot surface, in their SMPL-X template positions, and projected onto the partner capsule surface. Each colour denotes the G1 link a vertex is registered to, and the connecting lines join the same representative vertices across the three configurations, so that any contact vertex can be carried onto the corresponding robot or capsule surface by forward kinematics. The columns are drawn at true relative scale, exposing the proportion mismatch between the human template and the shorter G1 that the registration must bridge. The dense map covers the full template at a mean vertex-to-surface residual of 0.89mm, well below the ϵ = 10 cm contact threshold.

Figure 11: VLM contact filtering, qualitative examples. Distance candidates and their VLM verdicts on the five contact-rich Inter-X actions (rows: hug, hand-shake, pat-on-back, high-five, link-arms), sampled at 1 s intervals over a 4 s window (columns). Green markers are candidates kept after VLM verification, labelled essential or incidental. Red markers are Stage 1 distance candidates the VLM removes as spurious near-contacts. The proximity test fires on many transient arm passes; the VLM stage prunes them while preserving the genuine contacts, which is the precision gain quantified in Tab. 8.

Figure 14: User-study web interface (one trial). The original demonstration (3-view orbit, top) and the four blinded retarget conditions A–D (middle) are played synchronously; the participant gives a strict 1–4 ranking for each of the three questions (bottom). Full ranking criteria are in Sec. E.5.

Figure 5: Generalization across partner distance and orientation. REACT performs pat-on-back with the partner at 70 cm and 130 cm and with the partner back-on or side-on to the robot; the per-interaction student reaches and holds the back contact in every condition from onboard depth alone.

Figure 8: One continuous rollout with VLM skill selection. No interaction is specified in advance. From left to right: the partner opens their arms, and the VLM selects the hug student; the partner is then displaced mid-rollout, and the robot re-finds them, approaches, and switches to the hand-shake student, all without a reset.

Figure 9: In-loop human depth rendering closes the sim-to-real gap. Egocentric depth of a hug frame. Capsule: the partner as collision primitives, blocky and non-human. SMPL-X Mesh: the partner rendered as a realistic body mesh. SMPL-X Mesh + Scene (Ours): our full rendering with the randomised scene. This last variant closely resembles the real-sensor depth shown in Figure 1 of the main paper.

Table 2: Teacher tracking results. Contact recall at 15 cm, mean ± std over 3 seeds.
Table 3: Student policy results. Contact recall (%) at 30 cm on the held-out evaluation split, mean over 5 room layouts.

Ext. human pose (HMR2.0) drives the policy from partner state produced by an external human-pose estimator while Ours (E2E) outputs actions end-to-end from egocentric depth and proprioception. Both rows use earlier model settings than Table 3 and are evaluated on the same held-out motions.

Peraction and total precision, recall, and F1 as across-clip mean ± std under per-frame vertex-distance matching at ϵ = 10 cm on the SMPL-X rest-pose template, after symmetric-pair deduplication. The verifier removes spurious near-contacts rather than acting as a stricter detector.

Table 10: Per-action retargeting Recall and Precision (ϵ=10 cm, per-event, across-clip mean±std, %). For each action the two columns are Recall (R, vertex-pair-targeted) and Precision (P, body-part τ0); the Total columns equal the Recall and Precision columns of the main paper’s retargeting table. Recall uses 16 GT clips per action (58 in total for OmniRetarget, whose collision solver makes the rest infeasible); Precision averages over clips with at least one predicted event.

Relaxing ϵ shows that for Ours the contact is in fact established but slightly displaced: Recall rises from 59.4% at 10 cm to 80.0% at 15 cm and 92.0% at 20 cm.

papers.abstract: Understanding contact and tactile magnitude in hand-object interaction is a key step toward physically intelligent systems, yet learning such representations is limited by the cost and restricted coverage of tactile measurements. We present Touch-JEPA, a framework for learning tactile representations from hand-object videos with limited tactile supervision. We first introduce a self-supervised pretraining objective that learns from video alone without tactile supervision. Using video-derived hand geometry, Touch-JEPA predicts masked visual features at corresponding hand-surface locations from spatial and temporal context, encouraging the representation to capture latent contact dynamics. We then extend this formulation to joint representation learning, where masked prediction is applied to all videos while tactile supervision is available only for a labeled subset, grounding the shared representation in measured contact and magnitude. With self-supervised pretraining alone, simple supervised readouts on frozen Touch-JEPA features outperform supervised baselines in contact discrimination and tactile magnitude estimation across three human-hand benchmarks, and transfer to robotic hands without robot tactile training data. Joint learning with limited tactile supervision further improves contact and magnitude estimation on the human-hand benchmarks. Together, these results show that hand-object video can provide scalable self-supervision for tactile representation learning, while limited tactile measurements provide complementary physical grounding.
authors: Minseong Kweon, Qiao Feng, Yiming Huang, Lingjie Liu
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited coverage of tactile measurements for learning contact and tactile magnitude.
Uses video-only self-supervision to predict masked visual features at hand-surface locations from spatial and temporal context.
Extends to joint learning by applying masked prediction broadly while grounding representations with tactile labels from only a subset of videos.
Frozen pretrained features outperform supervised baselines on contact discrimination and tactile magnitude estimation across three human-hand benchmarks.
Transfers to robotic hands without robot tactile training data; limited tactile supervision further improves human-hand performance.

When tactile annotations are available, joint training additionally supervises contact and magnitude predictions decoded from masked x-encoder states before the predictor, providing complementary physical grounding for the shared representation.

papers.abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.
authors: Qiayuan Liao, Yiyang Shao, Junfeng Long, Kevin Zakka, Roberto Horowitz, Pieter Abbeel, Koushil Sreenath
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of learning across large human-motion datasets.
Fits a shared differentiable dynamics model from simulator transitions and trains it jointly with the tracking policy.
Uses short imagined rollouts and backpropagation-through-time to provide analytic policy gradients.
On the reported benchmark, it exceeds a 7-day, 128-GPU baseline after 3 hours on one GPU, with 25 versus 179 failures; zero failures are reached after 9.8 hours on two GPUs.
Transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions, while maintaining stable prediction error as motion data scales from 1 to 264 hours.

papers.abstract: While large-scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV (Fast Retargeting with Dynamics Validation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second, approximately up to 136 times faster than GMR and ProtoMotions, while robot-specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics-based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact-related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state-of-the-art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/.
authors: Daniel Marew, Sangjun Park, Nisal Perera, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Addresses the computational cost and manual effort of adapting diverse human motion capture data to different humanoid robots.
Uses constrained kinematic retargeting with a custom SQP solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk processing.
Incorporates robot-specific constraints to reduce ground penetration and self-collision artifacts.
Applies contact-implicit iLQR dynamics validation to detect infeasible motions and refine foot floating or skating.
Evaluations include motion-tracking reinforcement learning and sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree G1 humanoid.

papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal models have shown promise as direct robot action policies, yet whether they grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions and can apply that understanding to guide action remains underexplored. We investigate this question using contact-rich manipulation as a representative testbed, examining tactile understanding as a concrete instance of this broader capability. Contact-rich manipulation requires interpreting tactile feedback and adjusting actions after obstruction. Existing learned tactile policies acquire these capabilities through specialized pretraining and per-task optimization, with substantial data and training costs. We present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, which summarizes expert demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for contact assessment and corrective action. GPT-6-Astra combines this context with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate control commands and adjust actions through contact feedback. Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves 93.8\% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks. Overall performance is comparable to state-of-the-art policies, with higher success on selected tasks. On Insert Hole, tactile feedback improves success from 31\% to 99\%. Execution analysis further demonstrates contact-guided probing and correction, supporting manipulation progress through explicit expert experience and online feedback.

papers.abstract: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks. However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress. In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages, existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, i.e., a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion. To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world--action generation toward intended future. We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation.Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, TaskWAM provides strong plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid robots.

The approach transfers across WAM architectures and diverse robot embodiments, including single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots.

papers.abstract: Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) requires a robot to rearrange objects that block access to its goal. For a pushing robot, progress may depend on a setup push that enables a later opening without itself clearing a passage. The number of candidate sequences can grow exponentially with sequence length, making physics-based search costly. We introduce the Search-trained Push Action Ranker (SPAR), which learns to prioritize push primitives from simulated search outcomes. Searches over sequences of up to two pushes per object provide supervision that distinguishes immediate openings from setup pushes. A transformer trained with regression and ranking losses scores primitives using contact tokens conditioned on scene geometry and reachability regions. The same model guides simulator evaluations in SPAR Search and selects actions for direct execution in SPAR Policy. Both modes solve successive keyhole problems that open access to neighboring free-space regions within a NAMO planner. Across successful runs on $300$ simulated two-push keyhole problems, SPAR Search reduces median simulator calls by $7.0\times$, leading to a $3.8\times$ reduction in planning time relative to Random Search. Without retraining, the same ranker guides search on $600$ keyhole problems which have no solution within two pushes. At a depth limit of five pushes, SPAR Search achieves $50.7\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $20.2\%$ for Random Search. These gains carry over to NAMO planning: on hard simulated scenes, SPAR Search achieves $47\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $21\%$ for Random Search. In real-robot experiments, SPAR Policy succeeds in $37/40$ trials without a physics-based digital twin, compared with $33/40$ for SPAR Search and $27/40$ for Random Search.

Supports both search guidance (SPAR Search) and direct action selection (SPAR Policy) within a keyhole-based NAMO planner.
On simulated two-push problems, SPAR Search reduces median simulator calls 7.0× and planning time 3.8× versus Random Search.

papers.abstract: Trajectory tracking for compliant robots is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and modeling uncertainties, often requiring learning-based methods to avoid explicit parameter identification. Iterative Learning Control (ILC) ensures theoretically high precision and preserves the passive compliance of the robot. However, traditional ILC requires a separate learning phase for each new trajectory. Conversely, Reinforcement Learning (RL) generalizes to new trajectories, but practically suffers from high sample complexity and limited tracking precision. This work proposes Reinforced Iterative Learning Control (RILC) that combines the strengths of both approaches to achieve fast adaptation and guaranteed tracking convergence across diverse trajectories. By establishing a concurrent coupling between the two controllers, RILC overcomes the high initial errors and slow adaptation of traditional ILC, enabling high-performance tracking from the very first trials. In this architecture, ILC provides high-quality samples, while RL contributes as a generalizing best-effort policy across iterations. Additionally, a theoretical proof is presented to show that the RL component preserves ILC stability and, under specific conditions, can also reduce the error bound asymptotically. The efficacy of this framework is demonstrated through simulation and experiments on an underactuated 4-degree-of-freedom serial elastic robot using different trajectories and modeling mismatches.

Theoretical analysis shows RL preserves ILC stability and can asymptotically reduce the tracking-error bound under specific conditions.
Simulation and experiments on an underactuated 4-DOF serial elastic robot demonstrate tracking across trajectories and modeling mismatches.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework. We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions. Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination. To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences. GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion. Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment. Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.
authors: Youwei Zhou, Bohan Hou, Yankai Fu, Yaoxu Lyu, Yifan Ye, Shilin Shan, Chen Guo, Jiaming Liu, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Shanghang Zhang, Jianfei Yang, Zhihe Lu
bullets: Evaluates GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation with a lightweight agent execution framework.

Introduces LIBERO-GeoMotion, where GPT-6 Astra achieves 11.1% zero-shot success on geometry-constrained tasks; reported results also include 26.92% on RoboDojo and 76.0% on RoboTwin 2.0.
Real-world tests show simple zero-shot execution is feasible, but motion feasibility, physical safety, precise control, and inference latency remain deployment barriers.

papers.abstract: We introduce JAXbounce, a continuous control pong-like benchmark designed to evaluate active inference beyond discrete, low dimensional environments. JAXbounce combines continuous states and stochastic dynamics in discrete time with flexible and composable observation models that allow representing the environment as a state vector or a pixel grid, corruptible through the rich family of noise models we provide. It is fully differentiable and parallelisable in JAX. We run over 10,000 agent simulations on our environment comparing a baseline deterministic solution, to a state-based active inference agent with Unscented Kalman Filter perception and expected free energy planning, and a pixel based agent whose measurement model is a pretrained neural network encoder. All agents are evaluated across three scenarios of increasing difficulty with eight different noise conditions. Our experiments characterise how performance of continuous state agents scales with planning, planning horizons, observation modalities and knowledge of the noise process, exhibiting preference-oriented behaviour even in the presence of increasing uncertainty. We release JAXbounce as a reproducible benchmark for continuous control active inference research.
authors: Chaitanya Kaul, Markus Klar, Sebastian Stein, Fraser C. Paterson, John H. Williamson, Roderick Murray-Smith
bullets: Targets active inference beyond discrete, low-dimensional environments using continuous states and stochastic dynamics.
Supports composable state-vector or pixel-grid observations with varied noise models.
Provides JAX-based differentiability and parallelisation for scalable, reproducible experiments.
Compares deterministic, state-based, and pixel-based agents across three difficulty levels and eight noise conditions.
Findings characterise effects of planning, horizon, observation modality, and noise knowledge, including preference-oriented behaviour under uncertainty.
