papers.abstract: Object-centric reinforcement learning agents typically receive each object's position in a fixed global frame, even though their decisions usually depend on where objects are relative to one another. These absolute views often fail to capture the local context that is most relevant to the agent's behavior. As a result, an agent must relearn the same response at every location where a configuration can occur, and its performance collapses when the scene is merely shifted. In this work, we propose a shift toward Object-Relative Coordinates fixed to Anchor (ORCA), where entities are described in a relative frame of reference. To operationalize this idea, we introduce Object-Relative inductive-Bias Transformers (ORBiT), a transformer-based architecture for processing anchor-relative inputs in reinforcement learning. Our results suggest these relative representations improve performance for both MLP and transformer agents. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ORBiT outperforms the pixel-based PPO baseline, achieving an aggregate HNS IQM greater than 1.0 over 13 Atari games. ORBiT learns the game of Foosball from scratch, dominating all baselines. In our controlled Tag environment, we further show that ORCA extends to rotations, that ORBiT generalizes to unseen numbers of distractors, and that these gains require a decision-relevant anchor.
authors: Cedric Derstroff, Jannis Bl\"uml, Janosch Moos, Michael Girstl, Zihan Ye, Debora Clever, Kristian Kersting
bullets: Absolute coordinates force agents to relearn equivalent behaviors at different scene locations and can fail under simple shifts.
The proposed ORCA representation encodes entities in anchor-relative coordinates, while ORBiT uses a transformer to process them.
Relative representations improve both MLP and transformer agents; ORBiT also outperforms a pixel-based PPO baseline across 13 Atari games.
ORBiT learns Foosball from scratch and dominates the evaluated baselines.
In controlled Tag experiments, ORCA handles rotations and unseen distractor counts, but requires a decision-relevant anchor.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with $\pi_0$, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.
authors: Matteo Cercola, Katie Z Luo, Milan Ganai, John Alora, Simone Formentin, Marco Pavone
bullets: Existing VLA reasoning compresses alternative valid plans into one representation, limiting revision and control.
GPL models the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over choices such as objects, grasps, or routes.
Plans can be sampled for coverage, selected on request for steering, or reweighted using deployment outcomes without retraining.
In SimplerEnv, steering increased request-following executions from 0.48 to 0.94; native action-distribution guidance showed no reliable gain.
Explicit plans help most when they encode decision information not already determined by the observation.

papers.abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.
authors: Xiaoxu Xu, Hao Li, Hongtao Zhang, Yili Tang, Jiafei Cao, Junhao Cai, Haoxiang Ma, Weixin Li, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the gap between predicting how scene geometry evolves and using those predictions to generate actions.
Pretrains predictive geometric representations from dense 3D features in multi-view video, preserving scene structure and temporal evolution.
Uses action supervision on geometric transitions to learn a complementary motor representation emphasizing action-relevant changes.
Transfers geometry through queries and uses motor features to guide intermediate action-generation features during downstream training.
Improves policies across simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks, including a 10.4-point absolute gain on WidowX, with transfer across VLA architectures and WAMs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of complementary predictive representation pretraining. A frozen 3D foundation model extracts dense geometric features from multi-view video observations, which are compressed by the Hierarchical Geometric Tokenizer and temporally modeled by a causal Slot-Temporal Mixer to produce the predictive geometric representation. Geometry reconstruction, masked geometric representation prediction, and geometric transition prediction jointly shape this representation to preserve scene structure and capture its temporal evolution. The resulting geometric transitions are used with action supervision to extract an action-aware motor representation, providing complementary predictive and motor information for policy learning.

Figure 3: Overview of representation-guided policy post-training. The frozen pretrained model provides the predictive geometric representation G and motor representation Z as privileged supervision. The two representations are transferred through role-specific pathways: G supervises dedicated geometry queries, while Z aligns with intermediate features along the action-generation pathway.

Figure 1: Comparison of geometry-guidance paradigms for policy learning. (a) Input-centric methods augment policies with spatial information derived from current observations. (b) Prediction-centric methods use future-world or predictive targets as additional supervision. (c) Our approach learns a predictive geometric representation from dense geometric features and derives a complementary motor representation from the evolution of scene geometry. The two representations are transferred through role-specific guidance pathways during training and are not required at inference time.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure. Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy. To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target. Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type. When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.
authors: Jiatong Li, Jisheng Dang, Qiangqiang Ma, Bimei Wang, Jingwen Zhao, Wenjun Ma, Juncheng Li, Hong Peng, Bin Hu
bullets: Targets VLA failures caused by deviations from nominal task conditions, including object-position and instruction perturbations.
Uses Planner, Grounder, Verifier, and Correction Agents to parse tasks, bind references, monitor execution, diagnose failures, and select recovery actions.
Retains the pretrained VLA as the default action generator when no intervention is needed.
Demonstrates improved robustness across multiple VLA backbones on LIBERO-PRO, with state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.

papers.abstract: Tactile representation learning for dexterous manipulation often requires substantial robot-side data collection, limiting its scalability across different hands and sensors. We explore whether large-scale human hand-object interaction (HOI) data can provide a useful prior for robotic tactile learning. To this end, we propose HuTact, a framework that pretrains tactile-aware hand representations from human HOI data without requiring real tactile signals during pretraining. HuTact transfers the interaction structure learned from human hand motions to robotic tactile observations and can be further adapted with a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data. We evaluate HuTact on tactile perception and manipulation tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning. Across these tasks, human HOI pretraining improves data efficiency and provides a strong initialization for downstream learning. Notably, with HOI pretraining followed by midtraining on unlabeled robot play data, HuTact achieves 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using only 25\% of the labeled downstream data, comparable to training from scratch on the full labeled dataset (88.23%). These results suggest that human interaction data can serve as a scalable complementary source for robotic tactile representation learning.
authors: Yeonguk Yu, Jaehong Kim, Byungok Han
bullets: Addresses the need for costly, robot-specific tactile data collection across diverse hands and sensors.

Improves data efficiency across grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning.
With HOI pretraining and unlabeled robot play-data midtraining, reaches 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using 25% of labeled data, comparable to 88.23% from full-data training.

papers.abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.
authors: Junha Song, Geonmo Gu, Jeongeun Park, Heejeong Nam, Lucas Maes, Byeongho Heo, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Trains one language-conditioned future predictor on simulation, robot trajectories, images, and videos.
Uses language to unify numerical actions and visual changes across heterogeneous data.
Achieves higher average MPC planning performance than domain- or task-specific latent world models.
With additional image/video data, planning robustness to action phrasing improves.
Matches an RAEv2 video-generation baseline with 6× lower training cost and 13.9× faster planning; its policy initialization enables competitive performance with up to 5.5× faster inference.

papers.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/
authors: Oliver Hausd\"orfer, Felix Minzenmay, Mani Majd, Maximilian P. Christof, Shiyuan Zhang, Angela P. Schoellig
bullets: Single-view latent action models ambiguously infer 6D movements, especially out-of-plane actions and occluded interactions.
The proposed model combines cross-attention over multiple views with sequential flow matching between latent and action experts around a frozen VLM.
Dual-view pretraining improves 6D-action decodability by 17% over single-view and yields a +13.5% downstream success-rate gain versus +6.2% for single-view.
One cross-embodiment source is sufficient for skill transfer; adding a second viewpoint is more beneficial than adding up to four additional embodiments.
Hardware experiments using human-hand demonstrations improve success by 20% over action-only policies across 850 rollouts, with benefits varying by task.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Method: We combine latent action pretraining from in-domain cross-embodiment videos with a downstream flow-matching policy. First, latent actions are inferred from a large cross-embodiment video dataset. Second, a sequential policy is learned on the latent actions and a small set of demonstrations on the target embodiment. The LAM uses a spatio-temporal transformer to merge multiple viewpoints before computing the latents. The spatial block attends to patches of other viewpoints, yielding latent actions grounded in 3D space. Latent action labels and real robot actions are jointly used to train a hierarchical downstream policy. The policy uses sequential flow matching experts and outputs actions applied to the robot.
Fig. 8. Failure modes. Models struggle with object grasping (44% of failure cases). The push task requires precision to align the gripper with the milk.

Fig. 4. Real World Tasks: We evaluate the policies and skill-transfer on six tasks consisting of novel movements, novel background, novel objects, and novel placements. For each eval task, we collect 50 human demonstrations and evaluate under settings with 0–50 robot demonstrations per task. We additionally collect an off-task play dataset across 32 tasks, totaling 1000 human demonstrations and 600 robot demonstrations.

Fig. 3. Left: Latent Action Probing. An MLP probe reconstructs ground-truth robot actions from the latents. Adding the second view improves decodability in the directions that are only ambiguously observed by single-view. Right: Cross-embodiment Learning. t-SNE showing 2D correspondence of latent actions to embodiments. Separation by color indicates separate latent per embodiment before training, while mixed colors show a latent space shared between embodiments. Shared latents already occur for a single cross-embodiment present in pretraining.

Policy success rate (SR) when scaling (left) the number of action-annotated demonstrations per task on the deployed embodiment Franka Panda, (middle) the fraction of LIBERO-90 used as off-task play data for latent video pretraining increasing task diversity. Top row shows mean success rate over all 40 tasks; bottom row split by in-distribution and heldout tasks (see Sec. IV). Successes on heldout tasks prove transfer from crossembodiment video demonstrations. (Right): The number of cross-embodiments contained in the video dataset (1 = iiwa, 2 = +kinova3, 3 = +sawyer, 4 = +ur5e) for single- and dual-view pretraining. Dual-view pretraining outperforms adding up to four cross-embodiments.

The multi-view LAM shows significantly better reconstruction of the ground-truth robot motion in y-direction. See more qualitative results in the supplementary video.

On average, using human demonstrations without any robot demonstrations increases SR by +20%, and with 5 robot demonstrations by +19%. Tasks with novel placement locations ([place]) are easiest to solve, followed by novel objects ([obj]). Middle: Multi-view video pretraining scores 46% against 21% for single-view significantly increasing SR. papers.abstract: 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) is used in indoor environments, such as smart homes, to analyze human movement and monitor human states. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar is suitable for this task because it is robust to lighting variations and does not capture images of human appearance. However, radar observations often provide insufficient information about certain body parts or contain overlapping reflections from multiple body parts, limiting accurate 3D joint localization. To address these limitations, we propose the Initialization-to-Refinement Pose Framework (I2R-Pose), comprising two stages: Motion-Aware Pose Initialization and Observation-Guided Refinement. In the first stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations and human skeletal structure to compensate for insufficient joint information and estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the second stage, separately extracted radar observation features predict joint-wise positional corrections that refine the initial pose and generate the final pose sequence. The framework supports individual and fused inputs of time-Doppler/time-range (TD/TR) maps and radar point clouds (PCs). To evaluate performance across indoor activities, we construct the Radar Motion and Spatial Information for 3D Human Pose Estimation (RaMoS-Pose) dataset, providing synchronized TD/TR maps, radar PCs, and 3D joint ground truth (GT). Evaluations on RaMoS-Pose and the publicly available MVDoppler-Pose dataset show that I2R-Pose reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and by 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose with fused inputs, compared with the best-performing existing methods evaluated on each dataset.
authors: Woo-Jin Jung, Chan-Bin Lim, Seung-Hyun Kong
bullets: Addresses missing or overlapping mmWave radar reflections that hinder accurate 3D joint localization.
Uses a two-stage pipeline: motion-aware pose initialization followed by observation-guided joint correction.
Supports TD/TR maps, radar point clouds, and their fusion.
Introduces the RaMoS-Pose dataset with synchronized radar data and 3D joint ground truth.
With fused inputs, reduces MPJPE by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose versus the best evaluated existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the I2R-Pose framework. The TD/TR-only configuration with two observation views is illustrated as an example. The Motion Branch learns joint-wise features from radar observations, while the Pose Branch sequentially performs initial pose estimation using these features and pose refinement using separately extracted observation features. The GT-based Keypoint Motion Encoder and Keypoint HPE Head are used only during training, and Cross-Modal Motion Feature Alignment guides the learning of joint-wise radar features. For visual clarity, the feature tensors are illustrated with the temporal dimension (T ) along the X-axis, the joint or token dimension (J or NO) along the Y-axis, and the channel dimension (C) along the Z-axis.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of 3D human pose estimation results on (a) MVDoppler-Pose and (b) RaMoS-Pose. Each row shows the ground-truth (GT) pose and the poses estimated by existing methods and I2R-Pose (Ours) for a representative motion. The numbers below each estimated pose indicate the MPJPE (mm) for the corresponding frame, with bold values indicating the lowest MPJPE in each row. RGB images in (b) are provided solely for visual reference.

Fig. 1. Conceptual overview of I2R-Pose. In the Motion-Aware Pose Initialization stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations (TD/TR maps, PCs, or both) and human skeletal structure to estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the subsequent Observation-Guided Refinement stage, radar observation features extracted separately from the same radar input are combined with the joint-wise features used for initial pose estimation to predict joint-wise positional corrections. These corrections are applied to the initial pose to generate the final pose sequence. The refinement process and changes in MPJPE are illustrated using a representative frame, while RGB images are provided solely for visual reference.

Fig. 3. Main feature extraction and representation processes in I2R-Pose. (a) Generation of joint-wise radar motion features through TD/TR feature extraction and Time–Joint Cross-Attention. (b) Generation of PC spatial tokens through voxel-based feature extraction and global and local tokenization. The illustrated motion features are generated in the Radar Motion Encoder, while the same tokenization structure is independently used in the Radar Observation Encoder with separate weights. (c) Construction of joint-wise motion descriptors from GT joint sequences and their transformation into keypoint motion features.

papers.abstract: Human-collected real-world robotic manipulation demonstrations often contain mixed-quality trajectories, including hesitant, indirect, or inefficient action segments. While diffusion- and flow-based policies can model such multimodal data, standard behavior cloning (BC) assigns equal likelihood to all demonstrated actions and may therefore reproduce suboptimal modes. Offline RL value estimates offer a natural signal for biasing policies toward higher-value behavioral modes, but directly fine-tuning the generative policy or using critic gradients for policy steering can amplify critic errors and induce prior drift. We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS), an offline post-training method for improving frozen one-step generative manipulation policies without updating their decoders. AWLS learns a residual noise shaper, an observation-conditioned residual correction to the policy's latent noise, and trains it with an advantage-weighted action reconstruction objective. The advantages are detached, scale-normalized, and used only as supervised weights on demonstrated actions, avoiding critic-gradient policy updates while preserving fast single-step inference. We further introduce a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for selecting pretrained checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise perturbations. Experiments on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks with clean and mixed-quality demonstrations show that AWLS improves over the frozen base policy while limiting drift from the pretrained behavior prior. Project page: https://awls-corl2026.github.io/
authors: Jiahong Tang, Jiaju He, Zhiyuan Yang, Ruyang Han, Haiyue Zhu
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality demonstrations where standard behavior cloning treats inefficient and high-quality actions equally.
Learns an observation-conditioned residual noise shaper using advantage-weighted action reconstruction.
Detaches and normalizes advantages, using them only as supervised weights to reduce critic-error amplification and prior drift.
Introduces a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for selecting checkpoints responsive to latent perturbations.
Experiments in simulated and real manipulation tasks with clean and mixed-quality data show improvement over the frozen base policy while preserving fast single-step inference.

papers.abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.
authors: Zhipeng Cao, Taoran Wu, Weiru Cui, Luke Ong, Bai Xue
bullets: Addresses degradation of learned barrier certificates when deployment dynamics differ from training dynamics.
Formulates the conditional barrier-drift condition as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test.
Uses nonnegative test supermartingales to provide anytime-valid, finite-sample false-alarm control.
Adds deterministic temporal boundary shaping for greater conservatism early in a prescribed deployment horizon.
Empirically evaluates alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates; the monitor does not guarantee pre-unsafe-entry detection or subsequent safety.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human-scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.
authors: Jiushu Li, Haoran Wang, Yumeng Liu, Zhiyang Dou, Yuan Liu, Yuexin Ma, Cheng Lin
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified models and scarce, costly data for multi-skill long-horizon HOSI generation.
Uses 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes, natural-language instructions, and a shared structured scene state.
A harness plans action stages, invokes experts through their native interfaces, and updates the evolving world after each action.
Bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation reduce motion and manipulation artifacts.
Experiments and a perceptual user study report the best task completion and interaction quality among evaluated methods, with greater data diversity.

papers.abstract: Simulation-ready world reconstruction demands physical interactivity beyond visual realism, which existing black-box 3D generation fails to deliver. We present NeoWorld-3, a coding-agent framework that reconstructs interactive 3D worlds from visual observations via tunable, executable programs. At its core, NeoSDK provides the underlying computational engine for low-level geometries, part composition, differentiable parameter refinement, and physics validation. At the same time, NeoMCP exposes these capabilities as structured, tool-callable APIs for vision-language agents to visually inspect, edit code, and iteratively refine programs. Through a hierarchical coordinator-worker architecture, the framework scales seamlessly from standalone articulated objects to complex compositional scenes. Evaluations across object-level and scene-level reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate that NeoWorld-3 achieves state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness. Crucially, manipulation trajectories planned within our reconstructed twins achieve successful zero-shot execution on a physical dual-arm robot, completing the Real-Sim-Real loop.
authors: Eachen Soong, Zijian Niu, Haoran Xu, Yihong Dong, Yunbo Wang, Xiaokang Yang
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually realistic 3D generation and simulation-ready physical interactivity.
Uses NeoSDK for geometry, composition, differentiable refinement, and physics validation.
Uses NeoMCP tool APIs with vision-language agents to inspect, edit, and iteratively refine reconstruction code.
A hierarchical coordinator-worker design scales from articulated objects to complex scenes.
Reports state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness, with successful Real-Sim-Real execution on a dual-arm robot.

At the object level, vision-language agents construct tunable geometry programs, revising program structure based on real-sim feedback and optimizing geometric parameters through differentiable refinement, with parts and joints added for articulation. At the scene level, object subagents reconstruct individual assets, while a scene agent coordinates object integration and manages global layout using multi-view observations. Object- and scene-level feedback loops guide reconstruction and revision, producing simulation-ready scenes for sim-based policy optimization and sim-to-real deployment.

NeoWorld-3 achieves higher geometric and visual fidelity at the object level, along with more accurate spatial layouts, object correspondence, proportions, materials, and colors at the scene level.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.
authors: Zhan Yi, Yuchen Wang, Chao Li, Lei Hong, Boyuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of full future-image prediction and the loss of local detail in heavily compressed latent dynamics.
Predicts spatially structured future latent changes from visual and language inputs.
Uses change-aware supervision to emphasize regions expected to change most.
Feeds predicted future changes into action generation through a future-to-action interface.
Achieves 79.0% success on LIBERO-Long and raises CALVIN average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564, while updating 2.95% of parameters in the second training stage.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our world-to-action framework. The shared multimodal backbone produces action-query representations, from which a future-change decoder predicts patch-level future latent change. During training, a frozen visual encoder provides change-aware supervision using current and future observations. The predicted future latent change is then incorporated into the action representation through a gated future-to-action interface to generate the full action chunk. Future observations are not required during inference.

Figure 3. Patch-level future latent change and change-aware supervision. (a) A frozen visual encoder extracts patch-level features from current and future observations. Their differences at corresponding patch locations define the ground-truth future latent change ∆Z∗ t , preserving the spatial structure across camera views. (b) The magnitude of each ground-truth change vector is used to compute patch-wise supervision weights, assigning larger relative weights to patches with greater changes. (c) The predicted future latent change ∆̂Zt is supervised against ∆Z∗ t using weighted regression and directional losses. All patches contribute to the training objective with different weights.

Figure 1. Motivation for spatially structured future latent change. (a) In robotic manipulation, future changes are often concentrated around the robot arm and manipulated objects, while much of the background remains unchanged. (b) Highly compressed state representations do not explicitly preserve the spatial locations of these changes, whereas patch-level future latent change retains their spatial structure and provides future information for action generation.
Figure 4. Per-task success rates on LIBERO-Long. Comparison between the Action-only baseline and PLaCA across all 10 tasks, with 20 closed-loop rollouts per task.

Table 3. Ablation studies of PLaCA on LIBERO-Long. Patch Grid denotes the spatial resolution of the future latent representation. Uniform and Change-aware indicate the patch-wise supervision weighting scheme. F2A denotes the future-to-action interface.

papers.abstract: Handheld demonstration devices decouple data collection from the robot, but conventional designs burden the hand with a wrist camera, cables and a pose tracker (SLAM, an IMU, a VR controller, or a fixed external camera that the collector's body occludes), and burden the pipeline with as many data streams to timestamp, synchronise and cross-calibrate. We show that a single egocentric camera (USD 122) worn on the collector's head replaces the wrist camera, the pose tracker and their separate streams with one. It reads printed fiducials on an electronics-free glove (USD 22) against paper tiles taped around the workspace, giving the 6-DoF gripper pose and the jaw width from the same frames the policy will see; at deployment the same camera rides a low-cost (USD 120) arm beside the robot that mimics the collector's head from the robot's joint state. Against the robot's encoders the labels are accurate to 6.5 mm and 1.6 degrees median with 93-100% frame coverage, and a policy trained on them instead of encoders pays 3% in validation loss. Adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes lifts rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, level with 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25), and the full co-trained head-camera policy succeeds in 20/25 against 15/25 for the wrist-camera recipe, whose policies drop the object when the goal leaves their view, and 12/25 for a fixed camera.
authors: Yosub Shin, Yuan Liu, Igor Molybog
bullets: Replaces wrist cameras, pose trackers, cables, and separate synchronization streams with one egocentric head camera.
Printed glove markers and workspace tiles recover 6-DoF gripper pose and jaw width from deployment-relevant images.
Labels achieve 6.5 mm median position error, 1.6° orientation error, and 93–100% frame coverage against robot encoders.
Adding 194 glove demonstrations improves rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, while co-training reaches 20/25.
The approach depends on visible fiducials and a robot-mounted camera that mimics the collector’s head motion.

(b) The camera’s own frame: tiles (green), ball (red) and jaw tags (blue, yellow) give the pose and the jaw width. (c) The same camera on a six-joint positioner beside the robot during a rollout. The wrist fisheye on the glove and the fixed camera on the post serve the ablations only.

papers.title: A Head Camera Is (Almost) All You Need: An Electronics-Free UMI Glove Labelled and Observed by One Moving Camera

papers.abstract: Visual manuals communicate procedural knowledge through stepwise diagrams, but translating these instructions into reliable long-horizon robotic execution remains challenging. We introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution without additional language instructions. JARVIS comprises 236,679 LEGO assembly tasks across 8,987 scenes, with a carefully curated JARVIS-v1 suite of 50 tasks for interactive robotic evaluation. Tasks span varying initial structural complexities and assembly horizons, requiring agents to interpret manuals, ground actions in an evolving workspace, and execute the intended procedure. A structure-aware evaluation protocol captures geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion. We further introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that composes robot primitives into executable programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery, without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates. Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives increase the average assembly score. Performance nevertheless declines sharply with assembly horizon, and execution errors remain difficult to correct. Prior-task experience improves initial performance, while repeated reflection provides inconsistent benefits, highlighting persistent limitations in connecting visual procedural reasoning with reliable physical execution.
authors: Fan Ding, Fucai Ke, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Xuewen Luo, Wenyu Liang, Vishnu Monn Baskaran, Hamid Rezatofighi, Yan Wu
bullets: Introduces a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous assembly from visual manuals without extra language instructions.
Includes 236,679 tasks across 8,987 scenes and a 50-task interactive evaluation suite, JARVIS-v1.

papers.abstract: Can embodied task agents use tactile experience to perform fine manipulation without task-specific model training? We investigate this capability through Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates tactile experience into an embodied task agent through in-context learning. Successful expert demonstrations show how contact changes during manipulation. We pair each recorded robot movement with its camera views and bilateral tactile observations. We keep tactile observations at the start and end of each movement and add two neighboring time points when the tactile images change markedly in between. The agent combines these demonstrations with current vision, tactile observations, and proprioception to select actions through general-purpose robot tools, without updating model parameters. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, adding tactile observations to the same two expert demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Further experiments show that performance depends on the sensory content and representation of demonstrations, while comparing agent models on Lift Bottle reveals substantial differences under the same system configuration. On the real-robot tasks, demonstrations with aligned visual and tactile observations increase the task success rate from 0% to 60%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile experience in context for fine manipulation and suggest a path toward extending embodied task agents to additional sensory inputs.

papers.abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.
authors: Aidan Sirbu, Charles Y. Zhang, Yuanjia Yang, Bence P. \"Olveczky, Talmo D. Pereira, Blake A. Richards

Combining the priors supports realistic exploratory behavior while exploiting task structure.
The behavior prior enables learning from sparse rewards by inducing diverse movements.
Designed for modeling rodents performing realistic neuroscience-inspired tasks.

papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment requires AI systems to learn from diverse populations whose preferences may reflect heterogeneous or even conflicting objectives, and to personalize their behavior to individual users. Existing approaches in pluralistic alignment often assume access to annotator identities and rely on powerful pretrained representations to model individual preference variations. We propose Preference-PCA Pluralistic Learning (P3L), a novel framework for pluralistic alignment that jointly learns trajectory embeddings and the shared basis of preference directions via PCA decomposition from heterogeneous crowd feedback without requiring annotator identities. At test time, our approach enables rapid and accurate personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization. Experiments across multiple embodied control tasks demonstrate that P3L enables steerable personal alignment that generalizes beyond the offline dataset to out-of-distribution new users and attains competitive RL and test performance, while substantially reducing computational cost and supporting variable adaptation query budgets.
authors: Akansha Kalra, Ellen R. Novoseller, Vernon J. Lawhern, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses pluralistic alignment when user preferences are heterogeneous and annotators are anonymized.
Jointly learns trajectory embeddings and a shared basis of preference directions using PCA decomposition.
Supports rapid personalized reward learning and downstream policy optimization at test time.
Across embodied control tasks, generalizes to out-of-distribution users and supports variable adaptation-query budgets.
Achieves competitive reinforcement-learning and test performance while reducing computational cost.

papers.abstract: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
authors: Rui Shi, Xunjian Yin, Jiacheng Sang, Zichuan Liu, Shuyan Zhou
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting and the need for different capabilities across long-horizon trajectories.
Trains independent LoRA adapters on a frozen backbone and exposes adapter selection as internal tool-calling actions.
Enables on-demand capability composition instead of fixed parameter configurations or static adapter merging.
On eight deep-research benchmarks, reports 6.2% higher average accuracy than full fine-tuning and 27.5% higher than static LoRA merging.
Supports modular continual adaptation by adding or updating individual adapters without changing the backbone or other capabilities.

papers.abstract: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet's shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.
bullets: Problem: Human monitoring and corrective interventions do not scale as robot fleets grow.
Method: FERT retrieves relevant successful trajectory segments using failure contexts and fine-tunes the policy with their actions as supervision.
System: FATS asynchronously coordinates experience collection, training, and policy distribution despite robot interruptions.
Results: Across five real-world manipulation tasks, policies reached 93.3–99.2% success on robots excluded from data collection; larger fleets generally improved performance.
Scope: Demonstrated for deployment-time learning in real-world manipulation, including phone packaging, where 96 robots improved success from 79.2% to 98.3%.

papers.abstract: Data-driven learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation presents a fundamental trade-off between data-collection cost and adaptability to real-world environments. Imitation learning (IL) requires costly human demonstrations, whereas simulation-based learning is vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps in dynamics and sensor observations. We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), a framework that decouples control learning from perception learning to learn image-based policies in the real world. A state-based teacher policy trained in simulation is executed on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student policy using the collected trajectories. Observation Alignment resolves observation mismatches between data collection and deployment. This framework collects successful, efficiently executed trajectories paired with real-world visual observations, without requiring demonstrations from human experts. In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation, our method achieves better overall performance when jointly considering task success and execution efficiency than both IL based on human demonstrations and policy distillation in simulation. https://isri-aist.github.io/redoa-project-page/
bullets: Addresses the cost of human demonstrations and the sim-to-real gap in dynamics and visual observations.

papers.abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

Collects recovery trajectories over 2× faster than a human-in-the-loop approach.
Improves task performance by up to 4.1× over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and enables cross-architecture distillation.

papers.abstract: Flow policies capture rich and diverse action distributions, and fine-tuning them with off-policy RL to improve beyond the demonstrations has drawn growing interest. However, fine-tuning a flow policy against a learned value function is not trivial, because the policy generates its action over many flow steps. Adjoint matching offers a principled way to update the flow model itself by propagating value information from the final action back to each flow step, but it requires a vector--Jacobian product through the policy at every step, a cost that grows with the number of flow steps and the policy size. We observe that the batch-averaged velocity Jacobian of pretrained flow policies concentrates on its diagonal. Motivated by this finding, we derive a closed-form scalar adjoint that scales the value gradient at the final action by the flow time, eliminating the per-step vector--Jacobian products. We further find that controlling the critic's value at policy-generated actions is particularly important under the scalar adjoint. Based on these findings, we propose Q-learning with Scalar Adjoint Matching (SQAM), which combines the scalar adjoint with a value penalty at those actions. SQAM's gains concentrate on the four hardest OGBench domains, where its success rate exceeds that of the strongest baseline in each domain by 18 to 35 percentage points. To test whether SQAM extends to large pretrained policies, we also fine-tune a vision-language-action policy on a real bimanual robot. SQAM improves over supervised fine-tuning on all three tasks.
bullets: Flow policies require value information to be propagated through many generation steps, making standard adjoint matching expensive.
The method uses a scalar adjoint that scales the final-action value gradient by flow time, avoiding per-step vector–Jacobian products.
SQAM adds a value penalty on policy-generated actions to control critic estimates.
On the four hardest OGBench domains, SQAM exceeds the strongest baseline by 18–35 percentage points in success rate.
It also improves over supervised fine-tuning across all three tasks in a real bimanual-robot evaluation.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory. At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes. To address this, we propose DiVeR, which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.
bullets: Verifier-guided test-time scaling selects among sampled action candidates to improve robot task success without collecting more robotic data.
Existing trajectory-level verifiers treat all states equally, despite only a sparse subset being important for distinguishing candidates.
DiVeR estimates state criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations and reweights verifier learning accordingly.
It requires neither step-level annotations nor additional environment interaction and adds negligible verifier inference overhead.
Experiments on LIBERO, RoboCasa, and a Franka Research 3 robot show consistent task-success improvements.

papers.abstract: Quadrupedal robots are increasingly deployed in environments where locomotion must remain robust to disturbances and constrained terrain. Gait type, such as walking or trotting, is commonly used to characterize quadrupedal locomotion. However, gait type does not uniquely define locomotion, as parameters such as duty factor, speed, and stance width can vary within a single gait type. In this work, we investigate the relationship between these gait parameters using three distinct quadrupedal locomotion control approaches. First, using whole body trajectory optimization with LQR feedback, we show that duty factor is a stronger predictor of local error convergence than nominal gait type. Second, we investigate duty factor selection with a learned locomotion controller, suggesting how duty factor may serve as a low-dimensional parameter for adapting locomotion robustness in narrow-terrain environments. Finally, we show that these trends persist under a centroidal model predictive control framework and validate them through narrow-terrain experiments on a physical quadruped. These results show that duty factor provides a simple and effective basis for understanding and selecting robust quadrupedal locomotion across gait types and control architectures.
bullets: Gait types such as walking and trotting do not uniquely determine locomotion behavior because duty factor, speed, and stance width vary within each type.
Whole-body trajectory optimization with LQR feedback finds that duty factor better predicts local error convergence than nominal gait type.
A learned controller suggests duty factor can serve as a low-dimensional parameter for adapting robustness in narrow terrain.
The same trends appear with centroidal model predictive control and are validated on a physical quadruped.
The study focuses on constrained or narrow-terrain locomotion and does not establish that duty factor alone determines all aspects of gait performance.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data can reduce the cost of collecting and annotating training data for robotic perception, but generating sensor observations that preserve the characteristics relevant to downstream perception remains challenging, particularly for sonar imagery. In this work, we investigate whether conventional image-fidelity metrics adequately reflect the downstream perception performance of GAN-generated synthetic sonar data. We employ a Pix2Pix conditional generative adversarial network with four discriminator configurations characterized by different receptive fields: PixelGAN, PatchGAN-16, PatchGAN-70, and ImageGAN. The models are trained using sonar imagery from two datasets and evaluated using conventional image-fidelity metrics, including Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and Mean Squared Error (MSE). To complement these pixel-level measures with task-oriented evaluation, YOLOX-S, YOLOX-L, and Faster R-CNN detectors are trained exclusively on real sonar imagery and subsequently evaluated on the GAN-generated images using identical test samples and annotations across all discriminator configurations. The results reveal a discrepancy between image-fidelity and downstream object-detection performance: the configuration achieving the best SSIM, PSNR, and MSE does not consistently yield the best detection performance. In particular, PatchGAN configurations achieve strong downstream detection results despite not achieving the highest pixel-level similarity scores. These findings suggest, for the datasets and models considered, pixel-level image-fidelity metrics alone may not consistently capture the task-relevant realism of synthetic sonar observations and motivate the use of task-aware evaluation for synthetic sensor data intended for robotic perception.
bullets: Problem: Conventional image-fidelity metrics may miss sonar characteristics important for downstream perception.
Method: Pix2Pix models with PixelGAN, PatchGAN-16, PatchGAN-70, and ImageGAN discriminators were evaluated using SSIM, PSNR, MSE, and YOLOX/Faster R-CNN detection performance.
Result: The discriminator configuration with the best pixel-level scores did not consistently produce the best detection results.
Finding: PatchGAN variants achieved strong downstream detection despite lower pixel-level similarity.
Scope: Conclusions apply to the datasets and models examined, motivating task-aware evaluation of synthetic sensor data.

papers.abstract: Active imitation learning reduces expert effort by allowing a learner to request the demonstrations it needs. Existing methods typically select these requests for their expected information gain about the expert policy. In structured multi-task domains, however, the number of start-goal tasks may grow combinatorially despite their solutions sharing reusable behavior. This makes composable behaviors especially valuable, since a single demonstration may help solve many tasks at once. Prior methods do not explicitly account for this value when selecting which demonstration to request. We introduce Adaptive Agents via Latent Topologies (AALT), which requests demonstrations that maximize expected gains in start-goal connectivity. We further show that this objective is formally tied to information gain about task reachability. AALT organizes existing demonstrations into a topology of latent hub states connected by learned behaviors, identifies high-value bridge demonstrations that are likely to enable many tasks at once, and grounds each to an expert query. At inference, it plans through the resulting topology and conditions a diffusion policy on each successive hub transition. In a simulated UR5e robot ordered-retrieval domain with 72 tasks, AALT improved from 42/72 to 72/72 (100%) successful tasks consistently using only 3 demonstrations totaling 5 transitions beyond the initial dataset. After 20 demonstrations, the strongest baseline averaged 88.6% success using 98 transitions.
bullets: Problem: Standard active imitation learning prioritizes policy information gain but overlooks how one demonstration can compose solutions across many tasks.
Method: AALT builds a latent topology of hub states and learned behaviors, then requests demonstrations expected to improve start-goal connectivity.
It identifies high-value bridge demonstrations, grounds them to expert queries, and plans through the resulting topology with a diffusion policy.
In a 72-task simulated UR5e ordered-retrieval domain, AALT reached 72/72 successful tasks using 3 demonstrations and 5 additional transitions.
After 20 demonstrations, the strongest baseline averaged 88.6% success using 98 transitions; the reported evaluation is limited to this simulated domain.

papers.abstract: Video world models have emerged as promising candidates for high-fidelity world models, offering the potential to synthesize high-quality videos capturing fine-grained interactions between agents and their environments conditioned on multi-modal user inputs. Their impressive capabilities address many of the long-standing challenges faced by physics-based simulators, driving broad adoption in many problem domains, e.g., robotics. For example, video models can generate photorealistic, physically consistent deformable-body simulation without making prohibitive simplifying assumptions, which is a major bottleneck in physics-based simulation. Moreover, video models can serve as foundation world models that capture the dynamics of the world in a fine-grained and expressive way. They thus overcome the limited expressiveness of language-only abstractions in describing intricate physical interactions. However, despite their potential, video models still generate physics-violating future predictions, often manifesting as hallucinations. In this survey, we provide a review of video models and their applications as embodied world models in robotics, including efficient data generation and policy learning, dynamics and rewards modeling in reinforcement learning, policy evaluation, and visual planning. Further, we highlight important challenges hindering the trustworthy integration of video models, such as poor instruction following, hallucinations like violations of physics, unsafe content generation, in addition to significant data and compute overhead. We present potential future directions to address these open research challenges to motivate research and ultimately facilitate broader applications, especially in safety-critical settings. We provide a curated bibliography at https://github.com/irom-princeton/awesome-robotics-video-world-model-papers .
authors: Zhiting Mei, Tenny Yin, Ola Shorinwa, Apurva Badithela, Zhonghe Zheng, Joseph Bruno, Madison Bland, Lihan Zha, Asher Hancock, Jaime Fern\'andez Fisac, Philip Dames, Anirudha Majumdar
bullets: Covers applications in data generation, policy learning, reinforcement-learning dynamics and reward modeling, policy evaluation, and visual planning.
Video models can represent fine-grained world dynamics and photorealistic interactions, including deformable-body simulation beyond simplified physics models.
Key limitations include physics-violating predictions, poor instruction following, unsafe content generation, and substantial data and compute requirements.
Highlights future research directions for improving reliability and enabling broader use, particularly in safety-critical robotic settings.
Provides a curated bibliography of robotics video world-model research.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.
authors: Shiao Xie, Siyu Chen, Jianwei Lv, Xiandong Li, Yujin Wang
bullets: RL with verifiable rewards provides task-level supervision but limited guidance for localizing visual-reasoning errors.

Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG) validates corrections by comparing teacher outputs with evidence-present and evidence-degraded views.
VAG uses verifier-derived advantages as anchors and admits only directionally visually supported corrections.
Across six visual reasoning benchmarks, VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD, achieving new state-of-the-art average performance.

papers.abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $\Psi_0$, $\omega$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.
authors: Tianqi Liu, Hanfei Zhao, Qifeng Liang, Hui En Pang, Jiarui Xu, Sayang Mu, Penghao Qiu, YingSheng Zhang, Jun Wang, Ziang Cao, Mingze Sun, Yukang Cao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision in joint loco-manipulation modeling.
Introduces Xp-Data with 10k hours of human and 3k hours of robot egocentric data, plus unified multimodal annotations and quality control.
Uses a unified kinematic representation combining camera poses for locomotion with projected skeletons for manipulation.
Introduces Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon dexterous humanoid teleoperation benchmark.
Reports strong performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks and held-out human video; distilled models support real-time, minute-long rollouts and VR interaction.

papers.abstract: Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3\% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6\% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.
