Across 16 model–benchmark pairs, it reduces inference cost in every case, with up to 1.48× speedup.
Success rate improves in 14 pairs, by up to 15.08 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Nowadays, robotic telemanipulation enables humans to control robots so as to execute tasks in a manner similar to how they perform them, and serves as an essential approach for collecting on-robot data for robot learning by human demonstrations. The quality of collected demonstrations directly impacts the performance of the learned policy. However, existing telemanipulation systems rely heavily on human operation, particularly for large-scale data collection. Collecting dozens or hundreds of demonstrations is a demanding process, as operators tend to fatigue quickly, especially during the execution of dexterous tasks that require sustained concentration. Recently, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation has emerged as a promising direction that reduces operator workload while preserving human-in-the-loop control for task execution. We therefore introduce a scalable, intuitive, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation system that leverages a mixed reality (MR) headset for on-robot data collection. The system autonomously executes the majority of the task trajectories and only requires the operator to make fine adjustments at key stages. We validate the effectiveness of our system by collecting data and training imitation learning policies on the execution of a high-precision, fine-grained bimanual peg-in-hole task. With lower data collection effort, our system obtains high-quality demonstrations that can be used to train fully autonomous task execution policies.

papers.abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.

Achieves 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long and handles challenging real-world bimanual tasks such as box folding and packing with unseen object combinations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.
authors: Boyi Liu, Yite Wang, Xinyu Lian, Fan Shu, Sida Li, Feng Yan, Mingjia Zhang, Yuxiong He, Zhewei Yao
bullets: Targets the difficulty of separating algorithmic gains from an under-tuned RL baseline for long-horizon agents.
Uses small-pool overfitting to expose failures hidden by early reward gains and integrates gated rewards, importance-weight control, aligned training/inference engines, and consistent policy state.
Reaches 62.0% pass@1 with Qwen3.5-4B on raw R2E-Gym data, comparable to FrogNano while using about one-sixth as many rollouts.

papers.abstract: Quadruped robots often switch gaits to traverse mixed terrain safely. Many practical supervisors enforce hardware constraints (e.g., dwell or guard intervals) using a transition handler. However, the switch decision itself is often driven by near-field thresholds, which can delay commitment when rough terrain is only detected shortly before contact in the local height map. We propose a lightweight height-map-only gait supervisor that unifies look-ahead and locomotion constraints in a single decision policy. A robot-centered height map is partitioned into near-, mid-, and far-field bands, each discretized into a terrain class, and band evolution is modeled as a Markov process. Gait selection is cast as a look-ahead Markov Decision Process whose transition model and cost explicitly encode platform-specific switching constraints. Indoor and outdoor experiments on a Unitree Go2 platform show reduced late switching, lower time spent using ineffective gaits on rough terrain, and improved roll stability compared to tuned reactive baselines. Overall, the MDP formulation yields anticipative constraint-aware gait switching that improves robustness without course-specific retuning.
authors: Kelvin Aladum, Justin Peel, Nisar Ahmed
bullets: Addresses delayed gait changes when rough terrain appears only shortly before contact.
Partitions robot-centered height maps into near-, mid-, and far-field terrain bands modeled as a Markov process.
Selects gaits with a look-ahead MDP whose transition model and cost encode platform-specific switching constraints.
Indoor and outdoor Unitree Go2 experiments report less late switching, less ineffective rough-terrain gait use, and improved roll stability versus tuned reactive baselines.
Improves robustness without course-specific retuning; evaluation is scoped to the tested platform and environments.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation is particularly challenging because it requires coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction, making it difficult to learn from limited demonstrations or from scratch through Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce DiPLO (self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation), a framework that combines a self-distilled diffusion planner with a low-level whole-body tracking policy. Our planner is pretrained via supervised learning on motions derived from human-to-humanoid retargeting, while the tracker is trained via RL to execute them. DiPLO centers around two complementary post-training stages. First, we introduce Self-Distillation Diffusion Policy Optimisation (SD:DPO) to remove the planner's dependence on strong task conditioning, which we identify as a crucial ingredient for effective pretraining, as downstream fine-tuning does not recover comparable performance when it is omitted.. We then fine-tune this distilled model with Diffusion-Augmented Proximal Policy Optimization (DA:PPO), a maximum-entropy RL method for diffusion models, to improve task success and align generated plans with the frozen tracker's execution capabilities. Together, these stages enable motion generation through state-history and goal conditioning alone, enabling 99% task success in pick-carry-place tasks, compared to just 45% for the pretrained model. The resulting planner also generates motions for unseen object goals, with further evaluations on kicking and pushing/pulling tasks. Finally, we deploy our pipeline on the hardware, using our DA:PPO planner-tracker on a Unitree G1, achieving repeated successful executions without any real-world fine-tuning.
authors: Shafeef Omar, Sebastian Sanokowski, Elham Daneshmand, Dian Yu, Daniel Cremers, Cordelia Schmid, Majid Khadiv
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction in humanoid loco-manipulation.
Pretrains a diffusion planner on human-to-humanoid retargeted motions and trains a low-level tracker with RL.
Uses SD:DPO to remove dependence on strong task conditioning, then DA:PPO to improve success and match plans to tracker capabilities.

(b) The diffusion motion generator Gϕ is pretrained to generate an n-step feasible motion conditioned on the IK-retargeted motion prior, the state history and the goal, while the tracking policy πθ is trained separately with RL to track sD. (c) Self-distillation with SD:DPO removes the need for the task prior: the student Gϕ, with the prior token nulled, rolls out with the frozen tracker πθ; each plan it produces is noised to a random denoising step k and denoised twice by the same network, with and without sIK , and the student’s reverse kernel pϕ is matched to the self-teacher’s stop-gradient kernel sg(pϕ). In closed loop, Gϕ plans n steps, πθ executes the first m ≤ n of them, and Gϕ re-plans from the reached state. papers.abstract: Wheeled planetary rovers immobilised in loose regolith have no principled recovery controller: scripted maneuvers are terrain-specific, and naive driving deepens entrapment. We introduce a recurrent policy that learns to escape without a predefined maneuver. The framework rests on a verified trap: in a continuum material point method (MPM) simulator we identify a configuration at sinkage-to-radius ratio z/r = 2.0 where the strongest of ten scripted controllers succeeds in only 7/32 trials, yet the regolith retains traction and continues to shear, confirming granular entrapment rather than a numerical artifact. A frozen entrapment detector, trained on 81,771 windows spanning three materials and six sinkage levels, supplies a three-state belief to the policy observation. A separate simulator mobility latch gates training rewards. Across five training seeds, mean action evaluation achieves 62.5% escape (range 28.1-81.3%; 32 trials per seed) versus 7/32 for the strongest scripted controller and 0/32 for action noise. A numerical audit identifies a coupling-buffer fault that silently discarded 9.7% of contact nodes at 16 parallel environments. Results establish recovery in the tested simulation regime; physical transfer remains unverified.
authors: Meraj Hossain Promit, Chandak Chakma, Md Jubair Ahmed Sourov, Sejuti Rahman
bullets: Addresses terrain-specific scripted recovery and the risk that naive driving worsens entrapment.

A numerical audit found a coupling-buffer fault that discarded 9.7% of contact nodes in parallel simulation.
Physical transfer is unverified, and results are limited to the tested simulation regime.

papers.abstract: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.
authors: SeongJun Jeong, Chungwoo Lee, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Addresses adapter and task-selection module growth under fixed onboard storage and compute budgets.
Reuses frozen adapters and adds new adapters only at selected layers, with a penalty discouraging redundant information.

GPU memory and control frequency remain comparable to the backbone as tasks accumulate; retention is also shown on a real UR5 arm.

papers.abstract: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce \textit{Reciprocal Q-Augmentation} (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and \texttt{CleanUp-Lite}. Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.
authors: Francesco Morri, Adel Abusitta, Quentin Cappart, Margarida Carvalho
bullets: Targets general-sum settings where defection can trap agents in low-welfare equilibria.
Uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment each agent’s Q-function with estimated effects of its actions on others.
Learns both cooperative and defecting policies using only the agent’s own Q-function.
Experiments across four social dilemmas show faster and higher cooperation than fully cooperative methods with shared rewards.
A single RQA agent can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard reinforcement learning.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of the different modules of the RQA method.

Figure 5: (a-c): Plots of the cooperation rate (time passed in cooperative mode by the RQA agent), and the cumulative return for the test with a frozen RQA agent implementing the switching logic against a PPO agent. The dashed lines represent the theoretical maximum welfare. (b-d): Same plots but for a learning RQA agent, implementing the switching logic while training its policies. In both cases and for all matrix games we see that the cooperation rate is very close to 1 by the end of training, and the cumulative reward converges toward the optimal solution.

papers.abstract: Quadruped locomotion requires coordinating body motion,contact forces, foothold placement, and gait timing. We present a hierarchical controller in which reinforcement learning adapts these structured locomotion references while a gait scheduler, reactive footstep planner, and whole-body impulse controller retain responsibility for high-frequency execution. The model-based backbone can sustain a nominal trot independently, allowing the policy to focus on when and how to modify an already functional locomotion controller. We train the complete hierarchy in a vectorized controller-in-the-loop environment using a six-direction disturbance curriculum. Under a common simulator and evaluation protocol, the proposed controller achieves 77.29% mean survival across the tested disturbance grid, compared with 50.35% for the model-based reference controller. Training-time channel ablations identify adaptive foothold placement as the largest marginal contributor to grid survival and reveal direction-dependent effects of gait-rate adaptation. Together, these results demonstrate the viability of the proposed hierarchical controller architecture for integrating learned adaptation with optimization-based whole-body control through structured locomotion references.

papers.abstract: The scan-then-revisit workflow of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy requires bringing a previously observed suspicious region back into view for closer inspection. Acquiring such targets requires translating anatomical and appearance descriptions into camera motions from partial observations of a confined, deformable environment. We present EndoVLA-OOV, a language-conditioned vision-language-action policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy. The policy adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands and combines initial, intermediate, and current images to guide search. To support policy learning, we provide an open-source VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k observation-action pairs. Physical evaluation spans wet-lens and low-light conditions, two unseen stomach phantoms, and cross-embodiment transfer to an unseen ex-vivo environment. In the cross-embodiment evaluation, the full-data policy achieves 93.3% target acquisition success (28/30). In a controlled training-data comparison, expanding the corpus from 312 to 1,050 episodes increases acquisition success from 40.0% to 90.0% under the same model, training, and test configuration. Instruction and observation interventions further support the use of language and temporal context in the evaluated acquisition tasks. These results support language-guided endoscopic revisitation across the evaluated environments and robot embodiments and demonstrate the benefit of expanded task-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.
authors: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying task-level planning with interaction-specific, state-dependent whole-body control.
Projects independently learned skill policies into the latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM).
Trains a single offline perceptive flow planner on aggregated closed-loop latent rollouts from multiple skills.
Introduces AH-BFM with adaptive horizons for both precise control and extended whole-body behavior.
Across three simulated tasks, achieves 42.0% mean success versus 11.6% for latent replay and 3.5% for kinematic planning; real-robot tests show transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of FIBER. (a) Heterogeneous interaction experts are acquired through motion imitation, reward shaping, or successorfeature-guided behavior reuse. (b) Action-aligned latent policy projection maps their short-horizon control responses into a frozen adaptivehorizon BFM; closed-loop rollouts produce executable latent trajectories. (c) These trajectories train a unified perceptive planner entirely offline. Language commands or waypoint conditions are encoded as steering tokens, and a DiT planner predicts future latent trajectories. During deployment, the planner replans from onboard observations while the frozen BFM provides high-frequency feedback.

Fig. 4: Qualitative real-world behaviors of FIBER. (a) During box carrying, the robot reacts to an unstable grasp by briefly lifting the box and repositioning its hands underneath for more secure support, illustrating high-frequency closed-loop adjustment. (b) After picking up the box, the same policy follows waypoint commands while carrying it; after stumbling, the robot stabilizes on its knees and recovers before continuing, demonstrating interaction-preserving skill chaining, steering, and recovery. (c) For a heavy door, the robot leans its whole body into the interaction to generate sufficient pushing force, showing adaptive whole-body realization of contact-rich tasks.

Fig. 3: Skill chaining with FIBER. In a single rollout, the policy sequentially opens the door in (i), picks up the box in (ii), and carries it back through the doorway in (iii), demonstrating closed-loop chaining of multiple interaction skills under changing high-level commands.

papers.abstract: 3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability. This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects. We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth. This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert. We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact. Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.
authors: Zhiyuan Yang, Jiaju He, Ruiteng Zhao, Anqi Cheng, Haiyue Zhu, Kezhi Mao
bullets: Commodity RGB-D sensors produce missing, distorted, or incorrect geometry, causing a sharp performance drop in modern 3D policies.
NISE learns trustworthy spatial features using Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision with calibrated multi-view depth.
Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention propagates position uncertainty instead of treating corrupted 3D tokens as exact.
Simulated sensor-corruption benchmarks and real-robot tasks with transparent and reflective objects show improved noise robustness.
The approach targets deployment with imperfect commodity RGB-D sensors, beyond clean-depth evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: NISE framework. Per-camera RGB-D is encoded by a frozen visual backbone ViT and a trainable DPT-style head [21] into a shared spatial feature map. NISE acts on this shared map: during training, Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision attaches a cross-view geometry head to encourage view-consistent geometry in the same features consumed by the policy; at deployment, this head is removed. Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention remains in the deployed policy and carries per-token coordinate uncertainty into 3D attention, so lifted tokens influence action features according to their spatial reliability.

papers.abstract: Pedipulating a freestanding articulated object requires controlling its pose and internal configuration while maintaining balance. We demonstrate this capability by autonomously solving a giant Rubik's Cube with a quadruped using only its feet. The task demands repeated precise interactions, since unintended layer motion can invalidate subsequent operations. We develop an onboard RGB-D perception pipeline that estimates the cube's metric pose and its full color state from partial views acquired through locomotion and flipping. A planner converts the computed solve into robot-executable skill sequences. Learned whole-body skills reorient the cube while preserving its layer configuration and turn its layers with one foot pinning the cube as the other pushes. We train these skills using reinforcement learning with privileged observations and distill them into policies that map onboard depth and proprioception to joint targets. The deployed policies tolerate variations in relative robot-cube placement and recover from external disturbances. The system completes three autonomous hardware solves, each about 30 steps over 8-9 minutes. These results show that combining onboard perception with coordinated pedipulation enables a quadruped to complete extended multi-step physical tasks. Additional material can be found at: https://leggedrobotics.github.io/rubik-skills/
authors: Lukas Amiet, Gabriel S\'anchez-Blanco Repgen, Mayank Mittal, Victor Klemm, Andrei Cramariuc, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
bullets: The task requires precise control of the cube’s pose and layer configuration while maintaining robot balance.

A planner translates the cube solution into executable skills, including reorientation and one-foot-pinning layer turns.
Reinforcement-learned whole-body skills are distilled into policies using onboard depth and proprioception, with recovery from placement variation and external disturbances.
The system completed three autonomous hardware solves of roughly 30 steps each in 8–9 minutes.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in embodied AI for robotic manipulation and planning, but their deployment in physical systems exposes vulnerabilities such as jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mainly evaluated on short instructions containing a single hazard, whereas realistic tasks may interleave safe and unsafe sub-tasks, conceal hazardous steps, or combine individually safe actions into unsafe outcomes. Such compound instructions make it harder for a single safety decision to distinguish hazardous sub-tasks from legitimate ones, risking either overlooking the hazard or rejecting the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-enabled robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this problem, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules planning framework that distributes safety enforcement across multiple reasoning and verification stages. Five cooperating agents are used to ground general safety principles into world-specific rules, assess the instruction's sub-tasks in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is then organized as a graph of rule-specific nodes, where higher-level nodes inherit the union of their parents' rules, and candidate plans are progressively verified and aggregated until a single plan satisfies every relevant rule. In this way, RuleGraph reduces reliance on a single centralized safety decision. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions across two benchmarks in two environments using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reduces ASR to 0% on both benchmarks while achieving the highest TSR among all methods, reaching 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 84.54% on our long-horizon compound instructions.

papers.abstract: LIBERO has emerged as a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating robotic manipulation policies. However, strong performance on LIBERO does not necessarily indicate robust embodied capabilities, as models may exploit benchmark-specific regularities rather than generalize to diverse operating conditions. In this work, we introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0, a comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of embodied foundation models under distribution shifts. LIBERO-Pro2.0 encompasses 22 static perturbations and 20 runtime interventions across six dimensions: Condition, Environment, Observation, Execution, Robot State Configuration, and Language, yielding 1,648 validated shifted task instances. To support robustness-oriented learning, we further collect 39,390 training trajectories through model-generated and human demonstrations. All shifted task instances undergo six rounds of iterative human review and correction to ensure physical plausibility and task validity. We evaluate 17 representative robot policies spanning vision-language-action models, world-action models, and robustness-oriented policies. Our results reveal substantial robustness gaps across all evaluated paradigms: under runtime distribution shifts, the evaluated models exhibit an average performance drop of 26.5 percentage points, with individual drops reaching 32.5 points. These findings highlight the gap between nominal benchmark performance and robustness under distribution shifts, underscoring the need for systematic robustness evaluation of embodied foundation models.

papers.abstract: Most simulation benchmarks for robotic manipulation keep target objects static and treat policy inference as instantaneous. These assumptions simplify evaluation but hide how a moving target evolves during computation and how stale an observation is when an action is executed. We introduce LIBERO-Dynamic, a dynamic extension of all 40 LIBERO tasks. It drives objects through contact friction along three trajectory families and speed tiers, while advancing the physical world according to calibrated, model-specific inference latency. The same mechanism supports training by replaying verified static demonstrations and compensating robot actions online for target displacement, producing 9,000 quality-filtered dynamic trajectories. We evaluate six pretrained policies on 1,800 dynamic conditions per configuration, compare execution strategies and action horizons with fixed checkpoints, and fine-tune three architectures using dynamic and mixed data. Faster motion degrades every policy but not uniformly; execution timing and horizon can change the behavior of the same policy; and asynchronous replanning benefits from frequent feedback only when the action queue avoids underflow. Dynamic demonstrations improve each architecture under at least one recipe, with gains varying by temporal conditioning, data composition, and training budget. A small-scale physical study shows task-dependent execution-strategy differences consistent with simulation. LIBERO-Dynamic makes object motion, inference latency, and action execution explicit and controllable for evaluating and improving robot policies in moving-target manipulation.
authors: Shaojie Ren, Jingwen Sun, Zezhi Liu, Hongjin Chen, Xin Jin, Wei Zou, Zhibo Chen

Across six pretrained policies, faster target motion consistently reduces performance, while timing and action horizon alter behavior.
Dynamic data improves each of three fine-tuned architectures under at least one training recipe; a small physical study shows similar strategy differences.

papers.abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots' ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight recurring skill categories that provide a practical framework for studying these capabilities. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support reproducible fabrication using consumer-grade 3D printers, and are paired with simulation models with tunable resistance loads. Controlled task variations enable evaluation of policy generalization. We evaluate recent vision-based and vision-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that the evaluated vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, while the evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance. By providing shared tasks and physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes a foundation for reproducible evaluation of contact-rich manipulation research. The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench
authors: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Defines eight recurring skill categories for everyday contact-rich manipulation.

Uses tunable resistance loads and controlled task variations to test policy generalization.
Evaluations show vision-only policies struggle with contact perception and reaction, while visual-tactile policies provide no meaningful improvement on the tested tasks.
The benchmark is open-sourced for shared, reproducible research.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies must ground language instructions in the right objects, contact points, and target locations for reliable manipulation. Human gaze provides a natural signal for this grounding, but existing robot datasets rarely pair real human gaze with the multi-camera observations used by modern policies. We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-equipped real-robot manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view VLA policies. Using screen-based teleoperation, we record gaze directly on the robot camera feed viewed by the operator, yielding 12000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains with 300 Hz gaze synchronized with images, proprioception, and actions. We transfer gaze from the operator-selected view to the remaining synchronized cameras, producing spatially consistent targets across the policy's visual inputs. We then use these gaze-derived targets to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training while keeping inference gaze-free. Across 18 real-world tasks, our method improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6%, with gains up to 25 percentage points. Ablations show that gaze works best as soft supervision and that real human gaze provides stronger attention targets than generic attention-shaping priors. The gains transfer to LIBERO-Spatial (57.9% to 69.6%) and different VLA backbones.These results show that gaze collected in the robot observation space can provide effective training-time targets for improving visual grounding in VLA manipulation.

bullets: Introduces a real-robot, multi-view gaze dataset with 12,000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains.
Synchronizes 300 Hz human gaze with images, proprioception, and actions, then transfers gaze targets across camera views.
Uses gaze as soft supervision to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training; inference requires no gaze.
Improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6% across 18 real-world tasks, with gains up to 25 percentage points.
Benefits transfer to LIBERO-Spatial and different VLA backbones; real gaze outperforms generic attention-shaping priors.

papers.abstract: Visual imitation policies can organise task motion, yet contact-rich object use demands gripper adjustments beyond coarse opening and closing. We study fine-grained gripper control as a local feedback problem within ongoing task execution. Our approach assigns tactile feedback a dedicated control role during contact-rich task stages. We introduce ContactPolicy, a learned local controller that takes over the gripper while a visual base policy continues to control the arm. ContactPolicy combines tactile and force histories with current robot state to jointly predict gripper increments and their modulation, updating the gripper target from each new observation. An Intent policy manages control handover between the visual base policy and ContactPolicy. Real-world experiments on container opening, object handling, and tool operation show improved task success over both the Visuomotor Policy and Tactile-Force Policy baselines. Execution analysis illustrates how the gripper adjusts contact within an ongoing task, including periods of target retention and fine-grained changes as interaction conditions evolve. Arm-state ablations and failure analysis further examine how execution context supports local regulation. These results support task-local tactile policies for fine-grained gripper control within visual manipulation.
authors: Mingyuan Ba, Yanan Zhou, James Zhao, Weiming Zhi
bullets: Addresses the need for gripper adjustments beyond coarse opening and closing during contact-rich tasks.
Combines tactile and force histories with robot state to predict gripper increments and their modulation.
An Intent policy hands gripper control between the visual base policy and the tactile local controller.
Real-world tests on container opening, object handling, and tool use report higher task success than two stated baselines.
Analysis shows target retention and fine-grained contact adaptation, while ablations and failure analysis examine the role of execution context.

papers.abstract: Individually competent robot skills can fail when composed: tools may lack a required capability, completion signals may misrepresent physical progress, and one skill may leave a state that violates its successor's prerequisites. We introduce Recursia, a recursive self-improvement framework that treats the shared executable stack, rather than individual task programs, as the persistent unit of improvement. The stack integrates tools, skills with execution contracts, handoffs, and verifiers. Source-side execution traces guide failure attribution and the generation of missing tools or repairs to existing shared components. Generality checks, mechanism tests, and paired selection and regression gates determine which changes become the next parent. The resulting stack is frozen and reused through declarative task adapters, allowing source-derived changes to support new compositions without target-side code repair. Experiments cover LIBERO-Pro Long simulation and a physical Franka FR3 equipped with a Franka Hand. In simulation, Recursia improves success over ASPIRE by 5.8 percentage points under Pos perturbations and 15.1 points under Task perturbations. Across three physical compositional target tasks, it improves mean success over the Skill Document Only baseline by 40 percentage points. Analyses of constituent execution, candidate rejection, and inference drivers distinguish local mechanism improvements from complete task success and characterize the cost of feedback-conditioned orchestration. These results examine shared executable interfaces as a concrete mechanism for compositional transfer in robot programming.
authors: Yangzhi Chen, Feiran Liu, Zishuo Wang, Zijian Jin, Xin Zhu, Lecheng Ruan, Wenjuan Han
bullets: Targets failures in skill composition caused by missing capabilities, misleading completion signals, and incompatible handoffs.
Uses source execution traces for failure attribution, generates repairs or new tools, and filters updates with generality, mechanism, selection, and regression checks.
Freezes the improved stack and reuses it through declarative task adapters, avoiding target-side code repair.
Improves success over ASPIRE by 5.8 and 15.1 percentage points under two simulation perturbation settings, and by 40 percentage points over a document-only baseline across three physical tasks.
Evaluations cover LIBERO-Pro Long simulation and a physical Franka FR3 with a Franka Hand; analyses separate local mechanism gains from complete-task success.

papers.abstract: Large, unlabeled datasets of prior experience have become increasingly available for agentic tasks in domains such as robotics and coding. A common recipe for these tasks is to train a policy using the prior data, and then further improve it with online rollouts. But while much work has studied how to use both the offline and online data for policy extraction, far less work has been done to understand how the prior data can be used to efficiently \textit{explore} during the online learning phase. Previous work has attempted to formalize this idea by defining the \textit{empowerment}, a measure of how many future states an agent can realize; states with higher empowerment require more exploration as there are more futures to explore. However, existing methods for estimating empowerment require online policy rollouts in the environment. We propose the first method for estimating empowerment from unlabeled prior data, without any environment interaction. By jointly learning an empowerment-maximizing policy together with its discounted state-occupancy measure, our estimator can be trained on unlabeled trajectories generated from any unknown policy. We demonstrate that our empowerment estimator qualitatively gives intuitive empowerment measures and show that the pretrained estimator can be used to improve exploration in the online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning setting. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/ishirgarg/offline-empowerment}.
authors: Ishir Garg, Vivek Myers, Qiyang Li, Catherine Ji, Benjamin Eysenbach, Sergey Levine
bullets: Targets the underexplored use of prior offline data for exploration rather than only policy learning.
Introduces an estimator trained without environment interaction or knowledge of the data-generating policy.
Jointly learns an empowerment-maximizing policy and its discounted state-occupancy measure.
Shows qualitatively intuitive empowerment estimates and improved exploration in online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.
Scope: demonstrations are based on qualitative estimation and exploration improvements, without reported quantitative results in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Human video demonstrations provide rich manipulation strategies for dexterous manipulation learning. We study a setting in which a fully specified simulated scene is used to generate videos that specify the demonstrated manipulation behavior. This setup provides access to scene information such as object geometry, articulation, and camera parameters, while allowing direct control over task and scene configuration. However, generated videos may contain geometric distortions, inaccurate contacts, and other physical inconsistencies, making the recovered motion difficult to execute directly on a robot. We present an end-to-end framework for converting such simulation-grounded videos into physically executable dexterous robot demonstrations. Our perception pipeline leverages the known scene through model-based object tracking with dense foundation-model features and depth-based hand-object alignment. The recovered human motion is then retargeted and physically grounded using residual reinforcement learning, where a backward curriculum and a cache of physically valid reset states enable the policy to correct imperfect video-derived references while preserving the demonstrated manipulation strategy. On clean ARCTIC demonstrations, our method achieves competitive performance with prior dexterous retargeting approaches and shows greater robustness when applied to references extracted from generated videos. We further demonstrate diverse rigid and articulated manipulation tasks in simulation and successful open-loop transfer of the optimized trajectories to a real dexterous robot.
authors: Xiaowen Qiu, Yian Wang, Haoxiang You, Chuang Gan
bullets: Addresses geometric distortions, inaccurate contacts, and other physical inconsistencies in generated video demonstrations.
Uses known scene information with model-based object tracking, dense foundation-model features, and depth-based hand–object alignment.
Retargets recovered human motion and applies residual reinforcement learning with backward curriculum learning and valid reset states.
Shows competitive performance on clean ARCTIC demonstrations and greater robustness to generated-video references.
Demonstrates diverse rigid and articulated tasks in simulation and open-loop transfer to a real dexterous robot.

papers.abstract: With advancements in learning-based policies, robots are increasingly being deployed in human-centric environments, such as manufacturing floors and homes, where safe and precise operation requires compensating for unknown loads while remaining compliant during human interactions. Reliably distinguishing between these interaction types is challenging with a single sensing modality, as force signals cannot separate payloads from human pushes, and vision is susceptible to occlusions. We propose a task-agnostic interaction estimation and adaptive control framework that addresses this challenge by fusing force history and 3D point cloud through a transformer-based classifier. Trained with modality dropout for occlusion resilience and fine-tuned from simulation to hardware, the classifier achieves 91.89% accuracy and maintains above 90% under complete occlusion of one modality. The classifier drives a system identification framework that selectively compensates for unknown payloads and a variable-impedance controller that switches between adaptive and reactive modes, while simultaneously estimating interaction forces for downstream tasks, such as human intent estimation. We validate the framework under external perturbations and unknown loads across single-arm manipulation, deployment with an imitation-learning-based policy, intent-driven target switching, and zero-shot bimanual deployment on two Franka arms lifting a box of unknown mass, demonstrating generalization to closed kinematic chains and unseen setups, enabling safe and precise deployment.
authors: Mateusz Jaszczuk, Paris Perdikaris, Nadia Figueroa
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity between unknown payloads and human pushes, which neither force sensing nor vision resolves reliably alone.
Fuses force history and 3D point clouds with a transformer classifier trained using modality dropout and adapted from simulation to hardware.
Achieves 91.89% classification accuracy and remains above 90% when either sensing modality is completely occluded.
Uses the estimate to selectively compensate payloads, switch between adaptive and reactive impedance control, and estimate interaction forces.
Validated across single-arm manipulation, imitation-learning deployment, intent-driven switching, and zero-shot bimanual box lifting, including unseen setups.

papers.abstract: Policy gradients for autoregressive sequence models differentiate each token's log-probability while holding the conditioning history fixed. This discards information about how earlier decisions shape later conditional distributions, creating a credit-assignment bottleneck when rewards are sparse. We introduce History-Reparameterized (HR) policy gradients, which replace the frozen prefix in the score function with a differentiable reparameterized or relaxed history, allowing gradients of downstream log-probabilities to propagate backward through the generated trajectory. The resulting history-pathwise term is generally biased when added directly, so we derive Optimal HR (OHR), a centered control-variate estimator with a closed-form coefficient that minimizes the trace of the gradient variance at the population level. The variance reduction is governed by temporal structure in the policy dynamics: random or weakly structured policies provide little benefit, while policies with learned sequential dependencies yield informative history-pathwise corrections. For discrete tokens, the choice of relaxation is crucial: embedding-level relaxation yields substantial variance reduction that grows with horizon, whereas straight-through Gumbel-Softmax yields essentially none in our diagnostics. We validate the method on a Gaussian linear Markov model, a sparse-reward T-maze with a recurrent policy, and an autoregressive Transformer model for small Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) instances.
authors: Mohammad Hossein Amani, Leonardo Bocchieri, Maxime Peyrard, Cl\'ement Hongler, Robert West
bullets: Standard autoregressive policy gradients freeze prior histories, limiting how downstream decisions inform earlier actions.
HR gradients use differentiable or relaxed histories to add a history-pathwise gradient term, while OHR centers it and chooses a closed-form variance-minimizing coefficient.
Benefits depend on policy dynamics: weakly structured or random policies gain little, whereas learned sequential dependencies provide useful corrections.
Embedding-level relaxations reduce variance increasingly with sequence horizon; straight-through Gumbel-Softmax shows essentially no reduction in the reported diagnostics.
The approach is evaluated on a Gaussian linear Markov model, a sparse-reward T-maze, and small autoregressive Transformer TSP instances.

papers.abstract: Video generative models are an emerging tool for embodied agents: they can serve as scalable visual planners, generating videos that depict how to complete previously unseen tasks. However, executing these plans typically requires a video-to-action or "inverse dynamics" model trained on large, human-collected video-action datasets, severely limiting scalability. We introduce Mirror, a self-supervised approach that learns video-to-action mappings through environment interactions, without prior action data or hand-crafted rewards. Mirror learns by attempting to follow a visual plan by executing its best guess of the underlying actions in the environment. Mirror then trains on the resulting video-action pairs, incrementally self-improving and following the visual planner more closely. Across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control, Mirror outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods with learned video plans, and achieves near-expert performance with oracle plans. On Minecraft BASALT, it outperforms methods with access to expert actions or hand-engineered task knowledge. In Minecraft survival, it is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe through self-improvement alone, without rewards or expert action labels. In the offline setting, with expert action labels but no environment interaction, it sets a new state of the art in obtaining diamonds. Our results suggest that advances in video models can translate into increasingly capable agents without a corresponding need for hand-crafted rewards or large collections of expert action data.
authors: Hyunwoo Ryu, Eric Ming Chen, Max Wilcoxson, Vincent Sitzmann
bullets: Addresses the scalability bottleneck of training inverse-dynamics models on large human-collected video-action datasets.
Learns action mappings by attempting to execute visual plans, collecting resulting video-action pairs, and iteratively retraining.
Outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control with learned video plans.
Achieves near-expert performance with oracle plans and strong results on Minecraft BASALT and survival tasks.
Also performs competitively offline using expert action labels without environment interaction.

(a) Tokenized frames and text are fed into the 14B-parameter Cosmos3-Nano (NVIDIA, 2026) model, forming a causal stream of contexts whose keys and values are cached and reused. The denoiser generates K future frames while cross-attending to the context KV cache, so each observation and instruction is encoded only once. (b) Attention mask. While our self-improving approach is able to solve many tasks, it struggles on tasks with fine-grained environment interactions such as placing torches in the cave. Figure 6: Emergent in-context learning from failure. (a) We challenge our agent to escape a lava lake without fine-tuning. (b) Retaining context between deaths causes a directional bias in the agent’s trajectories, indicating in-context adaptation. (c) Shared history allows the agent to learn from its past failures in-context, leading to higher escape rates. Retaining recurrent state does not provide a comparable benefit for VPT BC.

Figure 18: MakeWaterfall comparisons. Mirror is capable of the long horizon planning necessary for MakeWaterfall. The agent must make a waterfall, remember its location, and move to another location to take a picture of it. Even though BC, UniTeam and KAIROS are trained with action labels, they achieve 0% success on this long-horizon task. They often go out of distribution. GoUp, which relies on scripted actions, cannot adapt to unseen scenarios such as when underwater. papers.abstract: Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal. We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter. CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1%, a relative improvement of over 16% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes. We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8%, and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.
authors: Sungsu Kim, Vineet Bhat, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, Ramesh Karri, Farshad Khorrami

Achieves 89.1% average success in simulation and benchmarks, with an 88.8% success rate on a real robot arm.
Shows generalization across object classes, lighting, clutter levels, and from simulation to reality.

papers.abstract: When a robot possesses more degrees of freedom than a task requires, multiple trajectories can achieve the same objective using distinct motion styles. Compositional robot control aims to preserve a selected style while simultaneously executing an independent task command, effectively balancing these potentially competing objectives. In this paper, we present CODES, a framework for compositional robot control that discovers a coherent style repertoire from diverse recordings and composes it with independent commands. First, motion retargeting maps the recordings to motions executable by the target robot; next, weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering identify styles within and across recordings without a prescribed count; finally, reinforcement learning trains a policy to compose the discovered styles with independent commands. We evaluate CODES on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across two simulators and physical hardware. Compared to baselines, CODES significantly improves kinematic coherence. Furthermore, our controller successfully tracks velocity commands that generalize beyond the support of the recorded data, exhibiting robust and distinguishable style characteristics during both cross-simulator and real-world hardware deployments. Project website: https://www.proroklab.org/compositional-motion-styles/
authors: Heedo Woo, Antonio Marino, Eduardo Sebasti\'an, Amanda Prorok
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving distinct motion styles while executing separate task commands on robots with redundant degrees of freedom.

Retargets recordings to the target robot, uses weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering to discover styles without preselecting their number, and trains a reinforcement-learning composition policy.
Evaluated on a Unitree Go2 in two simulators and on physical hardware.
Improves kinematic coherence over baselines and tracks velocity commands beyond the recorded-data support while retaining distinguishable styles.
Demonstrated across cross-simulator and real-world deployments.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Learning and composing motion styles for quadruped control. This makes recorded motion characteristics available under independently selected commands.

Fig. 3. Style switching on hardware under a fixed task command. Deployment of the CODES policy on the Unitree Go2 at a constant 0.5 m/s forward command with zero lateral and yaw-rate components, while the selected reference switches among C04, C00, C14, and C11. The colored band indicates the active style, and dashed lines the switch instants. The policy, reference bank, and state estimation run onboard, without external motion capture or offboard inference. The top row shows a time-lapse composite of the traversal, with numbered markers at successive instants of the run. (21) with respect to the active reference; the base-relative height ∆z of the four feet (FL, FR, RL, RR); and the kinematically inferred contact states. The command is identical across all four segments, while foot-swing amplitude, contact timing, and base posture differ, indicating that the reference changes how the command is executed rather than which command is tracked. papers.abstract: Robotic rearrangement tasks require planning sequences of actions that fulfill high-level specifications while also being geometrically feasible. Symbolic abstractions make the combinatorial structure of rearrangement tasks tractable, but they usually do not fully capture the geometric constraints that determine which actions a robot can actually realize. These constraints are hard to express in the symbolic model. We propose REAP (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions), a framework in which a relational graph neural network heuristic is learned over a simple symbolic abstraction. A motion planner serves as a supervisor that elicits the hidden geometric preconditions of the problem during training. Deployed with greedy best-first search, the learned heuristic generalizes out-of-distribution along object count, plan length, and object arrangement, and can be trained jointly on several domains. Compared to classical heuristic search and learning-based baselines, REAP solves more problems, requires roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods, and the action it ranks first is geometrically feasible in 94% of sampled states, against 22% for a random choice.
bullets: Addresses the gap between tractable symbolic abstractions and real geometric constraints in robotic rearrangement.
Uses a relational graph neural network over a simple symbolic model, supervised by a motion planner that reveals hidden action preconditions.
Combines the learned heuristic with greedy best-first search and generalizes across object counts, plan lengths, arrangements, and multiple domains.
Solves more problems than classical and learning-based baselines while using roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods.
Ranks a geometrically feasible action first in 94% of sampled states, compared with 22% for random choice.

figures.caption: Figure 1: REAP learns which symbolically applicable actions are geometrically feasible, without modeling the geometric constraints. (1) Grasping the target o1 is symbolically applicable, but not geometrically feasible since other objects block the target. (2) A relational GNN, whose input state includes the goal, predicts a cost Q(s, a) for each applicable action and applies to any number of objects. Feasible picks of blocking objects get low costs, infeasible picks high costs. (3) At test time, a plan is found by greedy execution or greedy best-first search on Q, with the motion planner checking each expanded action. Q is learned by an RL algorithm that uses ε-greedy WA⋆ to guide the exploration and penalizes infeasible actions.

Figure 2: REAP instantiates the same relational-GNN architecture trained with motion-planner feedback over hidden geometric preconditions across five evaluation environments, each with a different hidden geometric precondition. Gripper clearance on the open table, lateral grasp clearance in the confined shelf, blocking in a multi-level shelf, front-facing retrieval past blockers (Access-19), and finger/arm interference in 3D stacking. At the same time, REAP also learns the cost-to-go of the underlying planning problems, to guide search towards efficient solutions.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.
authors: Yanjun Li, Jiarui Ye, Weiyu Guo, Zixiao He, Kangjie Ye, Dihan Wang, Yishuo Cheng, Zishang Xiang, Mingju Gao, Hao Tang
bullets: Addresses WAMs’ difficulty distinguishing task-relevant changes from incidental visual changes.
Uses a frozen vision-language model to describe plausible task-progressing state changes between current and future frames.
Aligns encoded descriptions with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features alongside existing WAM objectives.
Adds no inference-time overhead because language components are used only during training.
Achieves 79.17% average success on HumanoidArena and improves real-world task success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.

papers.abstract: A robotic agent operating in an unknown environment must gather sufficient task-relevant information before acting. However, determining when the available information is sufficient remains a challenge. We propose a conceptual hybrid neuro-symbolic framework for task-sufficient active perception in unknown environments. After interpreting a requested task, the agent generates an initial plan and iteratively reevaluates it as new information becomes available. At each iteration, it can acquire a more informative viewpoint, inspect or manipulate candidate objects, ask the user for clarification, or perform the task. Neural perception modules update an object-centric belief state, while a symbolic decision layer determines whether the remaining uncertainty justifies further information gathering. The framework will be implemented on a mobile manipulator comprising a humanoid torso and a mobile base, with complementary evaluation in simulation. The proposed approach aims to enable robots to determine not only how to gather additional information, but also when further perception is no longer necessary.
authors: Mariana da Silva Barros, Matthias Kerzel, Cornelius Weber, Stefan Wermter
bullets: Addresses the challenge of determining when task-relevant information is sufficient in unknown environments.
Combines neural object-centric belief updates with symbolic decisions about whether further uncertainty warrants more perception.
Iteratively chooses among changing viewpoints, object inspection or manipulation, user clarification, and task execution.
Plans implementation on a mobile manipulator with simulation-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: Multi-object grasping is a fundamental yet challenging problem, constrained by data collection costs, varying spatial layouts, and the need for broad generalization. To address these challenges, we propose MoDex, a data-efficient framework that provides the first unified solution for universal multi-object dexterous grasping across diverse spatial layouts. MoDex accomplishes this by formulating the task as a single-step decision problem of learning residual corrections to a reference trajectory, and introducing a spatially adaptive dual-strategy that performs single-shot grasping for proximal objects and sequential interaction for separated objects. Extensive evaluations show that MoDex significantly outperforms baselines in proximal configurations, achieving 61.24% success on unseen objects, and achieves high success rates in separated layouts. Further experiments demonstrate its generalization across robot embodiments, scalability and zero-shot sim-to-real deployment through a vision-based policy trained solely on simulation data. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Aurora-Xiong/MoDex.
authors: Jing Xiong, Jiale Xie, Haoqi Yuan, Chaoyi Xu, Zongqing Lu
bullets: Addresses costly data collection, varying spatial layouts, and generalization in multi-object grasping.
Learns residual corrections to a reference trajectory as a single-step decision problem.
Uses single-shot grasping for proximal objects and sequential interaction for separated objects.
Achieves 61.24% success on unseen objects in proximal configurations and high success in separated layouts.
Demonstrates cross-embodiment generalization, scalability, and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer using simulation-only vision training.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich insertion requires precise geometric alignment despite uncertainty in perception, geometry, and con- trol. When this uncertainty causes unintended contact, the re- sulting contact provides local information that can guide correc- tive motion. Sampling-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) is well suited to this setting because it optimizes through forward simulation without requiring gradients through contact dynamics. However, standard SMPC methods typically use generic proposal distributions that do not exploit observed contact to determine where to search next. We introduce ContactKernels, a contact-adaptive proposal kernel that uses geometry-conditioned wrench measurements to estimate contact location and local contact geometry. The estimated contact state directly adapts the proposal distribution: contact location biases the search toward corrective motions, while the contact normal shapes the sampling covariance. We evaluate ContactKernels with Predictive Sampling (PS) and Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control across multiple insertion geometries in simulation and on a real robot. In simulation, ContactKernels improves mean insertion success by over 50 % points across both controllers. On the real robot, it increases insertion success from 53.3 % to 90.0 % and reduces mean time to insertion by 33 %. These results show that contact information can improve sampling-based control not only as feedback, but also by directly determining where the controller searches

Evaluated with Predictive Sampling and MPPI in simulation and on a real robot across multiple insertion geometries.

papers.abstract: Long-range throwing on unstructured terrain is a key capability for mobile robots in delivery and retrieval tasks, but it requires high release velocity, coordinated whole-body motion, and robustness to terrain-induced disturbances. We present a whole-body kinetic-coordination framework for a wheeled-quadruped manipulator that combines kinetic-chain arm modeling with SQP-based trajectory optimization and a reference-guided reinforcement learning policy for coordinated base motion. The manipulator is first reduced to a kinetic-chain model and optimized under kinematic and dynamic constraints to produce a high-speed throwing reference. On a stationary base, the optimized arm trajectory reaches a release speed of 12.75 m/s and a throwing distance of 16.68 m. When whole-body coordination is enabled, the system further increases the release speed to 16.64 m/s and the throwing distance to 28.25 m. We then integrate the mobility of the wheeled-quadruped platform and validate the complete policy through hardware experiments on flat ground, grass, slopes, and rough roads. The results show that kinetic-chain optimization and whole-body coordination together enable robust long-range throwing across diverse unstructured terrains.

papers.abstract: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.

papers.abstract: Transporting unsecured payloads with legged robots over uneven terrain requires balancing locomotion performance and payload stability, since aggressive motion can destabilize the payload even when the robot remains stable. We study quadrupedal transportation of unsecured stacked boxes on an edgeless torso-mounted board without dedicated payload sensors or active carrier mechanisms. To address this trade-off, we propose Payload-Adaptive Multi-Objective Reinforcement learning for Transportation (PAMORT). PAMORT trains a multi-objective base policy conditioned on a preference vector that weights locomotion and payload-stability reward groups, then trains a weight adjuster on the frozen policy to adapt this preference online from proprioception. In simulation, PAMORT achieves comparable or better overall transportation success than a corresponding single-objective baseline across different payload configurations, including an unseen three-box stack, despite training only with two boxes. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 demonstrate zero-shot transfer to slopes and steps at or beyond the training difficulty, with mean success rates of 0.850 for PAMORT and 0.675 for the baseline across eight tasks. These results demonstrate robust unsecured-payload transportation with online adaptation of the locomotion--payload trade-off from proprioceptive information.

papers.abstract: Self-motion manifold (SMM) characterizes the geometric structure of the infinite inverse kinematic solutions set of a redundant manipulator at a fixed end-effector pose, and its efficient recovery underpins feasible and global optimal motion planning. Existing methods such as null-space continuation and learning-based methods are formulated around the assumption that an SMM is a curve, and do not extend to higher redundancy orders. We instead adopt a probabilistic view: SMMs are the support of the conditional posterior over configurations given a target pose, so that recovering it reduces to sampling from a learned distribution and separating its disjoint components by clustering. The formulation is independent of the manifold dimension and requires no architectural change as the redundancy order grows. In this work, we demonstrate that our method can approximate 1-D SMMs with performance comparable to the latest null-space continuation and learning-based approach, and that it is the first method capable of approximating highly redundant 4-D SMMs in a 7R manipulator for position tasks. Project website: \href{https://github.com/accuracy-maker/high-dimenstional-self-motion-manifold-approximation}{https://github.com/accuracy-maker/high-dimenstional-self-motion-manifold-approximation}

papers.abstract: Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints. Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials. Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower. Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or MuJoCo's signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at https://younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/.
