papers.abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.
authors: Runhan Huang, Xiangcheng Zhang, Haoyu Chen, Yitong Li, Yen-Jen Wang, Bohan Lyu, Haotian Ye, Chuye Hong, Yixuan Wang, Chloe Su, Haoyu Xiong, Yangzhen Wu, Enze Xie, Travis Manderson, Stefano Ermon, Pieter Abbeel, Antonio Torralba, Dawn Song, Weirui Ye, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the need for new teleoperation datasets when adapting robot policies to new embodiments or tasks.
Uses a coding agent to generate executable robot-control programs and discover goal-achieving decision sequences through exploration.
Compiles successful experiences into modular perception-planning-control programs that can be reused and composed.
Evaluated across multiple simulated and real robot embodiments and manipulation tasks, with generalization improving as exploration scales.
Reports emergent active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration capabilities.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | System architecture and self-improving loop of RAX. The coding agent, powered by a frozen LLM, interacts with physical hardware across an isolation boundary using multimodal perception and control SDK interfaces. By reflecting on execution outcomes, the agent continually updates a persistent memory system containing working context, task notes, and a versioned repository of verified skills. During exploration, the agent compiles its perception and planning logic into standalone Python control programs that execute high-frequency loops directly on the robot. When encountering perception or planning failures due to environment variations, the program raises an exception (raise Unsure()), delegating control back to the agent to make adjustments and refine the codebase.

Figure 5 | A long-horizon task on the real RB-Y1. The agent composes six sub-tasks from skills learned in earlier sessions. It finds the cups from Gemini’s rim points and depth, measures the desk edge by picking points in the head image, and plans the base routes on a model of the scene.

Figure 3 | Agentic 3D perception and motion planning on a real robot. (a) The articulated air fryer model constructed programmatically by the agent from point-cloud measurements and fit to RGB-D observations, consisting of a fixed chassis and a drawer articulated via a prismatic joint along pull direction d relative to central axis c. (b) Action trajectories planned on the instantiated model with the drawer opened by 13.1 cm. End-effector poses are visualized as pyramids whose bases face the approach vector and whose thick edges indicate the finger closure axis. The underlying geometric estimator maintains high fidelity, yielding only a 6.5 mm displacement between the predicted basket rim and the post-opening physical measurement. Figure 27 illustrates the corresponding execution sequence on the physical robot.
Figure 4 | Frontend–backend separation. The agent and its programs act only through the tool interface; the backend owns control, sensing, and safeguards on every platform.

Figure 34 | The Bandu assembly program, running fully automatically. It finds the pieces with both exterior cameras and Gemini, keeps a slot model of the demonstrated tower, and places each piece by a guarded place, a tactile search for the seat (with a tilt check for the urn), or a camera alignment of the knob over the urn’s opening.

Figure 19 | The stance model and the crossing window. (a) How far a left step from a squared stance places the left sole ahead of the right one, against the step amplitude: the agent’s measurements and the piecewise-linear model it wrote. (b) The positions of the two soles before the bar at every start of a crossing in exploration, rehearsal, and formal episodes, with the window that the program uses.

Figure 15 | Measuring the fingertips with the wrist camera, in the agent’s first episode, re-run on its stored frames. (a) The right wrist camera with the hand in its grasp posture; the agent segments the white fingertip caps and splits them into two clusters. (b) The hand’s point cloud in the frame of the measured flange, with the two clusters and the tip offsets the agent adopted (stars). (c) A side view of the clusters, their centroids and the adopted offsets, with the fingertips of the official hand model, which the agent never saw, for comparison.

Figure 32 | The peg-insertion procedure. The agent fits the board’s CAD model and each peg’s top outline to the wrist camera’s image edges. It drops the peg into the 3 mm row, probes by touch for the 1 mm hole, and tilts a corner into the 0.1 mm hole before turning the peg upright and pushing it down.

Figure 20 | The outcome of every stage in every program run, in interactive and rehearsal episodes grouped by version (left), and for the submitted version on the 60 formal episodes, ordered by outcome (right). Each column is one episode; the counts give completed episodes.

Figure 24 | The find-the-cube program. During the shuffle it follows every cup on the wrist camera and remembers the cup that covered the cube (top); it also catches a cube that is moved or dropped into a cup (middle). It then lifts the cup that hides the cube and picks the cube up (bottom).

Figure 14 | Why the program transfers to LIBERO-Pro. (a) Mean object positions over the 50 official and the 50 perturbed layouts, seen from above with the robot at the top; the perturbation exchanges the soup with the ketchup and the tomato sauce with the orange juice. Crosses mark the program’s first estimate of each can in every perturbed episode. (b) The distance between the program’s estimate of a can’s axis and the nearer can in the simulator, for the first agent-view estimate and for the wrist refit before each grasp, against the displacement of the two cans. The task takes the cans in either order, and in two perturbed episodes Gemini exchanged their labels; the rejected refits are those on the ketchup bottle.

Figure 17 | Perception on an unseen layout and precision over the 150 formal episodes, re-run with the agent’s code. (a) The egocentric point cloud, coloured by height, with the measured disks, the peg axes, the target peg, the thumb and index targets of both pinches, and the predicted seat of the red disk. (b) The height of the red disk measured after placement, minus the height the program predicted. (c) The program’s estimate of the target peg against the hidden pose of the board, both relative to their means over the 150 layouts.

(a) An official layout of the third Long task and (b) the same layout under the LIBERO-Pro perturbation, which moves the cabinet to the other side of the table. (c) The adapted program’s check of the side, re-run on both first frames: level cells of the cabinet top above 1.08 m (orange) on either side of the robot, counted on the height map of the agent-view point cloud. (d) The adapted program on the perturbed layout, with the bowl in the drawer.

Figure 27 | The air fryer task on the real robot. The agent’s final run, from the continuous recording of an exterior camera, with the time since the start of the run under each frame. Each row is one planned action, numbered as in Figure 3(b): grasping the handle, pulling the drawer open by 13.1 cm in 3 cm steps, carrying the banana and releasing it with the hand tilted 60◦ over the basket, releasing the ball, and closing the drawer by a push that stops about 2 cm short followed by a push with closed fingers, which leaves the handle within 3.5 mm of its initial position. This camera was moved by a collision earlier in the session and was not used for perception.

Figure 6 | The program RAX writes for boxing books on BEHAVIOR-1K (Table 3). It detects the books, shelves and box in the head camera, tracks the robot’s motion by visual odometry, maps the scene, and plans paths with A*; the policy flow shows the camera view at each step.

Figure 7 | From exploration to code. Inference time (left) and output tokens (right) of each successful exploration episode, on base-2 logarithmic vertical axes; for rehearsals, inference time is the program’s computation time as measured by the harness, without the overhead of running in isolation. The token axis is linear below one thousand tokens so that zero can be shown. Filled dots mark episodes in which the agent takes part, alone or together with its program; hollow circles mark rehearsals, in which the program runs alone. On loading the car, raw points are faint and the line is a running median over five successes; output tokens of parallel episodes are attributed to the environment an agent was assigned, or split evenly across the episodes active at that moment.

Figure 12 | Adapting skills and programs on the real Franka. Each row is one program that already worked, with the task it learned (left image) and the operator’s change (green). Right: the program’s entry point after the change, condensed from the agent’s code, with new lines in green, modified lines in blue, and reused lines in black. Top: find the cube, where each image overlays frames from the left camera a quarter of a second apart, earlier ones fainter, to show how the object is hidden; the cube is first dropped into a cup and then replaced by a red wedge. Bottom: wiping with paper towels from a box; S and P are the towel program’s modules, imported unchanged.

Figure 9 | Error recovery and safety on real robots. Each incident and the rule the agent derived from it. RB-Y1: a turn planned by hand pushes a cabinet, after which every base move is checked against the area the base sweeps; squatting to lift a bucket overloads a wrist, and standing up first resolves it. Franka: an unusual arm posture hits a camera, after which the agent plans only natural postures that keep the arm away from the cameras.

Figure 23 | Find the cube, trial 11: a red wedge instead of the cube. (a)–(d) The operator tosses the wedge into an upright cup, turns the cup over, and shuffles; (c) is the wrist camera, which the agent’s detector watches. (e)–(f) On the resumed run, the robot sets the predicted cup aside and grasps the wedge on the first attempt. Left exterior camera except (c); time is from the first frame.

Figure 22 | Find the cube, trial 9: adapting to a new way of hiding the cube. (a)–(d) Left exterior camera: the operator drops the cube into an upright cup, turns the cup over, and shuffles the four cups. (e)–(f) Right exterior camera: after the agent added a detector for this case, the robot sets the identified cup aside and grasps the cube. The identification comes from the updated detector run on the recorded wrist stream, and the run resumed from locating the cups. Time is from the first frame.

Figure 11 | Continual learning on the real-world RB-Y1 mobile manipulator. Top: Modular skills acquired during prior exploration sessions and stored in the skill repository, complete with descriptions from their respective skill files. Middle: The final execution of a complex tidy-up task—a single high-level instruction carried out across six sequential stages, annotated with completion timestamps and invoked skills. Bottom: The agent’s generated code for each stage (condensed from execution logs with passed arguments). Code invoking pre-stored skills is color-coded by skill (chair, cups, bucket, and box correspond to each skill’s run.py), while ad-hoc control logic written directly by the agent is shown in black.

Figure 29 | Wiping with paper towels, second wet run, from the left exterior camera. (a) The poured stain, the tissue box, and the bin behind it; (b) a sheet pulled from the box; (c) six sheets piled on the stain; (d) the pile pressed and grasped as a wad; (e) wiping, with the towel program’s zig-zag; (f) the wad released over the bin; (g) a leftover sheet picked up by the sweep; (h) the table afterwards, with a flat wet scrap the sweep missed. Time is from the first frame.

Figure 13 | Perception and planning on a LIBERO-Pro layout, re-run with the agent’s code on the stored frames of one evaluation episode. (a) The agent-view image with Gemini’s points (diamonds) and the geometry that the program derives from depth: the top and axis of each can and the basket rim. (b) The point cloud of the agent-view camera, completed over the basket by the wrist camera and coloured by height above the table on the scale of (c) and (d), with the fitted cans, the basket rim, and the two planned placements, numbered in the order of execution. (c) The basket measured by the wrist camera in 4 mm cells, with the interior outlined. (d) Footprint reach, the highest point under the footprint of a can, and the two spots that minimize it; the circles show the footprint.

Figure 18 | Perception on an unseen DoubleDesk scene, re-run with the agent’s code on the stored frames of one formal episode. (a) The head camera at the start, with the hammer the program finds and, enlarged, its axis and length. (b) The point cloud in the level frame, coloured by height, with the hammer and the bar fitted to it. (c) The last stance before the crossing, seen from above in the frame of the bar: the soles, the window from which the program starts a crossing, and the position of the left sole that the stance model predicted. (d) The basket found at the placing stance.

Figure 8 | Active perception. Simulation, DexJoCo bimanual Tower of Hanoi (Section D.2): (1) in its first episode, the agent moves single joints of the Allegro hand and finds the white fingertip caps in the wrist camera; (2) from the caps’ points it fits the fingertip offsets relative to the flange, and, without a model of the hand, its thumb tip lies 1.1 mm from the official model; (3) after each placement, the program measures the disk again, on average 0.66 mm below the height it predicted over 150 evaluation episodes. Real robot, ManipulationNet peg-in-hole (Section G.4): the agent probes with closed fingers to measure the height of the transparent board and the tilt of the table.

Figure 25 | The air-fryer program. After its elbow hit the left camera in run 2, the agent re-registered the camera and planned only postures clear of both cameras; it releases the banana with the hand tilted 60◦. One program handles four fryer layouts; the bottom row follows the run with the fryer rotated.

Figure 30 | The wiping program. It finds the stain by comparing both exterior cameras with a clean reference and the towel heap in depth, grasps the heap as a wad, and wipes a zig-zag fitted to the reachable area. The wrist camera catches thin streaks that the exterior cameras miss, so the table is checked at both scales.

Figure 16 | The grasps the agent tried, seen by the wrist camera of the grasping hand in its exploration episodes, with panels 3 and 4 rotated so that the peg stands upright. The first four failed for the reasons given below them; the rolled vertical pinch carried both disks and became the grasp of the program.

Figure 26 | The agent’s estimators on its final run, computed by its own code. (a) Lid points from the wrist camera above the fryer; blue points are kept and grey points discarded by the trimmed least-squares circle fit (red), whose centre is the axis c. (b) Handle-arm points seen from above, around the lid circle; points outside the ±0.25 rad window (dashed) are discarded, and d points to the median of the rest. (c) Handle points in the plane along d: the outer face in each 1.5 cm height slice (red bars) and the top of the arm (dashed). (d) Banana points along their principal axis, with the fitted centre line, its ends, and its middle (the grasp point). (e) Rim points after opening around the model’s prediction (dashed), and the fitted rim (green), 6.5 mm apart. Distances are in centimetres.

Figure 10 | Human–robot interaction. Requests that the agent sent to the operator, summarized, with the scene before and after. Right: the fryer poses that the agent requested across runs 6 to 10, from its own measurements of the fryer’s axis and handle direction.

Figure 31 | The ManipulationNet peg-in-hole challenge, final run, from a crop of the left exterior camera. (a) A peg inserted into L1 (3 mm clearance); (b)–(d) the rectangle peg entering L3 (0.1 mm clearance) corner first, turned upright, and seated; (e) the three pegs seated in L3. Time is from the first frame.

Figure 28 | Wiping a stain, trial 7b, from the left exterior camera. (a) The poured stain and the towel heap; (b) the grasped wad pressed on the stain; (c) scrubbing; (d) the towel is carried back; (e) the table after one pass. Time is from the first frame.

papers.selection_reason: Online exploration framework for robot agents that synthesizes executable programs and improves manipulation skills fits robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
papers.tldr: RAX enables robots to learn and continually improve through scalable online exploration and generated control programs, without demonstrations or policy training.

papers.abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

bullets: Evaluated across 12 benchmarks covering tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands using in-context demonstrations and extended execution.
A System 2 reasoner paired with a low-level System 1 controller is costly but effective for embodied control.
Real-world tests across 8 robot configurations expose gaps in affordable demonstration collection and the usefulness of longer execution under physical constraints.
Key open challenges include generalizable in-context learning, execution cost and time, state verification, recovery from irreversible failures, and preserving progress over long horizons.
Proposed benchmark principles emphasize real-world tasks, no in-domain demonstrations, and evaluation under a continuously running world clock.

figures.caption: Figure 7 Token cost versus performance on RoboDojo for different System 1–System 2 collaboration strategies and action interfaces. Each point represents an experimental configuration, with token cost measured in millions and performance measured by the unweighted mean of category scores. Dashed lines intersect at the Agentic GPT-6-Astra baseline reference point, defining four shaded quadrants.

Figure 8 Zero-shot real-world control, from simple to complex embodiments. Frames from released videos in temporal order. Chips give successes over all counted trials. (c) GPT-6-Astra re-plans after contact displaces the receiving bowl. (e) Dexterous grasping with the Wuji hands of the Tianji M6S, given human-written grasp scripts (the successful bottle run; the toy grasp succeeds in 3/3). The full gallery is in Fig. 13, and all tasks per platform in App. E.

Figure 6 Residual failures under ICL with the extended budget. Each pair shows the state before a key event and its outcome; purple arrows mark the relevant objects. (a) Verifying physical success: apparent or self-reported completion diverges from the actual task state. (b) Recovering from consequential actions: an early mishap, such as a spill or a dropped part, cannot be undone and derails later subtasks. (c) Preserving progress over long horizons: progress that later steps depend on, such as an open lid or a placed object, is lost and blocks the task.

Figure 5 (a) Average per-task token usage and (b) average per-task time for each benchmark, stacked from bottom to top as ICL preparation, the 1× run, and the additional cost of extending to 10×. Here, 1× and 10× denote maximum action-step budgets, not token or time budgets. The relatively small additional token and time costs primarily reflect early termination of extended runs upon success or terminal failure, before the full 10× budget is exhausted. We observe that the vast majority of tokens consumed are cached input tokens (approximately 98% in our runs). Accordingly, we use a simple rule of thumb for cost estimation: 1M tokens ≈ 1 USD.

Figure 12 GPT-6-Astra in the household proof of concept. All runs are zero-shot, with contact-based grasping and no demonstrations. (a) While moving a book during tidying, the robot displaces desk items, knocks objects onto the floor and pushes the monitor out of place with its elbow. (b) Having opened the refrigerator to store the milk, the robot turns to carrying fruit to the table, and the door stays open from 300 s to 765 s of world time. (c) Making breakfast, the robot holds the refrigerator door open with one arm, but from where it stands the door blocks its other arm from the bacon inside; when it releases the handle to reach in, the door swings shut. (d) The running tap is not closed, and with the drain closed the sink fills until water spills down the cabinet onto the floor. (e) GPT-6-Astra watches an egg through the robot’s head camera and decides to turn the burner off once it has set; deciding takes 8 s of world time with the burner still on, and by the time the burner is turned off, about 90 s after the egg has set, the egg has charred. Purple outlines highlight relevant objects; timestamps denote elapsed world time. External camera views are used for visualization; the agent sees only through the robot’s onboard cameras.

Figure 4 Success rate versus step budget. The budget is expressed as a multiple of each benchmark’s official step limit; dots show observed success rates and pink curves show fitted trends. We evaluate budgets up to 10× the official limit (1× for BEHAVIOR). The gray line marks the upper bound, which assumes that every episode that exhausts the evaluated budget without succeeding has the potential to succeed with an unlimited budget.

Figure 10 Two specifications of a breakfast task. Left: the BEHAVIOR-1K activity cook_bacon [8], with its complete goal. The goal is tested against the current state at every step, and the episode succeeds at the first step at which it holds. Nothing requires the stove to be turned off, and since cooked holds once an object’s maximum temperature has passed a threshold, it remains true for bacon that has burned. Right: what a judge for the request “make breakfast” needs to express. Any acceptable refinement earns credit, graded by what is served and by when, with a value that decays once the resident has left [56]; items count as served only if they never burned. Predicates are defined on physical quantities known only to the judge. The :never and :whenever clauses are the absence [38] and bounded-response [84] specification patterns, expressible in metric [85] and signal [108] temporal logic and checked over the whole trajectory on the world clock, which keeps running after the agent declares that it is done. All constants are illustrative.

Figure 11 Building and using the household environment. Publicly available assets (1) and a floor plan (2) are composed into an interactive home. Coding agents place everyday items at real-world scale on named supports under human review (3), and every part is bound to physics: articulation, liquids, cloth and contact (4). A task states only a need (5): asked to make breakfast, the agent must work out the fridge, air fryer and toaster by itself, and is to be judged both on the request (Intent) and on obligations no one stated, such as closing the fridge (Duty). The agent sees only through the robot’s onboard cameras, and its deliberation advances world time (6).

Figure 3 Contents of an ICL knowledge package. GPT-6-Astra decides what to retain, yet packages share six recurring components; file types are typical and content varies by benchmark. At test time, K is read alongside current observations to retrieve, adapt and check actions.

Figure 2 In-context learning protocol. For each task, GPT-6-Astra studies the training data and writes a knowledge package K, which is frozen before testing. Each test episode starts a fresh session with K and runs under the standard (1×) or extended (10×) budget. Model weights remain fixed throughout, and K remains unchanged during testing, and no information passes between episodes.
Figure 19 Galaxea R1 Pro: (a) washer task and (b) flower collection, from the task records; (c–h) tabletop manipulation tasks.
Figure 20 AgileX Tracer + xArm7: one recorded run per navigation task, third-person phone video. Chips give successes over all trials of the task.

Figure 18 Tianji M6S with Wuji hands: (a) toy grasp with grasp code written by GPT-6-Astra (round 1; the toy is never lifted), (b) toy grasp and (c) bottle grasp with human-written grasp scripts. Frames from the head-camera recordings.

Figure 9 What GPT-6-Astra can do depends on what it can see. Flower insertion, main view and wrist views. Frames are from third-person recordings; GPT-6-Astra received the head-camera RGB view and tool-returned robot state. Binary hand profiles were used.

Table 2 Benchmark-level success rates (%) underlying Fig. 1. For each benchmark, we list the best published result (SOTA) with its method, the best published agentic method (Agentic SOTA), and GPT-6-Astra + ICL under the standard (1×) and cumulative extended (up to 10×) budgets. Benchmarks are grouped by embodiment. Published baselines are reported under the standard budget. papers.abstract: Robot policies are expected to generalize across deployment environments, including variations in the robot itself: cameras are bumped and remounted, calibrations drift, controllers run at different rates, and end-effector pads wear down. We present LIBERO-RIG, a benchmark that perturbs only the robot's hardware and setup while holding every LIBERO task fixed. The benchmark spans eleven perturbation axes, including camera mounting and optics, camera-to-arm calibration, actuation gain, control rate, proprioceptive noise, base pose, table height, and gripper pads. Each axis has five severity levels, yielding 210 conditions across the four LIBERO suites. We evaluate nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and substantiate each finding with rigorous statistical tests. Pooled success falls from 0.932 to 0.767 at the middle severity and 0.509 at the highest severity. Performance degradation varies substantially across perturbation axes and action interfaces, and training on visual perturbations does not mitigate faults that leave camera images unchanged. We release the benchmark together with manifests specifying the fixed perturbation parameters for each episode.
bullets: Benchmarks robustness to 11 hardware/setup perturbation axes across four LIBERO suites, with five severity levels and 210 conditions.
Evaluates nine recent vision-language-action models using 500 episodes per condition and statistical testing.
Pooled success decreases from 0.932 under nominal conditions to 0.767 at medium severity and 0.509 at the highest severity.
Robustness varies substantially by perturbation axis and action interface.
Training on visual perturbations does not address faults that do not alter camera images; fixed-parameter episode manifests are released.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for vision-language-action robot policies under hardware perturbations, directly fitting VLA and robot learning/manipulation.
papers.title: LIBERO-RIG: A Hardware-Setup Robustness Benchmark for Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) have recently shown that a single humanoid policy can support diverse whole-body control, but extending such generality to physical interaction remains challenging. We introduce I-BFM, to our knowledge the first BFM for humanoid-object interaction. Rather than relying on task-specific policies or reference tracking, I-BFM learns a shared representation of the coupled dynamics among the humanoid, objects, and their contacts using forward-backward representations and unsupervised reinforcement learning. Given a downstream task reward, the same policy can be directly conditioned on a latent command to execute closed-loop interaction without task-specific policy optimization. To improve interaction control over different time scales, we further train the policy with both short-horizon interaction targets and longer-horizon goal targets. A single I-BFM policy performs carrying, pushing, and kicking, while also supporting goal reaching, motion tracking, stylistic control, and long-horizon task chaining. More importantly, it remains effective after large deviations from nominal execution: on Carry, I-BFM achieves 94.3% nominal success and retains 89.3% success after robot falls, compared with 1.3% for a planning-based baseline. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 further demonstrate diverse loco-manipulation behaviors, rapid recovery from interaction failures and external disturbances, and task chaining without task-specific retraining.
bullets: Learns shared representations of coupled humanoid–object–contact dynamics using forward-backward representations and unsupervised reinforcement learning.
Conditions one policy on downstream task rewards through latent commands for closed-loop interaction.
Combines short-horizon interaction targets with long-horizon goal targets to support multiple control time scales.
Supports carrying, pushing, kicking, goal reaching, motion and stylistic control, and long-horizon task chaining.
On Carry, achieves 94.3% nominal success and 89.3% after robot falls; real-world tests on a Unitree G1 show recovery from failures and disturbances.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables robot policies to improve through physical interaction, but the assistance they require changes as their competence evolves. Existing intervention strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules can therefore become mismatched to the current policy. To address this, we propose UniIntervene++, an adaptive intervention agent that learns to allocate control between autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors during online RL. Specifically, UniIntervene++ first formulates the evolving RL policy, trajectory correction, and a task-structured CodePolicy as Options in a unified semi-Markov decision process and learns their relative values online. Building on this, competence-adaptive intervention periodically probes the RL policy through unassisted execution, keeping control allocation responsive to its evolving capability. Finally, coupled experience learning allows assisted behaviors to improve the RL policy, whose evolving outcomes in turn reshape future intervention decisions. In this way, UniIntervene++ jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene, and when to return control as the RL policy improves. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of 89.67%, outperforming all baselines by at least 6 percentage points, while reducing human intervention to 0.77%, a relative reduction of at least 94.6% from the best baseline. Code is available in our \href{https://github.com/dannyyudong/An-Adaptive-Intervention-Agent-for-Efficient-Real-World-Reinforcement-Learning}{GitHub repository}.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between fixed or offline intervention rules and an RL policy whose competence changes during learning.
Models autonomous execution, trajectory correction, and structured CodePolicy assistance as Options in a unified semi-Markov decision process.
Learns option values online and periodically probes unassisted behavior to keep control allocation competence-aware.
Uses coupled experience learning so assisted behaviors improve the RL policy and the policy’s progress updates future intervention choices.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks, reaches 89.67% average success with 0.77% human intervention, outperforming baselines by at least 6 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Pretrained robot policies offer strong manipulation skills but are typically limited to single-agent settings, where a robot acts in isolation. In this work, we study how to adapt pretrained single-agent diffusion policies to multi-agent settings using minimal collaborative data, co-optimizing for two key objectives: high coordination performance and single-agent skill retention. To this end, we introduce ALTER, an adaptation method for coordination on demand: the adapted policy coordinates with other robots when deployed in a team while remaining capable of acting independently when operating alone. Execution is decentralized: each robot acts only on its own visual observations, without explicit inter-agent communication. Our method trains a coordination head that predicts a residual denoiser to transform single-agent behavior into coordinated multi-agent behavior when necessary while also preserving single-agent capabilities. To preserve single-agent capabilities, we augment a small number of collaborative demonstrations with self-distilled data generated by the base policy during training of the residual denoiser. In simulation, ALTER achieves higher coordination success over our baselines while retaining much higher source-skill retention. In our hardware experiments, we find similar trends where ALTER better co-optimizes for coordination success and single-agent skill retention than the baselines.
bullets: Targets on-demand coordination: robots collaborate in teams but act independently when alone.
Trains a coordination head that predicts a residual denoiser to modify single-agent behavior when needed.
Uses self-distilled data from the base policy alongside a small number of collaborative demonstrations to retain source skills.
In simulation and hardware experiments, ALTER improves the coordination–skill-retention trade-off over baselines.

papers.abstract: This study asks whether training-time motion-prior regularization can improve insertion success when a diffusion policy is learned from only 15 demonstrations. Minimum jerk discourages abrupt changes in predicted translational acceleration; speed-curvature regularization instead couples movement speed to path geometry. These are candidate mechanisms for task completion, not safety guarantees. We compare the priors individually and jointly, neither prior, and generic smoothness, with 80 real-robot trials per setting pooled over four recorded condition classes. Joint and minimum-jerk-only settings each achieved 70/80 successes (87.5%), versus 69/80 (86.3%) for speed-curvature only, 66/80 (82.5%) for neither prior, and 67/80 (83.8%) for generic smoothness. Success rates and Wilson 95% confidence intervals are visualized for direct comparison. Joint regularization exceeded neither by 5.0 percentage points but provided no observed gain over minimum jerk alone. The results motivate minimum jerk as the simpler candidate for replication, without establishing synergy, biomechanical specificity, improved safety, or distribution-shift robustness.
bullets: Evaluates motion-prior regularization for diffusion-policy robotic insertion under data scarcity.
Compares minimum jerk, speed-curvature, their combination, no prior, and generic smoothness.
Uses 80 real-robot trials per setting across four recorded condition classes.
Minimum jerk and joint regularization each achieved 70/80 successes (87.5%); no prior achieved 66/80 (82.5%).
Findings support minimum jerk as the simpler replication candidate, with limited scope for safety or distribution-shift claims.

papers.abstract: Agent skills adapt frozen models through editable external instructions. Revising several rules at once makes changes difficult to inspect, while judging each local edit only by its immediate score can discard useful intermediate states. We introduce AtomSearch, which keeps revision actions local while using subsequent skill states to guide search. Contrastive atomic editing links each primitive rule edit to failed and successful executions, a behavioral hypothesis, and an intended scope. Skill-State Tree Search (STS) evaluates short edit compositions and selectively retains them as executable states that can be revisited and extended. Outcome memory supplies later proposals with observed repair and regression statistics. We evaluate AtomSearch across four tasks and five target models. With deepseek-v4-flash, it exceeds SkillOpt on three of four tasks, including a 9.68-percentage-point gain on LiveMathematicianBench, and SkillOpt's final skills contain 2.3-19.7 times as many characters. In 67% of completed searches, the best validation state passes through an ancestor that was not highest-scoring at its depth. These results show how local rule edits can support the exploration of useful revision paths and yield compact skills, with additional offline evaluations used to explore alternative states.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of inspecting multi-rule revisions and the risk of discarding useful states based only on immediate scores.
Uses contrastive atomic editing to connect each rule change to execution evidence, behavioral hypotheses, and intended scope.
Skill-State Tree Search evaluates short edit sequences, retains executable states, and revisits or extends them; outcome memory informs later proposals.
Across four tasks and five models, it outperformed SkillOpt on three of four tasks for deepseek-v4-flash, including a 9.68-point gain on LiveMathematicianBench.
Searches often benefited from non-greedy paths: 67% of completed searches passed through a best-state ancestor that was not top-scoring at its depth.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) systems already bring together two valuable resources for robot learning: rich visual representations and demonstrations of successful task execution. Intrinsic Robot Rewarding (IRR) proposes to use these resources for a second, complementary purpose: evaluating the robot's own outcomes and providing feedback for policy improvement. Successful demonstration endpoints define task-specific references, and the policy's frozen visual encoder provides the feature space in which new outcomes are assessed. The core reward mechanism adds a reference bank and a scoring operation to the existing pipeline, without requiring a separate learned evaluator or an additional perception backbone. Our position is that this reuse offers a promising route to lower integration effort, efficient reward computation, and reduced recurring human outcome scoring. Building on established research in visual rewards and learning from experience, IRR brings these ideas into the robot's existing perception and demonstration pipeline. An operational COMAU Racer 3 demonstrator is available at technology readiness level 4 (TRL 4). This laboratory foundation supports the next research step: connecting internal outcome evaluation to physical policy improvement. We present the reward formulation, central research questions, and an evaluation methodology linking reward reliability to task success and supervision effort. The intended contribution is a reusable approach to learn and improve from the data and experience already available in industrial robot systems.
bullets: Uses successful demonstration endpoints as task-specific reference outcomes.
Scores new robot outcomes in the frozen VLA visual encoder’s feature space.
Adds a reference bank and scoring step to the existing pipeline, avoiding an extra perception backbone or learned evaluator.
Targets lower integration effort, efficient reward computation, and less recurring human outcome scoring.
The work defines a reward formulation and evaluation methodology; physical policy improvement remains a future research step, with a TRL 4 COMAU Racer 3 demonstrator available.

papers.abstract: Action Chunking Transformers (ACT) are widely used to learn robot manipulation from demonstrations. Their conditional variational autoencoder includes an encoder meant to capture differences between demonstrations during training. The original ACT paper reported that encoder removal dropped the mean success rate from 35% to 2% on two simulated tasks with human demonstrations. We re-ran this ablation in the original code and checked whether the findings depend on the implementation or training data. The published drop does not reappear in our tests, although smaller gains or losses in success rate remain uncertain. To investigate the discrepancy, we varied training length and how checkpoints are selected for evaluation. Both can reverse which policy scores higher, but the published drop's cause remains unknown. Success rates alone leave open whether the encoder provides information that helps the policy reconstruct demonstrated actions. On the tested ACT benchmark, the sampled latent provides little reconstruction benefit at every tested nonzero weight of the penalty on latent information. At inference, ACT leaves this latent unused and sets it to zero. Skipping the encoder increases training throughput in both implementations we timed. We release code, evaluation tools and results so others can repeat the comparisons and test the encoder on other tasks.
bullets: The original 35%→2% success-rate drop after encoder removal was not observed in the re-run.
Training duration and checkpoint-selection rules can reverse which policy performs better, but do not explain the published discrepancy.
The latent provides little reconstruction benefit across tested nonzero information-penalty weights and is set to zero during inference.
Removing the encoder improves training throughput in both timed implementations.
Code, evaluation tools, and results are released to support reproducibility and testing on other tasks.

papers.abstract: Reward shaping is fundamental to modern robotic control with deep reinforcement learning (RL), yet practitioners still rely heavily on heuristic principles borrowed from classical optimal control and trajectory optimization. Existing methods rarely distinguish reward terms that are intrinsic to the control objective from numerical regularizers, leading to brittle hyperparameter tuning. To determine which quantities a reward must contain, we study the stabilization control problem with a focus on zeroth-order (configuration) and first-order (velocity) information. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that policy gradient methods can successfully solve stabilization tasks without first-order reward terms, adding such terms can instead introduce severe sensitivity as their scale grows. Conversely, our findings confirm that reward functions must be zeroth-order complete over goal-relevant coordinates, while the first-order state remains necessary in the policy observation under our low-dissipation assumptions. Overall, these results provide actionable and principled guidance for reward design in robotic RL.
bullets: Studies whether stabilization rewards require zeroth-order configuration information, first-order velocity information, or both.
Theoretically and empirically finds that velocity-based reward terms are unnecessary for successful stabilization under the studied assumptions.
Adding first-order reward terms can introduce severe sensitivity as their scale increases.
Rewards must be zeroth-order complete over goal-relevant coordinates.
Velocity remains necessary in policy observations under low-dissipation assumptions.

papers.abstract: Existing adaptive reasoning methods for driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily focus on whether to reason, overlooking how reasoning should differ across driving situations. Our key insight is that while scene complexity informs reasoning depth, dynamic risk is equally critical for deciding how to reason in time-critical situations. We therefore propose CAR-VLA, a unified driving VLA model that jointly considers scene complexity and dynamic risk to guide reasoning depth, urgency, and focus. CAR-VLA maps four complexity--risk categories to three reasoning modes: \textit{Fast Intuition} for direct trajectory generation in simple low-risk scenes, \textit{Slow Thinking} for deliberate reasoning in complex low-risk scenes, and \textit{Reflex Response} for compact, hazard-focused reasoning in high-risk scenes regardless of complexity. Rather than merely shortening deliberation, Reflex Response centers reasoning on the most critical hazard and the immediate safe response. We train CAR-VLA through progressive supervised learning that links scene assessment, reasoning-mode selection, and trajectory generation, followed by reasoning-augmented reinforcement learning to improve driving quality and reasoning behavior. Experiments on NAVSIM v1(91.1 PDMS), NAVSIM v2(90.3 EPDMS), and Navhard(35.0 EPDMS) demonstrate competitive driving performance. Qualitative comparisons on navtest and in-house high-risk scenarios further illustrate risk-aware reasoning and hazard-responsive trajectory generation. The code for this paper will be released publicly at: https://github.com/chenxl124578/CAR-VLA.git
bullets: Addresses the limitation of methods that decide only whether to reason, not how reasoning should vary by situation.
Maps complexity–risk conditions to Fast Intuition, Slow Thinking, and Reflex Response modes.
Uses progressive supervised learning followed by reasoning-augmented reinforcement learning to connect scene assessment, mode selection, and trajectory generation.
Reports competitive performance on NAVSIM v1, NAVSIM v2, and Navhard, with qualitative evidence of risk-aware, hazard-responsive behavior.
Scope: high-risk situations receive compact, hazard-centered reasoning regardless of overall scene complexity.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of CAR-VLA. (b) Teacher-assisted data construction produces two complementary datasets: scene assessment data containing assessment reasoning and scene labels, and mode-adaptive driving data containing scene labels, driving reasoning, and trajectories. (c) Progressive supervised fine-tuning jointly learns general driving knowledge and scene assessment in Stage I, then learns scene classification, mode-specific reasoning, and trajectory generation in Stage II. (d) Reasoning-augmented reinforcement learning updates the policy through GSPO using driving, geometry, format, and reasoning rewards. papers.abstract: Co-training offers a straightforward way to build a multi-task vision-language-action (VLA) policy, but can fall short of the performance achieved by training each task independently. The challenge is to retain these task-specific gains in a multi-task policy without joint post-training. Combining independently trained experts through model merging is a natural approach, yet strong individual experts do not necessarily yield a strong merged policy. We identify one source of this incompatibility: task-specific changes to the action interface, comprising action normalization and the action encoder and decoder. We propose PolicyWeave, combining merge-compatible post-training with context-guided sparse merging. During post-training, all experts retain the common base policy's action interface, while task adaptation is restricted to LoRA updates in the hidden layers of the action model. This makes the experts more compatible with existing model merging methods. However, merging all experts can still introduce interference from unrelated tasks at deployment. PolicyWeave scores each expert's LoRA updates using the initial visual-language context, determines the expert set through leave-one-layer-out ranking stability, and forms a sparse weighted merge of the selected updates that remains fixed for current task. We evaluate PolicyWeave with GR00T N1.5 on 18 RoboCasa365 tasks, using only 10% of the target-task demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Preserving the shared action interface raises the average success rate across four static merging methods from 17.0% to 52.8%. PolicyWeave achieves 64.7% success with these SFT experts and 74.1% after task-specific reinforcement learning (RL), compared with 60.7% for joint RL. Further evaluations on LIBERO-10 and an AgileX Piper arm support the deployment of independently learned skills in long-horizon and real-world manipulation.
bullets: Independent task experts can outperform jointly trained policies, but incompatible action normalization and encoders/decoders make merging unreliable.
PolicyWeave keeps the base policy’s action interface fixed and restricts task adaptation to hidden-layer LoRA updates.
It scores expert updates from the initial vision-language context, selects stable experts, and creates a sparse weighted merge for each task.
On 18 RoboCasa365 tasks with 10% of target-task demonstrations, shared-interface merging increased average success from 17.0% to 52.8%; PolicyWeave reached 64.7% with SFT and 74.1% after RL.
Additional evaluations on LIBERO-10 and a real AgileX Piper arm support long-horizon and real-world manipulation use cases.

papers.abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.
authors: Zhixu Li, Keqian Tang, Litian Gong, Jingyu Yao, Wenqian Zhang, Tianze Xu, Zehao Wang, Yuping Wang, Junge Zhang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Covers five questions: zero-shot preference following, learning from demonstrations, sample efficiency, cross-task/layout generalization, and preference conflicts.
Defines language-expressible preferences spanning motion, skill, and user-profile choices, with automatic preference-satisfaction metrics.
Provides five task suites totaling 312 simulated tasks, paired demonstrations, metadata, and reusable procedural generation.
Current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization; supervised fine-tuning makes preferences learnable.
Mixed training preserves no-preference behavior better than sequential adaptation, while generalization, decomposition, conflict handling, and some motion-preference learning remain challenging.

papers.abstract: Real-world post-training of generalist robot policies faces two challenges: partial observability makes action selection ambiguous, while offline post-training methods delay feedback from deployment experience. We present Value as Memory (VaM), a framework that addresses these challenges through value caching and online real-world reinforcement learning (RL). Value caching conditions actions on recent value predictions as task-progress memory, while online updates enable timely policy improvement by combining offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient adaptation. As a result, VaM transitions from offline RL warmup to online autonomous learning with sparse rewards. Across long-horizon tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulation, VaM yields a mean absolute success-rate gain of $29.4\%$ with value caching, while achieving a $32.8\%$ gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training. The evaluated online schedule performs $8\times$ as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than $2\times$ lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.
authors: Wenye Yu, Yijin Chen, Kaiyi Xiong, Wenbo Han, Wendi Chen, Yang Jin, Han Xue, Jun Lv, Cewu Lu, Chuan Wen

The evaluated schedule performs 8× more policy iterations and records over 2× lower time per gradient step through concurrent data collection and training.

papers.abstract: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. papers.abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies benefit from large-scale visual pretraining but often struggle with contact-rich dexterous manipulation, where force, compliance, and incipient slip are hard to observe from images. We present Spark-0, a spatially aligned vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) model that uses touch in two complementary ways. During pretraining, image-space contact maps derived from tactile gloves, together with features from a frozen 3D geometry teacher, supervise the visual tokens; these objectives are removed at inference. In parallel, a tactile pathway encodes regional force histories and 3D taxel states to condition the action expert. A single checkpoint therefore supports both vision-only and tactile-conditioned deployment. To scale this supervision, we build HumanTouch, a 1,000-hour dataset of full-hand tactile human manipulation, and pretrain Spark-0 on it together with egocentric video, robot data, and simulation. We also release SparkArena, which pairs vision-only simulated tasks with tactile-conditioned real-robot tasks on one dexterous embodiment. Spark-0 achieves the highest mean success rate on both SparkArena tracks and ranks first on all eight aggregate metrics of the Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark. Compared with vision-only pretraining on the same data and compute with touch discarded, retaining the touch of 1,000 hours of HumanTouch raises vision-only success on Ego Humanoid from 52.5% to 71.7%, and success on SparkArena-Real, where touch is also used at deployment, from 44.0% to 52.0%, indicating that touch serves not only as a policy input but also as scalable supervision for dexterous visuomotor pretraining. The Website is available at: https://xsparkai.com/Spark-0.

papers.abstract: How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Botao He, Yiming Dou, Yiannis Aloimonos, Jitendra Malik, Akash Sharma, Ruoshi Liu
bullets: A behavior-cloned play policy autonomously gathers hours of contact-rich interaction data for training a world model.
The play policy guides model-predictive control by proposing candidate action sequences evaluated by the learned model.
Self-play in the world model distills faster closed-loop, goal-conditioned policies.
Evaluated on underactuated pushing and multifingered in-hand pose reorientation in simulation and the real world.
In real-world tests, DSP improved success by 69.6% over hindsight behavior cloning and matched reinforcement learning using 490× less interaction data.

papers.abstract: Robotic harvesting requires precise manipulation to ensure accurate positioning of the end-effector, especially in a constraint workspace. This study introduces the Path-Safe Approach Proximal Policy Optimization (PSA-PPO), a target-conditioned local reaching framework designed for robotic harvesting of nutrient film technique (NFT)-hydroponic lettuce in greenhouses. The proposed PSA-PPO preserves the standard clipped PPO objective while introducing a harvesting-oriented policy formulation that integrates target-conditioned observations, corridor-aware spatial constraints, trajectory-history-based safety encoding, and task-specific success criteria for constrained robotic manipulation. PSAPPO was trained entirely in Isaac Lab and successfully transferred to a physical UR10e robotic arm without any real-world policy fine-tuning. In a controlled physical benchmark against 150 scheduled targets, PSA-PPO achieved the highest reaching rate of 94.7%, outperforming Cartesian+TOTG (86.0%), RRTConnect (88.0%), and RRT* (80.0%), while reducing median RMS jerk by 39.8 to 73.0% relative to the classical planners during the final approach segment. A formulation ablation evaluated over 200 simulation targets demonstrates that path-safety and side-corridor shaping are the principal drivers of harvesting-compatible performance: removing either term substantially degrades strict success even when terminal endpoint accuracy is preserved or improved, confirming that optimization toward the endpoint alone is an insufficient objective for constrained crop-proximal manipulation. Finally, PSA-PPO was integrated with an RGB-D vision module and an end-effector and evaluated as a complete greenhouse harvesting system across 144 lettuce harvesting attempts, achieving 94.4% vision-guided target reaching and 86.1% complete harvesting success.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation fundamentally requires memory: agents must retain task-relevant information from past observations and interactions and use it to guide future actions. Existing approaches typically preserve raw historical observations, compressed visual tokens, or language summaries, but these representations either expose the action policy to increasingly long histories or risk discarding task-relevant temporal, semantic, and perceptual information. We introduce Mem4Act, a framework for learning effective latent memory as a fixed-size representation explicitly optimized for long-horizon robotic control. Mem4Act addresses three coupled challenges: how to efficiently cover long histories, what information memory should retain, and how to ensure the policy actually relies on memory. To this end, it organizes history via multi-granularity temporal aggregation, preserves complementary semantic and perceptual information through question-answering supervision and key-frame DINO feature reconstruction, and employs memory-first two-stage training to encourage greater use of memory by the action policy. The resulting memory captures both high-level task state and fine-grained perceptual evidence while providing a bounded interface to the action policy. Across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, Mem4Act achieves state-of-the-art performance on memory-dependent control, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%, respectively. Extensive ablations further demonstrate the importance of temporal aggregation, complementary memory supervision, and memory-first training.
authors: Yun Zhang, Zhiyu Huang, Tianhui Cai, Chen Tang, Wei Wang, Jiaqi Ma
bullets: Addresses the limitations of raw histories, visual-token compression, and language summaries in memory-dependent control.
Uses multi-granularity temporal aggregation to efficiently cover long interaction histories.
Combines question-answering supervision with key-frame DINO feature reconstruction to retain complementary semantic and perceptual information.
Applies memory-first two-stage training to encourage the action policy to rely on the learned memory.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across RoboMME, RMBench, and four real-world manipulation tasks, with success rates of 49.88%, 61.0%, and 81.5%.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation and overview of Mem4Act. (a) Mem4Act consolidates retained interaction history into a fixed-size latent memory, providing a bounded context to the action policy. (b) Mem4Act addresses coverage, content, and utilization problems through structured multigranularity attention, semantic and perceptual supervision, and memory-first training. (c) Mem4Act improves memory-intensive control across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks.

Figure 4: Mem4Act reliably leverages memory for long-horizon robotic manipulation. Across simulation and real-world tasks, it preserves historical semantic and perceptual information, tracks task progress, and supports correct actions in long-horizon tasks.

Figure 2: Mem4Act structure. (a) Historical observations are encoded as compact visual tokens with state, phase, and time embeddings. (b) The latent memory tokens first attend within fine temporal windows, then are regrouped to attend broader windows. Global self-attention produces the final latent memory Mt. (c) Memory-related question answering and multi-keyframe DINO feature reconstruction supervise what this memory retains. (d) The resulting memory conditions action generation through memory modulation in the action expert. papers.abstract: Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
authors: Helena Merker, Nick Walker, Andreea Bobu
bullets: Human teaching often covers some task features better than others, leaving rewards underspecified.
The method uses teaching data to identify uncertain features and build an informed prior for targeted preference queries.
Each query includes an explanation that directs human attention to the relevant features.
In simulation, targeted queries improve performance over a standard baseline by up to 30.8% in low-query settings.
A user study finds that targeted queries and explanations independently improve reward recovery and work better together.

papers.abstract: In robotic manipulation, the same observation often admits multiple feasible actions. Generative policies such as diffusion and flow matching naturally capture such multimodal behaviors, yet which mode is executed is left to random sampling and cannot be actively controlled. We propose Mode-Oriented Source Shaping (MOSS), which turns mode selection into an explicit choice of where generation starts. We first reveal, both empirically and theoretically, that deterministic flow transport induces mode-dependent structure in the source space. Under ideal deterministic ODE transport, distinct behavioral modes have distinct source-space preimages, while practical approximation errors can blur their boundaries due to imbalanced data, limited model capacity, and few inference steps. Motivated by this source-space structure, MOSS constructs semantically aligned mode-specific Gaussian sources that encode mode identity in the initial noise. A modality-strength estimator predicts the local degree of multimodality, which adaptively controls the geometry of the mode-specific sources. It contracts them toward a shared Gaussian where behaviors are similar and separates them near behavioral branching points. During deployment, the desired behavior is selected at inference simply by sampling from the corresponding component. Across 6 simulated and 3 real-world manipulation tasks, MOSS steers to the target mode up to 100% of the time with high task success, recovers minority modes at over 90% guidance rate under a 10:90 imbalance dataset, and surpasses mode-conditioned flow policy by 43.3 points of guidance rate on real robots.
authors: Zirun Ma, Jindou Jia, Tuo An, Jiaqi Bai, Jiahua Dong, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Deterministic flow transport creates mode-dependent structure in source space, but approximation errors can blur mode boundaries.
MOSS builds semantically aligned, mode-specific Gaussian source distributions to represent behavior choices.
A modality-strength estimator adaptively contracts or separates these sources based on local behavioral multimodality.
At inference, users select a behavior by sampling from its corresponding source component.

Across 6 simulated and 3 real-world tasks, MOSS achieves up to 100% mode guidance, over 90% minority-mode recovery under 10:90 imbalance, and a 43.3-point guidance-rate gain over a mode-conditioned flow policy on real robots.

papers.abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans' ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.
authors: Conor Mc Gartoll, An Dang, Pranay Thangeda, Arjun Gupta, Carolina Higuera, Nima Fazeli, Mustafa Mukadam, Manikantan Nambi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of end-effector-only grasping for bulky-object manipulation.
Builds a feasible whole-body grasp dataset, trains reinforcement-learning experts for grasp-to-grasp repositioning, and distills them into one policy.
The policy uses proprioception and object geometry and transfers zero-shot from simulation to a real Unitree G1.
Demonstrations include repositioning a basketball and box, plus carrying and stowing a box in a long-horizon task.
Across real-world tasks, it completes 90% of trials versus 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.

papers.abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
authors: Juliette Marrie, Paul Pacaud, Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Shizhe Chen, Moritz B\"ohle
bullets: Pretrained exclusively on curated public robot, egocentric human, and vision-language data.
Combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert.
Uses register tokens to summarize recent VLM outputs in the action expert’s cache at negligible cost.
Improves simulated and real-robot success, while making pose oscillations about four times rarer.
Outperformed only by roughly twice-as-large models on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand, and RoboCasa365.

Figure 3: REKI. (a) Camera views and instruction are encoded as context Et, which every expert block reads by cross-attention. The state embedding gt and the flow time modulate the actions through adaptive normalisation. The noisy chunk enters the expert’s stream, and the flow loss compares the predicted velocity with its target. The register keys and values of past frames are kept in a cache and read by self-attention, which is the memory of §4.1. (b) One of the ten blocks, holding nr=32 registers and the action tokens of the current frame. Arrows run from a query to what it reads. Action tokens read the current and past registers and themselves, and registers never read them.

Figure 2: How VLAs carry the past. Each panel shows one training window of three frames, with a loss under each frame that receives one. The VLM takes the whole window as input, and only the last frame is supervised. (b) A state is written at each step and read at the next, in the backbone (Cherepanov et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026) or as fast weights in the head (Jiang et al., 2026). Each step needs the output of the previous one, so the window is unrolled step by step. (c) Each frame is encoded on its own, and an added module mixes the memory tokens of past frames into the prediction for the current one. HAMLET (Koo et al., 2026) supervises the last frame only, and MemoryVLA (Shi et al., 2026) every frame, with the bank entries stored without gradient. (d) In REKI, the memory tokens are registers in the action expert. Their keys and values are kept across frames and read by the self-attention already present. The window is one batched pass, and every frame receives a loss.
