Procrustes similarity between each pair of models is highest for the gripper and lowest for wrist orientation, and all values exceed a shuffled null (0.00–0.02 for gripper and distance; 0.11–0.18 for wrist and EE position). (Gripper) Pullback steering vectors (379 per model) on their top three principal components, colored by whether they close (blue) or open (red) the gripper. (Wrist orientation) Activations on a (cos θ, sin θ) probe, colored by angle. (EE position) Activations on the (x, y, z) probe. (Distance to grasp) The real-world proxy for distance to target: activations on the meter and centimeter rulers of Fig. 3, with far (cool) and near (warm) points spreading along different rulers. Episode trajectories are overlaid in the last three columns.

Figure 2: MolmoBot’s VLM encodes its end-effector (layer 20) and the target object (layer 21) in separate, approximately Euclidean 3-D subspaces. Top: (a) held-out per-axis error relative to gripper width; (b) held-out R2 vs. readout rank; (c) singular values of the rank-3 readout; (d) residual of a linear map from world to activation displacements across layers (solid: general linear; dashed: orthogonal; reference line: no linear relation); (e) curvature of straight world paths inside each subspace vs. distance to the gripper, compared with a random 3-D projection. Middle, bottom: five gripper paths through the workspace (middle) and five target paths across its support surface (bottom), shown in world coordinates (upper) and projected into the corresponding subspace (lower). Subspaces are fit with the tested house held out.
Figure 34: The seven task variables. An overview of each variable we study.

Figure 5: MolmoBot’s action expert encodes task phase, but infers it from motion, so pauses are read as phase transitions (layer 24). Top: an example pick-and-place trajectory and its path through the phase subspace. Bottom: (a) LDA projection of natural rollouts, colored by phase. (b) First three principal components of natural activations, colored by true phase; the example trajectory is colored by the LDA probe readouts. (c) Freezing the arm shifts the decoded phase toward grasp during reach; frozen place landmarks are most often still decoded as place. Right: most frequent decoded phases when frozen (top two for reach and place). (d) Change in the fraction of executed-chunk steps commanding a closed gripper (frozen − natural; mean ± 95% CI across landmarks). Frozen reach and grasp moments close the gripper, while frozen place moments open it (Fig. 19).

Figure 33: Gripper steering vectors on real DROID episodes. (Top left) A linear probe decodes each model’s own gripper command from the activations projected onto the top-k principal components of the steering vectors. Dashed lines: each model’s full-activation ceiling. (Top right) Activations colored by the commanded gripper (red open, blue closed); the steering vectors point from each cluster toward the other. (Bottom left) One component captures 59 % of π0.5’s steering-vector variance (stable rank 1.69) but only 31% of MolmoAct2’s (stable rank 3.21).(Bottom right) One component flips the gripper (94–96% of attempts, both models) but leaks into the arm joints at 2.4–4.3× the full-δ optimum. Activations are recorded and steered at the final action-expert block (MolmoAct2 layer 35 of 36, π0.5 layer 17 of 18, counting from 0).

Figure 14: Direction to target object is observable with one probe, in contrast to the two distance rulers. Top: held-out decoded directions (VLM layer 21), averaged in 6 cm cells in a target-centered frame; arrow length is cell coherence. Decoded directions point toward the target throughout the workspace (median angular error 11.7◦ vs. a 33.1◦ floor); within 15 cm, per-read error increases but cell means still point toward the target (coherence 0.98 beyond 40 cm vs. 0.77 inside 7.5 cm). Bottom left: as in Fig. 3c, but for direction probes fit on different halves of the houses: the near/far cosine stays below its ceiling at every boundary (0.081 vs. 0.130 at c = 15). Bottom right: the range-split pair does not outperform a single recalibrated probe on near reads (up to 3◦ worse) and improves on it by at most 1.1◦ on far reads — a single probe suffices at all ranges.

Figure 22: After a full turn of the wrist joint the action expert’s activation does not return to its start; the VLM’s returns exactly. From one pose of the roll sweep (App. C.8; a single house), the wrist joint (Franka joint 7) is driven through successive full turns by writing the joint value directly into the simulator, far past the joint’s physical range (shaded band), so the sweep tests the models’ inputs rather than a reachable motion. At every full turn (dashed lines, large markers) the rendered frames and text tokens are identical to the start and only the raw joint value differs, and only the action expert receives that value. (Left) Action expert, layer 9, first action token: Euclidean distance of the activation at each step from the start activation; after one turn it is 28.8 units away and does not return over the following turns. (Right) VLM, layer 20, mean over image tokens: the same distance, which varies within each turn and is exactly 0 at every full turn; the two panels are in different activation units.

Figure 3: MolmoBot’s VLM encodes distance to the target in nearly orthogonal near- and far-range codes (layer 21). (a) Near (<15 cm) and far (15–70 cm) probe R2 after erasing the top-k directions of the other probe, computed against each range’s own variance. Erasing far directions leaves near decoding intact while far decoding collapses, and vice versa. The intact (k = 0) probes have errors of ∼1.3 cm (near) and ∼3.6 cm (far). (b) Near R2 (<c) vs. far R2 (≥c) as the cutoff c is swept. Clipped (‘round to c’) probes match probes fit separately on each range and outperform a single full-range probe. (c) Cosine between the near- and far-probe weight vectors as the cutoff c is swept, for range-split and clipped (‘round to c’) pairs (fold mean ± s.d.). For c ≲ 30 cm, both cosines stay below the cosine between two copies of the same probe fit on different halves of the data (dashed). On synthetic activations that encode distance along a single direction, the same probes are nearly parallel for c ≳ 15 cm (dotted). (d) Activations plotted by their meter- and centimeter-probe readouts, colored by true distance in meters (left) and centimeters (right). Far samples vary along the meter axis while the centimeter readout saturates, and near samples do the opposite, tracing an L.

Figure 9: The action expert (layer 12) also maintains a rank-3 EE position subspace. Panels as in the top and middle rows of Figure 2, for EE position read from the action expert, which receives proprioception; the paths are from a single scene excluded when fitting the subspace. The readout is near-exact and the paths are recovered almost without distortion. The gap between the general-linear and orthogonal residuals shows the subspace is a scaled, not isometric, copy of world coordinates.

Figure 10: The action expert (layer 22) also maintains a rank-3 target object position subspace. Panels as in Figure 9, for the target object’s position; the paths are from a single scene excluded when fitting the subspace. The action expert receives the object only through cross-attention to the VLM, and it carries target position with larger error than the VLM (Figure 2), recovering the paths with more distortion.

Figure 11: Within a scene, target object position is computed on the VLM’s instruction and final tokens between layers 12 and 21 and appears in the action expert from layer 18; EE position is present from the first layer in both. Held-out R2 of the rank-3 ridge readout of end-effector position (left) and target object position (right) at every layer, scored after removing each held-out house’s mean from the true and predicted positions, so only position changes within a scene count; one line per VLM token pool, the action expert dashed, rings on the readouts of Figure 2, values below the axis floor clipped. The target’s height is constant within a scene, so the target panel’s variance is horizontal and any within-scene variation in the predicted height counts as error; scores fall below zero where a readout’s predictions vary within a scene without tracking the object. On the instruction and final tokens the target read stays at or below zero until layer 12 and peaks at layers 18–21, while the image patches carry little of it at any layer. The action expert tracks EE position near-perfectly at every layer and the target only from layer 18 on.

Figure 12: Distance is compressive within the near range and closest to linear beyond 30 cm, and each ruler reads only its own range (VLM, layer 21). (Left) Held-out mean absolute error per bin of true distance for a single full-range ridge probe fit to d, log d, or 1/d and mapped back to metres; the compressive links have the lower error below 15 cm and the linear link in the farthest bins. (Right) Held-out R2 against true distance for the centimeter ruler and the meter ruler of Figure 3, scored separately on states below and above that cutoff; negative (saturated) values are drawn at zero and printed. Each ruler saturates outside its own range, as does a single unclipped metre-scale probe (not shown) on the near-range states.

Figure 29: DROID real world behavioral manifolds. Here we show the behavioral manifolds realized by MolmoAct2 and π0.5. The EE position and wrist orientation point clouds show the activations of all 3,321 queries, sampled from MolmoAct2 AE L16 of 36 and π0.5 VLM L7 of 18, demonstrating the structures appear across multiple streams. We plot a natural episode trajectory in the EE position subplots and the wrist roll sweep of Figure 30 in the Wrist Orientation subplots. In the Gripper plot we project the 379 landmark activations from each model’s final action-expert block onto the principal components of the pullback steering vectors, with binned steering vectors as arrows.

Figure 26: Gripper control for action expert layer 9 (Top left) A linear probe decodes the commanded gripper aperture; one principal component of the pullback steering vectors decodes it nearly as well as the full activation. (Top right) Natural-rollout activations colored by gripper state; notably, the steering vectors from each cluster do not point toward the other, unlike layer 32 in Figure 7. (Bottom left) One component captures ∼55% of steering-vector variance. (Bottom right) One component flips the gripper but leaks into the arm joints relative to using the full 768-dimensional steering vector; more components remove this excess leakage.

(Left) Held-out AUC of the contact discriminant at each of 10 layers, fit separately on five token groups: wrist-camera patches, exo-camera patches, text tokens, the final token, and the whole-sequence mean; reference lines mark a phase-timer baseline, a gripper-closure baseline, and the action expert. Left to right: action expert, VLM vision tokens, VLM language tokens. Figure 23: Even the most circular reachable wrist rotation does not close. Instead of rolling about the gripper’s approach axis, we tilt the gripper 30◦ off that axis and orbit the tilt about the vertical. If driven through a full turn, this precession returns the wrist orientation exactly to its start (a closed circle in SO(3)). The gripper position is held fixed within 5 cm while the whole arm reconfigures, and we record activations at each step. The arm’s joint limits (clipped to the 1st to 99th training percentile) stop the orbit partway: sweeping both directions from the start covers −70◦ to +158◦ (228◦ of the turn; angles are the realized rotation about the vertical axis). (Top) PCA over the sweep activations. Precession remains an open arc, with PC1 carrying 69% of the variance and PC2 25%. (Bottom) The exo camera image at different rotation angles along the sweep.

Robot-base frame viewed from above (left) and from the side, with height above the object’s resting position (right). Gray points are arm poses and violet diamonds object placements across all houses; the dashed outline is the box arm poses are sampled in. For one example house, the black point is the home pose, blue points its ten arm poses, and violet diamonds its five object placements; unlike Figure 15, both the arm and the object move.

Figure 21: The VLM maintains only a weak, pixel-derived trace of wrist orientation. A roll sweep from the same starting pose as Figure 6, over a 332◦ range (−156◦ to +176◦), read at the VLM; the VLM receives only images and text as input. (Left) PCA over the sweep activations (layer 35). The trace wraps — −156◦ and +176◦ land close together — but does not form a clean circle. (Right) The reduced-rank regression of Figure 24 at every VLM layer, on natural rollouts re-encoded at the VLM (19,089 states, 169 houses). Figure 27: In the VLM backbone, gripper steerability falls to the control floor by layer 28 although aperture readability stays high. The gripper pullback of App. C.9 with the edit δ added to every sequence token after VLM block L, at screen scale (32 edits per layer and objective, one query per landmark). (Left) Fraction of edits that flip the commanded gripper under the arm-hold objective of App. C.9 and under the gripper-only objective (the arm-hold and smoothness terms dropped), counted on the 29 edits whose unedited chunk has the opposite gripper sign; the gray band spans the flip rates of a control edit (the mean of the action-expert catalog, App. C.9). (Middle) Held-out R2 of a ridge probe from the pre-edit activation to the commanded aperture, best of the token pools at each layer; readability rises to 0.86 by layer 20. (Right) Absolute cosine between the first principal component of the arm-hold edits, a sample-limited estimate from the small per-layer catalog, and the close–open flip axis (dashed: the action-expert catalog of Figure 26); at the shallowest flipping layers (4 and 12) the leading component is only partly aligned with the flip axis.

Figure 28: The gripper steering vectors stay dominated by one component and aligned with the flip axis at every action-expert layer. The pullback catalog of App. C.9, re-fit at layers 9, 18, 27, and 32. (Left) Share of steering-vector variance on the first principal component. (Middle) Stable rank of the steering vectors. (Right) Cosine between the first principal component and the flip axis (mean close edit minus mean open edit), and held-out R2 of the aperture probe restricted to that component; dashed: a random direction.

Figure 36: The VLM keeps the target’s position but no map of the workspace; other objects are encoded per image patch. (Left) A table-occupancy map of the target, read from VLM activations (last token, layer 21), is no more accurate than the same readout applied to the target’s three true coordinates (dashed). (Middle) One readout shared across all image-patch tokens detects whether an object the instruction does not name is visible in that patch, well above patch-position and patch-color baselines (exo and wrist cameras, layers 8 and 20). (Right) With scene means removed, a readout of table position fit on all visible objects does not track the target as it moves, whereas one fit on the instructed target alone does on the exo camera.

Figure 31: MolmoAct2 and π0.5 encode distance to target object in 2 orthogonal subspaces. We find that similar to MolmoBot, as shown in Fig. 3 the tested DROID model also encode distance to target object with a multi-scale ruler. We sample 26,675 timesteps from 1,998 pick and place episodes. The distance is how far the gripper is from its initial grasp location. Figure 24: Full 3-DOF wrist orientation is decodable from natural rollouts at low rank (AE). Unlike Fig. 6, which rotates a single roll joint and reads the code with PCA, here “wrist orientation” means the complete 3-DOF orientation of the hand, represented by the first two columns of its rotation matrix (a 6-D target). We fit reduced-rank ridge regressions of rank 1 to 6 from the activations to this target on natural rollouts (6,555 queries, 191 houses) and report R2 on held-out houses at six action-expert layers. Rank 2 recovers most of the decodable variance and rank 3 nearly all of it; higher ranks add little. Decodability peaks at layer 9.

Figure 32: Task phase subspace in π0.5 and MolmoAct2. (Left) Example trajectory for a simple pick-and-place task, “Pick up the white and green brush from the table and hang it on the wall,” along with the predicted task phases. (d) Holding the edit at every step compounds the corrections, rotating the wrist opposite the written angle by about its magnitude (vertical lines mark action chunks).

(b) One principal component of the pullback steering vectors decodes the commanded gripper aperture nearly as well as the full activation. (c) Natural-rollout activations colored by gripper state; the steering vectors point from each cluster toward the other. (Top left) Held-out R2 of the near and far decodes as far-axis (solid) or near-axis (dashed) directions are erased; each decode drops only when its own axis is removed. (Top right) Held-out R2 of the centimeter and meter rulers on each side of the 15 cm cutoff; each ruler scores only its own range, and bars below zero are drawn at zero with the value printed. (Bottom) The two ruler readouts plotted against each other, colored by true distance on the meter (left) and centimeter (right) scales; the meter ruler resolves the far arm and the centimeter ruler the near arm, as in the VLM cell.

Gray points are all placements in the teleport datasets (906 houses). For one example house, the black point is the object’s natural placement and the blue points its 15 teleported placements, sampled uniformly over the supporting surface within the benchmark placement envelope; dashed arrows connect the natural placement to each teleport. Only the object is moved; the arm’s initial pose is unchanged.

Figure 17: MolmoBot’s task phase subspace in the VLM backbone (vision tokens, Layer 31). (Left) LDA projection of natural rollouts, colored by phase (0.86 balanced accuracy across held-out houses; AE: 0.92). (Middle) The full three-dimensional LDA subspace, with a held-out episode’s trajectory traversing the four phase regions in order. (Right) Freezing shifts the VLM’s decoded phase toward grasp, as in the action expert (Figure 5): frozen reach and grasp landmarks are mostly decoded as grasp, and frozen transport and place landmarks are most often still decoded as transport and place.

Figure 30: Wrist orientation PCA across models and streams. Following Fig. 6, we record a real-robot episode in which the wrist roll joint is swept from −79◦ to +84◦ while the other joints and the scene are held approximately fixed, and plot the top two principal components of the activations for MolmoAct2 and π0.5 in both the VLM and the action expert (color: roll angle). Figure 25: Cumulative variance of gripper steering vectors in layer 32. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes representational geometry in vision-language-action policies for robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied VLA and robot learning.
papers.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA policies encode task-relevant concepts as structured, often multi-dimensional geometries shaped by physical and task constraints—not merely as linearly readable variables.

papers.abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-trial gait rankings and long-term gait effectiveness after irreversible leg damage.
Uses persistent outcome profiles and conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot.
Evaluated across 108 MuJoCo tasks involving leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock.
Improved final gait quality and reduced low-quality failures versus an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline; gains appeared across all damage classes.
Ablations most strongly supported conservative uncertainty handling, while aggregate SRQ improvement versus no adaptation was inconclusive.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Holdout outcomes for the four methods. Bars show means and 95% task-bootstrap intervals. Higher is better for (a) SRQ and (b) final quality; lower is better for (c) low-quality failure rate (qF ≤ 0.05). Each damage class has 36 condition–seed comparisons. No-adaptation results are reused across seeds. Amputation and fracture remain difficult in absolute terms.

Fig. 2. PGRR from offline profiling to continuous online execution. (a) Repeated execution reveals behavior that a short probe can miss; twelve 0.75-s segments followed by a 3-s endpoint interval supply eight prediction targets. (b) Conservative selection, viability-gated probes, online correction, and incumbent bridges repeat until a stopping condition or the ten-trial budget. (c) Conventional independent-reset evaluation is shown only as a conceptual contrast. papers.abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $\pi_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Mozes Jacobs, Siddharth Boppana, Tal Haklay, Eric Bigelow, Andrew Lee, Conor Watts, Thomas Icard, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal

papers.abstract: Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfaction but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying request, creating an evaluation blind spot. We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content. Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To address this reward hacking, we introduce CALIF, a lightweight method that augments verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response quality. CALIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward model. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning modes, CALIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining response quality near or above pre-RL levels. It also outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model-metric comparisons across three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.
bullets: Introduces Tev-Gym, a dataset of 1,170 verified task environments spanning 7 domains.
Uses a latent-world-first design to specify task workflows and expected intermediate states before rendering environments.
Applies progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS) to convert task progress into dense per-step rewards.
Trains Tev-27B, which matches GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5 on ALE-CM.
Despite ALE-focused training, Tev-27B generalizes to Terminal-Bench subsets and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. Recent continuous alternatives mitigate this, but they are typically used as proxies for world modeling and require a further planning step to produce executable actions. We thus introduce UniLAP, a unified continuous latent-action policy that models the latent space via flow matching and bypasses reliance on future frames during inference. By distilling a LAM teacher with a flow-adaptive objective, UniLAP inherits the teacher's action representation while retaining the multimodal distribution of feasible behaviors. To decouple latent representations from task-irrelevant appearance, we extract a label-free motion target to isolate relevant kinematic cues from spurious visual dynamics. With the established embodiment-agnostic latent manifold, UniLAP can be easily adapted to novel platforms. Pretrained on multi-source videos at a compact 1.1B parameter scale, UniLAP outperforms state-of-the-art latent-action and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines across hand pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.
bullets: Addresses the granularity limits of discrete latent actions and the extra planning required by continuous world-modeling approaches.
Uses flow matching to model continuous latent actions and distills a latent action model teacher with a flow-adaptive objective.
Extracts label-free motion targets to separate task-relevant kinematics from task-irrelevant appearance.
Builds an embodiment-agnostic latent manifold that adapts to new robotic platforms.
At 1.1B parameters, outperforms latent-action and VLA baselines across pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots still struggle to plan contact-rich whole-body manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception. Workhorse learns such manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations. A visual planner predicts five-link targets: the poses of the torso, both wrists, and both feet. A reinforcement-learning whole-body tracker follows them on the robot. Both policies train separately on the same recorded human poses, without retargeting. We augment the training data of each policy to imitate the errors that the other makes at deployment. On a real Unitree G1, Workhorse transport boxes with its hands and a kick, catches a thrown box, and topples and climbs a suitcase. During box transport, we show recoveries after a person pushes the robot or takes the box away. In a simulated copy of the demonstration room, the system completes box transport in 77% of episodes, and in 64% under 40 N.s pushes. With both policies retrained from the same demonstrations, a simulated second humanoid completes box transport in 83% of episodes without pushes.
bullets: Addresses contact-rich humanoid manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception.
Predicts target poses for the torso, both wrists, and both feet, then tracks them with a whole-body RL policy.
Trains both policies separately on the same human pose recordings and augments data with the other policy’s deployment errors.
Demonstrates box transport, catching, kicking, and suitcase climbing on a real Unitree G1, including recovery from pushes and box removal.
Completes simulated box transport in 77% of episodes, 64% under 40 N·s pushes, and 83% on a second humanoid without pushes.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in unstructured environments must combine robust whole-body control with the ability to perceive and physically interact with surrounding objects. While large-scale human motion data provides powerful priors for natural and versatile humanoid control, effectively transferring such priors to perception-driven object interaction remains challenging. To address this bottleneck, we propose a framework that extends the recently proposed Generative Pretrained Controller (GPC) from general human motion to full-body humanoid-environment interaction. First, we adapt GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance cues and privileged state information. This adaptation begins with interaction and affordance pre-training on human motions paired with support scenes. These experts leverage the pretrained human motion prior while learning task-specific contact behaviors, including reaching toward objects, grasping environmental supports for stabilization, and pushing movable objects. Second, we introduce a perception-driven student that retains the pretrained GPC policy and distills interaction skills from the experts using onboard sensory observations. To bridge the gap between privileged expert observations and sensory inputs, we train the student's perception not only to reconstruct expert observations, but also to preserve the expert's motion decisions and resulting joint targets. Notably, our experiments across multiple whole-body interaction tasks demonstrate that large-scale generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for learning deployable policies for humanoid interactions in contact-rich real-world environments.
bullets: Targets humanoid interaction in unstructured environments, where control must combine natural motion, perception, and physical contact.
Adapts GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordances and privileged state information.
Pretrains experts to learn behaviors such as reaching, grasping supports for stability, and pushing objects.
Distills these skills into a sensory-driven student that preserves both expert observations and motion decisions.
Experiments across multiple whole-body tasks support the feasibility of deployable interaction policies in real-world environments.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos 3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune to a previously unseen robot, a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video-action asymmetry: the video renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We evaluate closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place. The native action succeeds only approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% of the time, respectively, and performs worse on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM, a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, that runs on the model's generated video to recover action estimates. Paired with the native prediction, these recovered actions provide preferred targets for fine-tuning only the action-related layers, while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare supervised relabeling with a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action gate reaches approximately 75%, 47%, and 42% pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success, compared with 17%, 10%, and 7% for the native action. A hybrid objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) performs best: on Oreo, the training object, it reaches 90% pre-grasp and 20% full-task success; on a held-out object, it reaches 80% and 30%. Plain Flow-DPO reaches 0% success despite 1.000 validation preference accuracy, indicating that the combination of training objectives, rather than the contrastive objective alone, drives the observed gains.
bullets: A LoRA-adapted WAM generates plausible video but systematically mis-targeted actions on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
The method estimates hand poses from generated video, converts them to actions with inverse kinematics, and uses them as preferred fine-tuning targets.
A hybrid DPO+SFT+DTW objective performs best, outperforming supervised relabeling and plain Flow-DPO.
Recovered-action gating raises pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success from approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% to 75%, 47%, and 42%.
On the reported objects, the best model achieves 90% pre-grasp/20% full-task success on Oreo and 80%/30% on a held-out object.

papers.abstract: Underwater manipulation couples visual decisions, contact forces and a thruster-controlled floating base. We introduce WasserMan, to our knowledge the first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of floating-base underwater contact manipulation. It provides ten expert-solvable tasks, two vehicle-arm platforms, a bimanual configuration and underwater dynamics. Nine tasks have learned-policy evaluations. We compare ACT, diffusion policies (DP) and behavioral cloning on six tasks, with three training runs and equal sampled-window budgets. Pretrained SmolVLA adds evaluations on three tasks. In the tested settings, removing integral action can prevent completion, while changing action interfaces can reduce learned-policy success despite successful expert replay. Currents produce task-dependent changes in completion and actuation effort. Versioned tasks, demonstrations and per-episode evidence support a protocol separating expert feasibility, learned completion and execution effort.
bullets: Covers ten expert-solvable tasks, two vehicle-arm platforms, a bimanual setup, and underwater dynamics.
Evaluates learned policies on nine tasks, comparing ACT, diffusion policies, behavioral cloning, and pretrained SmolVLA in selected settings.
Finds that removing integral action or changing action interfaces can hinder task completion, even when expert replay succeeds.
Shows that environmental currents affect completion and actuation effort differently across tasks.
Provides versioned tasks, demonstrations, and per-episode evidence to distinguish expert feasibility, learned completion, and execution effort.

papers.abstract: Large datasets and high capacity models have accelerated progress in vision and language. This work introduces a platform aimed at bringing comparable gains to embodied learning, world models, and robotics. We present EnvDreamer, a framework that uses large language and vision language models to generate Unreal Engine 5 environments for embodied AI and robot training. EnvDreamer enables sampling of large, diverse, interactive, customizable, and validator passed virtual environments for training and evaluation across navigation, interaction, and manipulation. We illustrate the platform with a large set of generated scenes and simple baselines. Policies trained on EnvDreamer generated environments, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve competitive results on multiple embodied benchmarks spanning navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation. EnvDreamer also supports image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies. Finally, we release EnvDreamer-20k, a dataset of 20,000 validator passed environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata to support reproducible benchmarking.
bullets: Uses large language and vision-language models to create interactive, customizable, validator-passed virtual environments.
Supports embodied learning without explicit mapping or human task supervision, including navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation.
Policies trained in generated environments achieve competitive results across multiple embodied benchmarks.
Enables image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies.
Releases EnvDreamer-20k: 20,000 environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EnvDreamer system overview. The system builds environments from scratch using vision–language models (vLLMs) to plan and control Unreal Engine 5. User-provided text or image prompts along with system information such as Remote Control API commands and viewport screenshots (left) are passed to a vLLM-based Home Agent which decomposes the request into sub-tasks with Chain of ThoughtWei et al. [2022], generates a structured layout plan and task list in JSON, and compiles them into EnvDreamer API Python code for execution (middle). An Evaluator Agent then performs iterative task-completion checks on scene layout, furniture placement, and rationality, providing feedback until the environment passes validation (right). Finally, users can inspect the completeness of the environment by entering a play session in either an ego-centric or bird’s-eye view.

Figure 5: Task-conditioned dataset generation pipeline for EnvDreamer–20k. A user specifies a scenario by providing a prompt and a high-resolution viewport screenshot plus the current environment JSON description (left). A language model decomposes the request into a sequence of grounded sub-tasks such as “Walk to the kitchen” or “Put pizza on the plate” (middle). The system then checks which preconditions are satisfied by comparing object relations and automatically adding missing objects required to solve each task (e.g., placing a plate on the table). Finally, the validated environment details and the set of available tasks are exported as JSON and rendered through the EnvDreamer API to produce entries in the EnvDreamer–20k dataset (right).

Figure 7: High-level architecture of the EnvDreamer Remote Control API. Python clients issue JSON commands to AJsonSceneBuilder, which resolves assets, spawns actors, and returns structured responses.

Figure 2: Diverse and realistic floor plan generation with EnvDreamer. Unlike traditional procedural methods that rely on fixed generation pipelines with limited variation, EnvDreamer leverages language-driven synthesis to create diverse, realistic home layouts. Each layout shown was generated from natural language prompts (e.g., "Create a modern 2-bedroom apartment," "Design a spacious family home with open kitchen"), producing architectural arrangements that follows realworld constraints. The diversity spans from compact studios (left) to complex multi-room residences (right), with rooms color-coded by type: bedrooms (yellow), bathrooms (green), living areas (red), and other spaces. This prompt-based approach enables researchers to specify exact requirements for embodied AI and robotics experiments while maintaining architectural realism that fixed procedural pipelines struggle to achieve.

Figure 4: Interactive scene in EnvDreamer. Ego-centric view from the embodied agent with annotated object relations (on, under, between, near, inside) and a bird’s-eye view of the procedurally generated multi-room layout. The robot is rendered in-scene, and objects are spawned with realistic and diverse geometry, materials, and placements that afford navigation and manipulation.
Figure 8: Remote web session for EnvDreamer. The live UE5 viewport is streamed to the browser, while a simple builder UI issues layout updates through HTTP endpoints backed by the RC API.

Figure 3: Interactive prompt-driven environment editing with EnvDreamer. A GPT-5–based vLLM-based smart agent receives natural-language chat prompts from the user to constantly edit the environment, translates them into EnvDreamer API calls, and applies edits to a running UE5 scene over the web. Users can inspect the updated environment, accept or refine the changes, and leverage additional web-session tools such as restoring prior states, direct drag-and-drop editing, and image-instructed edits, while the system maintains a synchronized JSON representation of the scene.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models tell a robot where to move, but not how hard to push. Contact-rich tasks depend on that second quantity, compliance, yet no widely used demonstration interface records it. The obstacle is identifiability as realized pose and measured force cannot separate the operator's intended equilibrium from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse and handheld grippers cannot supply compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies work around this with hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force and tactile hardware. Four-channel bilateral teleoperation removes the ambiguity directly by using the leader arm as a separate measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which we use to fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness alongside pose. On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, ours is the only policy of five whose contact force changes when the instruction asks for a firm wipe rather than a normal one (6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023
bullets: Compliance is essential for contact-rich tasks but is not captured by common robot demonstration interfaces.
Four-channel bilateral teleoperation uses the leader arm to measure intended equilibrium separately from realized pose and force.
Per-axis, direction-dependent stiffness is recovered by regression without dedicated force/tactile hardware or manual annotation.
The resulting labels fine-tune a VLA to output stiffness alongside pose.
In a Franka Research 3 wiping task, commanded contact force rose from 6.4 N for normal wiping to 9.1 N for firm wiping; the policy was the only one of five to respond this way.

papers.abstract: Capturing hand motion and interaction forces is critical for interactive computing, VR, and high-fidelity tactile demonstrations for robot learning. We introduce a wrist-worn pressure-sensing wristband that recovers continuous full-hand pose and distributed contact force on a single wearable. The system consists of flexible capacitive sensor arrays around the wrist, which require no electrical skin contact, and a recurrent network that maps the resulting pressure signal to hand state. Our key insight is that muscle contraction and tendon displacement produce pressure patterns, which correlate strongly with hand pose and interaction force. To validate this, we collect synchronized recordings of wrist pressure, optical motion-capture hand pose, and tactile-glove interaction force, covering isolated finger motion, fingertip-force stress tests, and natural hand-object manipulation. On isolated single-user motion the wristband attains $4.6^\circ$ mean finger-joint MAE, and across four users manipulating everyday objects it estimates per-finger contact force at $R^2=0.57$, which an external pose signal brings up to $0.75$. We see the wristband as one node in a constellation of everyday wearables -- e.g. paired with an egocentric camera -- adding the contact force that vision cannot observe and taking over when the hand is occluded.
bullets: Targets hand-motion and interaction-force capture for interactive computing, VR, and robot learning.
Uses flexible capacitive sensors around the wrist, exploiting pressure patterns from muscle contraction and tendon displacement.
Validated with synchronized wrist pressure, optical hand pose, and tactile-glove force recordings across motion, force, and manipulation tasks.
Achieves 4.6° mean finger-joint error for isolated single-user motion and force-estimation R² of 0.57 across four users, rising to 0.75 with an external pose signal.
The system is positioned as a wearable complement to vision, especially when the hand is occluded.

papers.abstract: Enabling human stakeholders to specify reward functions that lead to their desired outcomes is a key challenge in deploying reinforcement learning agents. Preference-based methods such as online RLHF can reduce the burden of manual reward design, but they require repeatedly training policies, sampling trajectories from the real world, and eliciting feedback, making them impractical in settings where environment interaction is computationally expensive or unsafe. We introduce Experience-Free Autonomous Reward Specification (EARS), a method for learning reward functions from preferences without environment interaction. Our approach uses a structured LLM-mediated process to construct a small set of expressive reward features from a task description and the environment observation space, then strategically samples imagined trajectories in this feature space and learns feature weights from preferences over the imagined trajectory pairs. We evaluate on three long-horizon domains: pandemic lockdown regulation design, insulin administration for diabetes patients, and autonomous vehicle control on a highway. We compare EARS to baselines that also enable reward specification without environment interaction--namely, methods that directly prompt an LLM to generate a reward function. When learning from either ground-truth preference labels or preferences labeled by a LLM, EARS designs reward functions that are more aligned with the ground truth reward function that produced the preferences or LLM context than these baselines. These results suggest that preference-based reward specification remains effective without environment sampling, enabling practical reward design in settings where collecting real trajectories is costly or infeasible.
bullets: Addresses the cost and safety barriers of online RLHF, which requires repeated policy training, real-world trajectories, and human feedback.
Uses an LLM to construct expressive reward features from the task description and observation space.
Strategically samples imagined trajectories in the feature space and learns feature weights from preferences over trajectory pairs.
Evaluated on pandemic regulation, insulin administration, and highway autonomous driving tasks.
EARS outperformed direct LLM reward-generation baselines in alignment with ground-truth or LLM-context rewards, using either ground-truth or LLM-labeled preferences.

papers.abstract: Robust point tracking in endoscopic videos is essential for computer-assisted intervention and autonomous robotic surgery, enabling continuous registration between intraoperative video and preoperative imaging despite soft tissue deformation. However, supervised tracking methods depend on large annotated datasets, while surgical conditions make reliable trajectory annotation challenging. We propose a self-supervised Track-Any-Point approach that learns from unlabeled surgical videos by establishing global pixel correspondences and inferring point trajectories through contrastive random walks. Trained without annotations, our method achieves performance comparable to existing semi-supervised approaches while implicitly handling tissue deformation. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of self-supervised point tracking in surgical environments and its potential to reduce reliance on annotated data.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of obtaining reliable trajectory annotations for endoscopic surgical videos.
Uses a self-supervised Track-Any-Point framework trained on unlabeled surgical videos.
Establishes global pixel correspondences and infers trajectories through contrastive random walks.
Implicitly handles soft-tissue deformation during tracking.
Achieves performance comparable to existing semi-supervised methods, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Generalizable bimanual robotic manipulation requires a reusable task prior that can persist across increasingly diverse tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and execution conditions, thus avoiding the prohibitive cost of large-scale teleoperated demonstrations and policy retraining. In this work, we present VLBiMan++, an extended framework that expands the generalization boundary of vision-language anchored one-shot bimanual manipulation. Starting from a single human demonstration, VLBiMan++ performs task-aware decomposition to identify reusable and adaptable skill components, and employs vision-language grounded geometric adaptation to transfer these skills to novel configurations without retraining. Building on this foundation, we systematically extend generalization along five dimensions: task generalization through diverse and long-horizon skill compositions; object generalization across unseen categories, varying geometries, and more complex articulated or deformable objects; scene generalization under clutter, occlusion, and dynamic interference; embodiment generalization across heterogeneous dual-arm robotic platforms; and deployment generalization through prolonged closed-loop execution under repeated external perturbations. To support this broader scope, we further introduce object-state-aware adaptation and lightweight trajectory optimization mechanisms that accommodate changes beyond simple rigid 6-DoF pose variations while preserving reliable bimanual coordination. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that VLBiMan++ maintains strong task success and adaptation capability across these increasingly challenging settings. Overall, VLBiMan++ advances one-shot bimanual manipulation from demonstrating isolated transferability toward a more systematic and scalable framework for generalization across tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and long-term deployment conditions.
bullets: Uses task-aware decomposition to separate reusable and adaptable skill components from a single human demonstration.
Applies vision-language-grounded geometric adaptation to transfer skills to novel configurations.

Adds object-state-aware adaptation and lightweight trajectory optimization beyond simple rigid 6-DoF pose changes.
Real-world experiments show strong task success and adaptation across increasingly challenging settings.

papers.abstract: Biological swimmers and flyers exploit unsteady vortices for propulsion, whereas engineered vehicles usually suppress them as disturbances. Learning such flow exploitation in machines is difficult because real-fluid interaction data are scarce and unstructured exploration is unstable in high-dimensional, history-dependent flows. Here we present REEF, a co-designed physical-learning framework that integrates SHOAL, an eight-channel high-throughput array for real fluid--structure interaction, with V-STAR, a staged algorithm that converts these interactions into policies through imitation, offline internalization, and online adaptation. Across lift-based, drag-based, and momentum-jet propulsors, REEF expands the attainable force envelope to more than twice that of parameterized search. Particle image velocimetry shows that these gains arise from coordinated vortex formation, growth, and force projection, rather than refinement of a fixed motion-to-force mapping. Force-trained policies transfer zero-shot to free-moving robots whose body motion changes the surrounding flow, suggesting that REEF learns transferable wake-coupling principles for embodied propulsion in unsteady fluids.
bullets: Addresses scarce, unstructured fluid-interaction data and unstable exploration in history-dependent flows.
Integrates SHOAL, an eight-channel fluid–structure interaction platform, with V-STAR’s imitation, offline learning, and online adaptation stages.
Works across lift-based, drag-based, and momentum-jet propulsors, expanding the attainable force envelope to more than twice that of parameterized search.
Flow measurements link performance gains to coordinated vortex formation, growth, and force projection.
Force-trained policies transfer zero-shot to free-moving robots, indicating learned wake-coupling principles.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of REEF, a co-designed physical-learning ecosystem integrating the SHOAL experimental array with the V-STAR learning algorithm. (A) Conventional engineering suppresses vortices to reduce disturbances, whereas biological systems exploit unsteady flows for propulsion; REEF advances toward deliberate vortex generation and manipulation. (B) Three representative propulsors, including a 3-DOF flapper, 2-DOF webbed foot, and 1-DOF caudal fin, span distinct locomotion modes and force-generation regimes. (C) V-STAR converts parameterized trajectories into flow-compliant policies through three-stage algorithm (imitation, offline internalization, and online adaptation). (D) SHOAL enables parallel real-flow learning with an eight-channel towing array, rapid flow reset, synchronized actuation, and real-time six-axis force sensing.

Figure 2: Each component addresses a distinct constraint. (A) Training reward of the full REEF pipeline and five ablation variants on the 3-DOF flapper benchmark. Curves show smoothed episode reward versus training time; shaded regions denote ±1 SEM across seeds. Dashed and solid segments indicate pre-training and online learning phases, respectively. Ablation configurations and equivalent baseline algorithms are defined in Table 1. (B) Kinematic trajectories and hydrodynamic force evolution across the three V-STAR stages. Top: representative flapping-cycle trajectories with instantaneous force vectors and foil orientations. Bottom: thrust (Cx) and lateral-force (Cy) coefficients along the same cycle, with stage transitions and cycle-averaged thrust Cx annotated. Abbreviations: SEM, standard error of the mean.

(B) Thrust–lift Pareto envelope of the 1-DOF caudal fin, with representative REEF and EMOA trajectories. (C) Force traces and PIV vorticity fields for webbed-foot paddling. (D) Wake structure and momentum-jet profile for the caudal fin. REEF forms a focused downstream jet, quantified by the time-averaged streamwise velocity increment ∆u along monitoring lines at c and 1.25c downstream of the trailing edge. Colorbars show spanwise vorticity; blue and red denote opposite signs.

(A) Quadrupedal flapper robot driven by SHOAL-trained REEF policies or the strongest parameterized representative (PARA) from the BF/EMOA pool. Image sequences show body displacement over time, with instantaneous streamwise force Fx below; bars report forward displacement of three REEF policies and corresponding PARA representatives as mean ±1 s.d. across three trials. (B) Quadrupedal webbed-foot robot under the same protocol. (C) Caudal-fin module tested in a circulating flow channel on near-frictionless air bearings; quadrupedal robots translate along streamwise guide rails with vertical spring compliance. Compared with EMOA4, REEF policies coordinate LEV formation, growth, and force projection with wing orientation, producing expanded thrust–lift performance.

papers.abstract: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website: https://hire-moma.github.io/
authors: Zhefei Gong, Hefeifei Jiang, Zehao Wang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Targets the difficulty of fine-tuning high-dimensional, tightly coupled mobile-manipulation systems on real robots.
Fine-tunes a frozen base policy with additive residuals, separated into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning.
Uses sparse human interventions covering under 20% of training to reshape value estimates and guide exploration.
Real-world experiments on TIAGo++ report improved task performance with about 30 minutes of online interaction across base-policy architectures.
Scope: demonstrated for dynamic, human-centric real-world mobile manipulation; specific task details and quantitative gains are not provided in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HiRe-MoMa Framework enables policy-agnostic real-world fine-tuning of mobile manipulators through an asynchronous residual reinforcement learning paradigm. (Right) Shared-Control Rollout: an onboard rollout worker augments a frozen base policy with learnable residuals; sparse human interventions during critical or hazardous phases are stored in an expert buffer. (Left) Asynchronous Central Learner: the residual policy is optimized along two pillars: a) a Hierarchical Residual Architecture (Sec. 4.1) that decouples the residual into mobile and manipulator heads with unidirectional conditioning, embedding the platform’s physical hierarchy directly into the policy; and b) an Expert-Guided Value Alignment loss (Sec. 4.2) that fuses sparse environment rewards with sparse human corrections to reshape the critic toward expert-preferred behaviors.

Figure 4: Training Dynamics. Comparison across methods over training time, where we construct the figure along the actual training time. (a) Success rate: HiRe-MoMa(full) attains a consistently higher success rate throughout training, validating the effectiveness of our design combining hierarchical residual architecture and alignment. (b) Human intervention steps: HiRe-MoMa requires fewer human interventions and converges faster than the baselines, and the comparison with and without alignment (+Hierarchical Decoupling) demonstrates the effectiveness of the extra alignment loss.

Figure 1: HiRe-MoMa System Overview. (a) Training Paradigm: A real-world dual-unit configuration consisting of an onboard controller for real-time interaction and a computing unit for policy optimization and action prediction. (b) Coordinated Execution: The red dashed lines illustrate the stringent spatiotemporal precision required for base-arm synchronization. In mobile manipulation, marginal tracking deviations are often magnified by kinematic coupling, causing even routine grasping maneuvers to fail.

Figure 7: Training-Step Progression vs. Wall-Clock Time. HG-DAgger advances through training steps faster than the SAC-based residual methods, but its higher step throughput does not translate into higher success rates (Fig. 4(a)). HiRe-MoMa adds only a modest per-step overhead over +Flat Residual (1–2×) while delivering clear gains in success rate and episode length.

Figure 3: Real-World Experimental Tasks. Our evaluation encompasses three tasks, Place Only, Sweep Litter, and Pick Place, that demand varying levels of inter-module coordination. These tasks are particularly challenging for mobile manipulators as they require the simultaneous optimization of base positioning and arm reaching, where minor misalignments in the platform’s pose propagate as significant errors at the end-effector.

Figure 6: Residual Correction Visualization. Base longitudinal velocity and manipulator vertical position throughout the Place Only task. HiRe-MoMa applies coherent corrections at critical trajectory phases, most notably during base acceleration and the manipulator’s lay-down motion.

Figure 5: Disentangling Decomposition and Conditioning. Training-time success-rate curves for +Flat Residual, +DecompositionOnly, and +Hierarchical Decoupling on Place Only and Sweep Litter; see App. A.1.

Table 3: Policy-Agnostic Generalization. Our HiRe-MoMa yields consistent gains when applied to ACT [47], demonstrating architecture-independent efficacy. While the performance ceiling is inherently tied to the base policy’s quality, the results confirm HiRe-MoMa’s capacity to fine-tune diverse base policies.

Table 4: Decomposition vs. Conditioning within Hierarchical Decoupling. Decomposition alone provides the dominant gain by mitigating gradient interference (+30 pt average success rate). Conditioning adds a targeted improvement (+5 pt on average) that manifests on the coupled dual-arm task (Sweep Litter).

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot's kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website: https://humanoid-weight-diffusion.github.io/
authors: Huixuan Cheng, Bike Zhang, Shankar Sastry, Koushil Sreenath
bullets: Targets direct generation and analysis of learned humanoid-control network weights, rather than conventional policy training alone.
Uses a linear autoencoder to compress actor parameters and a Diffusion Transformer to model their latent distribution.
Trained on reinforcement-learning policies for the Unitree G1, it generates real-world networks performing walking, dancing, and spin-kick motions.
Finds a consistent kinematic-prior structure in first-layer weights under both reinforcement and imitation learning.
Scope: results focus on Unitree G1 policies and initial understanding of the learned weight space.

papers.abstract: Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace. Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks. We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile humanoid doubles with safe team coordination. At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals, preferentially preserving the current striker's target. At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills combine agile movement with precise racket control. The skills are guided by human motion references, including footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from states produced by one another to support rapid transitions. A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements. In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline, while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance. In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of 2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive strikes in strict alternation.
authors: Haoran Jiang, Yichao Zhong, Kai Zhang, Cheng Liu, Yixuan Pan, Zhenjie Yang, Jingbo Wang, Tianyu Li, Li Chen
bullets: Addresses strict strike alternation, confined-space navigation, accuracy loss during repositioning, and collision risk between teammates.
A team-level planner jointly selects positions and filters risky actions, prioritizing the current striker’s target.
Individual footwork and striking skills use human-motion references and mutually generated training states for rapid transitions.
A simulator-calibrated racket-arm residual refines strikes using ball-flight and contact feedback.
Simulation improves ball-return success by 13.2% over the baseline; real robots achieve 2 cm clearance positioning, 2.4 s recovery cycles, and over 10 alternating strikes.

papers.abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.
authors: Weichen Lyu, Chong Xia, Mingyu Dong, Long Xu, Shengjun Zhang, Yueqi Duan
bullets: Targets difficult compositions such as hanging, gravity-driven settling, and hidden containment that static coordinate or image-generation approaches often mishandle.
Combines an Assembly Agent for geometric and kinematic planning with a Critic Agent for contact-dynamics diagnosis and closed-loop correction.
Uses Action Routers to convert semantic plans into executable simulator primitives.
Builds a self-evolving skill library from trial-and-error feedback to improve success and reduce exploration.
Experiments in Isaac Sim show improved relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality over existing methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2 . Overview of the PhySGA framework. Driven by a collaborative Feedforward-Feedback architecture, the Assembly Agent executes metric-grounded coarse adjustments, while the Critic Agent performs pixel-grounded fine-grained corrections via simulation feedback. Action Routers translate these semantic decisions into decoupled physical commands, and a Self-Evolving Skill Library distills successful interactions into reusable skills.

papers.abstract: We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/.

Across eight tasks, reduces penetration and foot skating versus video-based baselines while preserving over 90% of annotated contacts.
References satisfy prescribed object poses and support deployment of tracking policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands.

papers.abstract: Existing robot policy memories typically evolve with observation sequences, implicitly treating each update as the same amount of physical time. Yet identical observation histories can span different durations and require different actions, exposing physical time as a missing dimension of policy memory. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which learns memory dynamics to retain past events and evolve the memory state over measured time intervals. Observations and prior memory determine the content and time scales of each transition; elapsed time determines how far the state advances. TFP conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies through this memory state and is trained with their native imitation objectives. We evaluate TFP with Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$ through controlled comparisons of memory designs. These experiments show that successful timing depends on both measured intervals and retained history. TFP achieves higher average success than the recurrent and state-space memories we equip with the same intervals and than a variant that feeds the interval to a learned gate. Memory readouts recover the time since an event and motion information after occlusion. Changing the supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions, linking time inputs to behavior. Real-robot tasks requiring timing or memory, together with LIBERO evaluations, demonstrate benefits in physical and general manipulation. These results suggest viewing robot memory not as stored observation history, but as a state that retains past events and evolves with physical time.

bullets: Problem: Standard robot memories treat each update as equal time, so identical observations over different durations can produce inappropriate actions.

Method: TFP learns memory dynamics where observations and prior memory determine transitions, while measured elapsed intervals control state evolution; it conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies.
Results: Controlled comparisons with Diffusion Policy and π₀.₅ show higher average success than matched recurrent, state-space, and interval-gated memories.
Evidence: Memory readouts recover event timing and motion after occlusion, while changing supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon precise manipulation produces mixed-quality data for post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models: even successful demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts may contain detours, hesitations, failed attempts, and imperfect recoveries. The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91% success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels. More details and videos are available at: https://gr-bc.github.io
authors: Xiaoman Li, Zhiqiang Yang, Jiayu Hu, Jipeng Kong, Yang Zhang, Jingwei Zhang, Fangzheng Yan, Chunhua Shen, Chenjia Bai

Evaluated on four manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, reaching 91% success after a few offline iterations.
