papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning, an agent must explore an unknown environment to learn how to make good decisions. Unlike methods that can freely sample any state--action pair, an agent learning from a single trajectory must spend additional time navigating between states. It is therefore natural to expect that learning from a single trajectory requires more experience. In this paper, we show that this additional cost is not always necessary. For average-reward reinforcement learning, we develop an algorithm that learns where to collect information while ensuring that the required samples can be obtained efficiently. We establish an upper bound on the number of interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy. Furthermore, we prove a matching information theoretic lower bound, showing that, for a broad class of environments and at sufficiently high accuracy, learning from a single trajectory is no harder in the worst case than learning with unrestricted access to state action samples. Our results reveal that the additional complexity cost of navigation can be avoided by adapting information gathering requirements to how the environment provides information.
bullets: Studies policy identification when learning must follow one continuing trajectory rather than freely sampling state–action pairs.
Introduces an algorithm that adaptively chooses where to gather information while navigating efficiently.
Provides an upper bound on interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy.
Proves a matching information-theoretic lower bound for broad environment classes at sufficiently high accuracy.
Shows that, in the worst case, single-trajectory learning can be no harder than unrestricted state–action sampling.

papers.abstract: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.
authors: Parham Nooranbakht, Seyed Mahdi Basiri Azad, Joschka B\"odecker
bullets: Uses an adaptive action grid: high-value regions gain bins, while low-value bins are pruned.
Across eight DMControl tasks, SGQN is best on four and near-best on three; it trails Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run.
Analysis finds growth effectively activates all candidate bins, resembling uniform growth, while pruning has little impact.
Coarse initialization is important; starting with all bins causes collapsed seeds, and annealed softmax selection sharply reduces return.
Results may also reflect an uncontrolled difference in update frequency versus baselines.

papers.abstract: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations. Link for the webpage \href{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}
authors: Zeji Yi, Soham Dasgupta, Xinyang Zhang, Koushil Sreenath, Guannan Qu, Xi Chen, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Compares continuous and discrete single-step regression and multi-step flow policies in single-task and multi-task training, across simulation and real hardware.
Even naive uniform-bin quantization achieves comparable or better task success than continuous-action policies.
The key weakness of discrete policies is factorization error from product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions, rather than insufficient precision.
Iterative computation in discrete flows and classifier-free guidance improve responsiveness within predicted action chunks.
Geometric corruption processes inspired by continuous flow matching do not consistently improve discrete policies.

papers.abstract: We develop a self-supervised reinforcement learning algorithm that learns to build towers of up to eight cubes from scratch, without prior data, rewards, demonstrations, or pretrained models. Our method, Contrastive Planning via Spherical Linear Interpolation (C-Slerp), uses contrastive representations as reusable building blocks and repeatedly composes them to infer a sequence of intermediate waypoints. Under our hyperspherical parameterization, the learned representations allow intermediate waypoints to be inferred in closed form through spherical linear interpolation, without training a separate high-level policy or performing graph search. Importantly, the representation geometry also tells us how to adjust the number of waypoints based on the difficulty of each goal-reaching problem. Experiments show that our method succeeds on long-horizon navigation and robotic manipulation tasks, including settings where strong baselines fail to achieve a single success. Ablations further show that using a fixed number of waypoints substantially degrades performance, highlighting the importance of adapting the plan to task difficulty.

bullets: Learns from scratch in a self-supervised reinforcement learning setting, including tower-building tasks with up to eight cubes.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are today used largely for pretraining vision-language-action models, with little ability to use the same data for target-embodiment or task-oriented training, which scalable deployment of robots in industrial and general environments depends on. A human demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device such as a mobile phone can serve as post-training data for a robot whose body differs in structure and capability from the human who recorded it. This is made possible not by retargeting the hand's motion but the object's. A capture yields a body-free record: the object's pose over time, its contact intervals, and a reconstructed 3D object with provenance. Any robot, given as a URDF and a short descriptor, is solved against that record and scored in simulation against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth: the human-to-simulation leg of human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer, measured per robot. Each (robot, episode) pair gets one outcome: pass, failure with a named mode, or refusal, with its reason, before any motion. The method runs as a working system over a growing collection; the set analysed here is a sample of it: 42 captures solved on 8 robots, 157 pairs, of which 31.2% pass, 52.2% fail, 14.0% are refused and 2.5% are unauditable (kinematic feasibility, +/-50 mm / +/-15 deg, in simulation). Refusals held up: every pair the checks refuse on stored evidence yet ran anyway failed (13 of 13; 5 on a body whose public model welds its hand). A description file could not be shown to screen a robot: its outcomes were barely more predictable than guessing. No policy has yet been trained on the record. The record decides what a robot may post-train on; whether the policy then works on the real robot is the simulation-to-robot question, answered downstream.
bullets: Phone-recorded demonstrations capture object poses, contact intervals, and reconstructed 3D objects without tying data to a human body.
Each robot, specified by a URDF and brief descriptor, is evaluated in simulation against the demonstrated object motion before any policy execution.
For 157 robot–episode pairs across 42 captures and 8 robots, 31.2% passed, 52.2% failed, 14.0% were refused, and 2.5% were unauditable.
Refusal checks were reliable: all 13 pairs that ran despite being refused failed.
The study assesses data eligibility for robot post-training; it does not yet train policies or establish real-robot performance.

papers.abstract: Scaling embodied robot learning requires large and diverse manipulation datasets, but collecting real-world demonstrations remains expensive in human effort and robot time. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, yet converting a real workspace into a robot-learning-ready environment still requires substantial manual effort for object extraction, asset processing, coordinate calibration, and trajectory specification. We present AutoRSR, a highly automated real-to-sim-to real framework that converts scanned real-world workspaces into reusable embodied simulation assets and scalable manipulation data. Given multi-view observations, robot states, and open-vocabulary semantic queries, AutoRSR reconstructs the workspace, extracts individual object assets, and automatically registers the reconstructed scene to the robot base frame at metric scale. Starting from a small number of reference motions, AutoRSR then generates executable manipulation trajectories and scales them through trajectory interpolation and domain randomization. After workspace scanning and semantic queries, the remaining pipeline requires no manual object annotation, scene-to-robot calibration, or robot teleoperation. Across three real-world manipulation tasks, policies trained on 1K automatically generated episodes per task achieve 73.3--86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to pi 0.5 trained from 150 human teleoperated demonstrations, while reducing the human time required for data generation by an order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that real-world observations can be converted into metrically aligned, executable, and scalable simulation data with substantially reduced human effort.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Chang Liu, Litao Deng, Tao Zhang, Qin Jin
bullets: Addresses the cost and labor of collecting real-world manipulation demonstrations and manually building simulation environments.

Across three tasks, 1K automatically generated episodes achieved 73.3–86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to a policy trained from 150 teleoperated demonstrations.
The reported scope covers three real-world manipulation tasks and depends on workspace scans, semantic queries, and reference motions.

papers.abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints. We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and in a self-supervised manner during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate. Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift. TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic's predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value ("hard") observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions. Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.
authors: Motasem Alfarra, Pietro Mazzaglia, Markus Peschl, Daniel Dijkman, Christos Louizos
bullets: Addresses failures from terrain, payload, and sensing shifts when retraining or manual recalibration is impractical.
Adapts only the actor online using a frozen critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate.
TEMPO regularizes the critic’s predictive distribution to reduce overconfident extrapolation.
A score-based memory prioritizes hard, low-value observations and uses importance sampling under limited compute.
Improves performance across simulated robots and shifts, with gains up to 80%, and transfers to a physical Go2 with added payload.

papers.abstract: Despite the Markov assumption, safety failures in robot reinforcement learning rarely occur instantaneously; they typically emerge over several steps as the policy enters unfamiliar states under disturbances and domain shift. We address this limitation by learning a receding-horizon safety critic that predicts whether a state will remain non-terminating over the next receding horizon, enabling anticipatory detection of impending locomotion failures. The critic is trained from rollout-derived horizon labels with a composite objective that combines horizon classification, control-barrier-function-inspired temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization, and we aggregate an ensemble of critics with a conservative Conditional Value at Risk estimate to account for uncertainty. Building on the learned critic, we derive a closed-form, differentiable CBF-style safety filter that minimally modifies the policy action to improve predicted safety, and integrate it into PPO with an anticipation loss to reduce policy-filter mismatch during training. In simulated quadruped locomotion, our method improves robustness under action noise, external perturbations, and terrain shifts, reducing catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.
authors: Siwei Ju, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Targets safety failures that develop over multiple steps rather than occurring instantaneously.
Learns an ensemble safety critic using horizon labels, temporal-consistency constraints, and smoothness regularization.
Uses conservative uncertainty aggregation and a closed-form differentiable CBF-style filter to minimally adjust actions.
Integrates the shield with PPO through an anticipation loss to reduce policy–filter mismatch.
In simulated quadruped locomotion, improves robustness and reduces catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the training pipeline. Rollouts are collected in simulation under domain randomization and disturbances, and states are labeled by horizon-H safety to populate separate safe/unsafe buffers (with discounted weighting for delayed violations). A predictive safety critic is trained with a composite objective (labeling, temporal consistency, and smoothness), and an ensemble is aggregated via CVaR to obtain a conservative safety estimate and uncertainty σt. At each step, a differentiable closed-form safety layer projects the raw policy action to a minimally modified safe action, which is used both during PPO training (with an anticipation loss to reduce interventions) and at deployment for safety-shielded control.

Fig. 2: Top row: success rate; bottom row: average return. Columns correspond to four evaluation suites (action-noise and external-perturbation, each on flat terrain and heightfield terrain). Curves show mean performance over independent runs for PPO-RL, PPO-RL-NCBF, and our method, with shaded bands indicating standard error across different seeds. The x-axis denotes the perturbation/noise sampling probability.

Fig. 8: Comparison of SafeFall and our method in Safe RL training using each as a safety critic. The plot compares success rate (top row) and average return (bottom row) across different levels of action noise and external perturbations. Both methods show similar robustness under action noise, but our method outperforms SafeFall when faced with perturbations, demonstrating its superior generalizability.

Fig. 5: Comparison of state-only and state-action safety critics. The state-action safety critic demonstrates better generalizability and robustness, particularly under perturbations and domain shifts. The results are shown for success rate (top) and average return (bottom) across different perturbation settings. The result is aggregated over 5 seeds, and the shaded area shows the standard error. The state-action model outperforms the state-only model under external perturbation and domain shift.

Fig. 7: Safety predictions from the SafeFall predictor across several random episodes. The trajectory length is set to 250 timesteps. SafeFall’s predictions tend to be more binary, predicting failure only shortly before the event. This contrasts with our receding-horizon method, which provides earlier and more gradual safety estimates.

Fig. 6: Prediction of the state-based safety critic under domain shift. Top: ensemble safety predictions (gray), CVaR-aggregated safety prediction (black), and ensemble standard deviation σt (red dashed, right axis). Middle: action norms before and after shielding, ∥u0 t∥ (orange dashed), ∥ũt∥ (blue), and correction magnitude ∥ũt − u0 t∥ (green). Bottom: nominal-model-based one-step safety estimate hϕ(f̂nom(xt, ut)) (orange) versus the corresponding value evaluated on the realized next state h(xt+1) (black dashed). Under heightfield terrain with enlarged perturbations, the nominal estimate can diverge substantially from the next-state reference (e.g., around t ≈ 175–190), leading to spurious risk alarms and unnecessary interventions.

Fig. 9: Complete ablation on prediction horizon H . Success rate (top row) and average return (bottom row) under action noise and external perturbations on flat and heightfield terrain. The x-axis represents the action noise or disturbance sampling probability. Curves show mean performance over 5 seeds; shaded bands indicate standard error.

Fig. 3: Example rollout diagnostics of the predictive safety shield. Top: ensemble safety predictions (gray, “single prediction”), their CVaR-aggregated safety estimate p̂CVaR(xt) (black), and the ensemble standard deviation σt (red, right axis). Peaks in σt indicate increased epistemic uncertainty and coincide with sharp drops in the predicted safety. Bottom: action magnitudes before and after shielding, showing the raw action norm ∥u0 t∥ (orange), the shielded action norm ∥ũt∥ (blue), and the correction magnitude ∥ũt − u0 t∥ (green). Non-zero corrections occur primarily during high-uncertainty and low-safety intervals, illustrating successful interventions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.
authors: Huailiang Ma, Yuxuan Li, Ziyi Zhao, Xinkai Wang, Mingyu Li, Xinyu Guo, Lifeng Zhu, Aiguo Song, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
bullets: Targets weak fine-grained object understanding in existing image-level VLA models, especially under layout, clutter, and background shifts.
Encodes observations into temporal object slots with separate representations for persistent identity and changing object state.
Routes VLM attention toward relevant object tokens using identity-guided modulation.
Trains an action-conditioned dynamics module to predict future object states, while avoiding future prediction at inference.
Improves generalization across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation with novel arrangements and backgrounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of ObjDream. We introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework for robust manipulation. Unlike prior VLA models (a), which primarily rely on image-level understanding and entangled object representations, ObjDream (b) introduces explicit object-level representations and future object state prediction. This object-centric formulation improves manipulation robustness, leading to stronger performance than baseline methods (c).

Figure 2: Overview of the ObjDream architecture. The model integrates three main components: (1) a spatio-temporal object encoder that constructs factorized object slots by separately representing persistent object identity and time-varying object state; (2) an object-level dynamics module that decodes current object states and predicts action-conditioned future object states; and (3) a flow-matching action expert that predicts robot action chunks. ObjDream enhances object-level understanding through factorized object representations and future object state modeling, enabling more generalizable language-conditioned manipulation under object and scene variations.

Figure 3: Experimental overview. We evaluate ObjDream on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, a fixed 8-task subset of RoboTwin 2.0, and four real-world manipulation tasks, covering standard and perturbed evaluation settings.

Figure 5: Automatic offline annotation pipeline for object encoder pretraining. Qwen3-VL8B extracts task-relevant object phrases from demonstration instructions and initial observations, while a separate robot gripper label is used for robot annotation. Grounding DINO initializes the corresponding object regions, SAM2 propagates segmentation masks across frames, and DINOv2 extracts object-specific features from the initial grounded regions. Masks, geometry, visibility, and phrase–region correspondences are automatically constructed from this pipeline without manual frame-wise object annotation. The resulting annotations supervise encoder pretraining, while the DINOv2 features provide visual identity references.

The predictions are overlaid on the corresponding future RGB frames, which are used only for visualization and are not provided to the decoder.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird's-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments. BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors. Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance. Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations. Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC. This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.
authors: Eric Aislan Antonelo, Gustavo Claudio Karl Couto, Christian M\"oller, Pedro Henrique Fernandes
bullets: Targets behavior cloning for autonomous driving in simulated urban environments with scarce expert demonstrations.
Uses bird’s-eye-view inputs plus state variables to simplify policy learning.

A CNN predicts steering and acceleration actions.
In CARLA, weighted behavior cloning achieves higher route completion than standard BC, including in unseen test environments.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project
authors: Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang, Kai Hu, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses underspecified task instructions that do not clearly specify the next physical interaction.
Uses a vision-language reasoner to infer the next local motion from instructions and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict video and action chunks.
Builds temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations.
Introduces Execution-Grounded GRPO to train motion descriptions for appropriateness and execution success while keeping the WAM fixed.
Achieves 39.6% task success with default instructions and 31.6% with vague instructions in RoboLab real-to-sim evaluation.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Atomic-WAM overview. At decision step t, the reasoner predicts an atomic-motion description d̂t from the task instruction l and visual context ot−h:t, where each multi-view observation is formed by concatenating the wrist, left, and right camera views. The WAM conditions on d̂t, ot, and st to generate video latents x̂v and actions x̂a. The lower frames show selected decision steps from a full-task rollout, beginning at Start (t = 0).

Fig. 4: Closed-loop execution-grounded reasoner training. The reasoner samples four candidate atomic motions from a shared observation, while the frozen WAM executes them independently. An evaluator scores motion appropriateness and execution success, and the resulting group-normalized advantages update the reasoner. After each sampling round, one of the highest-reward endpoints is randomly selected as the starting state for the next round.

Fig. 2: Atomic-motion data curation. Displacement and gripper events first divide a demonstration into physical clips. We then annotate each clip from three views, then use temporal context to merge adjacent clips and refine their descriptions. Visible grasp details further enrich grasp-related captions. Finally, we check caption correctness and execution success; mismatched captions are revised and checked again.
Fig. 5: RoboLab success rate across training checkpoints. Results are averaged over three runs on RoboLab-120 with default instructions.

Fig. 1: Language specificity shapes predicted futures. Given the same initial observation and video backbone, we compare video predictions conditioned on (a) an abstract task instruction and (b) a concrete multi-step description. By explicitly specifying the target objects and action sequence, the latter produces a more coherent predicted manipulation sequence in this example.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at https://sites.google.com/view/touch-in-robot-learning-review.
authors: Kiyanoush Nazari, Luchen Li, Haoshu Fang, Nima Fazeli, Zhibin Li, Fumiya Iida, Thomas George Thuruthel
bullets: Reviews tactile representation learning, policy learning, foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and cross-domain generalization.
Organizes prior work by touch’s functional role throughout the learning and control pipeline.
Highlights challenges in learning transferable physical representations and linking semantic reasoning with contact-level control.
Examines scaling across objects, tasks, sensors, robot embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Representative architectures for integrating tactile information into foundation models for robotic manipulation. The paradigms include (a) direct multimodal conditioning, where tactile tokens are fused with vision, language, and proprioception within a VLM/VLA backbone; (b) semantic alignment of tactile representations with vision and language prior to policy conditioning; (c) physical grounding of tactile features through force-aligned representations; (d) predictive architectures that use tactile world models to generate future visuo-tactile interaction states for action generation; and (e) tactile-augmented reasoning, where tactile observations and retrieved interaction memories condition a VLM/VLA for semantic understanding and decision making.

papers.abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.

papers.abstract: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $\pi_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.

bullets: Fixed shared parameters can struggle when different robot operations require competing updates.
MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank updates for both vision-language and action modules.
Coupled generators follow the policy’s dependency structure, letting vision-language updates influence action-side parameter generation.
The framework is trained with the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets.
It reports gains of up to 16.30% on LIBERO and Meta-World and up to 14% over π₀.₅ in real-world evaluation.

papers.abstract: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, lim?its capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initi?ation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environ?ment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and het?erogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
authors: Xiangyi Wei, Hanzhe Yao, Jingwen Shang, Zhenhong Wu, Yang Li, Changbo Wang
bullets: Targets costly data collection, limited capability reuse, and cascading failures in complete-trajectory learning.
Represents each manipulation unit with a local goal, initiation condition, and observable success/failure criteria.
Uses language and vision to sequence units, select policies from a frozen capability registry, and verify outcomes before proceeding.
Supports checkpoint reuse for equivalent units and composes heterogeneous policies without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.
Evaluations on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks report higher complete-task success and verified progress, with better failure containment and lower error propagation than baselines.

papers.abstract: Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces enables scalable acquisition of human demonstrations for policy learning. However, existing handheld interfaces often provide limited intuitive force feedback, making contact-rich demonstration collection challenging for human operators. To address this, we present FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface with a scissor-shaped mechanism, which transmits object interaction forces directly to the operator's hands through actuation links without force sensors. This intuitive force feedback supports real-time action adjustment during robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Around FOMI, we build a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection. By further mapping pose changes and gripper opening of FOMI to robot end-effector poses and gripper commands, the system also supports teleoperation. Across four contact-rich tasks, FOMI improves collection efficiency by approximately 29% and 18% over the best baselines in robot-free collection and teleoperation, respectively. Demonstrations collected with FOMI in both modes enable policies to perform challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks with high success rates.

Improves collection efficiency by approximately 29% for robot-free collection and 18% for teleoperation across four tasks.
Collected demonstrations support policies that achieve high success rates on challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence. We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot's dynamics, independent of the learned DS. A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints. Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.
authors: Ashok Kumar, Mahathi Anand, Angela Schoellig, Abdalla Swikir
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of formally certifying flexible motions generated by dynamical-system learning from demonstration.
Uses a nominal controller to track the learned motion and a symbolic supervisory controller to monitor safety and convergence.
Automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan directly from the robot’s dynamics, independently of the learned dynamical system.
Intervenes non-conservatively when necessary constraints are violated.
Validated in simulations and on a real robot across 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting, and in complex dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning a policy that can outperform what is shown in the data. However, in practice, such systems suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity. In contrast, supervised learning provides a stable and scalable training objective, but is fundamentally limited by the quality of the demonstrated behavior. In this paper, we ask whether we can perform policy optimization with something as simple and stable as supervised learning but as performant as RL. Unfortunately, naively training the policy with supervised learning and conditioning on future rewards or advantages typically underperform dedicated RL methods. We introduce a new policy extraction method, Advantage Guidance, that retains the simple supervised learning structure with advantage conditioning while outperforming prior RL methods through effective conditional training and contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling. We show that Advantage Guidance can significantly improve a model's ability to respond to conditional advantage signals, and the contrastive guidance during sampling can use the learned advantage-conditioned policy to target the KL-regularized optimal policy. Empirically, we find that Advantage Guidance significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods on 26 long-horizon, sparse reward tasks across datasets with varying degrees of optimality.
bullets: Targets RL instability and hyperparameter sensitivity while retaining supervised learning’s simplicity.
Uses effective conditional training to improve policy responsiveness to advantage signals.
Applies contrastive diffusion guidance during sampling to target the KL-regularized optimal policy.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art RL methods across 26 long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks with varying data quality.

papers.abstract: Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71 times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations. Project page: https://rain-policy.github.io/.
authors: Hanlin Liu, Zichen Zhou, Jiacheng Zhang, Liuyuan Na, Jin Jin, Guangyan Chen, Yufeng Yue, Gen Li, Fangqiang Ding
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between lightweight, low-latency policies and slower iterative generative refinement.

Uses an ensemble trained from offline demonstrations without explicit labels for refinement needs, with calibration for uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency.
Evaluated on eight simulated ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks.
Achieves 66.6% simulation success with 5.71× lower policy latency than the best evaluated diffusion policy; real-robot success rises from 55.0% to 72.5% over ACT.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm--hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi-$\pi$, a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi-$\pi$ represents the right- and left-side arm--hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence--control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi-$\pi$ achieves state-of-the-art performance under both \textit{rand-obj} and \textit{rand-full}, improving the average success rate over $\pi_{0.5}$ from 31.9\% to 51.3\% and from 18.3\% to 32.3\%, respectively. Coordi-$\pi$ also consistently outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Yiming Meng, Yanming Shao, Weijie Shen, Kunyang Lin, Jiayu Sun, Ping Luo, Yao Mu
bullets: Targets the high-dimensional, structured action space of bimanual VLA policies, where cross-hand interactions are often implicit.
Represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as separate, interleaved action tokens.
Uses learnable hand-identity embeddings and factorized RoPE to encode hand identity, sequence position, and shared control timing.
On five DexJoCo tasks, average success rises from 31.9% to 51.3% under rand-obj and from 18.3% to 32.3% under rand-full, compared with π₀.₅.
Also consistently outperforms π₀.₅ across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.
authors: Julia Barth, Armin Sommer, Kunvar Thaman, Jannik Schilling
bullets: Identifies functional target substitution, policy shortcuts, and cue competition across Procgen and robot tasks.
Traces whether goal information is retained internally, influences the policy, and reaches the final decision.
Shows that steering can recover behavior when the goal reaches the decision, while new downstream wiring is needed when it does not.
Recovery fails when the goal is inert, linking intervention effectiveness to the depth of misalignment.
Frames goal misgeneralization as multiple policy-alignment failures rather than a single representation failure.

papers.abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors' epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.
authors: Sajad Marvi, Julian Schmidt, Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Jordan, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Exploring agents seek states that increase neighboring policies’ epistemic uncertainty, while other agents learn to drive safely through these challenges.
Epistemic uncertainty acts as an automatic difficulty signal, enabling curriculum generation without manual scenario design or ground-truth labels.
The approach improves zero-shot transfer on nuPlan Val14 and Argoverse 2 and also outperforms standard self-play on Waymo.
It produces 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage, suggesting a broader range of learned behaviors.
Highest-uncertainty agents have a 14.8× higher combined collision, off-road, and DNF failure rate than lowest-uncertainty agents.

papers.abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro
authors: Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Baekseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses failures caused by poor decisions about continuing versus intervening during VLA policy execution.
Uses a rollout-trained Critic to assess success prospects, choose intervention times, and select re-entry targets.
Applies Trajectory Retraction to return the robot to a selected point before resuming the same VLA with a fresh observation.
Evaluated with GR00T N1.7 and π₀.₅ in simulation and real-robot manipulation, improving success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points across the reported settings.
Also completes additional tasks when the available execution budget increases.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
authors: Jehun Lee, Hajun Lee, Jimin Ryu, Youhan Lee, Beomseok Kang, Jonghyun Choi, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Fixed-horizon execution can waste predicted actions and incur excessive policy calls at short horizons.
PICES is training-free and jointly selects an action chunk and how many actions to execute before replanning.
It compares nominal action chunks with versions generated from locally perturbed noise samples under shared conditioning features.
Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show up to 2.3× faster wall-clock inference on Jetson Orin and Thor, with improved success rate.
The method targets adaptive execution: longer horizons for stable predictions and shorter horizons for precise corrections.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of PICES. Step 1: Draw N initial noise samples and construct a perturbed variant of each sample. Step 2: The action expert processes the resulting N(1 + 1) inputs in a single batch under the shared condition C, producing N nominal action chunks and their corresponding perturbed chunks. Step 3: Stepwise action sensitivity G (n) k is computed by comparing each nominal chunk with its perturbed counterparts. Step 4: Compute a sensitivity score Si for each nominal chunk by averaging its sensitivity over the first W steps and use this score to determine its execution horizon hi. PICES retains candidates whose scores are at or below the median and selects the nominal chunk with the longest execution horizon from the pool.

papers.abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.
authors: Yuhang Hu, Junlin Lyu, Yuan Fang, Xiaoying Shen, Lechen Zhang, Jiong Lin, Judah Goldfeder, Steven Tian, Hod Lipson
bullets: Separates gaze target selection, fixation, and target-conditioned motion generation.
RGT uses a Transformer-VAE trained on retargeted markerless human gaze recordings in an 11-DoF robot joint space.
Self-supervised history encoding and autoregressive fine-tuning support realistic rollout behavior.
On a two-second shared-target benchmark, RGT-Base achieves the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE.
Physical demonstrations show integrated targeting and control, while perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary selection remain unevaluated.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) pipeline. The left panel illustrates our hierarchical perception system operating on a real humanoid robot. Egocentric video from the camera-embedded eyes, together with high-level natural language instructions, is processed by a slow-system VLM that reasons over the environmental context and designates salient targets. A fastsystem Visual Perception Module then tracks the selected faces in real time to produce a continuous target gaze direction. The right panel depicts the RGT architecture: a History Full-head Motion Tokenizer encodes recent facial dynamics while an Eyeball Trajectory Generator encodes the target gaze, and a Transformer-VAE fuses both streams into a latent representation from which it predicts future motion. The Action De-Tokenizer maps the near-future tokens to 11-DoF joint commands on the physical robot. The quantitative benchmark evaluates motion generation with ground-truth eye targets; target selection is illustrated by the physical demonstration.

Figure 2: Full pipeline of the Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT). Top: Data preprocessing stage. Raw human motion sequences (head pose, eye gaze, and blinks) are segmented into clips. Blink events are detected and extracted as separate blink templates (small eyelid motion sequences), and those blink segments are removed from the sequences to produce blink-free training data. Bottom: Model architecture and inference. Given a past full-head motion sequence and a planned eyeball motion sequence, the Transformer-VAE model (encoder and decoder) predicts a future blink-free trajectory along with blink probabilities for each future frame. At inference time, when a blink is predicted (high probability), a corresponding blink template is injected into the generated trajectory, yielding the final full-head motion with realistic blinks (red frames show the injected blink).

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of gaze behaviors across controllers. Each row shows a time sequence of robot face images during a representative leftward gaze shift. Top: Ground-truth human motion (GT) exhibits coordinated eye–head motion, with eyes leading the head. Second: RGT reproduces the illustrated sequence’s eye–head timing. Third: Eyes-Only rotates the eyes to mechanical extremes while keeping the head fixed, resulting in strained, unnatural motion. Bottom: Head-Only turns the head abruptly toward the target while leaving the eyes static, exaggerating head movement and yielding sluggish gaze redirection. Each column represents 1/3 second of motion.
Figure 4: Training Ablation Studies Comparison of pretraining and finetuning across different BIDs

Figure 5: (Top) Pearson correlation matrix across all head, eye, and eyelid degrees of freedom (DOFs), revealing strong coupling between head yaw and eye yaw, as well as head pitch and eye pitch. (Bottom) Lagged Pearson correlation peaks at a positive lag of approximately 20 frames (333 ms), consistent with eye motion preceding head motion in these recordings. Per-frame significance labels shown within the supplied plots are exploratory because adjacent frames are temporally correlated.

papers.abstract: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.
authors: Cheng Fan, Bingyang Zhou, Gang Yang, Zixuan Zhuang, Aoqian Zhang, Pengzhi Yang, Xin Liu, Chunzheng Wang, Yan Rui Tan, Fan Shi
bullets: Addresses gradient corruption from hard collisions and early termination in differentiable RL for legged obstacle avoidance.
Uses velocity-conditioned, stop-gradient shaping with penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints.
Distills a privileged SAPO teacher into a recurrent depth-based student using DAgger, then blends it with locomotion control through terrain-aware gating.
In simulation, shows higher sample efficiency than PPO and improved velocity tracking and obstacle avoidance versus PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC.

papers.abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.
authors: Fan Huang, Dezhong Tong, Changyu Chen, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An
bullets: Evaluates one-shot generation versus ICMC on UR5e cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks in MuJoCo using o1 and o4-mini.

Logged positive-reward rates increased from 31.6% to 35.3% over the reported five-step trajectory, but these rates were not always consistent with independently verified task success.
Audits found positive labels for geometric failures, including a case where all five rewards were 1.0 despite a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance.
Proposes independent evaluation against fixed task specifications to separate robot control from success assessment.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot's URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.

Evaluated in simulation on bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphologies and platforms.
Demonstrates real-world deployment on quadrupeds in multiple configurations without per-robot policy retraining.

papers.abstract: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.
authors: Xuan Han, Zinuo Jin, Tianlin Li, Yunfan Lou, Xin Liu, Yuchen Xue, Yuanpeng He, Boxian Yao, Shuhan Zhan, Ruihai Wu, Zhibo Pang

In real-world tests, Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion reach 63.00% mean success versus 40.00% for the baseline; only Prompt Fusion improves every task.
Predictive and temporal benefits are strongest for physical-property inference, while temporal designs underperform on assembly.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: A pretrained VLA succeeds on 80% of atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when skills are composed for mobile manipulation.

Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.

papers.abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20\% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.

On a physical 29-DoF robot, achieves over 20% higher task success than mainstream baselines across varied long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $\pi_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).
authors: Colton Crosby, Hao Wang, Mac Schwager, Somil Bansal
bullets: Addresses deployment-time failures that nominal policies cannot predict or recover from without retraining or new data collection.

Evaluated on LIBERO-Goal and a Franka Panda using π₀.₅ and a diffusion policy, with reported task-success improvements and real-time control.
Scope: interventions rely on offline training data and black-box query access to the nominal policy.

papers.abstract: We devise a dual-arm cooperative planning framework for wiping table surface in the presence of scattered objects. Unlike conventional surface-cleaning strategies that only cover free areas and detour around obstacles, our framework explicitly assigns one arm to rearrange objects while the other performs coverage wiping, thereby enabling access to previously obstructed regions. Specifically, we first construct a set of wiping and object-rearrangement action primitives. Based on these primitives, we introduce Geo-MILP, a geometry-aware task planner formulated as Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). By integrating Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD), Geo-MILP iteratively optimizes action sequencingand timing to resolve geometric conflicts, promoting efficient cooperation between wiping and object rearrangement. We then employ K-Order Markov Optimization (KOMO) to generate smooth, collision-free motions to ensure feasible execution. Simulation and physical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework not only increases reachable coverage by enabling access to obstructed areas, but also significantly improves time efficiency compared to Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) baselines, reducing planning time by up to 9 times and execution makespan by approximately 40%.
authors: Pengqi Zhang, Longchang Yu, Daohan Li, Liang Yan, Hangxin Liu
