papers.abstract: While multi-fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human-level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm-hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors. Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real-world learning. However, real-world demonstrations in the full arm-hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high-DoF multi-finger contact. Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off-nominal contact states important for robust execution. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks. Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm-hand coordination policy for arm control and hand-skill activation. This design enables effective real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation. Across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances. The project page is available at https://hly-123.github.io/HiFun/.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.

Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.

papers.abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. authors: Liqian Ma, Vaibhav Saxena, Utkarsh Aashu Mishra, Shuo Cheng, Yongxin Chen, Danfei Xu

figures.caption: Figure 2: MetaGenSim. We propose a meta-learning framework for Active Generative Simulation with three stages: (a) Rater network learning: We meta-learn a rater network that weights simulation samples according to their contribution to policy performance on a held-out validation set of real demonstrations. (b) Parameter utility landscape: We map these scores back to their corresponding simulation parameters and use kernel density estimation (KDE) to construct a probability landscape that identifies high-utility regions. (c) Targeted synthesis and co-training: We sample from the constructed distribution to generate a targeted simulation corpus, then co-train the final policy on this synthetic data and few-shot real demonstrations to maximize realworld success.

Figure 1: Active Generative Simulation via MetaGenSim. Sim-and-real co-training (top) boosts robot performance but traditionally relies on manual alignment (middle), where experts must laboriously tune data generation parameters (such as tasks, object placements, camera poses). We propose MetaGenSim (bottom), which meta-learns a Rater to score synthetic data based on policy utility. This induces a utility landscape over parameters, enabling active generation of targeted simulation data that matches the real-world distribution without manually tuning the generation parameters.

papers.abstract: Whole-body control plays a crucial role in enabling humanoid robots to execute expressive motions. Faithful execution requires preserving both the intended action and its expressive characteristics. Existing whole-body trackers typically balance joint and keypoint tracking with physical stability across diverse motions, but these objectives do not necessarily prioritize the expressive characteristics of each action. Our analysis shows that lower average positional tracking error does not guarantee better preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics. To address this gap, we propose a residual learning framework with compensation objectives targeting amplitude, energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height. To concentrate compensation while limiting interference with the underlying tracking behavior, motion-aware gating allocates correction capacity according to body-part activity, preserving larger correction ranges in more active parts and restricting them elsewhere. For each frozen tracker, we train motion-specific residual policies and distill them into a unified policy shared across motion categories. Simulation and physical experiments on the Unitree G1 across eight motion categories demonstrate superior preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics compared with the corresponding baselines.

papers.abstract: We present Keypoint Constraint Learning (KCL), a framework for learning task-relevant motion constraints from visual demonstrations and for planning safely with the extracted constraints. To make constraint learning tractable from RGB-D observations, we represent demonstrations using sparse 3D object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted through segmentation, visual feature clustering, and point tracking. In this reduced geometric space, we learn keypoint dynamics and infer distance- and orientation-based constraints that make the expert trajectories feasible and approximately locally optimal by enforcing KKT optimality conditions in the reduced state space. We then plan with the learned constraints under uncertainty, using robustness margins derived from accumulated prediction error, and provide a theoretical analysis of how keypoint perception error and learned dynamics error affect the recovered constraints. We evaluate KCL on visual demonstrations from navigation to rigid/deformable manipulation, showing that it recovers multi-stage geometric constraints and outperforms baselines in downstream safe planning.
authors: Zheng Qiu, Zhouyu Zhang, Ninghan Zhong, Glen Chou
bullets: Represents RGB-D demonstrations with object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted from segmentation, feature clustering, and tracking.
Learns keypoint dynamics and infers distance- and orientation-based constraints using KKT optimality conditions.

papers.abstract: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a practical path for adaptation, but limited and costly disassembly data cannot capture the distribution shifts arising from changing environments and product uncertainties. The policy's own rollouts record its approach attempts, and human corrections demonstrate recovery from its errors, but turning these experiences into better policy performance remains challenging. We introduce PACER, a Process-Aware Correction and Evidence Reweighting framework that learns from these experiences through SFT, using progress toward the target and each trace's source and outcome to weight valid action chunks in the native supervised action loss. PACER trains one policy per weighting setting and selects one of the resulting policies through held-out validation. We evaluate PACER on UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, where it achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.
authors: Zhi Cao, Yining Hong, Jiaolong Yang, Yejin Choi, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Huang Huang
bullets: Problem: Most human manipulation datasets lack force measurements, limiting force-aware human-to-robot transfer.
Method: FACT cascades a track-guided coarse planner with a force-action joint refiner that predicts future video, visual tracks, actions, and interaction forces.
Data: The model is pretrained on the EgoForce human tactile dataset together with robot demonstrations.
Results: Across ten fine-grained manipulation tasks, FACT improves success rates by up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex using as few as 10 robot and 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning.
Scope: Force supervision, visual-track prediction, and future-force prediction each support improved dexterous execution; the study focuses on tasks requiring fine coordination and force feedback.

papers.abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.
authors: Maria Attarian, Yifan Ruan, Claas Voelcker, Chenyang Cao, Amy Zhang, Peter Stone, Nicholas Rhinehart, Igor Gilitschenski
bullets: Compares supervised finetuning, critic-based steering, and offline RL across on/off-policy, offline/online, and optimal/suboptimal data scenarios.

With offline failure data, critic-based steering outperforms supervised finetuning.
Offline RL-trained critics do not outperform simpler Monte Carlo-based critics.
Online critic-based steering is more sample-efficient than policy-gradient finetuning but reaches a lower performance ceiling.

papers.abstract: Learning a collective policy for state-based Cartesian manipulation across diverse robotic embodiments presents a fundamental challenge due to embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. Collective learning aggregates multi-robot experience to discover shared task structure, yet naive aggregation can average incompatible action modes when different embodiments realize the same Cartesian command through different transition behavior. This leads to strategy ambiguity and performance collapse on dynamically outlying embodiments. To address this, we propose PACE, a two-stage collective learning framework that separates shared task-space intent from embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. The first stage employs a representation layer pre-trained on offline trajectories to extract task-level context from collective data. The second stage introduces a decision layer equipped with a predictive dynamics adapter. By forcing the latent state to predict future transitions, this adapter acts as a latent regularizer that grounds the policy in the transition behavior of the executing robot while preserving real-time inference without online planning. Evaluations across simulated embodiments demonstrate that our method prevents performance collapse on distinct robots. It achieves over 93\% overall success and 89\% on dynamically out-of-distribution zero-shot simulated robots, outperforming the Transformer behavior cloning (82\%) and diffusion policy baselines (66\%). Physical KUKA deployment further validates the feasibility of the full state-based pipeline under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Shaocheng Liu, Yuan Meng, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses performance collapse caused by aggregating incompatible action-transition behaviors across embodiments.

The adapter predicts future transitions to ground actions in the executing robot’s dynamics without online planning.
Achieves over 93% overall success and 89% success on dynamically out-of-distribution simulated robots.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real feasibility on a physical KUKA platform.

papers.abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.
authors: Daniel Lawson, Dhruv Sreenivas, Adriana Hugessen, Khimya Khetarpal, Glen Berseth
bullets: Addresses poor generalization from static offline datasets, especially on unseen tasks requiring composition of known skills.
Proposes TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model to generate achievable future outcomes.
Uses imagined outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned behavioral cloning policies.
Demonstrates significant generalization gains on stitching-based OGBench tasks.
Scope: focuses on zero-shot goal generalization and avoids the difficulty of long-horizon world-model generation.

papers.abstract: Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations. A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard. In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon. In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
authors: Elena Sorina Lupu, Hannah Grauer, Phaedrus Leeds, Nikhil Ranganathan, Connor Lee, Sulekha Kishore, Cailyn Smith, Shon Cortes, Brian Hardy, Benjamen Bycroft, Darren W. Rowen, Soon-Jo Chung
bullets: Addresses spacecraft autonomy under communication delays and limited bandwidth by moving learning pipelines onboard.

papers.abstract: Achieving human-like dexterous manipulation remains a central challenge in robotics. Learning from human hand-object interaction (HOI) datasets offers a promising pathway to diverse dexterous skills, yet existing physics-based approaches train specialist policies for individual trajectories, thereby limiting skill reuse at scale. We introduce DexMimic, a generalist dexterous hand-object tracking policy jointly trained across diverse HOI trajectories. Efficient joint training requires allocating each rollout to both an undertrained phase and a starting state that supports continued tracking. DexMimic realizes this insight through Value-Guided Reset Allocation, which adapts the initialization distribution online to prioritize difficult phases and select reset states with higher expected tracking returns. We further introduce a benchmark spanning training, fine-tuning, and generalization. Experiments show improved tracking success and training efficiency, faster fine-tuning, and the potential for zero-shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects; larger training sets further improve efficiency and generalization. Finally, we validate DexMimic on a real-world dexterous manipulation platform.
authors: Zhexi Luo, Zhixuan Xu, Rui Yang, Zeyu Xiao, Yiwen Hou, Lin Shao
bullets: Addresses the limited skill reuse of specialist physics-based policies trained on individual human hand-object trajectories.

Introduces a benchmark covering training, fine-tuning, and generalization, with experiments showing improved tracking success and training efficiency.
Demonstrates faster fine-tuning, potential zero-shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects, and real-world platform validation.

Physics rollouts from the sampled initializations update the policy and critic, replenish the reset map, and refine phase sampling probabilities, forming an adaptive training loop.

papers.abstract: Humanoid policies trained in simulation can transfer qualitatively to hardware while failing to transfer the force interactions learned during training, compromising torque efficiency, load regulation, and robustness to impacts. This failure can arise from actuator sim-to-real gaps because forces depend on actuator torques. We introduce Contact-UAN, a residual world model that preserves a simulator's physics priors while correcting actuator dynamics to align simulated rollouts with recorded hardware rollouts. For humanoid motion with contact, this requires contact-consistent replay: if hardware playback in simulation begins with misaligned contact wrenches, the residual model learns to correct reset artifacts rather than actuator discrepancies. Using only onboard proprioception, Contact-UAN infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose needed to initialize replay with consistent contact forces. We show that a UAN trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data generalizes to tasks that benefit from accurate force and impulse regulation and produces policies that transfer seamlessly to the real world, yielding 20% lower running torque, 43% lower force-tracking error, extreme compliance, accurate impedance control, and dynamic, robust jumps.
authors: Nolan Fey, Khai Nguyen, Yash Prabhu, Gabriel B. Margolis, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Addresses actuator sim-to-real gaps that degrade torque efficiency, load regulation, and impact robustness.
Uses a residual world model that preserves simulator physics while aligning simulated rollouts with hardware behavior.
Infers simulator-side stance-foot pose from proprioception to initialize contact-consistent replay and avoid reset artifacts.
Trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data, it supports force and impulse regulation, impedance control, compliance, and dynamic jumps.
Reports 20% lower running torque and 43% lower force-tracking error during real-world transfer.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly. Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution. We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion. Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination. We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations. Building on this pipeline, we develop $\lambda_0$, a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training. Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress. $\lambda_0$ achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks. We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world. Homepage: https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/

The system reaches 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations.

papers.abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.
authors: Mingxuan Yan, Litian Gong, Dihong Huang, Zhixu Li, Tianyu Zhang, Wenqian Zhang, Hefeifei Jiang, Peihao Li, Jian Zhang, Mengfei Zhao, Yikai Tang, Hai Zhai, Zehao Wang, Ruijian Liang, Yanjia Huang, Lin Shao, Changliu Liu, Kaiyu Hang, Zhiwen Fan, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Jianfei Yang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Benchmarks weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks.
Across three VLAs, approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning, while the best label granularity depends on the approach and model.
Constant-tag fine-tuning further improves mean success after conditioned pretraining, regardless of tagged or untagged inference.
AXIS-Bench provides replayable simulation trajectories with object and contact states for controlled, user-defined quality-label comparisons.
In a real-world experiment, simulation pretraining increased success from 9.6% to 31.7%.

papers.abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.
authors: Haldun Balim, Yilun Du, Na Li
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between short-horizon value bootstrapping and costly trajectory optimization.
Samples candidate action sequences from a learned diffusion prior rather than optimizing from scratch.
Refines proposals using learned dynamics, reward, and value models for trajectory-level reasoning.
Matches or exceeds reported baselines across continuous-control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, with improved stability in difficult regimes.
Reframes generative models as structured planning proposals rather than direct policies.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP). Planning proceeds via iterative beam search. Starting from an initial beam, GTP repeatedly (1) branches candidate trajectory prefixes by duplicating, (2) refines action suffixes through partial forward diffusion and denoising under the diffusion prior, and (3) prunes candidates using rollouts through learned dynamics, reward, and value models. The top-scoring trajectories are retained and expanded at the next depth, progressively constructing long-horizon plans toward high-return regions.

Figure 1: Generative Trajectory Planning. GTP combines the data-driven nature of RL with the long-horizon reasoning of trajectory optimization. A learned diffusion prior proposes candidate action sequences, which are evaluated and iteratively refined through learned models. By using a generative prior, GTP avoids computational cost of optimization while preserving long-horizon reasoning.

papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

papers.abstract: Expressive flow policies can represent multiple high-value actions, but sampling them with few integration steps while retaining tractable action densities remains challenging. We introduce DEFlow, a deep equilibrium flow policy that replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as an equilibrium system. We combine implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density, enabling off-policy training within soft actor-critic without backpropagating through solver iterations. DEFlow achieves an average relative improvement of approximately 10% in mean successful coverage over the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants. It also achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, while remaining broadly competitive across five MuJoCo tasks. These results support implicit flow policies for tasks requiring both diversity and precision, at the cost of additional nonlinear and linear solves. Primary

papers.abstract: Flow matching is a common generative recipe for robot foundation models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) generate action chunks, while world-action models (WAMs) additionally generate future visual states. Both start generation from a fixed Gaussian prior, despite temporal continuity between past and future states and actions. This requires costly training and iterative sampling, especially for WAMs with an additional visual branch. We introduce $Δ$-flow, which constructs the source from recent history with mild noise rather than from a fixed Gaussian prior. This moves the source closer to the target, reducing transport to a small residual $Δ$ that can be learned efficiently and enables single-step inference. We integrate $Δ$-flow into the VLA policy $π_{0.5}$ and the WAM policies ImageWAM and Fast-WAM. On LIBERO, ImageWAM reaches 90% success in one epoch rather than six, and Fast-WAM reaches 95% in two epochs rather than eight. With LoRA fine-tuning, $π_{0.5}$ exceeds its baseline's five-epoch performance after one epoch. Single-step inference gives $1.54\times$, $2.49\times$, and $4.45\times$ speedups on $π_{0.5}$, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, respectively. It preserves action smoothness, achieving a $4.5\times$ reduction in action jerk compared with one-step Gaussian sampling. $Δ$-flow reaches state-of-the-art generalization performance on LIBERO-Plus. Action-history sources can be applied to pretrained WAM policies without retraining. Replacing the Gaussian action source at inference largely preserves task success with a single sampling step and can slightly improve it. We further study how action representation and visual information in action learning affect history-to-future prediction in $Δ$-flow. These results show that $Δ$-flow is simple yet effective, improving the efficiency and generalization of robot foundation models.
bullets: Targets costly iterative sampling and training in vision-language-action and world-action robot models.
Builds the flow source from recent action and visual history, learning only the residual transition to future actions and states.
Integrated into π₀.₅, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, it achieves faster training and 1.54×–4.45× inference speedups on LIBERO.
Maintains smooth actions, reducing action jerk 4.5× versus one-step Gaussian sampling, and reaches state-of-the-art generalization on LIBERO-Plus.
History-based action sources can be applied to pretrained world-action models without retraining, though visual and action representations affect prediction quality.

Figure 1 ∆-flow matching learns past-to-future changes for efficient robot foundation models. This shorter transport substantially improves training efficiency, enables fast single-step inference, strengthens generalization under distribution shift, and preserves smooth action generation across chunk boundaries.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. This paper presents SurgiCLAW, a hierarchical skill-based framework for precision surgical manipulation. SurgiCLAW confines an MLLM to intraoperative visual understanding, structured explanation, and atomic surgical-skill selection, while delegating physical execution to verifiable deterministic control programs. For brain--machine-interface implantation, a representative high-precision surgical task, we construct a state-to-skill invocation dataset and expand it through visual and state perturbations. The model first learns structured skill invocation through supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized using three rewards for action correctness, operation prerequisites, and format validity, improving action selection, operational safety, and output parseability. We evaluate subtask success, offline model comparison, real-robot performance, and ablations. On a fixed test set, SurgiCLAW achieves 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1). Across 50 closed-loop real-robot implantation trials, it achieves an 88.0% task success rate.
authors: Angen Ye, junjie xie, Yujia Song, Junkai Huang, Dapeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the precision, opacity, and data-scarcity challenges of end-to-end low-level action prediction in surgical robotics.
Uses an MLLM for visual understanding, structured explanations, and skill selection, while verified control programs execute actions.
Trains on a state-to-skill dataset augmented with visual and state perturbations, then optimizes correctness, prerequisites, and output validity.
For brain–machine-interface implantation, reaches 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1 on a fixed test set.
Achieves 88.0% task success across 50 closed-loop real-robot trials.

Fig. 1. Multi-MLLM collaborative data-generation pipeline. Starting from raw image, robot-state, instruction, and skill-label samples, the pipeline expands the data through image/text augmentation and constructs structured rationales using three MLLMs. Candidate outputs are filtered by rule-based checks, leaveone-generator-out cross-validation, and human spot inspection before being retained in the final structured dataset.

Fig. 3. Closed-loop decision example for flexible-electrode implantation. At each step, SurgiCLAW receives the current microscopic image, robot state, and operation query, then outputs a structured rationale, an operator-facing answer, and a single atomic-skill call. The example illustrates a typical decision sequence from spatial registration and image-quality correction to needle alignment and final insertion. surgical data: a multi-MLLM data-generation pipeline expands 5,000 state–skill samples into 30,000 structured ones, and a three-reward group reward-decoupled normalization policy optimization objective improves skill selection, prerequisite safety, and output parseability. On the fixed test set SurgiCLAW reaches 94.6% accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1, and it completes 88.0% of 50 closed-loop implantation trials. We interpret these results as a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of clinical efficacy: the evaluation covers a single high-precision task using phantom and ex-vivo material, and the closed-loop comparisons are constrained by the modest number of paired trials. Whether the safety and interpretability benefits generalize to other tasks, to more stringent clinical conditions, or to long-horizon unattended operation remains to be established.

papers.abstract: Visual world models predict the consequences of actions from images, but planning with them is typically done by optimizers such as CEM and MPPI. However, these optimizers stall on long-horizon tasks where progress requires motion the objective does not reward, such as moving around a block before pushing it. This paper revisits kinodynamic sampling-based motion planning for world models, using the learned model as the propagator of a tree search in latent space. Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model, where they rapidly expand through intermediate states that myopic optimizers never sample. We present two exploration strategies for the high-dimensional latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE, with GPU-native batched expansion for efficient device utilization. We evaluate with an off-the-shelf DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task. Our approaches match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at up to 13.8x lower planning time in simulation, and improve the success rate by 20% on the real robot.
bullets: Addresses optimizer failures when successful actions require temporarily unrewarded intermediate motion.
Uses the world model as a latent-space propagator for kinodynamic tree search.
Introduces nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE with GPU-batched expansion.
Evaluated in four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task.
Matches or exceeds CEM/MPPI success rates with up to 13.8× lower simulation planning time and 20% higher real-robot success.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Planning paradigms and receding-horizon execution in latent space. (a) Shooting methods (CEM) iteratively collapse trajectories toward a mean, risking entrapment in local minima around non-convex obstacles. (b) Tree search (RRT) finds a valid path through the latent space, committing only its first 𝑛exec actions. (c) System execution introduces minor drift from the planned path, requiring re-grounding and replanning from the new observation. (d) KPIECE projects states onto a grid and prioritizes under-explored frontier cells (shaded) for subsequent expansions.

It first traverses around the block, keeping the block stationary and leaving the cost flat for ∼ 60% of the trajectory. papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves reasoning, while the allocation of learning signal shapes which solutions remain accessible under repeated sampling. Group-relative objectives assign equal advantages to equally rewarded responses, making aggregate credit proportional to sampled mode frequency. We introduce Exploration-Preserving Policy Optimization (ExPPO), a lightweight advantage-shaping rule that redistributes credit using prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate. ExPPO combines bounded shaping with shared normalization to preserve verifier polarity and approximately maintain each prompt group's total absolute sequence-advantage mass. Our analysis characterizes response-level credit allocation alongside sampled mode updates, deriving local conditions for gains in entropy and correct-mode discovery. Experiments show improved in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning coverage, higher aggregate response accuracy, and strong coverage at large sampling budgets. A controlled multi-answer evaluation further demonstrates increased correct-mode yield and gains in diversity among verified-correct responses. Code is available at https://github.com/jinhangzhan/ExPPO
bullets: Addresses group-relative objectives that can concentrate learning on frequently sampled solution modes.
Uses prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate to redistribute credit.
Applies bounded shaping and shared normalization to preserve verifier polarity and approximately conserve each prompt group’s absolute advantage mass.
Analysis links response-level credit allocation to entropy and correct-mode discovery.
Experiments report improved in- and out-of-domain coverage, aggregate accuracy, large-budget coverage, and diversity among verified-correct responses.

papers.abstract: Legged robots can learn expressive whole-body skills from the motions of humans and animals. Due to the morphology gap between the source and the robot, however, the motion must be tailored to the dynamic properties of the robot. In particular, dynamic motions such as a jump require careful adjustment, since their timing and control are interdependent. We propose dense temporal motion retargeting (DTMR), which jointly optimizes timing and control within a single optimization, where dense means that the timing is adjusted for every control step. This dense formulation enables DTMR to deform only the parts of the motion that need a change in timing. The problem is solved with sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) in parallel on a GPU. We evaluate DTMR against baselines on two hours of human motion with four humanoid robots, where the results show that DTMR outperforms baseline methods, particularly on dynamic motions. We also show that allowing more temporal deformation yields more precise retargeting. We further compare DTMR with a baseline that optimizes the temporal dimension, where the result shows that DTMR retargets more precisely under the same deformation budget while being ~19x faster. Lastly, policies trained on our references transfer to a real humanoid robot.
bullets: Addresses the morphology gap when transferring expressive human or animal motions to legged robots, especially timing-sensitive dynamics such as jumps.
Uses a single optimization combining dense per-control-step temporal deformation with control, solved via GPU-parallel sampling-based model predictive control.
Evaluated on two hours of human motion across four humanoid robots; outperforms baseline methods, particularly for dynamic motions.
Allows localized timing changes and achieves more precise retargeting than a temporal-optimization baseline under the same deformation budget, while being approximately 19× faster.
Policies trained from the retargeted references transfer to a real humanoid robot.

papers.abstract: Cross-structural motion retargeting aims to transfer motion between different skeletal topologies. Despite recent progress, existing state-of-the-art models struggle with reliability in zero-shot settings, i.e. skeletons with different topologies which were unseen during training, and recent Transformer-based attempts have failed to outperform specialized geometric methods. We bridge this gap with a Transformer Autoencoder that learns a topology- and translation-invariant latent space. Our core contribution is a learnable flattening of skeletal graphs that captures both local dependencies and global structure. Unlike the standard transformer architecture, which adds positional information to token content, we integrate graph-based positional encodings multiplicatively, a design choice that follows directly from our flattening formulation. The resulting model handles diverse skeletal topologies within a single unified architecture and trains in a fully unsupervised manner, requiring no paired retargeting data. Ablation studies show, that the graph encodings, multiplicative formulation, and Transformer backbone is critical for the performance. In zero-shot evaluations, our method reduces global joint position error by $43-47\%$ over current benchmarks. A user study ($n = 37$), including expert animators, further ranks our approach highest in motion alignment and physical plausibility ($p < 0.05$). These results demonstrate that our model design is key to making transformer architectures effective for motion retargeting, outperforming existing approaches.
bullets: Addresses poor zero-shot retargeting when test skeleton topologies differ from those seen during training.
Learns to flatten skeletal graphs while preserving local dependencies and global structure.
Uses multiplicative graph-based positional encodings in a Transformer Autoencoder.
Trains fully unsupervised and supports diverse skeleton topologies in one architecture.
Reduces global joint position error by 43–47% in zero-shot evaluations and ranks highest in a 37-person user study.

papers.abstract: Indirect manipulation of deep-seated deformable anatomy inaccessible to the robot is challenging in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) because intervening tissues spatially filter deformation transmission. Passive observations can be ambiguous because the Decoupled and Blocked modes may produce similar motion responses. We propose CADeT, a causal-aware deformation transmission framework that integrates structural causal model (SCM) with active sensing to infer a latent transmission mode and estimate a state-dependent adhesion Jacobian online. During normal manipulation, control actions update the mode belief; when ambiguity persists, an additional probing action is selected to improve mode distinguishability. The mode belief and learned Jacobian are incorporated into a belief-aware model predictive controller for indirect target-shape control. Validation in simulation and on the da Vinci research kit (dVRK), using phantom and ex vivo porcine tissues, shows higher mode-identification accuracy and faster shape-error convergence than the evaluated model-free and model-based baselines. These results show that active sensing improves mode identification and indirect deformation control under the evaluated conditions.
bullets: Addresses ambiguous deformation responses caused by intervening tissues in indirect manipulation.
Combines a structural causal model with active probing to infer latent transmission modes.
Learns a state-dependent adhesion Jacobian online and integrates it into a belief-aware model predictive controller.
Validated in simulation and on the dVRK with phantom and ex vivo porcine tissues.
Achieved higher mode-identification accuracy and faster shape-error convergence than evaluated baselines under the tested conditions.

papers.abstract: Behavior cloning provides an offline route to autonomous-driving policy learning, but mean-squared-error regression is poorly matched to demonstrations in which one observation admits several valid actions. Diffusion policies can represent conditional multimodal action distributions, yet their closed-loop performance may be unstable when visual features and control are learned from limited data. This paper presents Diffusion-2BC, which combines a diffusion denoising objective with an auxiliary deterministic behavior-cloning loss over a shared visual encoder. The auxiliary branch is used only during training; inference remains diffusion-based. The proposed method is evaluated in the controlled Claw environment and in bird's-eye-view CARLA navigation, including route-conditioned driving, route-free navigation through multiple intersections, and cross-map evaluation from Town01 to Town02. In the Claw task, Diffusion-2BC reduced the mean mask-distance error by approximately 10% relative to a diffusion-based behavior-cloning baseline and by 85% relative to standard deterministic behavior cloning. In route-free CARLA, Diffusion-2BC traveled substantially farther before termination under the evaluation protocol than both baselines in Town01 and Town02. Additional qualitative rollouts revealed distinct route choices, showing the multimodal behavior of the proposed diffusion-based agent. The results indicate that an auxiliary regression signal can improve the closed-loop reliability of diffusion behavior cloning while preserving multimodal prediction in the controlled benchmark.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between deterministic MSE behavior cloning and demonstrations with multiple valid actions.
Combines diffusion denoising with an auxiliary deterministic behavior-cloning loss through a shared visual encoder; inference remains diffusion-based.
Evaluated in the Claw environment and bird's-eye-view CARLA across route-conditioned, route-free, and cross-map navigation.
Reduced Claw mean mask-distance error by about 10% versus a diffusion baseline and 85% versus deterministic behavior cloning.
In route-free CARLA, traveled substantially farther before termination in both Town01 and Town02; qualitative rollouts showed distinct route choices.

papers.abstract: Existing LLM-driven robot task planners rely on a taken-for-granted assumption of an ideal user whose instructions are clear, complete, and task-focused. However, when interacting with real-world users, especially those experiencing cognitive impairments, such as people living with dementia (PLWD), the planners often make mistakes and even pose physical safety risks. We proposed TALK-Dem (Talking Attributes and Linguistic Knowledge in Dementia), the first benchmark for evaluating LLM-driven robot task planning under dementia-associated verbal communication. TALK-Dem contains 4,800 instructions and covers five typical communication patterns, including Referential Imprecision, Object Substitution, Empty Speech, Topic Drift, and Intrusion, at three intensity levels. Experiments across six open-weight LLMs reveal a substantial robustness gap. Across communication patterns, open-weight models exhibited performance drops of up to 22.3 percentage points compared to ideal instructions. This revealed a critical gap and even danger for real-world applications, especially in assistive robotics, where locally deployable models are necessary due to privacy concerns and connectivity constraints. To mitigate this issue, we proposed the Context-Aware Retrieval from Experience (CARE) method, which retrieves relevant previously resolved tasks to provide task-specific interpretation and planning context. CARE generally outperformed standard prompting baselines across the six open-weight models, improving average task success by 18.1 percentage points over the vanilla prompt. These results highlighted the importance of both evaluating communication robustness and developing effective adaptation strategies for locally deployable assistive robots. The TALK-Dem dataset is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TALK-Dem-A6B3/.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human demonstrations offer an accessible source of task experience, but differences in body scale and controller response, together with missing robot states, limit their value as humanoid training supervision. We present EgoAlign, a data-construction framework that converts these demonstrations into action and state supervision compatible with a general-purpose, continuous whole-body controller, without collecting physical-robot demonstrations. Using the target-robot model and simulator, EgoAlign guides demonstration collection through execution feedback. It preserves locomotion references for visually guided periodic stepping while adapting upper-body interaction geometry through scale alignment and controller-in-the-loop refinement. A final causal replay reconstructs the corresponding robot states and motion-token labels for training with the human observations. We assess the resulting supervision by fine-tuning a vision--language--action model solely on adapted human demonstrations and deploying it zero-shot on a physical humanoid. The resulting policies perform long-range object relocation, navigation to unseen goal positions, and independently evaluated foot interaction. Refinement improves simulated hand alignment and physical pickup success over kinematic alignment alone, while human collection reduces on-site acquisition time relative to teleoperation. https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/EgoAlign/
bullets: Addresses body-scale, controller-response, and missing-state mismatches between human demonstrations and humanoid training needs.
Uses robot-model simulation and execution feedback to guide collection, preserve locomotion references, and adapt upper-body interaction geometry.
Applies controller-in-the-loop refinement and causal replay to reconstruct robot states and motion-token labels.
A vision–language–action model trained only on adapted human data transfers zero-shot to a physical humanoid for long-range relocation, navigation, and foot interaction.
Refinement improves simulated hand alignment and physical pickup success over kinematic alignment, while human collection reduces on-site acquisition time versus teleoperation.

papers.abstract: Personal robots should adapt their co-speech gesture style to a new user without requiring model retraining. We present a training-free personalization pipeline that combines a frozen audio-conditioned diffusion prior with a gesture style encoder and lightweight conditioning adapters. The encoder is first trained to discriminate speaker identities and then jointly refined with the adapters using the diffusion objective, enabling a reusable style embedding to be extracted from approximately 10 seconds of enrollment motion through a single forward pass. To support this setting, we also release a Quest~3 capture application and a dataset of spontaneous co-speech motion from ten participants. We evaluate the system on held-out speakers using Style Recognition Accuracy (SRA) and Fr'echet Gesture Distance (FGD) to measure personalization and motion quality. Our approach improves SRA from 27.6\% for the frozen prior to 69.5\% while preserving motion quality (FGD 34.2 versus 34.8), and replacing the enrollment embedding with another person's reduces SRA to 11.4\%. The generated gestures are retargeted to a physical NAO robot, and this improvement also transfers to the robot deployment setting, where speech is synthesized using five TTS voices, retaining 67.3\% SRA.
bullets: Uses a frozen audio-conditioned diffusion prior with a speaker-style encoder and lightweight conditioning adapters.
Extracts a reusable style embedding in a single forward pass from enrollment motion.
Introduces a Quest 3 capture application and a spontaneous co-speech motion dataset from 10 participants.
Improves held-out speaker style recognition from 27.6% to 69.5% while maintaining similar motion quality (FGD 34.2 vs. 34.8).
Transfers to a physical NAO robot with synthesized speech, achieving 67.3% style recognition across five TTS voices.

papers.abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.
authors: Bingxin Xu, Wenrui Bao, Xinxin Liu, Jiawei Zhou, Yuzhang Shang, Emilio Ferrara
bullets: Agentic robots repeatedly invoke an LLM over the full interaction history, causing cost to grow with primitive count.
ChunkAct launches a chained chunk after each sub-goal decision and returns control to the planner only when the chunk fails.
Offline compilation converts memory into executable chunks, allowing memory-free test-time execution.
On LIBERO-Pro, it improves task success by 5.0 points while using 2.9× fewer LLM calls, 4.4× fewer input tokens, and 2.3× fewer output tokens.

Right: online, the LLM planner invokes ChunkAct via a single function call, which executes an entire action chunk autonomously and returns a typed error code to the planner only upon failure.

papers.abstract: Scaling expert demonstrations alone does not enable generalist robot policies to improve from deployment. Real-world rollouts contain successes, suboptimal behavior, and failures: imitating every recorded action can reinforce poor behavior, while filtering out failures discards evidence of physical interactions and their consequences. We introduce \textbf{LoopWAM}, a closed-loop world-action model that learns directly from this full quality spectrum, using rollouts from both itself and other deployed policies. Source-dependent noise sampling unifies behavior learning and action-conditioned world modeling, while quality steering and quality-weighted supervision retain full video supervision across qualities and regulate action imitation. Video and action tokens interact throughout parallel denoising, allowing learned consequences to inform action generation directly. On RoboChallenge Table30-V2, three deployment-and-training rounds raise success from 23.67\% to 43.33\%, a 19.7-percentage-point gain, with a final score of 56.80. LoopWAM also achieves 94.5\% average success on RoboTwin~2.0 and 49.5\% overall success on RoboCasa365 without additional embodied pretraining, obtaining the best overall results among the compared methods across all three benchmarks. On challenging shirt folding task, two rounds of deployment-driven improvement after single-task post-training raise success from 13.20\% to 55.56\%. These results demonstrate closed-loop improvement from mixed-quality experience under both multi-task learning and single-task post-training. \href{https://loop-wam.github.io/}{\textcolor{orange}{Project Page}}
authors: Wenxuan Guo, Yingping Liang, Zhaoguo Wang, Ziyuan Li, Angyuan Ma, Zhenyu Wu, Chengkun Wang, Bingyao Yu, Ze Chen, Borui Zhang, Xiuwei Xu, Meng Zhang, Erjin Zhou, Jiwen Lu

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid loco-manipulation from human demonstrations rests on observing how locomotion, posture, and object interaction evolve together as tasks unfold. Scaling collection across diverse environments, in turn, favors lightweight, portable capture systems. Yet, existing datasets provide only partial views of this coordination. Thus, we introduce EgoExplorer, a 100-hour vision-motion-touch observatory of human loco-manipulation built with a wearable system. With an emphasis on professional activities, its continuous recordings align egocentric video with reconstructed whole-body motion, fine-grained finger articulation, and tactile observations, accompanied by step-level descriptions. To achieve this coverage with sparse body sensing, we develop the Calibrate-Complete-Constrain pipeline. Concretely, reusable calibration fixes participant geometry and sensor attachments before motion inference to disentangle mounting offsets from articulation. A temporal prior then completes unobserved joint motion, while layered constraints promote measurement agreement, temporal continuity, and geometric consistency, properties that motion plausibility alone does not guarantee. Against tracker-fitted references, the method reduces body-point error by 71.9% relative to the strongest baseline; matched evaluations also show gains in hand stability and contact estimation. Preliminary studies explore multimodal generation and conditioning alongside humanoid retargeting with whole-body control in simulation.
authors: Yunsong Zhou, Xuekun Jiang, Haiqi Shen, Hangxu Liu, Chaojian Shi, Yujie Liu, Jingyuan Li, Haoran Yang, Jiafei Cao, Dongzhan Zhou, Dong Wang, Yao Mu, Chunhua Shen, Weinan Zhang

Reports a 71.9% reduction in body-point error versus the strongest baseline, with improvements in hand stability and contact estimation.

papers.abstract: Bringing general-purpose agents into the physical world calls for an executable representation of physical intelligence. Compared with vision-language-action (VLA) models, which map observations and language instructions directly to actions, code makes control logic explicit and reusable. Code can serve not only as a policy representation but also as the workspace in which the agent solves a task. Rather than following a prescribed workflow of planning, execution, and verification, the agent can autonomously inspect the state, revise and execute code, and use feedback to choose the next step. The success of this SWE-style loop in digital environments motivates its extension to physical tasks. Yet physical execution remains prone to recurring failures. To retain and refine experience for later scenes, we introduce EmbodiedEvo, where a coding agent evolves reusable Skills and Lessons through feedback on a single Playground scene, then freezes the resulting harness for diverse new scenes. On RoboDojo-Sim, EmbodiedEvo achieves an average score of 44.48 and a success rate of 37.82\%, surpassing all officially verified results. Paired tests show the largest gains on memory-dependent tasks and successful reuse of coordinated procedures, while fine contact control remains difficult. Experience from stronger models also improves weaker executors: Astra's experience raises Sol and Luna's success rates by 8.86 and 5.50 percentage points over no experience. Compared with raw interaction history, Skills and Lessons achieve comparable task performance at 53.0\% lower execution cost.
authors: Wenyi Li, Yizhe Chi, Youjie Zheng, Chunyu Liu, Xiaoqiu Wang, Mingju Gao, Zheng Jiang, Deyao Hong, Calvin Xiao, Kaisen Yang, Qinhuai Na
bullets: Targets the challenge of making physical intelligence executable, reusable, and adaptable beyond direct vision-language-action control.
Uses a self-improving code loop in which the agent inspects state, revises and executes code, and incorporates feedback.
Learns Skills and Lessons in a single Playground scene, then freezes the resulting harness for use across diverse scenes.
On RoboDojo-Sim, reports a 44.48 average score and 37.82% success rate, with strongest gains on memory-dependent tasks and coordinated procedures.
Skills and Lessons match raw interaction-history performance at 53.0% lower execution cost; fine contact control remains difficult.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to coordinate not only where to move, but also how contact and force should evolve throughout an interaction. Yet most robot policies represent actions primarily as motion trajectories, using tactile signals as inputs or auxiliary prediction targets without explicitly encoding contact dynamics in the action representation. We propose ILA (Interaction Latents as Actions), which uses decodable interaction latents that jointly capture the evolution of motion, contact, and force application as policy action units, providing a shared representation for action generation, evaluation, and offline improvement. We learn these latents through visually conditioned joint action-tactile reconstruction with a time-conditioned implicit decoder. Using them as flow-matching generation targets supports post-training of pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs), as well as training flow-matching policies from scratch. A shared decoder maps generated latents to executable actions. For offline improvement, we learn a tactile-conditioned expert reference model from interaction latents encoded from expert demonstrations. The resulting expert-consistency rewards guide weighted learning from successful rollouts, while observation-compatible expert references guide correction of low-reward predictions from failed rollouts. Across three policy families, ILA improves success rates averaged over four real-world tasks by 21.0-36.5 percentage points relative to tactile-conditioned direct-action baselines. Ablations highlight the benefit of encoding contact evolution in action targets beyond tactile conditioning, while the same latent space supports expert-guided offline improvement. Project website: https://mrsecant.github.io/ILA/.

papers.abstract: Expert demonstrations show how to complete contact-rich tasks, but provide limited coverage of how interaction forces respond to different actions. Task-agnostic play provides broader experience of contact dynamics without specifying task goals. To fully leverage these two types of data, we introduce ForceWAM, a force world action model that decouples knowledge of task-compatible interaction outcomes from knowledge of how local actions change contact. A world model learns from successful demonstrations to jointly predict future video and six-axis force/torque trajectories. Together, these futures describe the expected evolution of motion and contact during the task. A separate inverse dynamics model (IDM) learns from both task and play, mapping current observations and recorded visual-wrench futures to their associated robot actions. Play data thus provide knowledge of force responses for goal-directed execution. At deployment, the IDM reactively translates generated futures into actions, reusing them with fresh wrench feedback between world-model updates. Across real-robot force-regulated sliding, box flipping with and without disturbances, and ring placement, ForceWAM achieves $85$-$95\%$ mean success, surpassing world-modeling and reactive baselines. Our experiments further show that adding task-agnostic play data improves success by $15$-$45$ percentage points, demonstrating its value for learning contact-rich execution. Project page and code are available at https://force-wam.github.io/.

papers.abstract: In-context robot learning enables robots to acquire new behaviors from demonstrations without test-time parameter updates. However, visual and kinematic specifications alone may not distinguish contact-rich behaviors that share similar motions but require different interaction intensities or patterns. We propose Contact Trajectory Prompting (CTP), a framework for one-shot transfer of contact-rich manipulation behaviors. CTP encodes motion and contact information from a single demonstration into an ordered contact trajectory prompt that captures their temporal evolution and specifies the desired physical interaction behavior. During execution, the policy uses online sensory feedback to retrieve interaction-relevant information from the prompt, conditioning closed-loop action generation on the demonstrated contact behavior. Across real-world wiping, rotation, and insertion tasks on objects excluded from training, CTP achieves 78.7% overall success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 13.0 percentage points. Changing only the reference demonstration enables CTP to follow contact specifications for both intensity and direction, including an intermediate wiping force level and clockwise or counterclockwise cap rotation. These results demonstrate that contact trajectories serve as effective behavioral specifications, extending in-context robot learning beyond motion imitation to physical interaction transfer. papers.abstract: Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting updates to both a robot's capabilities and its improvement procedure, making subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. We present an L0-L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substantial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priorities in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/Physical-RSI.
authors: Hai Zhou, Fan Yang, Zeyi Chen, Lejun Zhang, Chenyang Fu, Jianping Li, Jiayi Zhu, Xianyang Liu, Yingxuan Yang, Lili Meng, Lu Wang, Xinyang Han, Jiankai Sun, Weirui Ye, Guanchu Wang, Wanhua Li, Ming Zhou, Boyi Li, Ming Jin, Kun Shao, Muhao Chen, Guang Chen, Lei Ma, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Costas Spanos, Xia Hu, Mac Schwager, Weinan Zhang, Qian Feng, Shangding Gu

Reviews methods involving harness adaptation, model training, safety, and control for robot self-improvement.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Physical Recursive Self-Improvement. (a) The task-execution system, consisting of the harness H and the parametric models Θ, proposes actions that pass through safety and control before acting on the physical world. The outcomes are stored as experience and feedback D, which is shared by the task-execution system and the improvement procedure Φ. Using D, Φ updates H through Adapt and Θ through Train, while Ver decides which changes are kept. Φ can also update its own stages. An independent evaluator E evaluates the task-execution system and thereby judges the updates made by Φ. (b) L1–L4 distinguish capability-level updates to the task-execution system from meta-level updates to the improvement procedure, within a single task or across tasks. L0 denotes systems that make no retained change on their own. L5 builds on L4 and requires independent, controlled evidence that subsequent improvement becomes more effective over successive rounds.

Figure 2: Update targets and task identity in the L0–L5 framework. (a) Task execution uses the harness H and learned weights Θ. Capability-level updates change H or Θ, whereas meta-level updates change the improvement procedure Φ. D denotes the experience and feedback store. (b) Tasks are distinguished by their required skill sequence κ. Grasping a cup from a table and from a cabinet top belongs to the same task set: κ remains unchanged, and only the instance parameters ξ differ. Retrieving a cup from an initially closed cabinet adds opening to κ and therefore belongs to a different task set. The two long-horizon examples share the same skill set κset but execute the skills in different orders. Their skill sequences κ therefore differ, so they belong to different task sets.

Figure 3: Selected systems by level, year, and evidence source. Each system sits in the sector of its level, and its distance from the centre gives its release year, from 2022 near the centre to 2026 at the rim. The border of each card gives the source of the feedback behind the update followed by the setting of deployment. R, real; S, simulation; O, model imagination, meaning a learned world model. A dagger marks a deployment that gave no feedback to the marked improvement loop: the update is driven by simulated (S) or imagined (O) feedback and the system is then deployed or validated on a real robot, which does not mean that the paper used no real data. L0 cards form a baseline of systems directed by humans or by execution feedback, and parenthetical labels name the branch evaluated. An asterisk is an affiliation note: SEFM* shows the affiliation at the time of the work rather than the first author’s current one, and HarnessPAI*, which is credited to a team, shows the affiliation of its first core contributor.

Figure 7: The meta-improvement loop. Improvement histories inform hypotheses and method changes. Current and candidate adaptation methods are compared through the subsequent harness updates they produce under matched budgets. Evaluation of subsequent gains and costs supports adoption, further revision, or rejection of the candidate method. Adopted methods govern future improvement.

Figure 10: Verification and evaluation in physical RSI. Proposed updates are applied to separate candidate system versions after harness adaptation and model training. Verification checks implementation validity, repair effectiveness, and capability preservation before updates are adopted. An independent evaluator assesses the updated system under external test conditions and scoring criteria, providing physical outcome evidence for meta-verification when the verifier itself is revised.

Figure 9: Safety and control in Physical RSI. System updates and environmental drift require reassessment of exploration, transfer, and runtime safeguards. Records in D inform later revisions of Φ. Acceptance determines inheritance, while release specifies permitted physical operation. Oversight of the evolving procedure spans the cycle.

Figure 8: Model-learning workflow in physical RSI. Environment generation and data selection organize experience from physical interactions for training policies, world models, and reward models through imitation, self-supervised, or reinforcement learning. Candidate updates undergo verification before adoption: model updates shape subsequent execution and learning, while mechanism updates revise how data are prepared and models are trained in later rounds.

papers.abstract: We introduce WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) against paired real-world executions. Given the same initial observation and low-level action sequence, WorldOracle asks whether a predicted rollout reproduces what happens in the real world, including physical consequences and task-state transitions. We evaluate models along four complementary dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence. To support this evaluation, we curate real-world training and evaluation suites that cover different interaction dynamics and embodiments. The evaluation suite contains long, multi-segment episodes with both successful and failed executions, enabling evaluation across varied action outcomes and behavior distributions. Experiments on seven representative ACWMs reveal distinct model strengths and failure modes. WorldOracle provides a systematic foundation for measuring and advancing action-conditioned world modeling for manipulation. We will release the datasets, evaluation code, and leaderboard.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of WorldOracle. (a) The human-operated trajectories are collected through robot teleoperation or direct human-hand execution. (b) The policy-rollout trajectories are collected by running a policy in closed loop on a real robot. (c) For both distributions, the recorded action trajectory is replayed open loop by the ACWM, yielding a generated rollout. (d) The predicted rollout is compared with the paired real execution along four dimensions: physical state correctness, interaction spatial alignment, key interaction area fidelity, and multi-view action coherence.

Figure 3 WorldOracle annotation pipeline. (a) Execution segmentation: each synchronized multi-view episode is divided into interaction segments Si,n, and the final frame of each segment is the outcome keyframe Ki,n capturing the observable physical outcome. (b) Physical criteria annotation: a VLM generates physical-state criteria for each outcome keyframe.
