papers.abstract: Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to robot teleoperation for collecting dexterous manipulation data. However, two challenges limit their use as reliable training data: accurate hand-object interaction (HOI) reconstruction from monocular RGB and high-quality robot demonstrations, especially visual observations. We present EgoMatrix, an end-to-end data engine that converts monocular egocentric human videos into bimanual dexterous trajectories and paired robot observation videos, with the trajectories directly replayable on real robots. It reconstructs HOI with emphasis on relative geometry and contact rather than exact metric scene recovery, then uses retargeting and reinforcement learning (RL) to reproduce the demonstrated tasks in simulation. We jointly render robot hands and objects from these simulated trajectories to produce physically faithful observations synchronized with state and control records. Rendering the same trajectories in diverse, task-compatible backgrounds expands paired training data while preserving robot-object motion and contact. Across TACO, OakInk2, and self-collected data, EgoMatrix achieves 54.84% end-to-end success in simulation versus 14.52% for the strongest baseline. Reconstruction reaches state-of-the-art performance on most metrics of the two public benchmarks. Qualitative results show more faithful hand-object interactions than prior methods, while feature-space analysis shows closer alignment with real-robot observations than GPT-6 Astra.Our project page is available at https://spikew726.github.io/EgoMatrix/.
authors: Ziheng Wang, Yanming Shao, Ting Mao, Kaihan Chen, Yiqun Wang, Xuanye Wu, Yao Mu

Reports state-of-the-art reconstruction on most metrics of two public benchmarks and closer feature alignment to real-robot observations than GPT-6 Astra.

papers.abstract: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.
authors: Xinyi Wang, Bangzheng Li, Hanyu Wang, Lin Zhang, Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Zhenggang Tang, Shyamal Buch, Dejia Xu
bullets: Evaluates three modes: code-as-policy, agent-as-policy, and auto-research fine-tuning of a vision-language-action model.
Introduces controls to distinguish retained learning from more attempts, familiar tasks, privileged state, larger budgets, and chance.
Across seven models, simulated tasks, and physical-robot tasks, longer learning helps mainly when tasks are difficult relative to model capability.
Reusable control code and routines transfer across tasks and simulators, but task-specific solutions transfer poorly; a real-robot gap remains for novel human-designed scenes.
Models differ in their best evolution strategy, and text-only models can match comparable multimodal models when reasoning and tool use compensate for weaker perception.

papers.abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC matches or improves control performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.
authors: Haodong Yang, Runhan Huang, Bowen Zhang, Iofai Lei, Zunzhe Zhang, Xiangcheng Zhang, Shaoting Zhu, Linzhan Mou, Yicheng Liu, Hang Zhao
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining reliable behavior during long-term autonomous operation.

Integrates with Diffusion Transformer and flow-matching vision-language-action policies.
Simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation experiments show maintained or improved robustness, with interventions expanding autonomous capability over time.

Rows 1–2 evaluate Hierarchical Block Stacking under nominal setups (two independent instances per category), while Row 3 evaluates Garment Folding. Left column (Delayed Detection): The detector remains silent throughout compounding drift, alarming only belatedly after the block arrangement is disrupted or a severe angular tilt has already occurred, missing the teleoperation recovery window. Middle column (Spurious Alarm): During nominal execution— including pristine, fully unfolded garment setups (Row 3)—noisy flow-loss expectation triggers false-positive alarms, needlessly aborting valid rollouts. Right column (Irreversible Failure): The detector triggers only after irrecoverable failures have occurred (e.g., mis-sequenced block placement or fabric bunched into an entangled knot), leaving no viable recovery path without a complete manual scene reset.

papers.abstract: A robot needs a world model that predicts how its actions will change the scene and a policy that chooses those actions. Models are usually built and evaluated for only one of these roles, and every robot records its actions in its own format. We ask whether one robot world model can serve both roles across different bodies, and what makes this work. We present GreenWAM, a world foundation model for robotics, together with the recipe that produces it: (1) a shared anatomical action space that describes 20 robot families, from bimanual arms to dexterous humanoids, in common joint coordinates; (2) joint training on these families in visual, action-conditioned and world-action modes; and (3) policies that split an action expert off the generator. As a world model, GreenWAM attains top-tier trajectory, depth and 3D accuracy on WorldArena 1.0, ahead of every world-action model and video generator in our comparison. As a policy, it scores among the top entries of the RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard, reaches the highest zero-shot LIBERO-plus success among the compared methods and is competitive with dedicated vision-language-action and world-action policies on CALVIN and LIBERO. We further adapt GreenWAM to a real humanoid, where it succeeds more often than policies adapted from $\pi_{0.5}$ and from Cosmos 3 Edge, and distill it into a single-step policy for real-time control. Controlled experiments yield three findings: robot specialization improves world prediction and control together; an action expert helps when split off at the start of adaptation; and keeping world-model modes during policy adaptation preserves robustness to scene changes.
authors: Gennady Sidorov, Valerii Kornilov, Denis Grankin, Polina Fedotova, Aleksey Postnikov
bullets: Addresses the challenge of building one model for robots with different bodies and action formats.
Uses a shared anatomical action space covering 20 robot families and trains jointly in visual, action-conditioned, and world-action modes.
Separates an action expert from the generator to derive policies, including a distilled single-step policy for real-time control.
Achieves top-tier WorldArena 1.0 world-model accuracy and strong results across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-plus, CALVIN, and LIBERO.
Real-robot adaptation to a humanoid outperforms the cited adapted baselines; specialization and retaining world-model modes improve robustness.

papers.title: GreenWAM: A World Foundation Model for Robotics

papers.abstract: Current recipes for robot learning require massive amounts of robot demonstrations to obtain robust and adaptive policies. In this work, we introduce Steertuning, a system that enables robots to learn new tasks in new environments from 5 human demonstrations in under 5 Steertuning consists of two parts. (1) We pretrain a 400M-parameter diffusion policy on our egocentric human dataset, which consists of 100 hours of densely annotated random interactions. This pretraining makes Steertuning robust to background differences and enables spatial and object generalization when deployed on new tasks. (2) Given 5 demonstrations of a new task, we finetune our model for only 2 minutes (2000 training updates) and steer the policy's actions during reverse sampling using the demonstration whose observation is closest to that of the deployment environment. Together with a carefully designed data processing pipeline for embodiment transfer, this enables Steertuning to achieve a 71% success rate across 12 tasks in 12 new environments, ranging from lab settings to kitchens in new homes. The entire process, from data collection for a new task to robot policy deployment, takes less than 5 minutes. Our full dataset, model weights, codebase, and robot videos will be made available at our website: https://steertuning.github.io.
authors: Billy Yan, Isaac Tu, Kelly Lee, Blake Chang, Kenny Ma, Kanad Patel, Dhawal Kabra, Neer Patel, Kevin Wu, Lerrel Pinto, Irmak Guzey
bullets: Addresses the need for large-scale robot demonstrations for robust, adaptive policy learning.
Pretrains a 400M-parameter diffusion policy on 100 hours of densely annotated egocentric human interactions.
Adapts to a new task using five demonstrations, two minutes of finetuning, and observation-based action steering during sampling.
Uses data processing for embodiment transfer to support spatial and object generalization across environments.
Achieves a 71% success rate across 12 tasks in 12 new environments, including homes and laboratories.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Policy. Our architecture and action steering mechanism. The policy takes four modalities as input: a point cloud, the manipulatedobject mask, the fingertip locations of both hands (10 3D points) in the anchor frame, and a text description of the task. Each modality is passed through its own encoder and the resulting tokens go through a self-attention transformer, after which we mean-pool them into a context latent that conditions the diffusion transformer via AdaLayerNorm [50]. The observation tokens are also fed to the diffusion transformer so that the noisy action tokens can cross-attend to them [51]. The point-cloud encoder (Utonia [52]) and text encoder (SigLIP [53]) are kept frozen; everything else is trained end-to-end with an MSE loss on the predicted ϵ. During finetuning, LoRA adapters are trained for 2k steps; at deployment, the predicted actions are steered toward the nearest human trajectory. A short finetuning combined with action steering enables robust yet quick task adaptation.

Fig. 5: Full-stack deployments of different policies from a single language command. The left-most column shows the language annotations used by the system. For example, Put the white cup into the trash is split into navigate white cup, pick up white cup, navigate trash, and drop white cup. Demonstrations for picking up and dropping the cup are collected and deployed in the same way as in Steertuning.

Fig. 4: In-the-wild and ablation tasks. We deploy Steertuning on 9 new tasks in new in-the-wild environments. For each task, we collect 5 new human demonstrations (top left) and deploy the policy on our robot YOR (top right). All ablation experiments are run on three tasks with spatial generalization (bottom). Steertuning achieves an overall success rate of 71% (7.1/10) across these 12 tasks; per-task success rates are given on our website.

papers.abstract: Evaluating robot policies before deployment typically requires producing new trajectories through real-world execution, simulators, or learned world models. These rollout-based approaches impose infrastructure requirements; simulator and world-model evaluators additionally face prediction errors that can compound over the evaluation horizon. In this paper, we study off-policy evaluation as an alternative to rollout-based robot-policy evaluation methods. Specifically, we introduce RoboFQE, an evaluator that estimates the discounted expected return of a target policy from offline robot trajectories without estimating a behavior-policy density, combining fitted Q-evaluation with a pretrained vision foundation model and learned terminal success annotation to bridge the gap between standard OPE benchmarks and continuous-control visual manipulation. Controlled experiments across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that RoboFQE produces accurate discounted-return estimates and preserves policy rankings even on long-horizon manipulation tasks where video world-model evaluators are degraded by autoregressive prediction errors. Ablation experiments show that pretrained vision encoders substantially outperform from-scratch alternatives, particularly on long-horizon tasks, and that learned terminal success annotation enables evaluation without ground-truth reward labels with only slight reduction of accuracy.
authors: Yunfu Deng, Sangwoo Shin, Brahma S. Pavse, Josiah P. Hanna
bullets: Addresses the infrastructure and compounding prediction-error costs of real, simulated, and world-model rollouts.

Experiments in simulated and real-world manipulation show accurate discounted-return estimates and preserved policy rankings.
Pretrained vision encoders help most on long-horizon tasks; learned success annotation causes only a slight accuracy reduction.

papers.title: RoboFQE: Rollout-Free Evaluation of Visual Robot Policies from Offline Trajectories
papers.tldr: RoboFQE evaluates visual robot policies from offline trajectories without executing rollouts, accurately estimating returns and policy rankings on long-horizon manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform manipulation tasks using camera images and language instructions, but object slip or visual occlusion can disrupt execution. Recovery is typically learned during policy training or delegated to a monitor that triggers a scripted repair after detecting a failure. We introduce ForkCast, a predictive recovery framework that compares counterfactual futures to determine whether and how to intervene in a frozen VLA policy. At each decision point, ForkCast evaluates three candidates: executing the policy's nominal action chunk (Commit), adjusting the camera viewpoint (Reobserve), and replanning the arm trajectory (Replan). A candidate-conditioned world model forecasts the latent outcome of each candidate at a common future horizon, and a shared task-progress head scores the predicted outcomes. By evaluating the policy's own continuation alongside the repair candidates, a single comparison based on task progress determines both whether and how to intervene, without a failure detector, an intervention threshold, or updates to the VLA backbone. On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with injected occlusion and object slip, ForkCast increases pooled success from 13.3% for the frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy to 30.0% and transfers to two additional VLA backbones without updating ForkCast. After adaptation on real-robot candidate rollouts, ForkCast also improves success over the base policy under both clean and visibility-limited conditions. Code will be released to benefit the research community.
authors: Chenru Wen, Huajian Zeng, Haokai Ding, Jian Kang, Anqing Duan, Dawei Zhou, Dezhen Song, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses manipulation failures caused by object slip and visual occlusion without retraining the VLA backbone.
Uses a candidate-conditioned world model to forecast common-horizon outcomes for Commit, Reobserve, and Replan.
A shared task-progress head selects whether to intervene and which recovery action to use, without a failure detector or intervention threshold.
On five simulated RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, pooled success increased from 13.3% to 30.0% for the frozen π₀.₅ policy.
Transferred to two additional VLA backbones and improved real-robot success under clean and visibility-limited conditions after candidate-rollout adaptation.

papers.title: ForkCast: Predictive Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Policies via Counterfactual Futures

papers.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.
authors: St John Grimbly, Nicolas Kuske, Evert A. Boonstra, Charel van Hoof, Rowan Hodson, Benjamin Rosman, Ryan Smith, Mark Solms, Jonathan P. Shock
bullets: Precision increases the reliability of interoceptive information, sharpening posteriors and improving survival.
Preference reweighting prioritises need-relieving outcomes, keeping bodily states farther from lethal boundaries.
Preference reweighting changes which bodily states are experienced and learned, narrowing model coverage while slightly improving accuracy in visited states.
Across 72 additional layouts, both interventions improved average survival and interacted positively, but the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts was not established.
Survival alone does not fully reveal how an agent prioritises needs or learns its body model.

papers.selection_reason: Explores interoceptive prioritization in an embodied agent using active inference, comparing precision and preference reweighting to learn body models and survival strategies.
papers.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
papers.tldr: Precision and preference reweighting are distinct routes to prioritising bodily needs, producing different effects on survival, perception, and learned body models.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks, allowing each stage to reuse behavioral and value knowledge acquired through prior RL. The inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides current-task actor learning, while prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes. Fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. Across contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware, ACCRUE accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and significantly reduces real-robot training time by 31.0\% to 68.5\%.
authors: Changyeon Kim, Kimin Lee, Yashraj Narang, Yijie Guo
bullets: Addresses the need for task-efficient adaptation without catastrophic forgetting during real-world robot deployment.
Carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks to reuse behavioral and value knowledge.
Adapts the critic using current-task transitions and preserves prior behavior by distilling the actor on a small set of retained episodes.
Uses fixed visual features to maintain compatibility between inherited learners and replay data during base-policy updates.
Across simulated and real contact-rich assembly tasks, it achieves near-zero forgetting and reduces real-robot training time by 31.0%–68.5%.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies excel at generalist robotic manipulation but generate actions without explicitly modeling their environmental consequences. World action models (WAMs) incorporate future prediction, yet most rely on costly video generation, while latent alternatives either use predicted futures only as auxiliary targets or infer latent actions from suboptimal visual transitions through costly large-scale video pretraining. We introduce WAVE-0 (World-model-Augmented VLA Execution), a framework that bridges VLAs and WAMs through a lightweight latent world model. By connecting the semantic understanding of pretrained VLAs with explicit future prediction, WAVE-0 allows anticipated action consequences to directly guide action generation. Built on a pretrained VLA, its 257M world model translates VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition the action expert, unifying latent planning, future prediction, and action generation. The world model is trained directly on ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, requiring neither pixel reconstruction nor large-scale video pretraining. WAVE-0 achieves success rates of 91.47% on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.7% on LIBERO, along with 88.0%, 61.4%, and 75.0% on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro, and LIBERO-Para, respectively. On real-world tasks, it improves the success rate of $\pi_{0.5}$ from 38.3% to 73.3%. These results demonstrate strong manipulation performance and generalization across diverse distribution shifts.
authors: Haomin Wang, Anqiong Ji, Ke Wang, Zhongshan Liu, Ru Ying, Ran Zheng, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit environmental consequence modeling in VLA policies without relying on costly video generation or large-scale video pretraining.
Uses a 257M-parameter world model to translate VLM-generated latent action plans into predicted future representations that condition action generation.
Trains the world model directly from ground-truth robot actions with a counterfactual ranking objective, avoiding pixel reconstruction.
Reports strong simulation performance across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and its distribution-shift variants.
Improves real-world success for π0.5 from 38.3% to 73.3%, demonstrating better generalization across distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.
authors: Thinker Team, Peng Gao, Jichao Jiao, Chen Liao, Daqin Luo, Yiming Ma, Baiyu Pan, Hailin Shi, Jiyuan Wang, Xiangming Xu, Xiongwei Zhao
bullets: Addresses fragmented world models that handle modalities and functions through separate interfaces or modules.
Uses modality-specific encoders and decoders around a shared Unified Dynamics Transformer that jointly evolves RGB, metric depth, and action representations.
Supports joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics.
A motion probe indicates that frozen visual representations retain recoverable action-related motion information.
Trained on heterogeneous egocentric-video, real-robot, and simulation data; the abstract reports top results on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad, and WorldArena.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Overview of the Data Factory producer–consumer pipeline. Heterogeneous multimodal data are organized into episode-centric catalogs Ei = (Vi, Si, Ai, Li,Σi,Λi) and accessed lazily through a SQLite offset index. The model specifies each training sample as qj = (ej , I V j , ISj , I A j , ILj ), including within-source window and modality selection, while source-level sampling controls the mixture of data sources across batches and ranks. The resulting samples are adapted, collated, and asynchronously prefetched into a rank-local ready-batch queue with occupancy 0 ≤ qt ≤ Q, from which the training process consumes prepared batches. papers.abstract: The fidelity of teleoperated demonstrations used for imitation learning is determined by how faithfully a robot hand can replicate the operator's posture. The posture retargeting law that the robot will execute is typically selected only once the hardware has been finalized, and conventional hand designs often neglect human-like grasping postures. We introduce PACT, an optimization based on human grasping postures that jointly optimizes the mechanical parameters of a 17-servo robot hand (link lengths, joint offsets, mounting angles, and base placements) and its nonlinear posture retargeter (a linear human-to-robot joint map, per-joint posture-IK weights, and damping). The optimization enforces full-finger correspondence (MCP, PIP, DIP, and tip of each finger) to human poses from the DexYCB dataset, and is constrained by servo interference, assembly clearances, and flat-hand protrusion, so the resulting design can be physically assembled. We fabricate the PACT Hand and validate it through teleoperation experiments and an imitation-learning demonstration. The hand reproduces all human hand keypoints with a kinematic RMSE of 3.9 mm, compared to 12.8 mm for the LEAP Hand baseline, and keeps all fingertips within 10 mm on every grasping posture, while the baseline achieves this for only 21.6% of the poses. Under matched per-joint torque limits, it lifts twice the baseline payload, 2 kg against 1 kg, and deforms a held paper cup seven times less, reaching a deformation level comparable to a human hand. It also achieves an 86% grasping success rate on YCB daily objects, compared to 64% for the baseline. Finally, as a demonstration, an imitation-learning policy trained on demonstrations collected with the PACT Hand achieved a 75% success rate at held-out placements in a can pick-and-place task. papers.abstract: Cooperative aerial manipulation is difficult under wind, payload motion, and noisy goal broadcasts because multiple Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are coupled through a shared payload. We present CALM (Cooperative Aerial Learned Manipulation), a decentralized controller for aerial manipulators carrying a basket while tracking a moving ground robot. CALM combines a parameter-shared Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) policy, trained using Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), with goal estimation, per-UAV Extended State Observers (ESOs), basket-mass estimation, and anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward. The anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward uses estimated goal motion to rotate the formation before position error develops, reducing basket-yaw lag without adding net commanded force. A disturbance-conditioned critic supports centralized training while execution remains decentralized. Across held-out trajectories, CALM achieves lower mean position and orientation errors than all evaluated baselines, including the matched arm baseline (7.68 versus 10.95 cm and 3.3 versus 4.7$^\circ$), the cable-suspended realization, and two model-based controllers. Under unseen full-information-path degradation, CALM remains statistically comparable or superior to the arm baseline. Videos are available at https://petreric.github.io/CALM/.

papers.abstract: Manipulation tasks such as unscrewing a cap or sliding a part in contact with a surface require imposing force along a high-friction direction: the robot must overcome a resistance rather than yield to it. Generative visuomotor policies predict the motion for such tasks but not the authority needed to realize it, and that authority is bounded by the impedance controller beneath them: when the resistance exceeds what a compliant controller can exert under a bounded tracking error, the task is unattainable however accurate the prediction is. The required amount cannot be anticipated either, since it depends on a contact state the observation does not reveal. In this paper, we propose a residual stiffening layer placed underneath an unmodified policy. Resistance is recognized, without force sensing, from the mismatch between the motion the policy commands and the motion the robot realizes, and a four-mode supervisor raises the stiffness along a single direction read off the policy's own action chunk, retains it while the task progresses and releases it afterwards. The layer needs no compliance labels, no retraining and no re-collected demonstrations. On two real tasks, unscrewing a bottle cap and pushing a T-nut along a T-slot groove against non-homogeneous friction, evaluated at six resistance levels of which two were withheld from the demonstrations, the layer raises the success rate from 52% to 90% while producing 61% less peak off-axis force than a uniformly stiff controller at the same resistance.
authors: Francesco Cufino, Carmela Mariniello, Mario Selvaggio, Andreas Sochopoulos, Fabio Ruggiero
bullets: Targets contact-rich tasks where compliant impedance control cannot overcome unknown resistance, even with accurate visuomotor predictions.

papers.abstract: Aerial mobile manipulation requires unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to traverse heterogeneous environments such as indoor and outdoor domains, and connect navigation with subsequent physical interaction within the same trajectories. Existing aerial benchmarks are typically confined to single-environment settings, limiting evaluation of agents across continuous environmental transitions. When interaction is evaluated, agents are often initialized near the target, leaving the transition from navigation to interaction largely unassessed. This work introduces CrossFly, a benchmark for long-horizon interaction-oriented aerial mobility across heterogeneous environments. CrossFly contains 15K trajectories across more than 20 reconstructed scenes under a unified simulation and evaluation framework, covering Indoor, Outdoor, and Indoor$\leftrightarrow$Outdoor trajectories. It further introduces Interaction Readiness Rate (IRR) to assess whether terminal navigation states provide suitable conditions for downstream interaction without assuming a specific manipulation policy. Experiments with five representative aerial vision-language-action (VLA) agents and the proposed CrossFly-Agent show that Indoor$\leftrightarrow$Outdoor settings are more challenging than single-environment settings, with the highest success rate reaching 9.7% on unseen scenes. A downstream manipulation case study further validates the relevance of interaction-oriented arrival to subsequent physical interaction. We hope CrossFly helps advance aerial embodied intelligence toward unified mobility and physical interaction in heterogeneous environments.

Experiments show indoor↔outdoor scenarios are more difficult than single-environment settings; the highest reported success rate on unseen scenes is 9.7%.
A manipulation case study supports the relevance of interaction-oriented arrivals for subsequent physical interaction.

papers.abstract: We introduce \textbf{ABot Embodied Reasoning (ABot-ER)}, a unified embodied reasoning foundation model that breaks the tension between breadth and depth in embodied reasoning. Embodied intelligence demands the joint mastery of perception, planning, and execution, yet reconciling generality with specialization across this spectrum remains an open challenge. Within a single unified model, ABot-ER commands specialist-level depth across all three competencies, spanning spatial, scene, and temporal reasoning in perception; long-horizon action organization in planning; and point grounding and affordance in execution. The \textbf{Agentic Data-Model Self-Evolution Engine} continuously adapts data strategies to the model's evolving capability state. The \textbf{Task-Conditioned Adaptive Training Strategy} uses task tokens to activate lightweight low-rank residuals over a shared backbone, separating updates from heterogeneous output formats while retaining shared embodied knowledge. Across a systematic evaluation on twelve benchmarks covering three core competencies and five capability dimensions, ABot-ER achieves \textbf{state-of-the-art overall performance} across perception, planning, and execution within a unified parametric framework, demonstrating that breadth and depth can coexist in unified embodied reasoning.

papers.abstract: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects. Our code and project page are available at https://youpengwen.github.io/Orchestra.
authors: Youpeng Wen, Gang Wang, Tianyu Huang, Weiwei Zhang, Zhijian Huang, Wei Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Yunhui Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving subtask order and monitoring progress as scenes change.
Separates task planning and execution management from low-level action generation.
Maintains shared context with the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations.
Introduces RMBench-Compose to evaluate composing atomic skills into longer subtask sequences.
Achieves 68.22% mean success across nine RMBench tasks and reaches 7.35 average successful subtasks on RMBench-Compose; real-world tests also show improved sequence length.

Patch embedding and spatial positional encoding are applied independently to each frame. Four spatial layers (S) alternate with a causal temporal-attention operation (T), giving temporal mixing after layers 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20. After layer 20, historical tokens are discarded and only current-frame features pass through the remaining spatial layers. The VLM receives 256 visual tokens per camera, matching the single-frame baseline. (b) Spatial attention is bidirectional within a frame; temporal attention operates across frames at the same patch index, with causal and valid-history masks. The temporal pathway reuses the corresponding spatial-attention weights and adds fixed sinusoidal age encodings, with zero encoding for the current frame. papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation systems commonly learn object affordances from human-annotated datasets, which reflect interaction possibilities for a human hand rather than the physical constraints of a specific robot. For example, a surface region of an object identified as graspable by a human annotator may be geometrically unreachable or mechanically infeasible for a robot, yet this mismatch is rarely addressed explicitly. To tackle this challenge, we proposed a framework that translates human affordance annotations into robot-executable affordance predictions conditioned on the physical properties of the robot. The network predicts which surface regions of an object are physically executable by the robot, given a 3D point cloud of an object and a descriptor encoding the robot's geometry and constraints. The model was trained using human-annotated affordances together with robotic execution outcomes from multiple sampled approach trials in simulation, where execution outcomes determined which regions are executable for the robot. The evaluation was performed on a household objects dataset using two parallel-jaw gripper configurations on a UR5e robot arm. The framework outperformed a model that does not receive information about the robot. The experimental results demonstrated that affordance prediction must be conditioned on the robot and that human annotations alone are insufficient for learning robot-executable affordance representations.

papers.abstract: Learning robot policies from demonstrations is often limited by the cost of collecting diverse, high-quality expert data. While an appealing alternative is to expand a single successful demonstration into a diverse set of successful trajectories, existing augmentation methods typically rely on manually designed transformation rules or complex trajectory planning, requiring substantial task-specific engineering and human effort. We introduce OneDemo, a reinforcement learning framework that learns to edit a single successful demonstration for new task configurations. We formulate demonstration editing as a structured reinforcement learning problem, in which an editor learns, from sparse task-success rewards, both when to transition between object-centric trajectory segments and how to geometrically adapt each segment. The learned editor serves both as a task policy and as a reusable demonstration generator. Across 15 Meta-World tasks, OneDemo reaches a 92.7% success rate within 53.7k environment interactions on average. Across 9 DexMimicGen tasks, it generates successful demonstrations with a 98.4% average success rate, and BC-RNN policies trained on the generated data achieve 99.6% average success at matched dataset scale. These results show that learning to edit a single successful demonstration provides a structured and effective basis for both policy learning and scalable demonstration generation.
authors: Ying Qian, Jianshu Hu, Han Fang, Shuguang Li, Yutong Ban
bullets: Addresses the cost and task-specific engineering required to collect or manually augment diverse expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation policies trained through imitation learning commonly rely on costly demonstrations recorded in one task direction and at one temporal resolution. We propose Reversal and Stride-based Trajectory Augmentation (RESTA), which exploits time-scaling data augmentation to improve data efficiency through trajectory reversal and temporal resampling. Trajectory-reversal augmentation reverses and relabels demonstrations between paired tasks with opposite objectives, reusing recorded rollouts without additional environment interaction. Because contact-rich manipulation is not exactly reversible, we treat reversal as an approximate paired-task prior rather than a physical symmetry. Temporal-stride augmentation varies observation and action sampling strides and conditions the policy on the resulting offsets, enabling fixed or randomized temporal schedules. Experiments across 16 paired bimanual manipulation tasks show that trajectory reversal is particularly effective in the low-data regime and that temporal-stride augmentation improves success under randomized temporal schedules. With 25 and 50 independently collected demonstrations per task, RESTA achieves 78.4% and 85.2% average success, respectively, matching or exceeding baselines trained with twice as many demonstrations (77.3% and 85.4%). These results show that RESTA can improve data efficiency in robot imitation learning.
authors: Yunpeng Jiang, Jianshu Hu, Han Fang, Zhiyuan Guan, Paul Weng, Yutong Ban
bullets: Targets costly data collection when demonstrations cover limited task directions and temporal resolutions.
Reverses and relabels demonstrations for paired opposite-objective tasks, treating reversal as an approximate prior rather than exact physical symmetry.

Across 16 paired bimanual tasks, reversal helps especially in low-data settings and stride augmentation improves robustness to randomized schedules.
Using 25 or 50 demonstrations per task, RESTA reaches 78.4% or 85.2% average success, comparable to baselines using twice as many demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Robotic harvesting of cherry tomatoes in greenhouses remains challenging due to dense fruit clusters, delicate skin, and the need for gentle yet effective detachment. This study presents a force-data-driven framework for autonomous cherry tomato harvesting that integrates six-axis force/torque sensing, a bio-inspired compliant gripper, and deployment on a mobile robotic platform. A wearable ATI six-axis force/torque sensor mounted on the index finger captured kinetic signatures of three elemental picking patterns (gripping, twisting, and lateral pulling) across 150 manual trials (50 per pattern) in laboratory and greenhouse settings. Gripping required a peak normal force of 3.92 and 0.45 N, twisting produced a dominant torque of 19.20 2.10 Nmm about the pedicel axis with minimal truss disturbance, and pure lateral pulling alone was insufficient for reliable detachment. These measurements informed a novel fingertip-localised Finray gripper, with compliant TPU 95A Finray geometry restricted to the fruit-contact region and a rigid PLA body, emulating the dual-stiffness human fingertip. A Dynamixel XM430-W350 servomotor under current-based torque control applies the measured gripping force and a 45{\deg} wrist twist. Finite element analysis showed a maximum von Mises stress of 0.24 MPa under the 3.92 N load, below the bruising threshold of cherry tomato skin. Integrated on a UR5 arm and Clearpath Husky A200 base, the system was validated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and in 50 autonomous trials at the SILAL commercial greenhouse, Abu Dhabi, UAE. The hybrid grip-twist-pull strategy achieved an 86.0% picking success rate, 2.3% fruit damage, and an 8.4 s cycle time per fruit, outperforming vacuum (66.3%), rotating (70.1%), clamping (76.0%), and suction-cutting (52.4%) end-effectors. These results demonstrate preliminary feasibility under the tested facility and cultivar conditions
authors: Rajmeet Singh, Manveen Kaur, Yusuf Adamu, Irfan Hussain
bullets: The study addresses reliable detachment of delicate cherry tomatoes in dense greenhouse clusters.
Six-axis force/torque measurements of gripping, twisting, and lateral pulling informed the harvesting strategy; lateral pulling alone was insufficient.
A fingertip-localized TPU Finray gripper with a rigid PLA body emulates dual-stiffness human fingertips and applies a controlled wrist twist.
The integrated system achieved 86.0% picking success, 2.3% fruit damage, and an 8.4-second cycle time in 50 autonomous trials.
Performance was evaluated under the tested facility and cultivar conditions, so broader generalization remains preliminary.

(c) Pattern C: Pulling direct horizontal pull (Fpull) perpendicular to the truss axis, causing tensile and bending failure. (d) Hybrid (Proposed) the proposed robotic picking strategy combining progressive rotation (Tz) with light lateral pull (Fpull), applying normal forces (Fn) axially to secure the fruit while minimising detachment force and truss disturbance. Blue arrows denote gripping forces (Fg); orange arrows denote detachment forces and torques. Dashed ellipses indicate the abscission zone at the pedicel calyx junction.

(c, f) Axial pull pattern showing smooth progressive force build-up with peak Fz of 0.22 N and transient torque peaks during the initial engagement phase. The distinct kinetic signatures of the three picking patterns provide the empirical basis for designing the proposed hybrid grip–twist–pull autonomous harvesting algorithm.

The seven sequential phases of the cycle are colour-shaded: APPROACH (grey), GRIP (yellow), TWIST (red), PULL (blue), TRANSPORT (green), RELEASE (purple), and HOME (light grey). papers.abstract: We present a real-time framework for expressive legged locomotion that enables independent control over velocity and style. Unlike existing data-driven controllers, which typically require explicit style labels for training, our method efficiently leverages large-scale unstructured motion data and generalizes to unseen styles. We disentangle style from functional locomotion through a tailored sampling strategy used to train a style encoder whose output conditions an autoregressive diffusion model. During inference, the user provides a style reference clip and a joystick velocity command. The diffusion model then generates a kinematic reference tracked by a reinforcement learning controller. To improve user controllability and stylization strength, we propose an attention biasing mechanism and a velocity command correction strategy. We demonstrate our method on a physics-based humanoid character in simulation and on a physical robot, showcasing robust real-time control and continuous style modulation. The results can be best seen in our supplemental video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=roFnS6N7nJ4).
authors: Joshua Aurand, Agon Serifi, Sammy Christen, Ruben Grandia, Espen Knoop, Marco Hutter, Moritz B\"acher
bullets: Separates locomotion function from style using a tailored sampling strategy and a learned style encoder.
Conditions an autoregressive diffusion model on style to generate kinematic motion references.
Uses reinforcement learning to track generated references on a physics-based character.
Adds attention biasing and velocity correction for stronger stylization and user control.
Demonstrated real-time control and continuous style modulation in humanoid simulation and on a physical robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview. We train an autoregressive diffusion model on unstructured motion datasets. We explicitly encode style in the style encoder, enabling generalization to unseen style references of varying length at inference. During inference, users can control the robot’s velocity through joystick commands, while selecting a desired style clip. The motion diffusion model’s output is autoregressively rolled out and passed to an RL-based tracking controller.
Figure 4: G1 Robot Deployment. Left: Continuous joystick control with dynamic style modulation. Right: Demonstration of the framework generating five distinct motion styles.

Figure 3: Style Encoding. Generated motions conditioned on interpolated style latents of styles from the 100STYLE dataset (top and middle row) and latents computed from unseen motions extracted from videos (bottom row).
Figure A.3: Baseline Comparison. We show two motion sequences generated by the same commands with CAMDM [6] and our model.

Figure A.2: Interactive Control. Example of interactive control where a physics-based humanoid follows velocity commands in various styles. The green dots indicate the trajectory generated from the given velocity commands.
Figure A.5: Attention Bias Quality. We compare unmodified inference with CFG and attention biasing for improved stylization.
Figure A.8: Velocity Correction. Qualitative analysis of applying velocity correction over a number of different trajectories.

Figure A.4: Sampling Scheme. We show the first frame of 5 consecutively predicted motion windows of models trained with and without our proposed sampling scheme. Without our sampling approach (“same window training”), the model collapses and keeps repeating the reference motion. With our sampling approach (“different window training”), the model learns to extract the style characteristic from the reference motion.

Figure A.1: Smoothing Scheme. To achieve smooth transitions between consecutive diffusion calls, we predict the next F states Mnxt fut at the current timestep t, then blend the first K states in Mnxt fut with the last K states of the previous prediction Mprv fut , then copy the next F − 2K states from Mnxt fut before incrementing the timestep t := t + (F −K) and repeating the process. More formally, we weight state mnxt i by w = i/(K+1) and state mprv (F−K)+i by 1 − w to form the blended states mt+i for i = 1, . . . ,K. The visualization shows the F = 6,K = 2 case.

Figure A.6: Attention Bias Sensitivity. We show how varying bias parameters affect performance by varying one weight at a time while keeping the other fixed at 0. Increasing either weight to large magnitudes worsens command adherence while increasing generation artifacts. Large positive wpst weights specifically result in frozen poses, which is why foot sliding is at zero.

papers.abstract: Broadcast spraying remains the dominant method of disease control in greenhouse tomato production, yet it treats healthy and diseased tissue alike, exposes workers to hazardous aerosols, and depends on operator skill. This paper presents MARTS (Modular Agricultural Robot for Targeted Spraying), a low-cost robotic platform that closes the loop from plant-level disease detection to leaf-localised spray delivery in commercial greenhouses. MARTS integrates a Clearpath Husky A200 mobile base, a UR5 manipulator, a novel modular spraying end-effector built around a single 12 V micro-diaphragm pump, and a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D camera. Disease detection reuses our previously published Tomato Leaf Disease Vision Language Model (TLDVLM; Grounding DINO, SAM-2 and LoRA-tuned BLIP-2, 97.27% accuracy over 10 classes); this work focuses on actuation, control and system integration. A ROS pipeline lifts detections into 3D targets, generates collision-aware nozzle poses at a 120 mm stand-off using fitted leaf normals, and scales pump pulse duration to lesion area. Water-sensitive paper calibration showed a linear pulse-volume relationship (R^2 = 0.994). In MuJoCo simulation, an adaptive base-repositioning strategy achieved 100% coverage of 18 waypoints with a maximum orientation error of 1.1 deg. Deployed at the SILAL commercial greenhouse (Al Ain, UAE) on cherry tomatoes under natural infection, MARTS treated 312 diseased leaves in 12 autonomous trials with 92.4% targeting success, 18.7 mm mean spray-centre error, 6.1% adjacent-leaf overspray, and a 71% reduction in pesticide volume versus broadcast spraying. Mean cycle time was 4.8 s per leaf, and the spraying subsystem costs USD 412, 6-10x lower than comparable systems, showing that accurate leaf-level targeting is achievable on commodity hardware.

papers.abstract: Visually similar actions can produce contact loss, jamming, slippage, or irreversible damage, while tactile feedback may arrive after a critical transition. Contact-rich manipulation therefore requires generative policies to anticipate and evaluate whether candidate actions will produce desirable contact outcomes, then adjust action generation before execution. We present ForeTac, a predictive contact-guidance framework organized as a represent-predict-evaluate-guide loop. ForeTac encodes the current tactile state, predicts the tactile consequences of a candidate action sequence, and evaluates the predicted trajectory using a contact-quality objective learned from successful and failed physical interactions. At deployment, its gradient propagates through the tactile predictor to guide action generation while the pretrained model parameters remain frozen. We evaluate ForeTac on four real-robot tasks (planar and curved-surface wiping, card swiping, and fragile-object grasping) with diffusion and flow-matching policies. Across these tasks, ForeTac raises the average task success rate from 36.3% to 71.3% and the average contact success rate (CSR) from 20.0% to 66.3% compared with vision-only Diffusion Policy. Component analyses support the tactile representation and action-conditioned foresight, and show that predicted touch preserves contact-quality ordering. Project page: https://foretac.github.io/.

Evaluated on four real-robot tasks with diffusion and flow-matching policies.

papers.abstract: Scaling interactive environments is important for training long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning. These environments often require further testing and refinement after initial generation, and correcting defects in a task may also require updating its work context and verifier. However, existing construction pipelines offer limited support for such iterative refinement while keeping these components aligned. We introduce WorkRover, a framework for training long-horizon cowork agents through recursive environment evolution. Its harness-driven synthesis enables construction agents to jointly build and validate semantically aligned work contexts, executable tasks, and evidence-grounded verifiers, adapting their actions to workspace state and execution feedback rather than following a fixed construction workflow. To support environment evolution, we introduce Factorial Compatibility Replay (FCR), which uses rollout feedback to evaluate combinations of component revisions through dependency-closed replay and selects the smallest validated repair among tested candidates while preserving task requirements and evaluation constraints. To provide finer-grained training signals, we propose Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment (VTCA), which augments trajectory-level GRPO advantages with signals from deterministic workspace-progress checks and assigns a bounded share of positive-progress credit to prerequisite turns using recorded tool-output and artifact dependencies. Using WorkRover, we post-train Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to obtain WorkRover-35B-A3B and evaluate it on several cowork-agent benchmarks. Its reported scores exceed those of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B by 26.27 percentage points on JobBench, 29.32 percentage points on OfficeQA Pro, and 413.25 Elo points on GDPval v2. These results suggest that WorkRover offers a promising foundation for scalable training of long-horizon cowork agents.

papers.abstract: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks. While orchestration remedies this, it remains bounded by physical execution errors of the low-level policy rather than high-level planning and achieves only ~25%. Tool selection orchestration with GPT-Policy on GPT-6 Astra significantly outperforms learned-policy methods, but incurs significant time and cost budget and succeeds only ~62%. Real-world experiments across two embodiments confirm the collapse of the low-level policy and the gain from orchestration. Project website: https://ladder.insait.ai

GPT-Policy with GPT-6 Astra reaches about 62% through tool selection, but requires substantial time and cost.
Real-world tests confirm both low-level policy collapse and the benefits of orchestration.

papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. We present TRACE, a framework for efficient cross-embodiment adaptation that preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.TRACE first injects kinematic priors into input and output projection layers and aligns nominal joint dynamics to reduce embodiment mismatch and support stable fine-tuning. It then combines encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning on a compact, quality-screened motion set, using a two-phase curriculum to establish stable tracking before refining difficult motions. We apply TRACE to transfer SONIC from Unitree G1 to Unitree H2 using 10 million motion frames and approximately eight hours of training on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, at less than 0.1% of the GPU-hour cost of training SONIC from scratch. The adapted controller achieves 96.08\% success on 67,953 evaluation motions under a height-scaled tracking criterion. Real-robot demonstrations span dynamic motion tracking and whole-body teleoperation, with collected demonstrations supporting downstream vision-language-action policy post-training. These results demonstrate practical reuse of a pretrained humanoid controller across robots with different body scales and dynamics.
authors: Qingyu Lan, Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Addresses kinematic and dynamic mismatch when transferring controllers across humanoid robots.
Injects kinematic priors, aligns nominal joint dynamics, and uses encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning.
Trains with a compact quality-screened motion set and a two-phase curriculum for stable tracking and difficult motions.

Achieves 96.08% success on 67,953 evaluation motions and supports real-robot dynamic tracking, teleoperation, and downstream policy post-training.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, such as $\pi_{0.5}$, have demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities by scaling behavior cloning across massive datasets. However, these models frequently suffer from distributional convergence, a phenomenon where the policy regresses to "safe" but suboptimal mean behaviors due to mode averaging in the training data. This often results in generic grasp strategies, Convergent Defaults, that fail in constrained or long-tail scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel framework to identify and correct these behaviors without parameter updates. We introduce a three-stage methodology: (1) Probing for Defaults, identifying task-specific mode collapse; (2) Diagnostic Root Cause Analysis, utilizing the VLA's latent reasoning capabilities to verbalize the logic behind suboptimal actions; and (3) Structured Guidance Injection, where concrete, distinct alternatives are encoded into reusable "Lens Prompts" that shift the sampling distribution. We validate this approach using $\pi_{0.5}$ in ManiSkill3 simulation environments. We hypothesize that our method outperforms vanilla $\pi_{0.5}$ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting by effectively breaking convergent defaults in complex manipulation tasks.
authors: Mohammed Daba (University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China), Waleed Abdulrahman Saleh AlAkwa (University of Sana'a, Sana'a, Yemen)
bullets: Targets distributional convergence in behavior-cloned VLA models, where mode averaging produces safe but suboptimal “Convergent Defaults.”
Probes task behavior to identify task-specific mode collapse.

Evaluated with π₀.₅ in ManiSkill3 simulations; the abstract states a hypothesis of improvement over vanilla π₀.₅ and standard Chain-of-Thought prompting, not confirmed results.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The Diagnostic Lens Framework. We treat the VLA as a reasoning engine to diagnose its own action priors. By extracting the root cause of a default behavior, we construct a textual ”Lens” that reshapes the flow matching distribution during inference.

Fig. 1. Breaking the Convergent Default. VLA models often regress to the mean of their training data, causing failures in constrained environments. Our method identifies these modes and injects structured guidance (Lens) to shift the action distribution toward expert behaviors.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires robust execution over sequences of interdependent actions. Existing methods typically handle execution deviations by replanning the remaining action chunk or correcting actions step by step as new observations arrive. However, a local deviation may affect only a few actions under distribution shift, yet replanning regenerates the entire chunk from an unfamiliar state, potentially introducing errors into otherwise valid actions. Step-wise correction may react too late, as it does not explicitly anticipate how the deviation affects subsequent actions. We propose ReEnvision, a future-guided selective action repair framework that updates a joint future-action belief using execution feedback. It then learns how the resulting belief revision affects each unexecuted action. The resulting belief revision enables selective repair of only the affected actions within a cached action chunk, preserving valid actions and reserving full replanning for severe deviations. On CALVIN, L-CALVIN, and RLBench, ReEnvision achieves 86.6% 5-step success, improves 10-step success from 56% to 63%, and reaches an average success rate of 88.8%, respectively. On five real-world manipulation tasks, it achieves an average success rate of 82.8%. Controlled repair experiments further demonstrate the benefits of localizing affected actions and preserving valid ones during execution.
authors: Xiyin Zeng, Xuewei Huang, Yi Lu, Weihao Yuan, Hao Wang
bullets: Addresses the risk that full replanning introduces errors into otherwise valid action sequences, while step-wise correction may react too late.
Updates a joint belief over future actions using execution feedback and estimates which unexecuted actions are affected.
Repairs only affected actions in a cached action chunk, reserving full replanning for severe deviations.
Reports 86.6% 5-step success, improves 10-step success from 56% to 63%, and achieves 88.8% average success across simulation benchmarks.
Achieves 82.8% average success on five real-world manipulation tasks; controlled experiments support localized repair and preservation of valid actions.

papers.abstract: Unknown payloads alter robot dynamics and make precise contact execution difficult when foothold margins are small. We present LOAD, a perceptive locomotion framework that combines explicit inertial estimates with implicit dynamics features for narrow-beam traversal. Separate recurrent modules infer torso inertial changes and task-relevant history from proprioception, while a height-map teacher is distilled into a depth-based student. We extensively evaluate LOAD and its variants in simulation and on hardware across beam widths and payload configurations. The results show that implicit dynamics features accelerate training, while explicit inertial estimation further improves traversal success; combining both enables LOAD to approach the performance of a privileged policy supplied with ground-truth inertial parameters. Hardware experiments demonstrate traversal with unilateral payloads of 6 kg on a 10 cm beam and 9 kg on a 15 cm beam, and an evenly distributed 11 kg payload on a 15 cm beam. These results support combining physical estimates and history features for precision locomotion under unknown loads.
authors: Kunzhao Ren, Zhishuo Zhu, Xiaobin Xiong
bullets: Targets precision footholds when payload changes make robot dynamics uncertain.
Uses recurrent proprioceptive modules for explicit inertial estimation and implicit task-history features.

papers.abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.
bullets: Multivariate distributional RL needs joint return distributions, but categorical critics scale exponentially and quantiles lack a canonical multivariate form.
The critic represents returns with Stein particles transported by Stein variational gradient descent along a learned score field.
Bootstrapped denoising score matching and a Bellman consistency loss learn and stabilize the score field across recursion.
A reverse-diffusion sampler supports tail-risk queries below the resolution of the particle set, with Wasserstein evaluation guarantees for bounded, possibly multimodal returns.
SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than equal-particle critics and performs comparably on MuJoCo continuous control.

papers.abstract: Can an AI agent turn high-level user intent into a functioning robot and teach it how to behave? We study this question from two complementary aspects: embodiment and behavior creation. For embodiment creation, we investigate how well current multimodal models capture mechanical requirements, and introduce computational metrics for evaluating generated designs before fabrication. For behavior creation, we present Roboforge, an agentic framework that turns task specifications into executable policies through motion generation, policy learning, and execution-grounded revision. Given a robot embodiment and task, the agent generates a reference motion, configures the learning objective, and trains a policy. Crucially, motion remains in the loop: rollout feedback can revise the reference motion, reward, or both. We evaluate a generated embodiment across multiple MLLMs and behavior creation across four diverse robots against reward-refinement and one-shot motion baselines. Our computational metrics expose recurring mechanical failures in generated designs, while behavior experiments show that execution-grounded refinement improves task-level behavior and execution quality. Finally, we fabricate an agent-generated Gorilla and directly deploy learned behaviors on the physical robot.

papers.abstract: Proactive dynamic grasping requires robots to predict the future state at which physical contact will occur, rather than reacting to the currently observed object pose. But what future must the robot predict, and at what level of abstraction? We argue that contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) is a compact task-sufficient abstraction for this problem: it directly determines where and when the robot should establish contact, without requiring visually complete future scenes. This insight leads to a lightweight object-centric forecast-then-select framework that predicts future rigid-body trajectories from short pose histories and uses a reachability-aware interception selector to choose feasible contact states under kinematic and timing constraints. Trained with randomized physics simulation over primitive shapes, the forecaster transfers to real objects once their metric geometry and SE(3) state histories are recovered. Experiments across simulation and real-world dynamic grasping tasks show that our framework improves the average success rate from \(24.5\%\) to \(62.0\%\) in simulation, and from \(15.3\%\) to \(67.3\%\) in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable interception. The SE(3) forecaster runs in \(15\,\mathrm{ms}\), orders of magnitude faster than dense visual future prediction, enabling real-time contact decision making. Our results suggest that effective proactive grasping does not require imagining the entire future scene. Instead, predicting the compact physical future that determines contact provides an effective and practical abstraction for real-time dynamic grasping.
authors: Yirui Zhou, Hongli Xu, Ying Zheng, Yi Wang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Frames contact-relevant rigid-body state in SE(3) as a task-sufficient abstraction for predicting when and where contact should occur.
Forecasts future object trajectories from short pose histories, then selects reachable interception states under kinematic and timing constraints.

Improves average success from 24.5% to 62.0% in simulation and from 15.3% to 67.3% in real-world catching, conveyor, and turntable tasks.
Runs in 15 ms, supporting real-time contact decisions while avoiding dense visual future prediction.

The forecaster encodes recent motion history, estimates initial velocities, and integrates a Newton–Euler-structured neural ODE to predict future rigid-body trajectories. The forecast-guided interception selector then propagates task-specific contact frames along the predicted trajectory and selects a reachable end-effector target under timing and kinematic constraints.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation has traditionally relied on end-effector-centric interactions. In contrast, humans routinely exploit whole-arm contacts to improve efficiency, robustness, and adaptability, especially when the hands are occupied or when precise grasping is unnecessary. Enabling similar capabilities in robots remains challenging: the robot must select where on its arm to make contact, generate effective non-prehensile interactions, and satisfy task-specific pose or safety constraints on the end-effector. We propose Whole-Arm Contact Learning (WACL), a hierarchical framework that describes each whole-arm contact task with three robot-agnostic representations and hands them to a quasi-static surface-contact optimizer: semantic keypoints that summarize the scene, a reference contact trajectory that specifies where and how the arm presses on the object, and safety-aware path constraints that a vision-language model generates from the task description to protect the end-effector's task. The robot's kinematic chain enters only in this optimizer, which grounds these representations onto the arm by jointly searching over which link makes contact, where on that link, and the joint configuration that realizes it. This decomposition lets WACL learn the contact trajectory from 10 bare-hand human demonstrations per task collected without teleoperation, while new end-effector constraints change only the optimizer's input rather than any trained component. Real-world experiments on a 7-DoF arm across four whole-arm tasks show that WACL sustains contact under end-effector constraints where a strong link-pose baseline fails (78% vs. 33% success) and generalizes to new constraints without retraining. Website: https://wacl-robot.github.io
authors: Bo-Ruei Huang, Daniel Seita, Erdem B{\i}y{\i}k
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing arm-contact locations while preserving task-specific end-effector pose and safety constraints.

A quasi-static surface-contact optimizer grounds these representations onto a robot by jointly selecting the contacting link, contact location, and joint configuration.
On a 7-DoF arm across four tasks, WACL achieved 78% success under end-effector constraints versus 33% for a link-pose baseline.
Demonstrations use bare hands rather than teleoperation; the method’s scope is whole-arm, non-prehensile contact tasks.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables driving policies to adapt to changing deployment conditions, but requires safe exploration throughout training. Safety filtering alone does not ensure stable policy improvement or reduced dependence on corrections. We propose Safe Online Adaptive Refinement (SOAR-Flow), a framework for safe and stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized Flow-based driving policies. A control barrier function (CBF)--model predictive control (MPC) filter corrects potentially unsafe actions before execution. To support stable policy updates, we introduce Gaussian-return-aware value calibration based on calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL), using recorded behavior returns and predicted return variability to smooth conservative critic updates and mitigate policy degradation. Paired corrective learning teaches feasible action adjustments, while an intervention-to-go predictor encourages decisions requiring fewer future corrections. Its predictions also regulate guidance strength, allowing recovery supervision to weaken as predicted dependence decreases. Together with gradually reduced calibration regularization, this supports continued task improvement while preserving hard execution constraints. We analyze conditions for safe execution at control steps and diminishing auxiliary learning influences. We evaluate SOAR-Flow in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV). The results demonstrate improved driving performance and reduced reliance on safety corrections during protected online fine-tuning. The demonstration video and project overview are available at https://lzqw.github.io/SOAR-Flow/.
authors: Zeqiao Li, Yijing Wang, Haoyu Wang, Zheng Li, Zhiqiang Zuo

Evaluated in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle, showing improved driving performance and fewer safety corrections during protected fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: A long-horizon manipulation task consists of primitive skills and the transitions connecting them. Learning skills that can be executed in sequence requires supervision for both, which is costly to collect on a robot. Human videos offer a scalable source of demonstrations, but transferring them to robots requires extracting robot-compatible observations and actions together with their skill structure. We present DexStitch, a framework that cuts long-horizon human videos into skills and transitions, converts them into aligned robot observation-action-skill data, and stitches the learned skills into a requested sequence. A skill classifier first segments the videos into manipulation skills and transitions. DexStitch then converts the human demonstrations into robot observations and actions while retaining their corresponding skill labels. During conversion, per-finger human-object contacts guide dexterous hand retargeting and robotic inpainting, preserving contact geometry and finger-object occlusion ordering. To stitch the learned skills into a sequence, a shared skill-conditioned policy is pretrained on the resulting synthetic data and finetuned on a mixture of synthetic data and a small set of single-skill teleoperation episodes. Conditioning on the current and next skills guides each transition toward the following skill, while predicted skill progression enables closed-loop switching. On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.
