papers.abstract: In embodied manipulation, Vision Language Action (VLA) models can execute atomic skills, but long-horizon manipulation requires recombining these skills without demonstrations for every skill combination. The full instruction route treats skill chaining as long-horizon imitation. In a controlled study, full instruction training on limited skill combination sequences reaches 40.0% ordered success on covered combinations but only 7.7% on recombination, suggesting memorization of sequence templates rather than robust skill recombination. We introduce Hierarchical Subtask Execution (HSE), a diagnostic framework that exposes skill recombination through a shared modular interface over the planner, trigger, and policy, decomposing long-horizon failures into separable modes. We introduce RoboCombine, a benchmark for skill recombination without combined skill training trajectories, with metrics for ordered success and transition conversion across subtask boundaries. RoboCombine reveals that atomic competence alone does not ensure ordered execution. Failures concentrate at transitions where downstream subtasks launch from handoff states from preceding subtasks rather than canonical atomic starts. We identify this mismatch as the start state gap. To address it, we introduce Pose Robust Task Initialization (PRTI), a lightweight atomic task post-training strategy that broadens start state coverage beyond canonical starts. Under oracle timed HSE on RoboCombine, PRTI reaches 18.16% ordered success, compared with 4.21% under random perturbation and 9.47% under a robot-reset oracle, without combined skill training trajectories. These results show that combinatorial generalization requires handoff robust atomic skills that convert first stage progress into reliable downstream execution, not merely decomposition into known subtasks. Code: https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/RoboCombine.
authors: Xupeng Zhang, Yantai Yang, Chang Guo, Zhaokai Yin, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: Full-instruction training appears to memorize seen sequence templates: 40.0% success on covered combinations versus 7.7% on recombinations.
HSE diagnoses failures across planning, triggering, and policy execution through a shared modular interface.
RoboCombine evaluates skill recombination without combined-skill training trajectories using ordered-success and transition-conversion metrics.

papers.abstract: VLMs provide promising solutions to embodied reward design. Most current methods that train VLMs as reward regressors not only require extensive annotations but are also primarily designed for finetuning pretrained policies, and perform less well in the more challenging from-scratch RL setting. This issue stems from a fundamental mismatch: regressing precise rewards is misaligned with what VLMs naturally excel at. We posit that it is more aligned with VLMs' inherent multi-modal VQA capabilities for the models to function as success detectors, and propose VLM success reward via Exploration-Augmented Key-Observation Gating (VLMeg) to well harness VLM for embodied reward design. As the core of VLMeg, the proposed exploration-augmented key-observation gating first determines whether the current RL episode is judgment-worthy based on its similarity to a generated success trajectory. Then, the key observation with the lowest confusion from the judgment-worthy episode will be selected for VLM evaluation as episodic reward. This gating mechanism not only avoids redundant calls but also enables higher detection accuracy of VLM. Considering the sparsity of judgment-worthy episodes, the advanced exploration incentives based on the generated trajectory are introduced, enabling more efficient exploration toward judgment-worthy trajectories for more VLM reward triggers and thus gaining higher RL efficiency. Extensive experiments in MetaWorld demonstrate VLMeg achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL, outperforming advanced VLM-based baselines on 12 challenging reward-free tasks. Furthermore, VLMeg also enables effective RL without any ground-truth reward in 3 challenging real-world experiments. Code will be open after acceptance at https://github.com/Raina915/VLMeg.
authors: Xin Liu, Yutong Jiang, Jian Su, Ziheng Wang, Chuang Wang, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the annotation burden and poor from-scratch performance of VLM reward regressors.
Uses exploration-augmented key-observation gating to identify judgment-worthy episodes and select a low-confusion observation for VLM evaluation.
Adds trajectory-based exploration incentives to reach more VLM reward-triggering episodes efficiently.
Achieves state-of-the-art from-scratch RL on 12 challenging MetaWorld reward-free tasks and works in 3 real-world experiments without ground-truth rewards.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of VLMeg. First, successful frames are extracted from the generated expert videos. During rollout, each observation ot is compared with the success frames. If the maximum similarity exceeds the threshold τsim, the trajectory is considered worthy of VLM verification; otherwise, rollout continues until the horizon T , and trajectories that never satisfy the threshold skip VLM evaluation. For qualified trajectories, the observation most similar to the success-frame set is selected as the key observation. The initial frame, success reference, and selected key observation are then sent to the frozen VLM for success detection, and the resulting episodic success reward is combined with exploration incentives to improve RL efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).
authors: Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma, Chuhao Zhou, Jingliang Li, Stefano V. Albrecht, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Uses a trained message channel and per-arm diffusion action heads on frozen VLA backbones with decentralised execution.
Communication is valuable mainly under partial observability, such as an occluded handover where only one agent sees the box marker.
With shared overhead-camera views, disabling messages has little effect on two- and three-arm handover performance.
On a wrist-only variant, messages improve success from 64.3% to 74.8%; on the occluded tray task, success is 76.0% with messages versus 1.3% when removed during training.
CoLA generalises across VLA backbones and matches a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline while using fewer trainable parameters.

figures.caption: Figure 1 CoLA framework overview. (a) Decentralised inference: each agent’s frozen VLA backbone (Octo-Base or π0.5) encodes its local observation. Its CoLA module compresses the backbone feature into a compact message (dm = 64), decodes the partner’s message, and concatenates the result with its own representation to form zi. This vector conditions a U-Net action head via FiLM, which predicts a coordinated action chunk (K = 10). (b) Adapter and action-head training: backbone features are cached offline and the backbones stay frozen. Only the CoLA modules are trained with a behavioural cloning loss, with gradients flowing end-to-end through the communication channel. (c) Multi-agent broadcast: each agent broadcasts its message to all other agents and receives theirs, so the same design scales to N ≥ 3 agents.
Figure 2 Multi-AgentManipulation Progression. Key milestones across evaluated tasks: (top) Occluded Tray-Handover Task, (middle) 2-arm Reactive Handover, and (bottom) 3-arm Handover Chain.

Figure 3 Qualitative Trajectory Comparison onHandover. Top: CoLA enables Arm A to maintain grasp stability until Arm B firmly closes its gripper. Bottom: Uncoordinated baseline desynchronises, causing premature release and dropped objects.

Figure 4 Linear probes of channel content. Left: on the occluded tray-handover task, the message decodes box colour well above chance while an untrained control does not, indicating channel-specific information transfer. Right: on the wrist-only handover, the message and an untrained control both decode Arm A’s presentation pose near ceiling, so pose is linearly recoverable from the raw features regardless of training, and this probe cannot isolate the channel’s contribution.

Figure 5 Validation loss for all training runs in table 1, one panel per coordination regime, ordered as in the main table. Octo steps are converted to epochs so both families share the matched 150-epoch budget. Decentralised rows train one policy per arm; the line is their mean and the shading their range.

Table 5 Trainable capacity and training cost by task and method. Every method within a task uses the same optimiser steps at batch size 128, which matches the optimisation budget but not compute or capacity: CoLA trains on cached backbone features, so it does a fraction of the work per step. Trainable parameters are the modules updated by gradient descent, summed over the policies a method deploys (two for the 2-arm tasks, three for the 3-arm task); the Octo baselines’ action head is U-Net at horizon 12 (68.5M), and the centralised variants differ only in output width (7 → 14), adding <0.1M. GPU-hours are job wall-clock on one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB, summed over the policies a method deploys; CoLA trains all arms in a single model. papers.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative and within-chunk future action flexibility,. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.
authors: Wenbo Yu, Jifan Li, Wenke Xia, Yuchen Li, Yizhuo Zhang, Pei Ren, Zhengping Che, Di hu
bullets: Addresses boundary misalignment between predicted action chunks and the committed execution stream.
Uses a lightweight Control Barrier Function-inspired constraint between consecutive chunks.
Computes corrections in closed form, avoiding backpropagation through the VLA action head.
Progressively tightens consistency during generation while preserving early and within-chunk action flexibility.
Improves success rates by 10%–15% on average and reduces per-chunk inference latency by over 45% versus RTC across simulated and real robotic settings.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Abu Hanif Muhammad Syarubany, Hwanhee Kim, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets the high training and inference costs of diffusion-based offline RL policies caused by iterative denoising and backpropagation through time.
Uses average-velocity modeling with a compositional formulation to learn a direct noise-to-action mapping across scales.
Combines the generative policy with behavior-regularized actor–critic learning using one policy network, without distillation, multi-stage training, or Jacobian computations.
Generates actions in one forward pass, with optional value-guided candidate selection for refinement.
Experiments on offline RL benchmarks and robotic manipulation tasks show performance comparable to or better than diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing training and inference time.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL) overview. (a) Standard flow-matching (diffusion) policies learn an instantaneous marginal velocity field v(at, t, s) and generate actions by multi-step integration. (b) InsQL instead parameterizes the policy with an average-velocity field u(at, n, t, s) over finite intervals, enabling single-step action generation by directly mapping noise to action. (c) Velocity composition: long-interval average velocity (blue) is recursively composed from shorter-interval average velocities (green/red); in the infinitesimal limit, this recovers the marginal velocity used in FM. (d) InsQL unifies the one-step policy into a non-BPTT behavior-regularized actor–critic framework, with optional Q-guided candidate selection for test-time refinement.

papers.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.
authors: Shutong Ding, Zhaoyang Liu, Yimiao Zhou, Jingya Wang, Jiayuan Gu, Ye Shi
bullets: Addresses reduced exploration diversity and capability loss when fine-tuning diffusion policies with RL.
Combines two policies’ score or velocity fields during sampling to control exploration–exploitation trade-offs.
Supports online RL with a frozen exploration branch and offline-to-online RL with a frozen pretrained exploitation branch.
Integrates with QSM, QVPO, and Flow-SDE+PPO across MuJoCo and RoboTwin manipulation tasks.
Provides a unified, plug-and-play framework without changing the underlying RL objectives.

papers.abstract: Multi-finger hands contact objects at different times, so a global close command can overload early-contact fingers while others are still moving. Dense tactile arrays address this problem but add hardware, calibration, bandwidth, and computation. We present an edge-native pipeline that uses only built-in joint-angle and pre-use-calibrated actuator-load feedback to recognize the grasped object and predict an independent Stop event for each finger. Four samples and their first differences form a 4-by-20 contact-evolution window. At its core is a heterogeneous dual-expert architecture, termed DualExpert, that assigns complementary tasks to a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and a Finger Graph Filter Network (FGFN). The TCN models short-term contact evolution and supplies all five Stop probabilities, while the FGFN encodes finger topology and contributes only to object classification. Fixed 0.7/0.3 class-probability fusion reaches 93.78\% trajectory-level classification accuracy on 225 held-out trials, improving the standalone TCN and FGFN by 4.00 and 2.22 percentage points, respectively. The TCN Stop path attains 95.25\% F1. The dataset contains 1,500 automatically collected trajectories from five object instances. In Flash deployment, mixed accelerator execution retains 93.78\% classification accuracy and 94.84\% Stop F1 with 2.890~ms mean inference time and 9.172~ms mean sample-to-stop latency. Across 50 physical trials, the system achieves 96.00\% recognition and 98.00\% grasp success while the complete embedded board draws approximately 0.80~W.
authors: Jiajian Zheng, Bin Zhang, Wen Fan, Yanan Liu
bullets: Addresses asynchronous multi-finger contact without dense tactile hardware, using pre-calibrated actuator-load and joint-angle signals.
Builds a 4×20 contact-evolution window from four samples and first differences.
DualExpert combines a TCN for temporal contact evolution and per-finger Stop prediction with an FGFN for finger-topology-aware object classification.
Fixed probability fusion achieves 93.78% trajectory-level classification accuracy and the TCN Stop path achieves 95.25% F1 on held-out trials.
Flash deployment maintains 93.78% classification accuracy and 94.84% Stop F1 with 2.890 ms inference, 9.172 ms sample-to-stop latency, and approximately 0.80 W board power.

papers.abstract: Robust motion planning and control for manipulators is the problem of guaranteeing safe execution and collision-free motion under disturbances. The Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF) is a recently proposed planner that comes with robustness guarantees and is particularly attractive for collision-free control as it guarantees closed-loop evolution inside a funnel, i.e., a collision-free region around a nominal trajectory. Despite its attractive theoretical properties, the current approach for computing funnels is computationally demanding, which limits its expressiveness and performance. We address its current limitations by proposing a novel funnel planning and control solution. Our key tool to enable this is a neural Signed Configuration Distance Function (nSCDF) which allows us to estimate collision-free balls and gradients in a computationally efficient way. We use the nSCDF in our planner to compute a nominal trajectory, where path length and clearance are balanced. To track the trajectory with collision-avoidance guarantees, we design a funnel controller that exploits the geometric information from the nSCDF. From numerical experiments, we observe that our planner produces nominal paths $2$ times faster, while at the same time obtaining $20 \%$ shorter path length and $5$ times the clearance. Finally, we also observe improved motion performance and robustness properties when using the nSCDF for funnel control.
authors: Bernhard Wullt, Christos K. Verginis, Per Mattsson, Mikael Norrl\"of, Thomas B. Sch\"on
bullets: Targets the computational cost and limited expressiveness of Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF).
Uses an nSCDF to efficiently estimate collision-free balls and gradients for planning and control.
Plans nominal trajectories that balance path length and obstacle clearance, then tracks them with a geometry-aware funnel controller.
Numerical experiments report paths computed 2× faster, with 20% shorter length and 5× greater clearance.
The approach also improves motion performance and robustness when the nSCDF is used for funnel control.

figures.caption: Fig. 5: Left: Illustration in world space, showing an example problem instance used in the experiments. The manipulator is 6 DOF colored black at a configuration along a collision-free path. The end-effector position is traced out along the path (blue curve). The start and goal configurations are colored transparent red and green, respectively. The obstacles are spheres (colored gray). Right: The learned configuration space representation of the world instance to the left, illustrated in the sub-space of the first three joints, i.e., main joints. The red, green and blue colored regions are the obstacle spaces for the main joints, wrist joints and self-collisions. The resulting path from our method is the black curve.

Fig. 3: All: A conceptual illustration of how the wrist configuration distance is computed for a 2 DOF arm, where qm is the main joint and qw is the wrist joint. The left plot is illustrated in the world space, the rest is illustrated in the configuration space. Left: The manipulator has two links (colored black). The main link is made transparent to emphasize that its collision with the obstacle is not considered. The obstacle is a disk (colored red). Its parameter vector is expressed in the base frame {0} as σ and in the wrist frame {w} as σlw. Computing the distance from the local wrist function results in a wrist movement (dashed blue arc) that moves the wrist to the obstacle boundary (transparent green). The distance or the movement does not include the main joint. Middle: Corresponding configuration space representation of the left plot. The configuration (red point); distance computed by the local wrist nSCDF (dashed blue line); the ground truth distance including the movement of the main joint (transparent red disk and green line). Right: To compute an estimate of the distance where the movement of the main joint is included, we discretize the space of the main joints (black points along the horizontal axis). For each grid point, we compute a distance, by forming the hypotenuse (red line) with the distance of the main joint (green line) and the wrist distance (blue line). This forms an estimated safe set (orange circle). From all estimates we take the smallest distance (blue circle).

Fig. 4: Illustrations in the configuration space. The SCDF, ψ, is illustrated as a colormap, with darker colors indicating lower distances. The zero-level contour, i.e., ∂Co, is represented by the solid purple curve. Left: Illustration of our medial-axis projection step. A discretized path (red points) is projected to points approximately on the medial axis (purple points), resulting in increased clearance. Middle: The projection steps result in a nonsmooth and distorted path. We solve a weighted shortest path problem by constructing a graph by using the points on the path as vertices. The edges are formed over intersecting balls (black lines). The weight function balances path length and clearance. Solving the problem results in an optimized path in the graph (red curve), which is continuously collision-free due to the intersection requirement of the resulting balls (red circles). Right: We smoothen the piece-wise linear path by solving a convex optimization problem. The key idea is to find a smooth path that is close to the original one (black curve). We do this by constructing collision-free capsules (transparent red) along the connecting line segments of the path. Each capsule is assigned a Bézier curve (colored curve within capsule). Continuity constraints are enforced with its neighboring curve. The closeness of the original path is controlled by the width of the capsules. Solving the optimization problem results in a smooth collision-free path.

Fig. 6: All: The vertical axis presents the integrated norm of the resulting jerk. Each data point is the average from 10 simulations in different funnels. If a run failed, then the average was not formed and no data point was added to the graph. The shaded region corresponds to ± one standard deviation. Funnel sizes: 0.10 rad (blue), 0.15 rad (orange) and with the nSCDF (green). Left: The horizontal axis represents different levels of model uncertainties. Right: The horizontal axis represents different amplitudes on the disturbance signal.

Fig. 1: Signed distance in the configuration space (brighter colors represent larger distance); the thick purple line (obstacle boundary) is the zero isoline. Our method computes a smooth trajectory (black curve) which balances path length and clearance. To track the trajectory, we develop a funnel controller such that the robot’s closed-loop trajectory (orange curve) stays within a funnel defined by the signed distance function (black circle and transparent red region).

Fig. 2: A conceptual illustration of the representation based on slices. The high-dimensional obstacle region (purple) is discretized into slices (dark purple), by forming the intersection with the hyperplanes (black). From a given query point (red point) we compute the distance to a slice (red line), by combining the normal plane distance (green line) and the in-plane distance to the slice boundary (blue line). The smallest distance from all the slices results in our estimate of the distance to the high-dimensional boundary.

The EFSS method is not able to give any clearance beyond the radius used to validate the region. All paths were collision-free.

papers.abstract: Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.
authors: Buzhen Huang, Xingchen Wu, Yuanwang Yang, Chenyi Xie, Kun Li
bullets: Targets collaborative manipulation tasks involving sequential actions, role specialization, and multiple agents.
A commander performs joint semantic and geometric planning, then decomposes tasks into role-specific subtasks and shared object-centric plans.
Executors use local observations and the commander’s strategy to learn physics-based coordination through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum.
Experiments across varied manipulation tasks show long-horizon collaboration and scaling from two agents to multiple agents.
The method reports higher success rates than state-of-the-art methods, though specific quantitative results are not provided.

papers.abstract: Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones. We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion. TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation. Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.

papers.abstract: Bilateral teleoperation with force feedback is becoming increasingly important, and the quality of external-torque estimation is critical to this process. However, manufacturer-provided disturbance-torque estimates on commercial robotic arms are often inaccurate, while the use of end-effector force/torque sensors adds cost and payload. We propose LETS, a physics-guided learning approach that assigns rigid-body dynamics to recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics and reserves learning for only the robot-specific residual. LETS uses only the robot's URDF model and joint feedback, deliberately excluding control commands and thereby decoupling external-torque estimation from control-command inputs. It trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute, without requiring a dedicated end-effector six-axis force/torque sensor. In bilateral teleoperation, LETS achieves real-time external-torque estimation that enables stable force feedback. Its free-space error is 69% lower than the manufacturer-provided estimate, substantially reducing coupled oscillations between leader and follower; its contact error is 28% lower, yielding more accurate haptic feedback.

bullets: Addresses inaccurate manufacturer disturbance-torque estimates and the cost and payload of end-effector force/torque sensors.

papers.abstract: Action chunking improves temporal coherence in visuomotor imitation learning by jointly predicting sequences of future actions. However, many existing policies regenerate entire action chunks even when errors are localized, potentially replacing otherwise valid predictions. We introduce Contextual Masked Action Policy (CMAP), a visuomotor policy that refines continuous action chunks through history-conditioned local regeneration. Specifically, CMAP introduces a history-conditioned action tape that combines executed commands with masked future positions to produce coarse action predictions and per-step uncertainty scores. An uncertainty-guided span regeneration mechanism then selects a high-uncertainty contiguous span and reconstructs it using the executed history and retained future predictions as context. By jointly reconstructing neighboring actions, CMAP models local temporal dependencies while preserving all predictions outside the selected span. Extensive experiments on nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that CMAP achieves superior overall performance over several competitive baselines. Ablation studies validate the complementary contributions of its key components, while held-out trajectory analysis shows that local regeneration reduces prediction errors within selected spans.

bullets: Addresses the problem of full action-chunk regeneration replacing valid predictions when errors are localized.

Experiments across nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks show superior overall performance over several baselines.
Ablations and held-out trajectory analysis support the complementary components and reduced errors within regenerated spans.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a stage-dependent sensory conflict: vision and proprioception are essential for localization and approach, when force is largely uninformative and potentially distracting, whereas force becomes critical after contact, when irrelevant visual details and correlated robot states may become shortcuts. We propose DEFT-VLA (Dual-Expert Force-specialized Training for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation), which retains the task-adapted base expert for vision-dominated non-contact behavior and introduces a force-aware contact expert for critical contact stages, localizing force-conditioned adaptation to where it is needed. We further introduce a contact-localized force-attending curriculum that applies force-attending post-training only to the contact expert, progressively restoring vision and masking state tokens to suppress shortcuts. Real-robot experiments on pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping show that DEFT-VLA effectively exploits force feedback to improve contact-stage performance while maintaining strong non-contact behavior and robustness to held-out grasp heights. It improves overall task success by 20-40 percentage points over the strongest baseline on each task.
authors: Zan Huang, Yibo Qiu, Kan Ding, Xuanping Zhang, Ao Tian, Ronald X Xu, Mingzhai Sun
bullets: Addresses the conflict between vision/proprioception before contact and force sensing during contact.

During contact-expert post-training, the contact-localized curriculum gradually restores image clarity and the original state tokens to suppress visual and proprioceptive shortcuts. At inference, a lightweight stage estimator fuses task-conditioned visual features, robot state, and causal wrench history, while a contact-stage router selects the active expert. papers.abstract: Synthesizing believable 4D hand-object grasping sequences is important for character animation, extended reality, and embodied agents. Grasping requires a hand to approach, contact, and lift or manipulate an object coherently. Existing synthesis methods often model only the final static grasp or rely on additional conditions, such as language, target grasps, or object trajectories, to specify the interaction. We instead study the underconstrained problem of generating a complete grasping motion from a single initial hand-object state. Our framework decouples hand-motion generation from object-motion recovery. Given an object point cloud in the initial wrist frame and the initial parameterized hand configuration, conditional flow matching predicts a sequence-level contact map and a hand pose at each normalized sequence time. This time-indexed formulation avoids the error accumulation of autoregressive rollout while representing the complete motion. We then infer an attachment frame and recover rigid-object motion through training-free, contact-guided weighted registration. We evaluate on held-out DexYCB objects and unseen object geometries reconstructed from in-the-wild videos by Open-CHOIR. Compared with LatentHOI, our method produces smoother hand and object motion in every setting, matches or improves on its contact and penetration metrics in the wild under a shared initialization, and is about 30x faster per generated frame. In a 15-participant study, our motions were preferred in roughly two thirds of (forced-choice pairwise) comparisons. Precise contact closure on novel geometry, however, remains a key open challenge.
authors: Nga Kiu Kelly Ho, Yilin Liu, Hao Xu, Niloy J. Mitra
bullets: Addresses underconstrained grasp synthesis without language, target grasps, or object trajectories.
Predicts a time-indexed contact map and hand poses using conditional flow matching, avoiding autoregressive error accumulation.
Recovers rigid object motion via training-free, contact-guided weighted registration after estimating an attachment frame.
On held-out and in-the-wild objects, motion is smoother than LatentHOI, about 30× faster per frame, and preferred in roughly two thirds of user comparisons.
Precise contact closure on novel geometry remains an open challenge.

papers.abstract: We present a learning-based framework that enables a full-scale bipedal humanoid to sprint at over 7 m/s with motion-prior-guided gait and perform aggressive cornering at high speed with a pronounced trunk lean of up to $25^\circ$. Achieving this combination is challenging: above approximately 4 m/s, periodic foot impacts induce severe, high-frequency yaw-rate oscillations intrinsic to high-speed gaits. This high-frequency temporal structure corrupts the history of proprioceptive feedback that flat-MLP policies rely on, while rendering conventional yaw-rate tracking rewards counterproductive, as they fight against the robot's natural oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, a single style prior shared across skills cannot tell which skill is commanded and inherently compromises the low-speed skill fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we adopt a causal multi-head attention (MHA) module to explicitly model the high-frequency temporal feedback. In place of the oscillatory yaw rate, we design a heading-direction reward that supervises only the low-frequency velocity direction, allowing agile turning at high speed without suppressing natural gait oscillations. We further introduce skill-conditioned multi-adversarial-motion-prior (MAMP) discriminators that condition the style reward on the commanded skill. Ablation experiments confirm that each mechanism is essential: replacing structured temporal encoding with a flat-history MLP caps the top speed; reverting to yaw-rate tracking prevents high-speed turning; and a single shared discriminator makes in-place turning collapse into a quasi-static stance. Our framework bridges the gap between raw sprinting speed and reference-motion fidelity, demonstrating stable high-speed sprinting and aggressive cornering in both simulation and real-robot deployment.
authors: Huaxing Huang, Ruidong Li, Jinchao Han, Ziyang Dong, Wenhao Cui
bullets: High-speed foot impacts create yaw-rate oscillations that disrupt flat-history policies and make direct yaw-rate tracking counterproductive.

Skill-conditioned multi-adversarial motion priors maintain distinct motion styles across sprinting and turning.
Ablations and simulation-to-real deployment demonstrate stable sprinting and aggressive cornering, including trunk lean up to 25°.

(3) The heading-direction reward supervises the low-frequency velocity direction at high speed, falling back to yaw-rate tracking below vmin. All three components feed into a shared PPO training loop.

papers.abstract: Robust manipulation under uncertain object dynamics and geometry remains a core challenge in real-world robotics. Policies trained under fixed assumptions often degrade when object mass, friction, scale, or shape vary. Embedding-based adaptation methods such as Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) address this by conditioning actions on latent representations of environment dynamics inferred from interaction history. We investigate whether this paradigm scales from single arm settings to coordinated bimanual manipulation, where higher dimensional control, coupled contacts, and shared object forces introduce additional complexity. We evaluate bimanual RMA on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties. Bimanual RMA, using observation-action history and dual wrist depth images, retains privileged policy performance on bimanual picking and lifting, while an otherwise matched stationary PPO policy without latent conditioning achieves low success; all methods remain limited on long-horizon stacking. We further demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer on a dual Franka lifting task without real-world finetuning. Together, these results suggest that latent conditioning provides useful structure for scaling robust control to coordinated bimanual systems, while longer horizon tasks require additional temporal structure.
authors: Seung-Bin Joo, Alessandro Albini, Luca Wiehe, Perla Maiolino, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Jo\~ao F. Henriques
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by uncertain object mass, friction, scale, and shape.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. Relative to Fast-WAM, BridgeWAM reduces single-sample inference FLOPs by 28.72% in simulation profiling and real-robot latency to 77.1 ms (a 2.47-fold speedup). Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.

Achieves 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus; reduces simulated single-sample FLOPs by 28.72% and reaches 77.1 ms real-robot latency.
Qualitative results suggest preferential attention to target objects and destinations under perturbations.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.
authors: Peizheng Guo, Cheng Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: WAMs can misjudge actions when predicted futures mix action-induced and environment-driven changes.
An SCM uses intervention and backdoor adjustment to isolate each candidate action’s future change.
CAG-WAM compares action-conditioned and environment-only futures to compute causal action gain (CAG).
CAG guides GRPO-based policy learning and supports inference-time action revision.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CAG-WAM Architecture. (b) Paired-Future World Model predicts action-conditioned and environmental futures under different action conditions and evaluates them using the same future evaluator.

Figure 3: Training and inference framework of CAG-WAM. (a) Training: candidate actions are evaluated by comparing their action-conditioned futures with the environmental future, and the resulting causal action gain is used as the policy-optimization advantage. (b) Inference: the initial action is evaluated using the same paired-future comparison; when its causal action gain falls below the revision threshold, future feedback is used for an additional action generation before execution.

papers.abstract: Coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with a diffusion or flow-matching action expert has become the mainstream vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm for embodied policies, yet they remain unreliable once a task demands precise manipulation, e.g., submillimeter cable insertion. We attribute this weakness to a training objective that averages flow-matching errors across contexts and flow times, allocating little supervision to the few decisive moments determining task success. Along the generative path, inference integrates a locally supervised velocity field, so equally penalized errors at different flow times can affect the executed action unequally. Consequently, precision-task performance deteriorates as physical tolerance tightens by orders of magnitude. We call this supervision imbalance across contexts and flow times Flow-Time Starvation. The remedy is to jointly align supervision allocation and representation learning with context-dependent precision demand, enabling the policy to recognize when greater precision is needed. We instantiate this precision-forcing strategy as Precision-aware Reweighting and Internalization for Skilled Manipulation (PRISM), which scores precision demand offline, strengthens flow supervision where errors are consequential and action signals are visible, and internalizes that demand in the VLM condition representation. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that PRISM preserves or improves general-task performance while raising mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% across drive connector insertion, bimanual connector mating, and screw tightening, substantially extending the precision boundary of existing embodied policies without new sensors or observation modalities.
authors: Chenghao Yue, Peiyan Li, Hao Wang, Lei Lv, Jiahao Chen, Huaping Liu, Yu Luo, Yuanlong Zhang

Raises mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% while preserving or improving general-task performance, without new sensors or modalities.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Test-time sampling promises to turn one action prediction into a set of distinct executable candidates that a verifier can choose among. Downstream fine-tuning works against that promise. A vision-language-action model trained to solve one task distribution concentrates its flow-matching decoder around the dominant demonstrated action, so repeated samples differ only marginally and the verifier receives many copies of one decision. We call this proposal contraction and identify it as a key constraint on test-time scaling: repeated samples can remain highly redundant as the candidate budget grows. Action Dynamic Sampling (ADS) alleviates the constraint on the proposal side, during training. At each training step, ADS integrates $K$ additional trajectories from the current policy under fresh base noise, scores each by the flow support along its path with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and corrects the policy's local action distribution toward this weighted set through a detached finite-set KL term. Training cost rises; deployment cost is unchanged. Across simulation and four physical-robot tasks, ADS raises proposal spread without the success penalty that Gaussian perturbation incurs, lifts oracle best-of-8 success on RoboCasa from 57.6% to 63.0%, improves fixed verifiers by 2.4 to 4.9 points in simulation, and raises TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on real-world manipulation.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Haitao Shen, Guanlin Li, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Problem: Fine-tuned VLA flow-matching policies contract around dominant demonstrated actions, producing redundant test-time candidates.
Method: Sample additional policy trajectories, weight them by flow support estimated with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and apply a detached finite-set KL correction.
Contribution: A training-time proposal-diversification method that increases candidate spread while avoiding the success degradation of Gaussian perturbations.
Results: Oracle best-of-8 RoboCasa success rises from 57.6% to 63.0%; fixed verifiers improve by 2.4–4.9 points in simulation and TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on physical-robot tasks.
Scope: ADS increases training cost, while deployment cost remains unchanged.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning has shown superior sample efficiency by leveraging the learned latent dynamics either in the form of derivative-free planning/imagined rollout training or dynamics gradient-based policy updates. While these approaches achieve comparatively fast learning, they all suffer, to varying degrees, from issues of recurrent compounding errors, high inference-time latency, and instability in backward propagation through time (BPTT). In this work, we propose a model-based RL approach that uses the chunk world model as a differentiable training-time evaluator to optimize the chunk actor without recurrent model invocation. Through the collaborative chunk-wise prediction of the world model and policy, we can generate H-step hypothetical rollouts in a single forward pass and directly optimize value expansion, avoiding the costly and unstable BPTT. We evaluate our method on 19 challenging high-dimensional humanoid tasks from HumanoidBench and deploy our method to the real-world for quadruped bipedal walking. papers.abstract: Most existing approaches rely on video or motion-capture data for reinforcement learning (RL) training; however, all of these methods require an upper-level module to generate reference trajectories in real time. In object carrying tasks, the humanoid can only lift objects from designated locations along the reference trajectory, resulting in poor spatial generalization. Moreover, existing policies can only be evaluated inside a motion-capture studio. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MOVER}, a multi-stage, Teacher-Assistant-Student, RL training framework for humanoid object carrying. We first collect data from videos and employ GENMO and GMR to retarget the video data, combining this with data augmentation techniques to generalize the data across objects of varying shapes and sizes. In the \textbf{first stage}, building upon the DeepMimic \cite{peng2018deepmimic} motion-training framework, we train the humanoid to transport objects from specified locations along designated trajectories. In the \textbf{second stage}, we relax the tracking of the reference motion and adjust the reward so that the humanoid learns to transport objects from different positions. In the \textbf{third stage}, we apply a Dagger-PPO distillation method to distill away the proprioceptive position observations and reference joint position of the humanoid. This allows the deployed policy to operate without relying on global position information from a motion-capture system; instead, the humanoid can directly perceive the object's pose from its onboard RGB-D camera to complete the carrying task. We design a series of simulation experiments to compare the success rates across stages (Stages 1 vs. 2) and before versus after distillation. We further transfer the policy to a real humanoid, successfully transporting objects at varying positions in a motion-capture-free setting.
bullets: Addresses poor spatial generalization and reliance on real-time reference trajectories and motion-capture systems in humanoid carrying.
Uses a three-stage Teacher-Assistant-Student RL framework based on retargeted human video, augmentation across object shapes and sizes, and progressive task relaxation.

papers.abstract: In multi-robot manipulation, an action's value depends on how teammates respond. We present \method{} (Cooperative Action--Response Belief Estimation), a framework for learning \emph{team-response beliefs} from local history. A predictive belief encoder represents the interaction and conditions a nominal action. Matched reactive and replay continuations separate each candidate's direct advantage from the utility contributed by teammate adaptation. A candidate-conditioned readout learns this response distribution alongside total advantage, and calibrated selection chooses an alternative or retains the nominal action. Our analysis characterizes when response changes the preferred action and how prediction and source errors limit the recoverable gain. With the representation, proposals, and data fixed, explicit response supervision improves candidate ranking and reduces selection regret relative to learning the same information through branch utilities. The benefit is concentrated in decisions where teammate adaptation changes the preferred action. Across RoboFactory, the MARS Control Track, and physical collaboration tasks, CARE achieves the highest average success among the evaluated policies, combining a capable nominal policy with selective coordination adjustments. Together, these results show that CARE turns predictions of teammate adaptation into effective decentralized action selection. Project page: https://jeong-zju.github.io/care/.

papers.abstract: Microsurgical anastomosis is one of the most challenging and sophisticated procedures for surgical robotics, requiring accurate manipulation of surgical instruments within a limited space to achieve precise operations. Accurate surgical trajectory anticipation is essential for surgical scene understanding, intraoperative planning, robotic manipulation, and reliable behaviour analysis. However, existing approaches mainly focus on features extracted from surgical videos and historical trajectories, while overlooking rich semantic and motion information that can provide more discriminative multi-modal representations for complex surgical instrument-tissue interactions. In this work, we propose a cross-modal feature fusion framework for long-term 2D and 3D microsurgical anastomosis trajectory anticipation. The proposed framework consists of a multi-modal representation extractor and a cross-modal feature fusion network. Semantic recognition of surgical objects and consecutive motion estimation are incorporated as multi-modal visual cues, providing complementary spatial and temporal guidance for instrument-tissue interaction characterization. A coarse-to-fine progressive fusion strategy with a long-short-term memory mechanism is introduced to capture temporal dependencies step by step. The training and evaluation are conducted on our established robotic platform and a comprehensive dataset containing both phantom and ex-vivo surgical scenarios is constructed. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing methods and exhibits improved robustness across different surgical scenes, highlighting its potential for both intelligent robot-assisted and autonomous surgical systems.

papers.abstract: A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop generalist robots that can perform tasks across a wide range of settings, flexibly specified with images and text. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward this goal by training on large collections of robot demonstrations. However, while VLAs perform well in-distribution, they often fail under minor test-time shifts, such as changes in object positions, lighting, textures, and camera poses. To address this, we propose Quality Diversity for Diverse Environment Generation (Q-DEG), a method for improving VLA robustness by generating adversarial environments and fine-tuning the VLA on its own successful rollouts. Q-DEG uses Quality Diversity (QD) optimization to find a set of high-failure environments, while promoting diversity using policy embeddings extracted from the VLA. These environments expose vulnerabilities that can be mitigated through self-imitation fine-tuning, thereby improving the VLA's robustness. In simulation, we conduct experiments across three representative VLA models, and our results indicate that Q-DEG improves robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) adversarial environments compared to the base VLA and VLAs fine-tuned using data collected from two red-teaming baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improving VLA robustness through Q-DEG facilitates sim-to-real transfer. Our anonymous project website is at: https://qd-env.github.io/qdeg/.
authors: Shihan Zhao, Henry Chen, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Minjune Hwang, Siddharth Srikanth, Freddie Liang, Akanksha Saran, Aaquib Tabrez, Stefanos Nikolaidis, Daniel Seita

papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.

papers.abstract: Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.
authors: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Wan Du
bullets: Dense task representations can diffuse inferred rewards across the state space, weakening goal-state contrast.
An L1 penalty concentrates reward-predictive information in a smaller latent subspace without changing the architecture or test-time closed-form inference.
Across 65 DMC Suite and OGBench tasks, Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons.
Average return rises from 661 ± 6 to 714 ± 3 on DMC; average success rate rises from 38.0 ± 0.8% to 48.4 ± 2.3% on OGBench.
The approach achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in 9 of 13 domains; analysis links gains to sharper, more task-informative reward landscapes.

papers.abstract: Retargeting human demonstrations into dynamically feasible dexterous hand trajectories requires resolving complex contact physics, yet current methods either omit physical constraints or rely on computationally expensive sampling-based optimization in simulation. Reinforcement learning has previously been used to achieve planning and control through contact dynamics; however, standard policies require object-specific training and fail to generalize across arbitrary geometries. This work reframes physics-based retargeting as a residual learning problem, where we demonstrate that zero-shot generalization across objects relies on structured state representations. Specifically, formulating the observation space to include a localized contact-error signal guiding each robot link to its target coordinate on the object surface enables a single, unified residual policy to successfully grasp novel, unseen object geometries. Rolling out this policy in simulation on a kinematic reference trajectory yields a physics-based retargeter, OATH. Operating at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, OATH achieves 2.4x faster-than-real-time performance and a 60-350x reduction in computational cost compared to sampling-based methods. The system recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories while maintaining a sub-2 cm tracking error.
authors: Solvin Sigurdson, Prasanna Sriganesh, Juan Borbon, Joel Burdick, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of producing dynamically feasible hand trajectories under complex contact physics without costly sampling-based optimization.
Uses a unified residual reinforcement-learning policy with structured observations that encode each robot link’s contact error relative to the object surface.
Generalizes zero-shot to novel object geometries, including held-out and unseen objects.
Runs at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, achieving 2.4× faster-than-real-time performance and 60–350× lower computational cost than sampling-based methods.
Recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories with sub-2 cm tracking error.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robot hands can receive useful motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but successful execution also depends on contact decisions that these commands rarely specify. We introduce DexFLEX, a contact-aware foundation controller that turns upstream fingertip-motion drafts into contact-consistent joint commands. Instead of treating a draft as a trajectory to copy, DexFLEX treats it as evidence about intent: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state, it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that best follows the command while preserving future contact stability. At inference time, a simple Draft-Dream-Select procedure combines pure-prior proposals for recovery with draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness, then decodes the selected motion into executable joint-space targets. Across degraded-command simulation, real-world shared control, and visuomotor policy learning, the same trained controller improves robustness without retraining, increasing real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3% and reaching 46.7% policy-learning success, 3.5 times direct joint-action prediction, and 1.56 times prior-only correction. Videos are available at dex-flex.github.io.
authors: Weikang Wan, Zeyu Lai, Jianyu Hou, Yuchen Zhou, Jiawei Fu, Henrik I Christensen, Hao Su
bullets: Addresses the missing contact decisions in teleoperation and learned motion commands.
Uses tactile-proprioceptive state to propose short-horizon motion chunks and predict their contact consequences.
Draft-Dream-Select combines command-seeded proposals with prior-based recovery, then selects stable, command-following motions.
The same trained controller improves performance across simulation, shared-control, and visuomotor policy-learning settings.
Reported success rises from 29.2% to 78.3% in real-world teleoperation; policy-learning success reaches 46.7%.

papers.abstract: World-action models inherit broad visual and physical priors from video pre-training. However, standard within-video next-frame prediction allows them to rely on appearance shared between the context and future, rather than learning interactions that transfer across scenes and embodiments. We introduce WATCH, a cross-video pre-training that learns from task-paired human demonstrations collected across diverse environments. Conditioned on the video and actions of one demonstration, the model jointly predicts another demonstration's actions and future frames from its current observation. Predicting one demonstration from another encourages the model to learn task-relevant interactions that transfer across scenes and demonstrators. Our pre-training shows that these capabilities can be learned from readily scalable human-human pairs alone, without requiring matched human-robot demonstrations. Analyses before robot post-training show improved motion alignment across embodiments and better action and video prediction on unseen robots, with representations closer to those learned from robot pairs. After robot post-training, WATCH improves MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3, with the largest gains on the unseen levels. Gains persist under context-free post-training across robot embodiments. WATCH outperforms within-video pre-training and co-training baselines, supporting cross-video prediction as a scalable approach to learning transferable world-action representations.
authors: Jeongeun Park, Taekyung Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of within-video prediction, which can rely on appearance overlap rather than transferable task interactions.
Uses cross-video pre-training on task-paired human-human demonstrations across diverse environments, without requiring human-robot pairs.
Jointly predicts the paired demonstration’s actions and future frames conditioned on the source video, actions, and target observation.
Improves motion alignment and action/video prediction on unseen robots before robot post-training.
Raises MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3; gains are largest on unseen levels and persist across embodiments.

papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant visual goal provides little guidance for preparatory actions, while uninformed action sampling makes local optimization inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy-Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize the cross-entropy method (CEM). CEM refines candidate action sequences toward each subgoal using an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop. In our primary real-robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push-T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy-guided action search improves both long-horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. Videos are available on the webpage: https://pilot-planner.github.io/.
authors: Yang Liu, Hanchen Cui, Karthik Desingh

papers.abstract: Humans and animals do not learn vision from a fixed set of data: they move, interact, and learn from the visual consequences of their actions. Motivated by this developmental view, we study whether robots can improve visual learning by actively collecting experience through curiosity-driven interaction. We introduce DySCOVER, a self-supervised framework for active robot visual learning. A robot observes RGB frames, learns a visual autoencoder that encodes and reconstructs them, and trains a recurrent world model to predict the next visual latent state conditioned on the current state and action. The agent's policy is trained only with intrinsic rewards: reconstruction error encourages visually novel observations, while the world model's error encourages transitions whose consequences are not yet predictable. This prediction error biases the policy toward more intricate trajectories that enrich the agent's set of experiences with observations beyond those encouraged by visual novelty alone. Our experiments conducted with robotic arms as the embodied agents show that adding predictive curiosity improves the vision model over using visual curiosity alone. Across variations in initial conditions, experience capacity, embodiment, and scene content, adding predictive curiosity consistently improved visual learning. These results show that predictive curiosity can improve active visual learning beyond reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
authors: Stelios Zarifis, Panagiotis Filntisis, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
bullets: Robots actively gather visual experience instead of learning from a fixed dataset.
A visual autoencoder reconstructs RGB observations, while a recurrent world model predicts future visual latents from states and actions.

The study evaluates varied initial conditions, experience capacities, embodiments, and scene contents.

papers.abstract: We introduce ClothCode, a unified generative framework for garment state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction in a shared discrete configuration space. A material-aligned tokenizer encodes garment configuration as residual vector-quantized patch tokens, while task-specific Masked Generative Transformers predict these tokens through parallel confidence-guided refinement. Across three garment templates, ClothCode reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction relative to the strongest baselines. Dynamics prediction requires only 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion. Integrated into the same model-predictive controller, ClothCode improves real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%. Further results and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ClothCode-DE32
authors: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Shiyu Fan, Zhuo He, Florent P. Audonnet, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our discrete generative framework for model-based garment manipulation. A garment configuration is encoded as a set of discrete patch tokens shared by two Masked Generative Transformers (MGTs). (1) The discrete garment representation captures local deformation states over fixed material patches. (2) For state estimation, an MGT iteratively predicts the complete token configuration from a partial point cloud. (3) For dynamics prediction, an action-conditioned MGT predicts future garment configurations for candidate actions, allowing MPC to select the trajectory with the lowest goal cost. (4) The resulting perception–prediction loop enables closed-loop garment manipulation on a real robot.

Fig. 2. Overview of ClothCode. ClothCode first learns a discrete representation of garment shape (top). Each mesh is divided into fixed patches that track the same material regions across deformations, encoded as two-level residual vector-quantization (RVQ) tokens, and reconstructed by a shared mesh decoder. This frozen representation provides a common prediction space for two tasks. For state estimation (bottom left), a masked transformer combines a partial point cloud with masked garment tokens to recover the complete garment configuration and its global position. For dynamics prediction (bottom right), a second masked transformer combines recent garment states with a candidate end-effector trajectory and jointly predicts the future garment sequence and its global motion. M denotes a masked token.
