papers.abstract: Reward design remains a major bottleneck for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation. Handcrafted dense rewards can compensate for the limited guidance provided by sparse rewards, but require substantial task-specific reward engineering. Learning rewards from videos provides a scalable, data-driven alternative to manual reward design. However, existing video-based rewards are often computed in entangled visual spaces where task-relevant state changes are confounded with extraneous visual variation. As a result, the learned reward may respond to visual distractors instead of actual task execution. To address this limitation, we propose DiTaR (Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling), a framework for learning dense rewards from heterogeneous videos. DiTaR learns a continuous task-relevant representation from multi-frame video latents through an asymmetric two-stage procedure that suppresses task-irrelevant visual variation. In the task-relevant latent space, we train a history- and language-conditioned rectified-flow model to capture task dynamics and derive a directional dense reward from temporal changes in dynamics compatibility. Together, these components enable reward modeling directly over task-relevant dynamics rather than generic visual variation. DiTaR substantially improves policy learning on MetaWorld-v3 and ManiSkill over video-based reward baselines, and transfers to real-world offline RL through reward relabeling. Reward analyses further show that DiTaR provides more reliable rewards.
authors: Dayou Li, Jionghao Wang, Peihao Wang, Jiuzhou Lei, Hao Wang, Jichen Chai, Hezhen Hu, Minghui Zheng, Zhangyang Wang, Xin Li, Wenping Wang, Zhiwen Fan

papers.abstract: Deformable-object manipulation requires accurate modeling of highly localized contact while maintaining simulation speeds suitable for interactive use. Uniformly fine tetrahedral meshes can resolve these interactions, but they introduce unnecessary degrees of freedom throughout the object. Coarse meshes are more efficient, yet they may under-resolve contact-induced deformation. We present a contact-adaptive mesh refinement framework that introduces spatial resolution only where it is most useful. The method uses geometric, elastic, and contact quantities already available from the deformable-body solver to score candidate edges. A fully GPU-parallel procedure then selects a conflict-free subset and updates both mesh topology and physical state directly within the simulation loop. We evaluate the approach on real deformable-object manipulation sequences. Adaptive refinement reduces simulation-to-real error, improves agreement with a fine-mesh reference, and remains substantially more efficient than uniformly fine simulation. These results show that local refinement can improve physical fidelity without incurring the cost of a globally fine discretization. The framework provides a practical basis for contact-rich simulation in interactive manipulation, sim-to-real modeling, and online physical digital twins.

papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra provides robust embodied reasoning, but frequent external queries increase inference time and token costs. We equip a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy with a lightweight CALL head that learns to predict when assistance is necessary. CALL reuses features from the standard policy forward pass and operates locally without consulting external models. Astra is activated solely for critical recovery events and returns control to $\pi_{0.5}$ upon stabilization. Evaluated across 40 LIBERO tasks (200 episodes), our system achieves a 97.5% success rate, outperforming the 95.5% baseline of pure $\pi_{0.5}$. In the Object, Goal, and Spatial suites, Astra executes only 5.49% of environment steps, consuming approximately 5,027 tokens per test episode. This selective intervention preserves the fast ordinary execution of $\pi_{0.5}$ while seamlessly integrating Astra's reasoning on demand. Our project page is available at https://kykgeek.github.io/Pi05_CALL_Astra/.

papers.abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.
authors: Lonnie Tankersley, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Soroush Korivand
bullets: Addresses the gap between plausible language-generated plans and physically feasible robot execution.
An API-hosted LLM produces symbolic task information, while a local Qwen3-VL verifier resolves ambiguous objects and container surrogates.
Deterministic modules handle scene grounding, reachability, collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasping, release verification, and visual assessment.
The system uses symbolic execution feedback for replanning without allowing the LLM or VLM to generate robot motions or coordinates.

papers.abstract: Multi-view perception is often treated as a safe design choice for robot manipulation: if one camera is useful, more cameras should be better. We revisit that assumption in tabletop bimanual manipulation by comparing policies trained with two large-field-of-view (FoV) wrist cameras against policies that additionally receive a head view, using controlled-variable experiments on a real bimanual platform. Across three tabletop tasks, adding a head view does not consistently improve task completion or execution quality: when the wrist cameras already observe the objects, grippers, and goal regions, wrist-only policies form a strong baseline. Restricting the wrist-camera FoV increases the potential value of a head view, but performance improves most reliably when the added view supplies concentrated, task-relevant information: region-of-interest (ROI) cropping yields more consistent head-view gains than the uncropped image, which is dominated by background and task-irrelevant regions. The data-scaling results further suggest an interaction between FoV and demonstration count: wide observations improve coverage but may require more data to stabilize, and they may reach a higher performance ceiling once enough demonstrations are available. These results suggest that camera design should be framed as a task-relevance and information-density problem rather than as a simple count of input views.

ROI-cropped head views yield more consistent gains than uncropped views dominated by background.
FoV and demonstration count interact: wider views may need more data but can achieve a higher performance ceiling.

papers.abstract: Competitive humanoid table tennis requires two distinct abilities: executing a desired return and deciding where to return the ball. We separate these two problems, with the ball landing target serving as an interface between motor control and strategy. (1) We first train a whole-body motor policy conditioned on the desired landing target, which maps the target to an executable humanoid stroke through a model-based strike planner and a learned controller. (2) We then improve the motor policy through self-play in closed-loop rallies, where the robot learns to handle incoming balls generated by another player rather than only prescribed incoming balls. At this stage, the landing targets are still sampled without considering the opponent, so the policy improves its execution without learning game strategy. (3) Finally, we freeze the entire motor stack and train a stroke-level strategic policy to choose landing targets through competitive self-play. Motor self-play improves both landing accuracy and legal-return rate during rallies. More importantly, with the entire motor stack fixed, changing only the target-selection policy leads to large differences in game outcomes: the learned strategy wins 89%, 82%, and 73% of points against center, random, and away-from-opponent baselines, respectively. The learned strategy also changes where it sends the ball according to the opponent's position and the previous target, showing that self-play learns more than simply aiming at fixed "good" locations. On hardware, the same frozen execution stack and strategic interface support complete 11-point games against a recreational human opponent, including multi-stroke rallies with both forehand and backhand returns.
authors: Fanrong Dong, Ziyi Sun, Ziqi Han, Junhan Sun, Lei Ye, Zetong Jing, Hao Zhao, Shaoxun Liu, Rongrong Wang
bullets: A target landing point serves as the interface between whole-body motor control and game strategy.
A model-based strike planner and learned controller execute strokes conditioned on desired targets.
Closed-loop motor self-play improves landing accuracy and legal-return rates without learning opponent-aware strategy.
With the motor stack frozen, strategic self-play selects targets based on the opponent and prior target, substantially changing game outcomes.
The system completes 11-point hardware games against a recreational human, including multi-stroke forehand and backhand rallies.

Opponent position enters only the strategic policy, preserving the separation between tactical selection and motor execution.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) is increasingly practical for contact-rich manipulation because GPU-based physics simulators enable real-time evaluation of large numbers of non-differentiable contact rollouts. However, this computation budget is finite and can be spent in competing ways, including denser control exploration, representing dynamics or state uncertainty, replanning more frequently, or aligning the simulation better with the physical state. Yet, the resulting trade-offs are not well understood in real-world sim-to-real control. In this work, we address this question through a systematic study of how to allocate a fixed computation budget for SMPC in contact-rich manipulation. To enable controlled comparisons, we develop a GPU-based framework named Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC), which runs on MuJoCo Warp and exposes dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment as independent dimensions of the computation budget while using the same control stack in simulation and on a real robot. Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, we find that the best budget allocation depends on the dominant sim-to-real error, with dynamics randomization not universally the most effective one.
authors: Magnus Dierking, Jo\~ao Carvalho, Vince Kurtz, Jan Peters, Nils Dengler, Georgia Chalvatzaki
bullets: SMPC budgets can be divided among control exploration, uncertainty representation, replanning frequency, and simulation–reality alignment.
The study introduces BAMPC, a GPU-based framework built on MuJoCo Warp for controlled budget comparisons.
BAMPC independently varies dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment within one shared control stack.
Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, optimal allocation varies with the primary sim-to-real error.
Dynamics randomization is not consistently the most effective use of computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC). The same control stack is used in simulation and on the real robot.

BAMPC provides a common framework to expose and compare these choices across different tasks.

papers.abstract: A longstanding goal for robot reinforcement learning (RL) is that robots learn from their own physical experience, as humans and animals do. A key obstacle to learning directly from physical experience, especially outside instrumented lab environments, is that the state of the world is usually unobservable to the learner and must be estimated from on-board sensing. Errors in that estimate corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward signal. We study this challenge using the contact-rich task of a bipedal robot learning to score soccer goals. We estimate all key state variables on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation (e.g., motion capture or overhead cameras). Because the UKF may incorrectly estimate state when the ball is unobserved, we learn a new state representation with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that, critically, only corrects the RSSM's latent state when the ball is observed. Building on RLPD, we introduce RSSM-RLPD and apply it to the task of a NAO robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal. We show that the robot learns to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget. We complement our physical robot experiments with a simulation study and show that RSSM-RLPD learns policies that achieve a higher success rate than behavior cloning, a feed-forward, and GRU baseline. Taken together, our results show that the addition of a learned state representation to existing on-robot learning methods enables RL from real-robot data even with a high degree of partial observability.

The robot achieved 100% success, compared with 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget.
Simulation results also show higher success than behavior cloning, feed-forward, and GRU baselines; the scope is demonstrated on soccer dribbling and complementary simulation experiments.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to be precise in free space to establish the intended contacts, and compliant once in contact to avoid excessive forces. Imitation learning has proven effective for simpler manipulation tasks, but the compliance underlying a demonstration is not directly observable and is therefore difficult to infer from demonstration data alone. We present a framework that makes compliance explicit at every stage. During data collection, the operator teleoperates the real robot while a synchronized digital twin visualizes the error between the commanded reference and the achieved pose, making the current compliance visible, and selects between two discrete compliance modes. To generalize across object poses, we combine Laplacian editing, which retargets trajectories efficiently but is not physics-consistent during contact, with simulation-based trajectory optimization, which enforces physical plausibility but offers no manual guidance. Finally, a residual reinforcement learning policy refines the interaction forces by adjusting the reference pose of the underlying admittance controller. We evaluate on three flipping and pushing tasks on a Franka FR3 based on a total of 7 demonstrations across tasks. Our method is successful on all 40 out-of-distribution trials, compared to 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines, with our base policy alone reaching 35/40.
authors: Chunyu Jiang, Yichen Cai, Shuai Li, Wenbin Sun, Jo\~ao Carvalho, Kostas Daniilidis, Oleg Arenz, Cristiana de Farias, Jan Peters
bullets: Targets contact-rich tasks requiring precise free-space motion and safe, compliant contact.
Uses a synchronized digital twin and two discrete compliance modes to expose otherwise hidden compliance during teleoperation.
Combines Laplacian trajectory editing with simulation-based optimization to retarget demonstrations while maintaining physical plausibility.
Residual RL adjusts the admittance controller’s reference pose to refine interaction forces.
Across 40 out-of-distribution trials, the method succeeds in all trials, versus 35/40 for its base policy and 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines.

(b) The collected human demonstrations are augmented via free-space motion Laplacian editing and in-contact trajectory optimization given randomly sampled positions and poses of the object in simulation. (c) A consistency flow matching-based policy is trained on the augmented dataset. (d) A residual RL policy is trained upon the base policy in simulation. (e) The system takes in the robot’s proprioception, stiffness of the admittance controller, external force feedback, and the object pose estimated by the digital twin to predict expected stiffness level and reference poses for implementing the task.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in learned whole-body controllers for humanoid robots has enabled robust free-space motion by tracking kinematic targets such as joint or end-effector trajectories. This interface provides a useful abstraction for upstream systems, including motion capture, teleoperation, or generative models, which can specify desired motion without reasoning about forces or balance. However, this abstraction has largely been limited to robot motion, requiring task-specific controllers or retraining for object interaction. We introduce OIL, an Object Interaction Layer that extends the kinematic command interface of whole-body control to include desired object motion and contact. OIL augments a standard controller with object-centric commands and translates them into coordinated whole-body behavior while preserving locomotion and balance. This design enables a single learned policy to execute non-prehensile interactions, including pushing, pulling, two-arm pick-and-place, and locomotion-coupled transport, directly from object-level kinematic targets without task-specific retraining. In simulation, we demonstrate that object-level commands improve performance over robot-centric controllers while matching task-specific policies across variations in object properties such as mass and size. We further demonstrate zero-shot generalization to novel behavior combinations and sim-to-real transfer on the Digit humanoid robot.
authors: Pranay Dugar, Mohitvishnu S. Gadde, Rajesh Mangannavar, Aayam Kumar Shrestha, Alan Fern
bullets: Addresses the limitation of robot-centric kinematic interfaces that require task-specific controllers or retraining for object interaction.
Adds desired object motion and contact commands to a standard whole-body controller.
Supports pushing, pulling, two-arm pick-and-place, and locomotion-coupled transport from object-level targets.
In simulation, improves over robot-centric controllers and matches task-specific policies across varied object masses and sizes.
Demonstrates zero-shot behavior combinations and sim-to-real transfer on the Digit humanoid.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of the Object-Interactive Controller. A behavior generator produces an object-interaction directive, split into an interaction directive dit (desired object position ôt, end-effector targets p̂Rt , p̂Lt , and contact conditions ĉRt , ĉLt ) and a base directive dbt (desired velocity v̂t, turn rate ω̂t, and base orientation b̂t). OIL (blue), running at 50 Hz, maps dit, object state (updated at 10 Hz), and robot proprioception to an arm joint directive ut. The Masked Humanoid Controller (MHC, green), also running at 50 Hz, combines ut and dbt with robot proprioception to produce PD targets at for all actuated joints, which are executed by a PD controller at 2 kHz. During training, the MHC weights remain frozen and only the OIL weights are optimized.

Figure 1: Overview of OIL. An object-interaction layer that augments a whole-body controller with object-level motion and contact directives, enabling a single controller to execute diverse loco-manipulation behaviors such as walking up to a box, picking it up from different heights and positions in front of the robot, walking while holding it up, placing it down at different locations, and pushing it on the surface with one or two arms. It further allows composition of these skills without any per-task finetuning.

papers.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation. All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation will be released as open source.
authors: Bince Qu, Wei Chen, Bo Zhang
bullets: Targets generalist embodied manipulation without directly training a vision-language-action model.
Provides LLM agents with a visual-geometric control panel for understanding and invoking robot tasks.
Uses Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with the RoboHarness interface.
Reports better performance than state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks.
The implementation is planned for open-source release.

papers.abstract: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.
authors: Mark K. Ho, Michael L. Littman, James MacGlashan, Fiery Cushman, Joseph L. Austerweil
bullets: Addresses the limited computational study of teaching by demonstration.
Distinguishes intentional “showing” from simply “doing” a task.
Develops a Bayesian model of how demonstrators teach through examples.
Two experiments find human teaching behavior matches the model’s predictions.
Standard inverse reinforcement learning algorithms benefit from demonstrations intended to teach.

papers.abstract: We present FoldBack, a self-correcting masked generative policy for long-horizon garment folding. Existing long-trajectory policies may continue after a missed or slipped grasp even when the garment has not reached the intended configuration. We structure FoldBack's recovery mechanisms around three inference-time decisions: when to refine and verify, how to roll back, and where and how to retry. FoldBack aligns refinement and grasp verification with pick-and-place events, returns the robot to a retryable pre-grasp configuration while preserving successful grasps, and selectively regenerates the failed segment and selected future actions while avoiding previous failed grasp locations. To our knowledge, FoldBack is the first editable full-trajectory policy to unify these decisions, enabling failed interactions to be detected, undone, and repaired before execution continues, without recovery demonstrations or base-policy retraining. Across 33 real garments from six categories, FoldBack achieves 75.2% final folding success and 0.837 final-mask IoU, versus 45.7% and 0.689 for the strongest prior baseline.
bullets: Addresses trajectory failures caused by missed or slipped grasps that would otherwise propagate through folding.
Uses inference-time refinement and grasp verification around pick-and-place events.
Rolls back to retryable pre-grasp states while preserving successful grasps, then selectively regenerates failed and future actions.
Avoids previously failed grasp locations and requires neither recovery demonstrations nor base-policy retraining.
On 33 real garments across six categories, achieves 75.2% final success and 0.837 final-mask IoU, exceeding the reported prior baseline.

papers.abstract: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) enables collaborative policy learning across distributed agents with heterogeneous environments. While recent methods based on variance reduction, divergence penalization, and momentum optimization improve FRL under heterogeneous settings, they still primarily synchronize policy or value-network parameters and do not explicitly address distributional mismatch among heterogeneous clients. Therefore, we propose \textbf{FedGuide}, a FRL framework that uses diffusion priors as behavior models to provide personalized data supported distributions for heterogeneous local policy learning. Instead of directly averaging local policies, FedGuide aggregates those diffusion priors through Optimal-Transport Mixture-of-Experts (OT-MoE), preserving heterogeneous behavior modes in distribution space. It further develops a Distribution Correction Estimation (DICE) value baseline to provide low-variance, return-aware guidance for local policy improvement. Experiments across heterogeneous environments show that FedGuide outperforms representative FRL methods in client-average returns, final-round performance, and worst-round robustness, while maintaining stable learning under stronger heterogeneity.
bullets: Targets distributional mismatch among heterogeneous clients, beyond synchronizing policy or value parameters.
Uses diffusion priors as personalized behavior models to support local policy learning.
Aggregates diffusion priors with an Optimal-Transport Mixture-of-Experts approach to preserve diverse behavior modes.
Introduces a Distribution Correction Estimation value baseline for low-variance, return-aware policy guidance.
Experiments report better client-average returns, final-round performance, and worst-round robustness, including under stronger heterogeneity.

papers.abstract: A robot's learned model of its own dynamics is only valid until those dynamics change: actuators wear, payloads shift, and joints stiffen. A model-based agent that keeps training as if nothing happened adapts slowly, dragged back by a replay buffer full of stale experience. We present Changepoint-Aware World Models (CAWM), a DreamerV3 agent that detects an abrupt dynamics shift from its own internal prediction error, using an online CUSUM test against a rolling baseline that fires only on abrupt change rather than on slow learning drift. It then forgets stale replay, keeping the learned representation while flushing obsolete data. On simulated locomotion under two robot-relevant shifts, doubled gravity and halved actuator gain, CAWM recovers substantially faster than passive retraining. It also beats a strong baseline that respawns a fresh dynamics model on detection, the deep-world-model analogue of model-bank methods. With the response triggered at the shift, CAWM gains +95 to +153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds, while matching that respawn at asymptote. Running the detector in closed loop reproduces this gain on the gravity shift. The benefit holds across both shift types, and is largest when the shift is severe enough that old data is genuinely obsolete.
bullets: Targets slow adaptation after actuator wear, payload changes, or joint stiffening make stored experience obsolete.
Uses DreamerV3 with an online CUSUM test on internal prediction error to detect abrupt shifts without reacting to gradual learning drift.
Flushes obsolete replay data instead of retraining from stale experience or replacing the entire dynamics model.
On simulated locomotion with doubled gravity or halved actuator gain, it recovers faster than passive retraining and fresh-model respawning.
With shift-triggered detection, it gains 95–153 return in the first 30k post-shift frames over three seeds and matches respawning at asymptote; benefits are largest for severe shifts.

Passive retraining stays stuck, CAWM recovers fastest, and the MBCD-style respawn crashes hardest immediately after the shift as its fresh model relearns before catching up. The green arrow marks CAWM’s asymptotic gain over passive.

Fig. 3. Windowed mean return for the gravity (top) and motor-wear (bottom) shifts, three seeds (error bars: std). Green annotations give CAWM’s gain over the MBCD-style respawn: large in the transient, shrinking to a tie at asymptote, on both shifts.

An online CUSUM test against a rolling trailing baseline fires only on an abrupt dynamics shift (blue: the changepoint machinery). On detection it forgets stale replay, capping the buffer while keeping the encoder, so the world model re-fits the new dynamics and the agent recovers. papers.title: Changepoint-Aware World Models: Detecting Dynamics Shifts and Recovering by Forgetting Stale Replay in Model-Based RL
papers.tldr: CAWM detects abrupt robot-dynamics changes and rapidly adapts by discarding stale replay while preserving its learned representation.

papers.abstract: We establish convergence bounds for deep $V$-learning with horizon $H$. The algorithm fits a scalar value function to targets from executed transitions and selects actions using a predictive model and the value function. For current observed-successor targets with fresh true-kernel outcomes, the conditional mean is $\mathcal{T}^βV$, which averages over behavior-policy actions. The Bellman optimality update is $\mathcal{T} V$. We decompose the update error into six residuals: fitting, transition reuse, target construction, replay, action selection, and exploration. Under $L^s$ concentrability, their $L^p$ norms ($p=s/(s-1)$) control expected $L^1$ policy loss. The bound explicitly weights residuals from only the last $H-1$ update blocks, plus an initialization term for shorter runs. We quantify the cost of a shared sampling distribution across horizon levels. For statistical error bounds of order $n^{-ν}$, we derive optimal continuous allocations and an integer allocation whose objective is within a factor $2^ν$ of the constrained optimum. A margin condition with exponent $α$ gives action error of order $Λ^{1+α/p}$, where $Λ$ combines network drift and score error; a one-step construction proves the exponent sharp. Bounds on the distance between frozen and optimal scores transfer an optimal-gap condition to frozen-iterate gap bounds while retaining the mass of optimal ties. Survival probabilities and coverage conditions at deployment yield bounds for policies selected with approximate scores. Separate spatial ReLU networks per horizon level give a conditional neural regression rate, and the finite-state case gives a log-free expected fit rate. These results give expected policy-loss consistency for the fixed-horizon generative-reset approximate-ERM procedure with exact action scores and provide an explicit residual-decay criterion for FIFO/interleaved SGD.
bullets: Decomposes update error into six residuals: fitting, transition reuse, target construction, replay, action selection, and exploration.
Under $L^s$ concentrability, controls expected $L^1$ policy loss using residual norms from the latest $H-1$ update blocks plus initialization.
Optimizes horizon-level sampling allocations and gives an integer allocation within a factor $2^ν$ of the constrained optimum for $n^{-ν}$ statistical errors.
A margin condition yields action error of order $Λ^{1+α/p}$; a one-step construction shows this exponent is sharp.
Establishes consistency for fixed-horizon generative-reset approximate ERM and gives residual-decay criteria for FIFO/interleaved SGD, with extensions to neural regression and finite-state settings.

papers.selection_reason: Establishes convergence bounds and sharp action-gap bounds for deep V-learning, a core component of reinforcement learning for robotics and embodied agents.
papers.title: A Convergence Framework for Deep $V$-Learning: Error Propagation and Sharp Action-Gap Bounds
papers.tldr: A convergence theory for deep finite-horizon V-learning decomposes learning and sampling errors, derives sharp action-gap bounds, and specifies conditions for policy-loss consistency.

papers.abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning has demonstrated remarkable capability in quadrotor control, yet learned policies offer no guarantee of respecting safety constraints during training or deployment. We present CALOS (Control-Affine Lyapunov On-manifold Safety), a runtime safety layer that enforces attitude constraints on a quadrotor without modifying the underlying learning algorithm. CALOS formulates four tilt-angle inequalities and a Lyapunov descent condition as a single quadratic program whose solution is the minimum-norm correction to the nominal torque output of the policy. The quadratic program is solved exactly via active-set enumeration over the three-dimensional torque space, with a computational cost low enough to enforce constraints in real time across thousands of parallel simulation environments, as required by modern massively parallel Deep Reinforcement Learning training. Evaluated on trajectory-tracking tasks in NVIDIA Isaac Lab, CALOS reduces lateral tracking error by 55-60% relative to an unconstrained Proximal Policy Optimization baseline while achieving zero attitude-constraint violations on the training trajectory. By restricting exploration to safe regions of the state space, the safety layer also accelerates training convergence and improves data efficiency without producing suboptimal policies.
bullets: Addresses the lack of safety guarantees in deep reinforcement learning for quadrotor control.
Applies four tilt-angle inequalities and a Lyapunov descent condition as constraints in a single quadratic program.
Computes the minimum-norm correction to the policy’s nominal torque without changing the underlying learning algorithm.
Uses exact active-set enumeration in three-dimensional torque space for real-time operation, including massively parallel simulation.
In Isaac Lab trajectory-tracking tasks, it reports 55–60% lower lateral error than unconstrained PPO and zero attitude violations on the training trajectory.

papers.abstract: The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation. Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts. Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences. Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble. But how much of the strategy must be specified? The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win. AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble. In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning. The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete. The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner. For videos, see our website: https://alpha-nist.github.io/
bullets: Trains from scratch on all 20 NIST Assembly Task Board #1 tasks using only binary task rewards.
Reaches 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning.
Handles episodes containing ten assembly pairs without a prescribed order, rewarding success only when all are complete.
Discovers dexterous and planning-like behaviors, including strategic grasping, geometry-based reorientation, and task interleaving.

ALPHANIST SOLVES THESE TASKS WITHOUT A PRESCRIBED ORDER OR EXPLICIT TASK DECOMPOSITION. FOR EXAMPLE, WHEN THERE ARE 10 ACTIVE PAIRS, THE POLICY RECEIVES A SUCCESS REWARD ONLY WHEN ALL 10 ARE IN THEIR ASSIGNED BOARD SLOTS.

papers.title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
papers.tldr: AlphaNIST shows that sparse binary rewards can drive a single robot policy to discover complex assembly strategies across diverse NIST tasks in simulation.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have made them capable generalist physical agents for a range of manipulation tasks. However, successful operation in an unfamiliar environment may require an agent to seek task-relevant information through interaction when it is absent from the observations: it may need to determine where a relevant object is, inspect an unobserved property, or discover the effect of an unfamiliar tool. We thus introduce RoboQuest, a benchmark for goal-directed embodied exploration, where agents must actively acquire task-relevant information through physical interaction, use the resulting evidence to adapt subsequent actions, and autonomously decide when to commit to task completion. RoboQuest comprises ten mobile manipulation tasks centered on three forms of uncertainty: search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing. We evaluate five frontier multimodal agents through a common visuomotor interface, as well as a $π_{0.5}$ policy fine-tuned on the full-episode demonstrations we release. The best agent succeeds in only 23\% of the episodes, and the fine-tuned policy almost never succeeds. Isolated tests of the execution skills the tasks are built from, with the hidden information supplied, show that the agents can carry out most of the required actions, and our failure analysis attributes only a minority of the failures to execution. Our failure analysis further finds that the agents often stop exploring too early as they make decisions before observing the required evidence for task completion. We also find that agents rarely prevent or repair the disturbances caused by their exploration. Moreover, learning by trial and error remains difficult for most models.
bullets: Introduces ten mobile-manipulation tasks spanning search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing.
Agents must acquire task-relevant evidence, adapt actions, and decide when to complete a task.
Evaluates five multimodal agents and a fine-tuned π₀.₅ policy through a common visuomotor interface.
The best agent succeeds in only 23% of episodes, while the fine-tuned policy almost never succeeds.
Failures primarily involve stopping exploration too early, neglecting disturbances, and difficulty learning through trial and error.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for robot policy learning, which predict actions in three forms: raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents. However, existing action representations primarily model action trajectories, with limited consideration of the visual dynamics induced by these actions. We introduce ViDAL, a Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space that anchors continuous action latents in the future visual dynamics of the scene. Specifically, ViDAL learns action latent space by training an Action Variational Autoencoder (Action VAE) to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent with future scene dynamics. When integrated into downstream robot policies, the proposed Action VAE serves as a plug-in action interface compatible with multiple VLA architectures and enables optional future-video prediction as an additional capability. Empirically, ViDAL outperforms competitive baselines on LIBERO with 98.1% average success, improves a multi-task $π_{0.5}$ policy on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and from 33.2% to 43.1% (Random) success rates over 50 dual-arm tasks, and yields 20.0% and 23.4% absolute success-rate gains on real-world single-arm Franka and dual-arm ARX robot platforms.
bullets: Existing VLA action representations mainly model trajectories without explicitly capturing the visual dynamics actions induce.
ViDAL trains an Action VAE to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent space with future scene dynamics.
The resulting plug-in action interface is compatible with multiple VLA architectures and can optionally support future-video prediction.
ViDAL achieves 98.1% average success on LIBERO and improves π₀.₅ on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and 33.2% to 43.1% (Random).
It also reports absolute success-rate gains on real-world Franka and ARX robot platforms, though the abstract does not specify the baseline setup or broader limitations.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). In this work, we propose a benchmark-agnostic evaluation framework to measure the behavioural robustness of models by characterising how successful trajectories are executed under perturbation. We implement this methodology by extending the widely-used LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. Across three state-of-the-art VLA models, four LIBERO task suites and seven perturbation conditions, we evaluate changes in both typical successful behaviour and its variability, including metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour. We find that perturbations can alter the behaviour of successful trajectories, a phenomenon which cannot necessarily be inferred from TSR alone. Across LIBERO suites, we identify cases where state-of-the-art VLA models achieve comparable TSR under the same perturbation condition, yet behaviour on successful trajectories diverges substantially. Therefore, to have a more robust assessment of task performance, we argue that suitable measures of robustness should capture not only whether a task is completed, but also how the robot behaves while completing it. When evaluating the robustness of VLA models, TSR may be complemented by behavioural evaluation metrics that characterise the nature and variability of successful task execution by robots.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark-agnostic framework for evaluating behavioural robustness in tabletop manipulation.
Extends LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus across four task suites, seven perturbation conditions, and three VLA models.
Analyses motion smoothness, efficiency, gripper behaviour, and variability in successful trajectories.
Finds that perturbations can substantially change successful behaviour even when task success rates remain comparable.
Argues that behavioural metrics should complement task success rate for more complete robustness assessment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation, but their zero-shot generalization in new tasks and environments remains limited, and their reliance on specialized training keeps them from benefiting directly from rapidly advancing general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs). In parallel, recent agentic robotic systems leverage VLMs for high-level reasoning or coding agents for robot control, but often depend on extensive external models and tools, introducing additional complexity and cost. This motivates us to ask: Can a general-purpose VLM itself operate a robot more like the human teleoperator by reasoning directly from observations, issuing actions, and continuously adapting to execution feedback, without relying on external models such as learned action experts, coding agents or grounding tools like SAM3? In this work, we introduce MotorMind, a robot manipulation harness that connects VLM-proposed mid-level actions to deterministic robot control and feedback, with asynchronous monitoring and background memory updates. Without task-specific policy training, coding agents, or additional grounding tools such as SAM3, MotorMind achieves 66.7% success on the base LIBERO-PRO suites and 53.8% under perturbations, compared with at most 13.3% and 19.2%, respectively, for the prior zero-shot methods we evaluate. The same interface reaches 95% average success on a real xArm6 robot across direct manipulation and human-perturbation settings. Replacing the backbone with a stronger VLM further improves performance, while the remaining failures - primarily due to visual grounding, embodied reasoning, and action knowledge - decrease as VLM capability improves. These results show that a general-purpose VLM, when equipped with an appropriate mid-level action representation and asynchronous execution harness, can perform effective zero-shot robotic manipulation.
bullets: Targets limited zero-shot generalization and the complexity of systems requiring specialized policies, coding agents, or grounding tools.
Uses a robot manipulation harness with VLM-proposed mid-level actions, deterministic control, asynchronous monitoring, and background memory updates.
Achieves 66.7% success on base LIBERO-PRO and 53.8% under perturbations, versus at most 13.3% and 19.2% for evaluated prior zero-shot methods.
Reaches 95% average success on a real xArm6 across direct manipulation and human-perturbation settings.
Performance improves with stronger VLMs; remaining failures mainly involve visual grounding, embodied reasoning, and action knowledge.

papers.abstract: Aerial manipulation in outdoor environments remains challenging due to the simultaneous requirements of reliable state estimation, stable aerial motion, and precise manipulation under external disturbances. In this work, we present a real-world outdoor aerial manipulation framework that integrates imitation learning, onboard LiDAR-inertial state estimation, and whole-body model predictive control. A Diffusion Policy is trained from manipulation demonstrations to generate desired end-effector motions from onboard observations. These learned commands are executed by a whole-body MPC that jointly coordinates the aerial platform and manipulator to realize the desired end-effector trajectory. To eliminate reliance on external motion-capture infrastructure, the platform employs onboard LiDAR-inertial odometry for state estimation during outdoor operation. We validate the complete framework on a physical aerial manipulator and demonstrate successful execution of outdoor manipulation tasks. The experimental results show that demonstration-driven manipulation policies can be effectively integrated with onboard state estimation and model-based whole-body control to enable aerial manipulation beyond controlled indoor environments.
bullets: Addresses outdoor aerial manipulation under disturbances, where state estimation, flight stability, and precise interaction must work together.
Uses a Diffusion Policy trained from demonstrations to generate desired end-effector motions from onboard observations.
Combines LiDAR-inertial odometry with whole-body model predictive control to coordinate the aerial vehicle and manipulator without motion capture.
Validated on a physical aerial manipulator through successful outdoor manipulation tasks.
Demonstrates feasibility beyond controlled indoor environments; the abstract does not quantify performance or specify task and environmental limits.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in data-driven robot manipulation policies have substantially improved task execution and generalization. However, real-world deployment still relies heavily on humans for failure assessment, correction, and environment reset, while models often fail to continually learn from failures and corrective experience. We present REVOLVE (Robot Evolving via Orchestrated Loops, Verification, and Experience), an automated closed-loop framework for evolving robot manipulation with minimal human intervention. Built on a unified software platform, REVOLVE integrates data collection, policy training and deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning into a single closed-loop workflow. Its Automated Reset and Correction (ARC) architecture automatically resets the environment and intervenes to correct policy failures. Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) continually improves the manipulation policy and agent by feeding real-world interaction and failure--correction data back into policy learning and using an external mismatch memory to refine agent judgments. Experiments across four real-world manipulation tasks show that, after five iterations, REVOLVE improves average policy success rate by 18.5% and agent judgment accuracy by 8.5%, while reducing human effort in data collection and deployment testing by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively. These results demonstrate that REVOLVE transforms real-world deployment into a closed-loop learning process that continually accumulates and uses execution experience, enabling continual evolution of both the policy and supervisory model with substantially less human intervention.
bullets: Addresses the need for humans to assess failures, correct behavior, and reset environments during real-world deployment.
Integrates data collection, policy training/deployment, failure recovery, and continual learning in one workflow.
Uses Automated Reset and Correction (ARC) for recovery and Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) to improve both manipulation policies and agent judgments.
Across four real-world tasks and five iterations, average policy success rose 18.5% and judgment accuracy rose 8.5%.
Human effort in data collection and deployment testing fell by 94.4% and 95.1%, respectively.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the REVOLVE framework. It integrates three core components: (1) REVOLVE, a unified software platform that streamlines data collection, policy learning, and active correction to significantly lower deployment barriers; (2) the Automated Reset and Correction (ARC) architecture, which leverages deterministic control for autonomous environment resetting and failure intervention to generate continuous correction data with minimal human effort; and (3) the Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) framework, employing dual memory banks to continuously co-evolve manipulation policies and VLM evaluation reliability during real-world deployment.

Fig. 3: Overview of the Dual-Loop Evolution (DLE) framework. Two synergistic loops operate concurrently during deployment: (1) the Corrective Evolution Loop updates pluggable policy backends using inference and recovery trajectories via a Correction Memory Bank; (2) the Judgement Evolution Loop accumulates agent-human evaluation discrepancies in a CLIP-indexed mismatch memory. This enhances agent state-detection via context retrieval without parameter updates, enabling continuous co-evolution of manipulation and evaluation capabilities.

Fig. 2: Overview of the REVOLVE software platform. The unified web interface provides three integrated workspaces: a user operation platform for data collection, a policy training workplace, and an agent monitor for test-time deployment. In the physical task arena, the system leverages deterministic control for automated data acquisition and environment resetting, automatically intervening upon policy failures. This mechanism continuously generates real-world interaction and failurecorrection data for subsequent policy optimization.

papers.abstract: A user who brings a generalist manipulation policy into their home or office wants it to pick up their objects from their shelves, counters, and tables. Yet even a strong generalist like $\pi_{0.5}$ achieves 0% pickup success in our captured deployment scenes without adaptation, and collecting real demonstrations in every user's environment is prohibitively expensive. We present Splat2Act, an automated real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that personalizes a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a specific scene and object set using only a handheld phone scan and images of the user's objects. Unlike prior real-to-sim work that reconstructs individual tabletops, Splat2Act operates on building-scale indoor environments: it builds a photorealistic digital twin with 3D Gaussian Splatting and collision geometry, automatically discovers tabletop and non-tabletop receptacles, constructs feasible pickup tasks, and generates successful demonstrations with a privileged simulation oracle, with only scene and object capture required from a human. Applied to 101 scanned campus environments with a median navigable area of 104.87 m$^2$ and 7 receptacles, the pipeline yields 852 receptacles and over 68,000 pickup demonstrations. We fine-tune $\pi_{0.5}$ in two stages: Stage 1 adapts to hundreds of public object assets, drawn either from the deployment scene alone or from all 101 scenes; Stage 2 personalizes to the user's own objects on the deployment scene's receptacles. Our strongest personalized policy reaches 62.5% aggregate pickup success in the target scene. Deployed on a real Stretch 3, the same policy achieves 63.9% success on a 12-task subset, closely tracking its 66.7% simulated success on those tasks. These results suggest that automated real-to-sim-to-real training can personalize VLA manipulation policies using only simulation-oracle data.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models encode broad manipulation priors, yet adapting them to specific tasks requires balancing limited robot interaction, computational resources, and safety constraints. Noise space learning (NSL) adapts flow-matching-based VLAs by learning a context-conditioned distribution over noise while keeping the pretrained VLA fixed. Building on prior noise-steering methods, we formulate NSL as an interface for VLA adaptation that accommodates different learning algorithms and instantiate it with PPO, SAC, and AWR. Theoretically, we provide an information-theoretic analysis of how NSL enables efficient adaptation. Empirically, we study these NSL algorithms on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks under interaction, computation, and execution constraints. Across these settings, we develop a suite of effective NSL variants and derive practical recommendations for choosing among them under different resource and deployment regimes.
authors: Junjie Lu, Chuheng Zhang, Yucen Wang, Yuhua Jiang, Xinyao Qin, Min Xu, Li Zhao
bullets: Addresses VLA adaptation under limited robot interaction, computation, and safety constraints.
Learns a context-conditioned noise distribution as an adaptation interface for flow-matching-based VLAs.
Implements the interface with PPO, SAC, and AWR, while providing an information-theoretic analysis.
Evaluates variants on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and four real-robot manipulation tasks across multiple resource constraints.
Offers practical guidance for selecting NSL variants under different training and deployment regimes.

papers.abstract: Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation-action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy, which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). We find that time-aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing.
authors: Changhao Wang, Jaden Clark, Shuran Song
bullets: Addresses failures caused by fixed-rate observation-action sequences under changing observation rates, delays, and inference latency.
Conditions a diffusion transformer on observation capture times and desired action execution times.
Compares timestamp token embeddings with time-aware rotary positional encodings; time-aware RoPE is more robust because attention directly uses physical time.
Uses temporal randomization during training to support varied sensing and execution schedules, including asynchronous and multi-rate data.
Improves dynamic and multisensory task performance while preserving nominal performance on quasi-static tasks and increasing timing robustness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Chronos Policy. Tokens are paired with their physical times. Figure 1: Timing-related issues in robot policy learning. These timing effects matter differently across tasks. (b) In dynamic tasks, the key temporal relationship is between when an observation is captured and when an action takes effect. (c) In multisensory tasks, the key temporal relationship is between when different observations are captured. (d) Even in quasi-static tasks, differences between data-collection and deployment timing can create temporal mismatch. Standard fixed-rate policy representations obscure these distinctions by treating sequence position as a proxy for time.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering module. We propose Dream to Remember (D2R), which continually steers a frozen generalist policy toward new tasks, while retaining its earlier skills. As the steering module learns a new task, a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, anchoring the module to its earlier behavior without a replay buffer or new data. When the world model is faithful enough, D2R learns the new task entirely in imagination. Otherwise, it learns the task in the environment while using the world model only to rehearse prior tasks. On CALVIN, D2R improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, raising average success from 63.7% to 74.8%, while LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence drops it to 11.7%. With a frozen off-the-shelf generalist policy and world model, $\pi_0$ and A2World, D2R learns unseen LIBERO-90 tasks in the environment while keeping $\pi_0$'s performance on the LIBERO suites it was fine-tuned on, even though the world model is not accurate enough for policy optimization. Finally, on a real Franka robot, D2R improves three tasks in sequence entirely in imagination while retaining the earlier improvements.
authors: Bahey Tharwat, Iman Nematollahi, Marvin Alles, Xingyuan Zhang, Akshay L Chandra, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when adapting robot policies to sequentially arriving tasks.
Learns a steering module for a frozen generative policy rather than changing the policy weights.
Uses a frozen pretrained world model to rehearse prior tasks via imagined rollouts, avoiding replay buffers or additional data.
Can learn new tasks entirely in imagination when the world model is sufficiently accurate; otherwise, it combines environment learning with imagined rehearsal.
Demonstrated on CALVIN, LIBERO, and a real Franka robot, retaining prior abilities while improving sequentially added tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of D2R. (a) Steering in imagination: A small steering module learns to shape the noise fed to the frozen policy through RL in a frozen world model. (b) Rehearsal in the world model: The world model imagines rollouts of prior tasks, where a KL penalty anchors the module to its earlier behavior. (c) Simulator or memory: A faithful world model supports both learning and rehearsal, while a coarser one can still support rehearsal as learning moves to the environment.

Figure 1: Dream to Remember (D2R): We adapt a frozen generative policy sequentially by steering its input noise with a small module trained inside a learned world model. While the module learns the current task, the same world model regenerates imagined rollouts of prior tasks, and we regularize the module toward its previous behavior on those states. Skills thus accumulate without revisiting prior tasks on the robot or storing their trajectories. Rehearsal requires less world model fidelity than optimization, allowing even a model too coarse for learning a new task to preserve prior skills.

Figure 3: Continual steering on LIBERO. Diagonal cells show the success when each task is learned, and cells below show the forgetting, the points lost after each later stage. DSRL forgets each task as soon as the next is learned, instruction KL reduces this, and D2R keeps the tasks to the end.

Figure 4: Continual steering on a real Franka robot. Heatmaps follow Figure 3, with the success rate when each task is learned on the diagonal and the forgetting score below it. D2R retains prior gains across the sequence, whereas DSRL without rehearsal loses about half of them. Adaptation occurs entirely in imagination, with the robot used only for evaluation.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video-diffusion world-action models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Rebuilds a pretrained 2B-parameter model’s inference interface using visual latents, cached text features, 12 transformer blocks, and a single rectified-flow step.
Achieves 95.5% success across 400 LIBERO episodes with 57 ms inference latency and 2.4 GiB of GPU memory.
Runs 11× faster than its teacher while using 18.5× fewer FLOPs and 3.2× less memory.
Its world head retains the ability to forecast scene motion.

papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.
authors: Hongrui Zheng, Aditya Singh, Rahul Mangharam
bullets: Addresses joint constraints whose team-level violation costs do not reveal which agents caused them.
Uses Signal Temporal Logic robustness with running-maximum cost increments to measure episode-level violations.
Applies differentiable dynamics and full-episode sensitivities to allocate delayed constraint effects among agents.
Evaluated on payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control.
Reports 1.6–5.1× higher safe-success in transport, 11.1% better navigation safe-success, and 50–68% higher traffic throughput than constrained baselines.

papers.abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Peidong Liu, Mingyang Li, Jiawei Li, Wenhow Li, Wenbo Ding, Xiang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting robot interaction data and the lack of action labels in human videos.
Learns continuous latent actions from frame transitions using perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals.
Pre-trains a vision-language-action policy, aligns it to the target robot embodiment, and applies task-specific post-training.
Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, it improves real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% when annotated human video increases from 1K to 5K hours.
The resulting policy generalizes to unseen visual conditions.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of LAPT-Scale. LAPT-Scale-LAM annotates egocentric human videos with continuous implicit actions. LAPT-Scale-Policy uses these annotations for human-video pretraining, followed by target-robot embodiment alignment and downstream post-training.
Figure 2: Human-video data overview. The corpus spans everyday egocentric manipulation across varied environments and interactions, providing broad coverage for latent-action learning.

Figure 8: Autoregressive LAM rollout comparison. Later predictions condition on the model’s own generated frames. papers.abstract: Standard Policy Gradient (PG) algorithms suffer from high estimation variance because they rely on Monte Carlo updates. While off-policy variance reduction mitigates this problem, establishing optimal sample complexity currently requires either restrictive assumptions, such as uniformly bounded importance weights, or impractical second-order operations. In this work, we introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced PG (LVR-PG), a unified theoretical framework that abstracts a class of first-order estimators that integrate recursive updates with defensive importance sampling, including known estimators such as PAGE-PG and STORM-PG. We prove that this algorithmic class achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ last-iterate global convergence under weak gradient domination for general parametric policies. We establish this guarantee using purely first-order updates, with minimal assumptions and without gradient preconditioners. By extending state-of-the-art lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, we establish an $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity limit, confirming our framework is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.
authors: Leonardo Cesani, Matteo Papini, Marcello Restelli
bullets: Addresses the high variance of Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimates and limitations of existing off-policy variance reduction methods.
Unifies recursive estimators with defensive importance sampling, including PAGE-PG and STORM-PG.
Proves last-iterate global convergence with approximately O(ε⁻²) sample complexity for general parametric policies under weak gradient domination.
Uses only first-order updates, without bounded importance weights or gradient preconditioners.
Extends lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, showing the rate is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.

papers.abstract: Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena, presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation. To enable systematic evaluation under these conditions, we introduce AutoBio+, a simulation benchmark and framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments. AutoBio+ comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation. We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures. To further enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed from 6 real laboratory scenes. For efficient large-scale data generation and evaluation, we further build a parallel simulation framework on top of mjlab, proposing Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) and integrating batched rendering with decoupled trajectory replay for demonstration generation and model-independent closed-loop policy evaluation. Our evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real-world experiments further demonstrate a reduced sim-to-real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for realistic manipulation evaluation. Supplementary materials are available at https://autobio-plus.github.io/AutoBioPlus.

Provides scalable evaluation through parallel finite-state machines, batched rendering, and decoupled trajectory replay.
Finds substantial task-dependent variation in policy performance, with real-world experiments indicating a reduced sim-to-real gap.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy-discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
authors: Faith Ogunwoye, Didar Seyidov, Konstantin Gubernatorov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: VLA commands arrive sparsely and irregularly, potentially causing abrupt motion near people.
The benchmark isolates controller effects by replaying the same commands and arrival traces across alternatives.
Interpolation reduced modeled p99 jerk by 83% on delayed human-motion traces, with a 2.0 cm tracking cost; jerk-limited generation reduced jerk further at greater cost.
Results across three VLA pipelines showed inconsistent links between entropy discontinuities and motion quality, and entropy gating helped only one pipeline.
On a physical UR3, interpolation reduced accelerometer-derived jerk in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not show the same contrast.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts. We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves representation features from pretraining with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy's representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations. Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning. By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/
authors: Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yan Zhuang, Tianle Zhong, Yen-Ling Kuo
bullets: Addresses representation drift and weakened out-of-distribution generalization when adapting pre-trained robot policies with few demonstrations.
Uses a two-stage process: retrieve similar pre-training features and align target representations, then fine-tune while constraining changes to retrieved representations.
Evaluated with Diffusion Policy and GR00T across 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot.
Improves average fine-tuning success by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, outperforming compared baselines.

(Right) Across 13 simulated and real-world tasks, RARA improves the average ID and OOD success over fine-tuning by 11.6 points.

papers.abstract: Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole-body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video-derived striking motions and uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task-conditioned whole-body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics-based teacher--student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine-tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference-motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of $90.00\%$ and $86.67\%$, respectively, and enables multi-shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/.
authors: Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Enzheng Zhu, Xun Yang, Jialong Qin, Mengbo Wang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Addresses the costly need for extensive task-specific motion-capture data covering diverse tennis states.
Uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching to build task-conditioned whole-body references from locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos.
Distills these references into a reactive physics-based policy with online DAgger, then fine-tunes it with PPO.
The deployed policy uses only robot and ball observations, without reference-motion inputs.
On a real humanoid, it achieves 90.00% forehand and 86.67% backhand hit rates and supports multi-shot rallies.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Overview of the ATHLETE framework. (3) We distill the teacher into a reactive student policy through online DAgger and privileged representation alignment. (4) We fine-tune the student using PPO with task-specific rewards and domain randomization to improve ball contact and return accuracy. (5) The resulting student policy is deployed on a humanoid robot to enable real-world tennis rallies with human players, using a motion-capture system for ball-state estimation.
