papers.abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $\tau=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.
authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Abdelwahed Khamis, Mohammad Ali Armin, Lars Petersson
bullets: Motivation: alarms can be too late to enable recovery, or can disrupt executions that would have succeeded.
Method: restore simulator and policy states at checkpoints, compare counterfactual interventions, and find the latest recoverable checkpoint.
Contribution: a framework for measuring recoverability and intervention cost jointly with monitor performance.
Findings: recoverability depends on the state–intervention pair; favourable detection scores do not necessarily reduce intervention cost.
Scope/limitation: under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, ideal detectors tolerate only a 2.0–3.3% false-alarm rate before resets become counterproductive.

papers.abstract: Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) can be applied to large nonlinear systems with complex objectives while enforcing constraints, but the cost of solving the underlying optimization problems limits real-time application for systems with fast dynamics or many states. Neural networks can reduce this online cost by approximating the control law, but may violate constraints and typically require many precomputed optimizer solutions for training. The learning-based iterative solver for constrained optimization (LISCO) instead learns to predict primal-dual steps toward satisfaction of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions through self-supervised training without precomputed solutions, but its dense, monolithic architecture grows with the prediction horizon. We remove this horizon dependence by exploiting the temporal structure of the problem in the solver architecture, which makes the network size independent of the horizon while leaving the training loss and the solver iteration unchanged. A closed-loop resampling strategy further aligns the training distribution with closed-loop operation at no additional sampling cost. On an economic NMPC benchmark of a CSTR cascade, the proposed solver scales to larger problems than monolithic LISCO and achieves median speedups of up to a factor of four over IPOPT. In closed loop, it achieves comparable control performance to IPOPT with no observed constraint violations.
bullets: Addresses the high online optimization cost of NMPC for large or fast nonlinear systems.
Uses a temporal-decomposition architecture to predict primal-dual KKT steps without network growth as the prediction horizon increases.
Retains LISCO’s self-supervised training and iterative solver procedure, requiring no precomputed optimizer solutions.
Adds closed-loop resampling to better match training data with deployment conditions without extra sampling cost.
On a CSTR cascade benchmark, scales to larger problems, reaches up to 4× median speedups over IPOPT, and achieves comparable closed-loop control with no observed constraint violations.

papers.abstract: Reliable real-time failure detection is critical for deploying learned robotic policies, yet defining failures explicitly is infeasible in open-world settings. This motivates failure detection from nominal demonstrations alone. Existing methods, however, struggle to balance robustness to benign variations with the ability to capture semantic and interaction-level errors. We introduce Robot-WATCHDOG, a self-supervised framework that models manipulation scenes as object-centric spatio-temporal graphs. Building on this representation, we investigate two complementary failure scores: Trajectory Projection and Correlation (TPC), a non-parametric measure of geometric deviation and relational consistency, and GnnT, a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer that predicts future object states. We evaluate both on a public benchmark and on a new dataset of semantically complex manipulation tasks, across six tasks and ten random seeds. Both scores outperform image-based failure detectors, particularly on semantic and interaction-level failures. TPC provides the strongest performance in AUPR and MCC on both dataset averages, with low variance across seeds. Qualitative results are made available at https://cea-list.github.io/Robot-WATCHDOG/.
authors: Quentin Rolland, Fabrice Mayran de Chamisso, Jean-Baptiste Mouret
bullets: Addresses open-world failure detection without requiring explicitly labeled failures.
Introduces two self-supervised scores: TPC for geometric and relational deviations, and GnnT for predicting future object states.
Evaluated on a public benchmark and a new semantically complex manipulation dataset spanning six tasks and ten random seeds.
Both methods outperform image-based detectors, especially for semantic and interaction-level failures.
TPC achieves the strongest average AUPR and MCC with low variance across seeds.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Siu Hing Lui, Hanlin Zhao, Huxin Gao, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Physical execution is isolated in a safety-constrained runtime and requires human authorization.
Validation evidence led the agent to reject an initial action representation and identify hazardous closed-loop behavior missed by offline data.

The final frozen policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and performed best among autonomous policies across six ex-vivo porcine specimens.

papers.abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.
authors: Chuxuan Huang, Zhanxiang Cao, Tianyue Zhan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang, Liyun Yan, Chenlin Ming, Keqi Zhu, Yizhi Chen, Shengcheng Fu, Zihao Zhou, Xinyi Peng, Kaixuan Zhang, Boyang Xing, Jiawei Bao, Yang Yang, Yue Gao

papers.abstract: Existing real-world reinforcement learning methods improve robot policies by combining human corrections with autonomous rollouts. However, accumulated experience varies in its value for policy improvement, and even successful trajectories can contain inefficient or redundant behavior, motivating more selective experience reuse. To this end, we propose Evo-RL, an iterative reinforcement learning method that combines human interventions with advantage-guided experience selection. Evo-RL uses human corrections and experience with positive estimated advantages from successful trajectories to iteratively refine the policy. To support learning from these different experience sources, we introduce RW-RL-Dataset, which spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments. On a real-world high-precision manipulation task, Evo-RL improves attempt success rate over RECAP by 30.46\%. Our code, model checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.
authors: Kai Ye, Yifan Jin, Qianhang Luo, Hongru Zhang, Jiedong Zhang, Shuyuan Hu, Song-Yuan Wu, Jihai Xu, Jie Zhao, Bo Zhao
bullets: Targets inefficient or redundant experience in real-world reinforcement learning.
Combines human interventions with advantage-guided selection of experience from successful trajectories.
Introduces RW-RL-Dataset, spanning over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments.
Improves attempt success rate over RECAP by 30.46% on a real-world high-precision manipulation task.
Code, checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy's primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves $50.97\%$ overall success, improving over $\pi_{0.5}$ and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.
authors: Min Lin, Bokai Zhou, Jianqi Lin, Kaiyuan Yang, Yicheng Chang, Junjie Yu, Xiaofan Liu, Jianhua Han, Rui Li, Shen Zhao, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets future-grounded Effect tokens rather than actions alone.
Builds temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrations, robot responses, and sparse visual transitions.
Uses flow matching to predict Effects, then a state-conditioned decoder generates action chunks.
Supports shared Effect modeling across single- and dual-arm embodiments.
On DexJoCo, achieves 50.97% overall success and leads on all five bimanual tasks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP
authors: Zekang Wang, Zhe He, Gaojie Jin
bullets: Partially observable RL commonly trains recurrent memory jointly with policy or value functions.
The paper tests fixed recurrent networks paired with a trainable nonlinear output module, inspired by Reservoir Computing.
Frozen networks support recall over hundreds of steps across varied memory demands, observations, and action spaces.
They achieve competitive control performance while requiring less than half as many trainable parameters as fully trainable recurrent models.
The approach is proposed as a simple, parameter-efficient baseline, though its effectiveness is evaluated within the studied POMDP tasks.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action-labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale. Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment-specific annotations. In this paper, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations. Grounded-Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines. Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task-relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories. These trajectories are used to post-train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images. To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded-Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks. The real-world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations. Empirical results in real-world tasks demonstrate that Grounded-Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.
authors: Feng Jiang, Shu Chen, Yuanfei Wang, Yuan Li, Zhenhao Shen, Jiaqi Liang, Yang Chen, Lei Wei, Chen Xie, Ruihai Wu
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability limits of collecting real-world robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs task objects and camera geometry from a small set of real initial-state images, then aligns them in simulation.
Post-trains a video world model and inverse dynamics model to generate realistic manipulation videos and robot actions.
Filters synthetic rollouts by replaying them in simulation and retaining only task-successful trajectories.
Uses only grounded synthetic data to train real-world policies, which facilitates policy learning in real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Grounded-Dreamer. Our framework automates the generation of massive, high-fidelity robot data from a small number of real-world reference images. By combining generative world models with simulation-based verification, Grounded-Dreamer produces data that is both visually realistic and physically consistent. This simulation verification loop effectively filters out the physical hallucinations common in purely generative approaches, allowing robot policies to be trained directly on scalable synthetic data that transfers robustly to complex real-world scenarios.

Figure 2: The Grounded-Dreamer Pipeline. Given several real-world reference images, our pipeline first reconstructs physically aligned simulation scenes and objects. Within these environments, task data is automatically collected and processed with interaction-aware masking to fine-tune Cosmos-Predict 2.5 as the core data generation model. An image refinement model then synthesizes diverse initial frames by combining reconstructed assets with real scene backgrounds and object appearances. Conditioned on these frames, the generation model produces manipulation videos, which are converted into action trajectories using an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM). Finally, all synthesized trajectories are replayed in simulation for closed-loop verification, filtering out physically inconsistent samples before policy training and real-world deployment.

papers.abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.
authors: Jiachen Zhang, Yuanyuan Li, Shaqi Luo
bullets: Addresses the need to repeatedly collect task demonstrations for each robot hand.

Retargets human motion to each hand and introduces GPIR for hand-centered object representation.
Evaluated on six real-world tasks: 90.8% success on Linker O6 and 80.8% on Wuji.
The complete configuration reaches 85.8% success across both hands, versus 26.3% with raw human demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
authors: Zipei Ma, Junzhe Jiang, Jiahui Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Chun Gu, Bozhou Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit future-state supervision in VLAs and the inference cost and error propagation of WAMs.
Uses an action-to-future paradigm: predicted futures condition on action features, not vice versa.
End-to-end training lets future-state prediction supervise the policy without allowing prediction errors to affect actions.
Backbone-agnostic design is instantiated with both vision-language and video-generative backbones.
Demonstrates a 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and up to 13% absolute gains over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our Forward Dynamics Models. The context expert encodes visual observations and the instruction to guide the action expert. During training, the generation expert predicts future states from context and action features; its loss backpropagates through these action features to complement action imitation. This asymmetric connection lets future supervision shape the policy while keeping action prediction independent of predicted futures. At inference, the action expert generates actions using the required context features, skipping future generation.

Figure 1: Architectural comparison of action prediction and future supervision. (a) VLA predicts actions directly from the current observation and instruction. (b) A future-conditioned WAM conditions action prediction on predicted future video, requiring future generation at inference. (c) FDM conditions future prediction on context and action features through action-to-future learning. During training, action imitation and future prediction are jointly optimized; the future loss backpropagates through action features to supervise the policy. At inference, FDM denoises action chunks using only the current observation and instruction, skipping the future-generation branch marked as training only while retaining context processing.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.
authors: Dijia Zhan, Zhuo Li, Xuemiao Xu, Sun Zheng, Jinyi Li, Wenjun Wang, Jie Tang
bullets: Addresses the unclear contribution of individual tokens in existing action tokenizers.
Builds each next token from the remaining action error after decoding the current prefix.
Evaluated across 19 manipulation tasks in three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings.
ReAT policies with 8 tokens outperform evaluated baselines; on LIBERO, 4 tokens outperform 8-token baselines.
Supports progressively refined action plans with fewer prediction tokens.

papers.abstract: People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop, creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way, while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.
authors: Chen Yu, Sudarshan S Harithas, Juan Borbon, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between disruptive full replanning and continuing along invalidated plans.
Combines online object-property estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control.
Partially inverts the old plan only where old and new beliefs disagree, then reconstructs the remainder under the new belief.
Across 18 simulated goals, reduced pooled final position error by roughly 33% and yaw error by 47% versus fixed-depth replanning.
Hardware experiments demonstrated translation and turning of a non-holonomic cart.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. An object-centric estimation–planning–control framework. Online estimation informs object planning and whole-body control (trajectory waypoint tracking). As estimates change, the planner can revise the remaining path using (A) BOPI, which uses belief overlap to decide how far to run the flow backward under the old belief, then runs it forward under the updated belief; (B) RDM [1], which blends the current plan with a fixed proportion of random noise, then runs the flow forward under the updated belief to reconstruct the path; or (C) FlowEdit [2], which uses shared noise to evaluate the flow under both beliefs, then edits the path using the difference between the flow directions under the updated and old beliefs. Orange/purple denote old/new plans and beliefs.

BOPI makes smaller changes between successive plans, producing consistent replanned trajectories as the robot progresses toward the goal. This consistency helps explain the lower final position and yaw errors reported in Table II. Grid spacing is 0.5m in both directions.

papers.title: Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion: Object-Centric Flow Replanning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

papers.abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.
authors: Dvij Kalaria, Bike Zhang, S. Shankar Sastry
bullets: Addresses contact-rich imitation under embodiment mismatch and changing runtime scenes.
Recovers human motion and task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, then performs contact-aware humanoid retargeting.
Uses high-priority Lagrangian penalties for user-specified contact poses and collision clearance while optimizing smooth motion.
Trains a contact-conditioned motion generator with movable contact points for adapting to new contact positions.
Demonstrated on ten skills—including table-tennis serves, object pickup, and ladder climbing—with hardware deployment.

papers.title: VICAR: Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting for Humanoid Interactive Skills

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R$^2$-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.
authors: Kai Liu, Jiangran Lyu, Tingyu Deng, Yixin Zheng, Jingtian Wan, Wenbo Cui, Mi Yan, Yizhou Zhou, Haoran Li, Dongbin Zhao, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang

Additional representations help only when they add task-relevant information beyond existing features; composition gains are secondary.

papers.abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.
authors: Catherine Ji, Vivek Myers, Joshua Lin, Alexandra Wingate, Sergey Levine, Benjamin Eysenbach
bullets: Connects empowerment with skill learning while distinguishing the two concepts.
Defines empowerment operationally as the number of executable skills available from a state.
Proposes a simple recipe that works with arbitrary underlying skill-learning methods.
Scales empowerment studies beyond tabular environments to realize theoretically predicted behaviors.
Demonstrates emergent behaviors, including house building in Crafter.

papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations. In contrast to resource-intensive and labor-intensive teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection. Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments, yet prior egocentric demonstration-based methods that require no robots or specialized teaching devices do not explicitly address occlusions. To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions. EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts the future camera-arm pose sequence from the current view and camera-arm pose, and the other predicts the future control commands from object keypoints and a history of control commands. EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility. In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
authors: Gangyi Li, LuYao Wang, Jingfu Sun, Jingyi Yuan, Hang Liu, Hao Zong, Yujia Hu, Tingting Gao, Jianyong Wang, Xu Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting multimodal observations and changing user goals into executable actions under product constraints.

Uses staged learning—supervised fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and reinforcement learning with DPER token-level evidence routing.
Combines generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency for training rewards.

Scores 77.44 on BFCL v4 and leads reported metrics on JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, while results on other public benchmarks are mixed; quadruped case studies demonstrate search, replanning, and failure reporting.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
authors: Zile Zhong, Yuxin Du, Tao Lin, Haoxiao Wang, Wei Dai, Binhua Zuo, Bo Zhao

Achieves a 91.1% tier-averaged success rate on Meta-World MT50, a 13.0% relative gain over a non-predictive baseline.
Shows stronger performance than evaluated baselines on real-world single-arm and bimanual AgileX tasks with 0.87B parameters, lower GPU memory use, and higher inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.
authors: Xule Gao, Xi Wang, Zehua Zang, Rui Wang, Changwen Zheng, Chuxiong Sun
bullets: Problem: Step-wise imitation can overfit to demonstration paths and offers limited guidance after execution deviates from them.
Method: Relabels offline trajectories with semantic key states and uses goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize key-state reachability.
Contribution: Shifts VLA post-training from trajectory imitation toward recoverable, goal-directed behavior from feasible off-demonstration states.
Results: Improves performance over standard supervised fine-tuning on LIBERO and MetaWorld, with stronger robustness under shifts and perturbations on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-ReAct.

papers.abstract: In the practical deployment of vision--language--action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.
authors: Weiwei Chen, Chenghao Xu, Meiling Yu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Long-tailed demonstration data can cause shared policies to favor action patterns from data-rich head tasks, harming under-represented tail tasks.
The method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence from instruction- and action-related signals, then removes it to create counterfactual observations.
Counterfactual predictions reinforce links among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with supervision adjusted by task demonstration frequency.
It requires no additional data or region-level annotations and adds no deployment-time computation.
Experiments across simulated benchmarks, multiple VLA architectures, and real robots show improved tail-task learning while maintaining head-task performance.

papers.abstract: In maximum entropy and behavior-constrained reinforcement learning (RL), the optimal policy is given by a Boltzmann distribution. Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic's action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data.
authors: Denis Blessing, Onur Celik, Gerhard Neumann
bullets: Targets maximum-entropy and behavior-constrained RL, where optimal policies are complex Boltzmann distributions.
Uses a fixed-point iteration based on the target flow identity to update the actor.
Trains flow policies with a regression objective whose targets come from critic action gradients.
Supports fine-tuning pretrained flow policies offline-to-online and training them from scratch in online RL.
Experiments show effective and accurate learning, though the abstract does not specify numerical results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Maximum Entropy Online RL. We have run FFM on all 20 MJX Playground tasks and on the four MJX humanoid tasks and present the aggregated results over all Playground tasks (left two panels) and the aggregated results over the humanoid tasks (right two panels). We have evaluated all methods on 10 seeds for every single environment (see Figure 4 and Figure 5 for results) and report the IQM with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals following Agarwal et al. (2021). FFM performs on par with the baselines on the Playground tasks (left two panels) but converges to the highest return much faster than TRUDI on the high-dimensional humanoid tasks. This result indicates that FFM’s benefits are most pronounced on high-dimensional tasks. Furthermore, we can boost FFM’s performance by leveraging its deterministic mapping properties and incorporating correlated exploration (FFM + OU), which leads to a significantly faster convergence to a similar return value as the best-performing baseline DIME (left two panels) (see Figure 15).

Figure 2: Per-domain aggregated offline-to-online success rate (mean over the five tasks and all seeds). Offline (≤ 1M) and online (> 1M) phases are shaded; FFM (ours) is drawn in bold with a ±1 standard-deviation band. Per-task curves and full tables are in Section E.3.

Figure 1: The FFM policy-improvement step. FFM repeats: (1) Clean actions X1 are generated from the current policy by integrating Equation (5) (forward only, no gradients); the grey curves are sampling trajectories. (2) Critic action gradients are required for the FFM regression target of Equation (12). (3) Fresh noise ε and the clean action X1 are used to sample a noised action Xt via Equation (3). (4) A flow-matching-style regression pulls vθ toward the FFM target. The optimal policy π⋆ ∝ eQ/λ is a fixed point of this loop.

Figure 4: Maximum Entropy Online RL: MJX Playground tasks. We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds. On most of the tasks, FFM performs similarly to or on par with baselines. However, we observe that there are some tasks such as AcrobotSwingupSparse, HopperHop, HopperStand, where FFM (and most of the baselines) perform badly, indicating that a more sophisticated exploration strategy is required. On a subset of the tasks, we have therefore run FFM with correlated exploration (FFM + OU), where we show the chosen τou hyperparameter on the respective plot. Please note that correlated exploration is only possible due to FFM’s deterministic mapping (Section 5) Correlated exploration can help improve performance, such as in HopperHop, or even more significantly in the HopperStand task. The aggregated results when using the correlated exploration curves whenever applicable are given in Figure 3 (left two panels).

Figure 13: Ablation. Deterministic evaluation (MJX Playground). We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on each of the 20 MJX Playground tasks for X0 = 0 (deterministic) and X0 ∼ N (0, I) (stochastic) during evaluation. While most of the results indicate that there are not many differences, for FingerSpin, or WalkerRun, deterministic evaluation seems to improve performance.

Figure 7: Ablation. Geometric versus linear interpolant schedule (MJX Playground). We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on the 20 MJX Playground tasks. The performance between the schedule types is the same for most tasks and differs only for some tasks such as FingerSpin or PendulumSwingup, which, however, lie within the confidence intervals. Therefore, there is no statistically clear result on which interpolant should be used for the Playground tasks.

Figure 5: Maximum Entropy Online RL: MJX Humanoid tasks. We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds. FFM converges faster to a similar performance level as TRUDI and performs significantly better than TRUDI on the T1JoystickRoughTerrain task. The high-dimensional humanoid tasks showcase FFM’s benefits more clearly.

Figure 11: Ablation. Action squashing mapping. We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on the four MJX humanoid tasks for the tanh and erf squashing functions. The results indicate that FFM is insensitive to the choice of the squashing function.

Figure 15: Ablation. Correlated Exploration. On a subset of the MJX Playground tasks, we analyze the effect of correlated exploration by varying τou ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32}, where we have run every curve on 10 seeds and report the IQM with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021). Correlated exploration can significantly boost FFM’s performance for the right choice of τou. For example, the HopperStand task is solved, while FFM without correlated exploration struggles on this task.

Motivated by diffusion-based methods, we have compared the performance of a linear schedule to the geometric schedule as described in Section D.4 and report the aggregated results over all 20 MJX Playground tasks (left two panels) and the four humanoid tasks (right two panels), where every single task was run on 10 seeds, and we report the IQM and the stratified bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021). While the results indicate that there is barely a performance difference in the Playground tasks, a slight improvement on the humanoid tasks can be seen, which is why we have chosen the geometric schedule as default for the online RL tasks. For all four tasks, deterministic evaluation shows significantly improved performance, indicating that stochasticity can harm performance, in particular for highdimensional action spaces. We use deterministic evaluation throughout all of our experiments.

Figure 10: Ablation. Number of Integration Steps. We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on the four MJX humanoid tasks for varying numbers of integration steps K. With increasing number of integration steps, the performance improves. However, the performance plateaus at K = 16 steps.

Figure 8: Ablation. Geometric versus linear interpolant schedule (MJX Humanoid). We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on the four MJX humanoid tasks. While for the G1JoystickFlatTerrain and for the G1JoystickRoughTerrain tasks there is no difference in performance, it seems that the geometric schedule performs slightly better on the T1 tasks, which is why we have chosen the geometric schedule as default for the online RL experiments.

Figure 20: Trust-region budget sweep. Success against εTR on four tasks (mean ± std over three seeds), offline (left two panels) and online (right two panels), for the pure tilt (first and third panel) and the product tilt (second and fourth panel). With the offline trust region off, the product tilt scores 0.41, 0.94, 1.00, and 0.81 on cube-double, scene, puzzle-3x3, and antmaze-large.

Figure 12: Ablation. Deterministic evaluation. We compare the effect of evaluating FFM using X0 = 0 (deterministic) and X0 ∼ N (0, I) (stochastic) on the 20 MJX Playground (left two panels) and four humanoid tasks (right two panels), where every task was run on 10 seeds, and we plot the aggregated IQM with stratified bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021). While there is almost no performance gap between both variants for the Playground tasks, a significant performance boost follows from the deterministic evaluation on the humanoid tasks. This indicates that deterministic evaluation matters most for high-dimensional tasks. Please see Figure 13 and Figure 14 for the per-task performances of each task suite.

Figure 9: Ablation. Number of Integration Steps (left two panels) and Action Squashing mapping (right two panels). Number of integration steps (left two panels): We analyze the effect of varying integration steps and report the aggregated results over all four humanoid tasks (left two panels). Every single task was run on 10 seeds, and we report the IQM and the 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021). The results indicate that with an increasing number of integration steps, the performance increases until it plateaus from K = 16 onwards, which is why we have chosen K = 16 as default in our experiments. Action Squashing Mapping (right two panels): We analyze the effect of utilizing the tanh and the erf as squashing functions for mapping the generated actions to a defined action bound. We have run experiments on the four MJX humanoid tasks and report the aggregated IQM with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (10 seeds per task) (Agarwal et al., 2021) in the two right panels. The results show that FFM is not sensitive to the choice of the squashing function. Please see Figure 11 for the per-task learning curves.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
authors: Minghao Fu, Tavis Siebert, Eryk Halicki, Randall Balestriero
bullets: Addresses the separation of representation, dynamics, and control training in prior JEPA pipelines.
Jointly trains next-latent-state prediction with action flow matching under an isotropic Gaussian latent constraint.
Supports direct policy execution and test-time planning by scoring sampled actions through learned latent dynamics.
Improves visual-planning success from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks.
Plans 32.3× faster than prior JEPAs and remains competitive on simulated and physical-robot behavior cloning tasks.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires maintaining a firm grasp while strictly avoiding both contact slip and structural damage to the object. Satisfying these inherent \textit{secure-and-gentle} grasping constraints is challenging for unknown objects. We present a novel online data-driven predictive control framework for safe dynamic robotic grasping of unknown objects. The proposed system features a pair of compact, single-channel tactile-sensing modules that characterize the gripper-object dynamic interaction in real time, entirely bypassing the need for prior knowledge or offline training. A finite-state-machine-based grasping force probing mechanism is developed to establish the initial grasping force and explicitly identify grasping force constraints. Through online dynamics learning, a Gaussian Process (GP) model captures gripper-object interaction dynamics. The model uncertainties are further used to form robust grasping constraints, which are embedded into a model predictive control scheme. We demonstrate error convergence in a probabilistic sense. The proposed control framework runs at 100~Hz in real time to dynamically manipulate and handle objects rather than static holding. Extensive experimental evaluations across diverse contact surface topologies and various types of objects validate superior performance and efficiency compared to baseline strategies. The proposed method is able to manipulate objects ranging from delicate items, such as raw tofu and marshmallows, to rough objects, such as rocks.

papers.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.

Stage 3 learns visual grounding by predicting the latent from RGB-D histories and camera ego-motion, using box-state supervision and DAgger rollouts. papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $\pi_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5-73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7-52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3-40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.

papers.abstract: Non-prehensile manipulation with mobile robots has primarily targeted placement in coarse goal regions. Precision placement has been studied with manipulators on benchmarks such as Push-T, where an omnidirectional end effector can readily re-approach an object from any side. For a mobile robot, correcting the same placement errors may require wide repositioning maneuvers around the object. We formalize multi-object pushing with a mobile robot as a multi-target assignment problem at tight tolerances. We propose a diffusion planner with a causal factorization: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. This factorization allows us to sample multiple object outcomes for a single robot plan, capturing the multi-modality of pushing. We also design a set of pushing-specific costs for mobile robots, used for both guidance and best-of-$N$ sampling at inference. On Push-T, our planner attains the highest success rate of the methods we compare, while having the lowest rate of implausible object motion. Across three multi-box pushing environments resembling warehouse scenarios, it raises the fraction of boxes placed by $21.5$ percentage points over an unguided baseline, and replans $1.8\times$ faster than a planner that denoises the two trajectories together. Lastly, we deploy the guided planner on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with object shapes absent from the training data, where it places $85.0\%$ of objects within tolerance against Diffusion Policy's $37.5\%$.
authors: Lance Pharand, Megnath Ramesh, Mark Chiu, Yash Vardhan Pant, Stephen L. Smith
bullets: Formulates tight-tolerance multi-object pushing as a multi-target assignment problem for mobile robots.
Uses causal diffusion: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the robot estimate, capturing multiple possible pushing outcomes.
Introduces pushing-specific costs for guidance and best-of-N trajectory selection.
Achieves the highest compared success rate and lowest implausible-motion rate on Push-T; improves box placement by 21.5 percentage points over an unguided baseline.
Replans 1.8× faster than joint trajectory denoising and places 85.0% of objects within tolerance on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with unseen shapes.

The Object phase denoises τO t while being conditioned on τ̂R 0 . The resulting chain τR t → τ̂R 0 → τ̂O 0 is differentiable through both decoder passes.

papers.abstract: Motion retargeting is a critical preprocessing step for transferring human motion data to humanoid robots. While existing methods are effective for single-character motions, interactions involving multiple characters and objects introduce additional contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved. Retargeting is commonly formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem, where conflicting objectives can require careful tuning of relative weights and can still compromise important motion characteristics. We introduce PriMoRetarget, a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces relative objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy. Lower-priority updates are constrained to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical characteristics such as foot placement and interaction contacts to take precedence over lower-priority pose objectives. The method is evaluated on four datasets spanning single-character motion, character-object manipulation, and character-character interactions. The resulting motions better preserve task-relevant interactions and provide reference trajectories that can be tracked more reliably than those produced by widely used retargeting methods.
authors: Nicholas Ioannidis, Dun Yang, Max Smith, Tue Vu, Ziyu Zhang, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Xue Bin Peng
bullets: Addresses motion-retargeting failures in multi-character and character-object interactions, where contacts and spatial relationships must be preserved.
Replaces manually tuned weighted objectives with prioritized optimization: lower-priority updates cannot compromise higher-priority objectives.
Prioritizes task-critical features such as foot placement and interaction contacts over lower-priority pose matching.
Evaluated across four datasets covering single-character motion, manipulation, and character-character interactions.
Produces motions that better preserve interactions and yield more reliably trackable reference trajectories than widely used retargeting methods.

papers.abstract: Prior research on learning from humans often requires real human demonstrations. But advances in video generation models offer a new paradigm: we can now prompt these generators to make synthetic videos of the task. On the plus side, these synthetic videos take place in the robot's current environment, and do not require actual human teaching. However, while the generated videos appear to show plausible motions, they lack both physical consistency and robot grounding, and thus the robot cannot directly roll out the trajectory shown by the video. In this paper we seek to formalize the process of going from synthetic video generation to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks. We recognize that this problem is an instance of constrained optimization. The object trajectories extracted from the synthetic video provide an initial guess at the correct motion, and the robot must refine these trajectories (for instance, within a digital twin) while enforcing physical feasibility and semantic consistency. Our optimization-based formalism provides insights into the video generation properties necessary for success. Specifically, we show that the video generation must probabilistically seed the search within a semantic basin of attraction where the trajectory can be locally modified without losing its task alignment. Our analysis further reveals that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified formalism with key simplifications. In our experiments we remove these simplifications to more closely match the underlying optimization, leading to more robust zero-shot trajectories from synthetic videos and improving average task success by 34.1% compared to the best-performing baseline. See videos at our project website: https://collab.me.vt.edu/CASTER
authors: Yinlong Dai, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Dylan P. Losey
bullets: Synthetic videos avoid real human demonstrations and can depict tasks in the robot’s environment.
Video-derived object trajectories serve as initial guesses, which are refined under physical-feasibility and semantic-consistency constraints.
Success requires generated videos to seed trajectories within a task-aligned semantic basin of attraction.
The framework unifies existing approaches and removes simplifying assumptions to better match the underlying optimization.
Experiments report a 34.1% improvement in average task success over the best-performing baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of CASTER. (Top Left) Given an initial RGB-D observation and a task prompt, we (Top) generate synthetic videos of a human performing that task in the current environment and (Bottom Left) build a digital twin of the scene. From the synthetic videos we extract the object trajectories, which then serve as initial guesses for trajectory optimization within the digital twin. (Bottom) The trajectories extracted from synthetic videos do not need to be perfect: instead, they must lie within a semantic basin of attraction where the optimization can locally modify the trajectory shape without removing its semantic meaning. (Bottom Right) We perform constrained optimization so that the robot’s actions in the digital twin cause the objects to move similarly to their video trajectories, while enforcing kinematic constraints so that the output can be directly executed by the real robot.

By matching these features while enforcing semantic consistency and physical feasibility, we can transfer erroneous videos to successful zero-shot trajectories.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment. To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact, a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing. authors: Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Zhian Ruan, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Ruihan Yang, Carmelo Sferrazza, Shuran Song, Guanya Shi

papers.abstract: Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision. Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot's view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active "View and Probe" framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe). Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation.
authors: Jaewoo Lee, Jeongyeon Seo, Sihyun Cho, Gyeongrak Choe, Yutong Wang, Bavin Saravanan, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Sebastian Scherer, Guanya Shi, H. Jin Kim, Seungjae Lee, Dongjae Lee

papers.abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.
